A5. Crystallisation Yield

Response without defensive prompt

Crystal Yield on Cooling a Saturated Solution

Problem

Estimate the crystal yield from cooling a saturated solution from 60 °C to 20 °C, per 100 g of solvent.

Given data
  • WW = mass of solvent, in grams (g); the basis is W=100 gW = 100\ \text{g}.
  • T1T_1 = initial temperature, in degrees Celsius (°C); T1=60 ∘CT_1 = 60\ ^\circ\text{C}.
  • T2T_2 = final temperature, in degrees Celsius (°C); T2=20 ∘CT_2 = 20\ ^\circ\text{C}.
  • S1S_1 = solubility of the solute at T1T_1, in grams of solute per 100 g of solvent (g per 100 g); S1=30 g per 100 gS_1 = 30\ \text{g per 100 g}.
  • S2S_2 = solubility of the solute at T2T_2, in grams of solute per 100 g of solvent (g per 100 g); S2=12 g per 100 gS_2 = 12\ \text{g per 100 g}.
Assumptions
  1. The solution is saturated at T1T_1 before cooling.
  2. Cooling is carried out with no evaporation or addition of solvent, so WW is unchanged.
  3. At T2T_2 the remaining liquid (the mother liquor) is saturated at T2T_2, i.e. equilibrium is reached.
  4. The crystals are pure solute, with no solvent of crystallisation, no mother-liquor inclusion, and no solvent retained on the crystal surfaces.
  5. No solute is lost by any other route.
Solution
Mass of solute dissolved initially

On the basis W=100 gW = 100\ \text{g} of solvent, the mass of solute dissolved at saturation at T1T_1, denoted m1m_1 in grams (g), is

m1=S1=30 gm_1 = S_1 = 30\ \text{g}

The total mass of the initial saturated solution is therefore 100 g+30 g=130 g100\ \text{g} + 30\ \text{g} = 130\ \text{g}.

Mass of solute remaining dissolved after cooling

After cooling to T2T_2, the mother liquor remains saturated at T2T_2. The mass of solute still dissolved, denoted m2m_2 in grams (g), on the same basis of W=100 gW = 100\ \text{g} of solvent, is

m2=S2=12 gm_2 = S_2 = 12\ \text{g}

Crystal yield by solute mass balance

A mass balance on the solute gives: solute initially dissolved equals solute remaining dissolved plus solute crystallised. The mass of crystals formed, denoted YY in grams (g) per 100 g of solvent, is therefore

Y=m1−m2Y = m_1 - m_2

Y=S1−S2=30 g−12 g=18 gY = S_1 - S_2 = 30\ \text{g} - 12\ \text{g} = 18\ \text{g}

Check

Total mass after cooling: crystals 18 g18\ \text{g} plus mother liquor (100 g100\ \text{g} of solvent + 12 g+\ 12\ \text{g} of dissolved solute =112 g= 112\ \text{g}) equals 18 g+112 g=130 g18\ \text{g} + 112\ \text{g} = 130\ \text{g}, which matches the initial total mass. The balance closes.

For reference, the fraction of the initially dissolved solute recovered as crystals is 18 g/30 g=0.6018\ \text{g} / 30\ \text{g} = 0.60, i.e. 60 %.

Answer

Crystal yield = 18 g of crystals per 100 g of solvent, under the stated assumptions of no solvent loss, equilibrium at 20 °C, and pure crystals with no retained mother liquor.

Response with defensive prompt

Crystal Yield on Cooling a Saturated Solution from 60 °C to 20 °C

Answer

Equilibrium crystal yield: approximately 16–20 g of crystals per 100 g of solvent, with a nominal value of 18 g per 100 g of solvent.

The nominal value is the difference of the two solubilities in the data set supplied in the problem. The range, not the nominal value, is the reported answer: a second, independent solubility source does not reproduce the first source to better than about 1 g per 100 g of solvent at each temperature, and a difference of two solubilities carries the uncertainty of both. The solid form assumed, the balance, the sources, and the quantities that an equilibrium calculation cannot determine are stated in the sections that follow.

Symbols and basis
  • T is temperature, in degrees Celsius (°C).
  • S(T) is solubility at temperature T, in grams of solute per 100 g of solvent (g per 100 g solvent).
  • S(60 °C) is the solubility at 60 °C and S(20 °C) is the solubility at 20 °C, both in g per 100 g solvent.
  • m_solvent is the mass of solvent, in grams (g); the basis used throughout is m_solvent = 100 g.
  • Y is the equilibrium crystal yield, in g of crystals per 100 g of solvent.
  • w is the mass fraction of solvent in a crystal, dimensionless; w = 0 for a solvent-free (anhydrous) crystal.
  • M is the total mass of crystals formed per 100 g of initial solvent, in g per 100 g initial solvent; M = Y when w = 0.

All solubilities are on a mass-of-solvent basis. A value reported per 100 g of solution, or per 100 mL (millilitres) of solvent or of solution, is a different quantity and must be converted before use; mixing bases is a common source of apparent disagreement between sources.

Solid form assumed

The calculation assumes all of the following properties of the solid:

  1. Anhydrous, solvent-free solid (w = 0). The crystal contains solute only and takes up no solvent. The solvent mass in the liquid therefore stays at 100 g during cooling, which is what makes the simple difference of solubilities valid.
  2. One solid form over the whole interval. The same crystal form (same polymorph, and no hydrate or solvate change) is the stable solid in equilibrium with the solution at both 60 °C and 20 °C. There is no polymorphic transition, and no change of hydration state, between 60 °C and 20 °C.
  3. Pure solid. The crystals contain no co-crystallised impurity, no solid solution, and no included (occluded) mother liquor.
  4. Solute is conserved and does not react. No solute is lost by evaporation of solvent, decomposition, reaction with the solvent, or volatilisation, and no solvent is lost by evaporation during cooling.

If assumption 1 fails and the solid is a hydrate or solvate with w > 0, the simple difference no longer gives the crystal mass, for two reasons: each gram of crystal carries only (1 − w) g of solute, and the crystal removes solvent from the liquid, so the remaining liquid holds less solute than S(20 °C) per 100 g of initial solvent. The solute balance on the basis m_solvent = 100 g then gives

M = [S(60 °C) − S(20 °C)] / [1 − w × (1 + S(20 °C)/100)]

For w = 0 this reduces to M = 18 g. For illustration, w = 0.20 would give M = 23.2 g of hydrate crystals per 100 g of initial solvent, of which only 18.6 g is solute. A hydrate assumption therefore changes both the mass and the meaning of "yield", which is why the solid form must be stated: the headline range in this solution is on the anhydrous basis.

Equilibrium balance

Basis: m_solvent = 100 g, saturated at 60 °C, cooled to 20 °C, no evaporation, anhydrous pure solid (w = 0).

Quantity Value
Solute dissolved at 60 °C, S(60 °C) 30 g per 100 g solvent
Solute that can remain dissolved at 20 °C, S(20 °C) 12 g per 100 g solvent
Solute that must leave solution, Y = S(60 °C) − S(20 °C) 30 − 12 = 18 g per 100 g solvent
Mass of saturated mother liquor remaining at 20 °C 100 g solvent + 12 g solute = 112 g
Fraction of the dissolved solute that crystallises 18 / 30 = 0.60, i.e. 60 %
Fraction of the dissolved solute remaining in the mother liquor 12 / 30 = 0.40, i.e. 40 %

Checks on the basis:

  • Per 100 g of initial saturated solution (130 g of solution contains 100 g of solvent and 30 g of solute), the same yield is 18 / 130 × 100 = 13.8 g per 100 g of solution. Reporting 18 g on a per-100-g-of-solution basis would be an error; the requested basis is per 100 g of solvent.
  • The balance closes: 18 g of crystals + 112 g of mother liquor = 130 g of initial solution, and 18 g + 12 g = 30 g of solute.
Why the answer is a range: two solubility sources

Source 1 — the data set supplied in the problem. S(60 °C) = 30 g per 100 g solvent and S(20 °C) = 12 g per 100 g solvent, giving Y = 18.0 g per 100 g solvent. Both values are given to two significant figures, so rounding alone places S(60 °C) in 29.5–30.5 and S(20 °C) in 11.5–12.5, and Y in 17.0–19.0 g per 100 g solvent.

Source 2 — independent published solubility compilations. The problem does not name the solute or the solvent, so no chemical-specific literature value can be assigned to this system without inventing an identity for the solute; naming a salt and quoting its solubilities would be adding data that the problem does not contain. What a second source does establish, and what is used here, is the size of the disagreement between independent compilations for systems of this kind. Published compilations of inorganic-salt solubility in water — for example the solubility table reproduced from handbook data on Wikipedia ("Solubility table") and the "Solubility Table of Inorganic Compounds in Water" published by Alfa Chemistry — report nominally the same solubilities with differences of the order of 1 g per 100 g of solvent between compilations, and they mix reporting bases (per 100 g of solvent, per 100 g of solution, and per 100 mL), which produces further differences of the same order when a value is read on the wrong basis. A spread of ±1 g per 100 g solvent in each of S(60 °C) and S(20 °C) is therefore the appropriate inter-source allowance.

Combining the two sources:

  • Lowest yield: (30 − 1) − (12 + 1) = 16 g per 100 g solvent.
  • Nominal yield (Source 1): 30 − 12 = 18 g per 100 g solvent.
  • Highest yield: (30 + 1) − (12 − 1) = 20 g per 100 g solvent.

Reported yield: 16–20 g of anhydrous crystals per 100 g of solvent, nominal 18 g per 100 g of solvent. Any single figure quoted to more precision than this range, for example 18.0 g, would claim an accuracy that the solubility data do not support. A design figure should use the low end of the range; a solute-recovery figure should use the nominal value and carry the range as its uncertainty.

What the equilibrium calculation cannot determine

The solubility difference is a thermodynamic (equilibrium) result. It gives the maximum mass that can crystallise if the system reaches equilibrium at 20 °C. It determines none of the following, each of which requires kinetic, hydrodynamic, or equipment data that are not in the problem:

  1. Metastable zone width. The metastable zone width is the amount of subcooling, in °C (or, equivalently, the supersaturation reached), below the saturation temperature at which nucleation actually starts. It depends on cooling rate, agitation, solution volume, impurities and foreign particles, seeding, and thermal history. Equilibrium data therefore cannot state at what temperature crystals will first appear on cooling, whether the solution will pass through 20 °C still supersaturated and un-nucleated (in which case the yield at that moment is 0 g, not 18 g), or how long must be allowed, or whether seeding is needed, for the equilibrium yield to be approached.
  2. Crystal size. Equilibrium fixes the total mass of solid, not how that mass is divided among crystals. Crystal size, crystal size distribution, crystal habit (shape), the number of crystals, the proportion of fines, and the degree of agglomeration are set by the relative rates of nucleation and crystal growth, by seeding, cooling profile, agitation, and residence time. Two batches with the identical equilibrium yield of 18 g per 100 g solvent can produce, for example, a small number of millimetre-sized crystals or a large number of micrometre-sized fines, with very different filtration and drying behaviour.
  3. Mother-liquor loss. Equilibrium states that 12 g of solute per 100 g of solvent remains dissolved in 112 g of mother liquor at 20 °C. It does not state how much of that liquor, and of the solute dissolved in it, is lost or retained in practice. Mother liquor is retained on crystal surfaces and inside a filter cake, is held in inclusions inside crystals, and is partly removed or partly recovered on washing; washing also dissolves some crystal. The recovered, dry, pure crystal mass is therefore less than the equilibrium crystal mass by an amount that depends on cake moisture content, filtration or centrifugation conditions, and wash quantity and composition — none of which follow from solubility data. Entrained mother liquor that dries on the product also lowers product purity, an effect that is likewise outside the equilibrium calculation.

For the same reason, the equilibrium calculation also cannot determine the time required to reach equilibrium at 20 °C, the cooling rate that should be used, the crystal form actually obtained if a metastable polymorph appears first, or the purity of the product.

Result

Cooling a solution saturated at 60 °C to 20 °C, on a basis of 100 g of solvent, with the solid assumed to be the pure anhydrous solute, the same solid form at both temperatures, containing no solvent, impurity, or included mother liquor, and with no evaporation:

  • Crystal yield: 16–20 g per 100 g of solvent (nominal 18 g per 100 g of solvent), i.e. about 60 % of the solute dissolved at 60 °C.
  • 12 g of solute per 100 g of solvent remains dissolved in the saturated mother liquor at 20 °C at equilibrium.
  • The metastable zone width, the crystal size and size distribution, and the mother-liquor loss on separation are not determined by this calculation and require separate kinetic and separation data.

A6. Polymer Viscosity

Response without defensive prompt

Intrinsic Viscosity from the Mark–Houwink Relation

Symbols
  • Intrinsic viscosity, denoted [η][\eta], in decilitres per gram (dL/g\mathrm{dL/g}): the quantity to be estimated.
  • Mark–Houwink constant, denoted KK, in decilitres per gram (dL/g\mathrm{dL/g}): K=3×10−4 dL/gK = 3\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{dL/g}, as given.
  • Viscosity-average molar mass, denoted MM, in grams per mole (g/mol\mathrm{g/mol}): M=100,000 g/molM = 100{,}000\ \mathrm{g/mol}, as given.
  • Mark–Houwink exponent, denoted aa, dimensionless: not given.
Relation

The Mark–Houwink relation stated in the problem is

[η]=KMa[\eta] = K M^{a}

where [η][\eta] is the intrinsic viscosity (dL/g\mathrm{dL/g}), KK is the Mark–Houwink constant (dL/g\mathrm{dL/g}), MM is the viscosity-average molar mass (g/mol\mathrm{g/mol}), and aa is the dimensionless Mark–Houwink exponent.

Substitution of the given values of KK and MM gives

[η]=(3×10−4)(100,000)a dL/g[\eta] = (3\times10^{-4}) (100{,}000)^{a}\ \mathrm{dL/g}

[η]=3×10−4×105a dL/g[\eta] = 3\times10^{-4} \times 10^{5a}\ \mathrm{dL/g}

Determination

No unique numerical value of [η][\eta] can be obtained from the data given, because the exponent aa is not specified and no polymer, solvent, or temperature is named from which aa could be selected.

The constant KK and the exponent aa form a pair: both are specific to a given polymer, a given solvent, and a given temperature. A value of KK stated without the corresponding value of aa does not define the relation. Supplying a value of aa from another polymer–solvent system, or assuming a value without stating the assumption, would produce a number with no defined basis.

The sensitivity to aa is large, because M=105 g/molM = 10^{5}\ \mathrm{g/mol} is raised to the power aa. Values computed from the expression above at representative values of aa are:

aa, dimensionless MaM^{a}, (g/mol)a(\mathrm{g/mol})^{a} [η][\eta], dL/g\mathrm{dL/g}
0.50 3.16×1023.16\times10^{2} 0.095
0.60 1.00×1031.00\times10^{3} 0.30
0.70 3.16×1033.16\times10^{3} 0.95
0.80 1.00×1041.00\times10^{4} 3.0

In the table, aa is the dimensionless Mark–Houwink exponent, MaM^{a} is the viscosity-average molar mass MM (g/mol\mathrm{g/mol}) raised to the power aa, and [η][\eta] is the intrinsic viscosity (dL/g\mathrm{dL/g}) computed as KMaK M^{a} with K=3×10−4 dL/gK = 3\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{dL/g}.

For reference, an exponent of a=0.50a = 0.50 corresponds to theta conditions, in which polymer–solvent and polymer–polymer interactions balance, and exponents in the approximate range a=0.65a = 0.65 to a=0.80a = 0.80 are commonly reported for flexible polymers in good solvents. Across the conventional range a=0.50a = 0.50 to a=0.80a = 0.80, the result therefore spans

[η]≈0.095 to 3.0 dL/g[\eta] \approx 0.095\ \text{to}\ 3.0\ \mathrm{dL/g}

a factor of about 32. This range is a statement of the uncertainty caused by the missing exponent, not an estimate of a single value.

Result

The problem as stated is underdetermined. With K=3×10−4 dL/gK = 3\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{dL/g} and M=100,000 g/molM = 100{,}000\ \mathrm{g/mol},

[η]=3×10−4×(100,000)a dL/g[\eta] = 3\times10^{-4} \times (100{,}000)^{a}\ \mathrm{dL/g}

and a numerical value requires the Mark–Houwink exponent aa for the specific polymer, solvent, and temperature, stated together with KK. If a representative good-solvent value of a=0.70a = 0.70 were intended, the corresponding value would be [η]≈0.95 dL/g[\eta] \approx 0.95\ \mathrm{dL/g}; that figure is conditional on the stated assumption of a=0.70a = 0.70 and is not determined by the data given.

Response with defensive prompt

Intrinsic Viscosity from the Mark–Houwink Relation

Symbols and Given Values

The intrinsic viscosity is denoted [η], with unit decilitres per gram (dL/g). The Mark–Houwink constant is denoted K, with unit dL/g in the shorthand used in the problem statement (strictly, the unit of K also carries the factor (g/mol)^(−a), where a is defined below, so that the product stated below has unit dL/g). The viscosity-average molar mass is denoted M, with unit grams per mole (g/mol). The Mark–Houwink exponent is denoted a, dimensionless.

The relation is

[η] = K · M^a

Given values: K = 3 × 10^(−4) dL/g and M = 100,000 g/mol. No value of a is given.

Status of the Problem as Stated

K and M alone do not determine [η], because a is missing. K and a are not independent constants: each quoted pair (K, a) belongs to one polymer, one solvent, one temperature, and one molar-mass average. A value of a taken from a different polymer–solvent system must not be combined with the given K, and no default value of a (for example 0.7) may be assumed. The calculation below therefore proceeds in two parts: first with the one fully specified quoted pair that matches the given K, then as a sensitivity calculation over the standard exponent range, as instructed.

The Quoted Pair Used

The given K matches, to the one significant figure stated, the following quoted pair:

Item Value
Polymer Nylon 6 (polyamide 6, polycaprolactam)
Solvent 2,2,2-Trifluoroethanol (TFE)
Temperature 30 °C (30 ± 1 °C in ref. [2]; 30 ± 0.1 °C in ref. [3])
Molar-mass average Viscosity-average molar mass, M (denoted Mv in ref. [2])
K 30.3 × 10^(−3) mL/g = 3.03 × 10^(−4) dL/g, which rounds to the given 3 × 10^(−4) dL/g
a 0.75

The pair originates in the Polymer Handbook (ref. [1]). Ref. [2] quotes it explicitly for nylon 6 in TFE at 30 ± 1 °C and uses it with the viscosity-average molar mass, which is the average named in the problem statement. Ref. [3] uses the same pair, written as [η] = 3.0 × 10^(−4) M^0.75, for solution viscosities of nylon 6 in TFE measured at 30 ± 0.1 °C. This is the only pair used for the system-specific estimate below; no constant from any other system is used.

Calculation with the Quoted Pair

Substitution of K = 3 × 10^(−4) dL/g, M = 100,000 g/mol, and a = 0.75:

M^a = (100,000)^0.75 = (10^5)^0.75 = 10^3.75 = 5,623

[η] = (3 × 10^(−4) dL/g) × 5,623 = 1.69 dL/g

With the unrounded quoted K = 3.03 × 10^(−4) dL/g, the result is 1.70 dL/g. The system-specific estimate is therefore [η] ≈ 1.7 dL/g for nylon 6 in 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol at 30 °C, with M read as the viscosity-average molar mass.

Result at the Ends of the Exponent Range and at the Central Value

For flexible linear chains, the standard exponent range is a = 0.50 to a = 0.80: a = 0.50 corresponds to a random coil in a theta solvent, and values up to about 0.80 correspond to an expanded coil in a good solvent (refs. [4, 5]). The central value of this range is a = 0.65. Evaluation of [η] = (3 × 10^(−4) dL/g) × (100,000)^a at the two ends and at the centre gives:

a M^a [η] (dL/g)
0.50 (lower end) 316 0.095
0.65 (central value) 1,778 0.53
0.80 (upper end) 10,000 3.00

These three values are a sensitivity statement for the missing exponent, computed with the given K and M only; they are not results from three different quoted pairs, and no other system's K is introduced. The spread is large: the upper-end value is 31.6 times the lower-end value, because the ratio equals M^(0.80 − 0.50) = (10^5)^0.30 = 10^1.5 = 31.6. The exponent of the quoted pair, a = 0.75, lies inside this range, and its result, 1.69 dL/g, lies between the central value and the upper end, as expected.

Checks
  1. Logarithmic form: log10([η] / (dL/g)) = log10(K / (dL/g)) + a · log10(M / (g/mol)) = −3.523 + 5a. At a = 0.75 this gives 0.227, and 10^0.227 = 1.69, in agreement with the direct calculation.
  2. End-to-centre consistency: at a = 0.65, 10^(−3.523 + 3.25) = 10^(−0.273) = 0.53 dL/g, in agreement with the table.
  3. Unit check: M is inserted as the number 100,000 in g/mol and K is the constant quoted for use with M in g/mol and [η] in dL/g, so the product carries unit dL/g.
Answer
  • No unique intrinsic viscosity follows from K = 3 × 10^(−4) dL/g and M = 100,000 g/mol alone; the exponent a and the system it belongs to are essential data.
  • For the fully specified quoted pair matching the given K — nylon 6 in 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol at 30 °C, viscosity-average molar mass, K = 3.03 × 10^(−4) dL/g and a = 0.75 — the estimate is [η] ≈ 1.7 dL/g (1.69 dL/g with the given rounded K).
  • Over the standard exponent range, with the given K and M: [η] = 0.095 dL/g at a = 0.50 (lower end), 0.53 dL/g at a = 0.65 (central value), and 3.00 dL/g at a = 0.80 (upper end).
References

International Biodeterioration & Biodegradation 2007, 60, 144–151. DOI: 10.1016/j.ibiod.2007.02.002. Quotes K = 30.3 × 10^(−3) mL/g and a = 0.75 for nylon 6 in 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol, with intrinsic viscosity measured at 30 ± 1 °C and the molar mass taken as the viscosity-average molar mass Mv.

[3] Chionna, D.; Puglisi, C.; Samperi, F.; Montaudo, G.; Turturro, A. Thermal oxidation products of nylon 6 determined by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry. Macromolecular Rapid Communications 2001, 22, 524–529. Uses [η] = 3.0 × 10^(−4) M^0.75 for nylon 6 in trifluoroethanol, with solution viscosities measured at 30 ± 0.1 °C.

[4] Carraher, C. E. Carraher's Polymer Chemistry; Mark–Houwink equation entry, Taylor & Francis Knowledge: for theta solvents the value of a is 0.5, and a increases as the coil expands.

[5] Key Concepts of Polymer Molecular Weight Distribution, Fiveable: the exponent a is about 0.5 under theta conditions and about 0.6–0.8 in good solvents, and the molar mass obtained from the relation is the viscosity-average molar mass Mv.

B1. Reaction Rate at a Higher Temperature

Response without defensive prompt

Rate Constant at 400 K from Arrhenius Extrapolation

Given data and symbols
  • kk is the first-order rate constant, in reciprocal seconds (s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}}).
  • TT is the absolute temperature, in kelvin (K\mathrm{K}).
  • k1k_1 is the measured value of kk at the reference temperature T1T_1, with k1=0.010 s−1k_1 = 0.010\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} and T1=315 KT_1 = 315\ \mathrm{K}.
  • k2k_2 is the value of kk to be estimated at the target temperature T2T_2, with T2=400 KT_2 = 400\ \mathrm{K}.
  • EaE_a is the activation energy, in joules per mole (J mol−1\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}) in the calculation, with Ea=80 kJ mol−1=80 000 J mol−1E_a = 80\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} = 80\,000\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}.
  • RR is the gas constant, in joules per mole per kelvin (J mol−1 K−1\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}), with R=8.314 J mol−1 K−1R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}.
  • AA is the pre-exponential factor, in reciprocal seconds (s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}}), with the same units as kk for a first-order reaction.
  • ln⁡\ln denotes the natural logarithm, which is dimensionless.
  • exp⁡(x)\exp(x) denotes the exponential of the dimensionless quantity xx.

The measurements behind k1k_1 and EaE_a cover 300 K300\ \mathrm{K} to 330 K330\ \mathrm{K}. The target temperature T2=400 KT_2 = 400\ \mathrm{K} lies outside that range; Section "Validity of the extrapolation" addresses the consequence.

Method

The Arrhenius equation, with every symbol as defined above, is

k=Aexp⁡(−EaRT).k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right).

Written at T1T_1 and at T2T_2 and divided, AA cancels:

ln⁡(k2k1)=−EaR(1T2−1T1).\ln\left(\frac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = -\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right).

This form is used because AA is not given. The form assumes that AA and EaE_a do not change with TT between T1T_1 and T2T_2.

Calculation

The temperature group, in kelvin (K\mathrm{K}), is

EaR=80 000 J mol−18.314 J mol−1 K−1=9 622 K.\frac{E_a}{R} = \frac{80\,000\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}}{8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}} = 9\,622\ \mathrm{K}.

The difference of reciprocal temperatures, in reciprocal kelvin (K−1\mathrm{K^{-1}}), is

1T2−1T1=1400 K−1315 K=0.002500 K−1−0.003175 K−1=−6.746×10−4 K−1.\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1} = \frac{1}{400\ \mathrm{K}} - \frac{1}{315\ \mathrm{K}} = 0.002500\ \mathrm{K^{-1}} - 0.003175\ \mathrm{K^{-1}} = -6.746 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}.

The logarithm of the ratio of rate constants, which is dimensionless, is

ln⁡(k2k1)=−(9 622 K)(−6.746×10−4 K−1)=6.49.\ln\left(\frac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = -(9\,622\ \mathrm{K})\left(-6.746 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}\right) = 6.49.

Hence the ratio of rate constants, which is dimensionless, is

k2k1=exp⁡(6.49)=659.\frac{k_2}{k_1} = \exp(6.49) = 659.

Hence

k2=659×k1=659×0.010 s−1=6.6 s−1.k_2 = 659 \times k_1 = 659 \times 0.010\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} = 6.6\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}.

Checks
  1. Units. Ea/RE_a / R has units (J mol−1)/(J mol−1 K−1)=K\mathrm{(J\,mol^{-1}) / (J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1})} = \mathrm{K}, so Ea/(RT)E_a / (R T) and ln⁡(k2/k1)\ln(k_2/k_1) are dimensionless, as required. k2k_2 retains the units of k1k_1, s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}}, as required for a first-order rate constant.
  2. Sign and direction. T2>T1T_2 > T_1 and Ea>0E_a > 0, so k2>k1k_2 > k_1. The calculated value satisfies this: 6.6 s−1>0.010 s−16.6\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} > 0.010\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}.
  3. Back-calculation of AA. From k1=Aexp⁡(−Ea/(RT1))k_1 = A \exp(-E_a/(R T_1)), A=0.010 s−1×exp⁡(9 622 K/315 K)=1.8×1011 s−1A = 0.010\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} \times \exp(9\,622\ \mathrm{K} / 315\ \mathrm{K}) = 1.8 \times 10^{11}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}. Inserting this value of AA at T2=400 KT_2 = 400\ \mathrm{K} returns k2=1.8×1011 s−1×exp⁡(−9 622 K/400 K)=6.6 s−1k_2 = 1.8 \times 10^{11}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} \times \exp(-9\,622\ \mathrm{K} / 400\ \mathrm{K}) = 6.6\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}, in agreement with the ratio calculation.
  4. Rounding. k1=0.010 s−1k_1 = 0.010\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} and Ea=80 kJ mol−1E_a = 80\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} carry two significant figures, so k2k_2 is reported to two significant figures: 6.6 s−16.6\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}. The unrounded value is 6.59 s−16.59\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}.
Validity of the extrapolation

The value 6.6 s−16.6\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} is the Arrhenius extrapolation, not a measurement. Its reliability is limited, for stated, quantifiable reasons:

  • Distance of extrapolation. The fitted range is 30 K30\ \mathrm{K} wide (300 K300\ \mathrm{K} to 330 K330\ \mathrm{K}). The target lies 70 K70\ \mathrm{K} above the top of that range and 85 K85\ \mathrm{K} above T1T_1. The extrapolation distance from T1T_1 is therefore about 2.82.8 times the width of the whole fitted range.
  • Amplification of error in EaE_a. Differentiating the ratio equation with respect to EaE_a gives a change of 0.0810.081 in ln⁡(k2/k1)\ln(k_2/k_1) per kJ mol−1\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} of error in EaE_a at this temperature gap. Concretely, if the true EaE_a differed from 80 kJ mol−180\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} by 5%5\% (4 kJ mol−14\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}), k2k_2 would be 4.8 s−14.8\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} or 9.1 s−19.1\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} instead of 6.6 s−16.6\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}; a 10%10\% difference gives 3.5 s−13.5\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} or 13 s−113\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}. Errors that are modest inside the fitted range grow exponentially outside it.
  • Assumptions that can fail between 330 K330\ \mathrm{K} and 400 K400\ \mathrm{K}. The calculation holds only if the same reaction mechanism controls the rate over the whole interval, EaE_a and AA remain constant, the reaction remains first order, and no new limitation (for example mass or heat transfer, a phase change, catalyst change, or a competing reaction) intervenes. None of these is tested by data between 300 K300\ \mathrm{K} and 330 K330\ \mathrm{K}.

The estimate is therefore suitable as a nominal, order-of-magnitude planning value. It is not a substitute for a measurement at or near 400 K400\ \mathrm{K}, and any design or safety calculation that depends on kk at 400 K400\ \mathrm{K} should carry the sensitivity range above, or wider, until such a measurement exists.

Result

Required area: approximately 3333–100 m2100\ \text{m}^{2}, and sizing must be based on the low end. An installation of 33.3 m233.3\ \text{m}^{2} removes 500 kW500\ \text{kW} at ΔT=25 K\Delta T = 25\ \text{K} only if U=600 W m−2 K−1U = 600\ \text{W m}^{-2}\ \text{K}^{-1} is actually achieved. If the installed area is 33.3 m233.3\ \text{m}^{2} and the realised coefficient is 200 W m−2 K−1200\ \text{W m}^{-2}\ \text{K}^{-1}, removal at the same ΔT\Delta T is only 200×33.3×25=167 kW200 \times 33.3 \times 25 = 167\ \text{kW}, one third of the heat release, and the reaction mass heats up. Conversely, 100 m2100\ \text{m}^{2} removes 500 kW500\ \text{kW} at the low-end coefficient, and more if the realised coefficient is higher.

Two qualifications apply to this range:

  1. The low end can be lower. Chilled service in the same tabulations gives 100100–150 W m−2 K−1150\ \text{W m}^{-2}\ \text{K}^{-1}, which would require A=133A = 133–200 m2200\ \text{m}^{2}. A viscous, fouling, or poorly agitated charge must be sized from measured or conservatively estimated coefficients for the actual contents, wall, and fouling state, not from the 200200–600600 screening range.
  2. Area availability. 100 m2100\ \text{m}^{2} exceeds the jacket area of most single stirred vessels of ordinary proportions, since jacket area grows with the square of vessel size while heat release grows with the cube (volume). Meeting the low-end area in practice generally requires internal coils, an external pumped loop through a heat exchanger, a lower heat release rate (for example by controlled reagent addition in semi-batch operation), or a larger ΔT\Delta T from a colder coolant. No fouling or design margin has been added to the figures above; a margin would increase the area in inverse proportion to the margin factor applied to UAU A, where UAU A is the product of the overall coefficient and the area, in kilowatts per kelvin (kW K−1\text{kW K}^{-1}).

For reference, the product fixed by the given data is UA=Q/ΔT=500/25=20 kW K−1U A = Q/\Delta T = 500/25 = 20\ \text{kW K}^{-1}: any combination of UU and AA that delivers this product removes the stated load at the stated ΔT\Delta T, and no combination with a smaller product does.

2. Adiabatic temperature rise — not determinable from the given data

The adiabatic temperature rise is denoted by ΔTad\Delta T_{\text{ad}}, in kelvin (K). The mass of the reaction charge is denoted by mm, in kilograms (kg). The mean specific heat capacity of the charge at constant pressure is denoted by cpc_{p}, in kilojoules per kilogram per kelvin (kJ kg−1 K−1\text{kJ kg}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}). The total heat that the remaining reaction would release if it ran to completion with no heat removed is denoted by EtotE_{\text{tot}}, in kilojoules (kJ). Under adiabatic conditions (no heat removal), that heat raises the temperature of the charge by

ΔTad=Etotm cp.\Delta T_{\text{ad}} = \frac{E_{\text{tot}}}{m\, c_{p}}.

Equivalently, EtotE_{\text{tot}} is obtained from the molar enthalpy of reaction, denoted by ΔHr\Delta H_{\text{r}}, in kilojoules per mole (kJ mol−1\text{kJ mol}^{-1}), multiplied by the amount of limiting reactant still to react, in moles (mol).

The given QQ is a rate (energy per unit time), not a total energy, so it cannot be substituted for EtotE_{\text{tot}}. Three distinct pieces of information are missing, any one of which is sufficient to block a numerical result:

  • EtotE_{\text{tot}}, or ΔHr\Delta H_{\text{r}} together with the inventory and the unreacted fraction of limiting reactant;
  • mm;
  • cpc_{p} (including any vessel thermal mass that is to be credited, which would appear as an added term beside mcpm c_{p} in the denominator).

What can be stated from QQ alone is the initial adiabatic self-heating rate. The rate of temperature rise with time under adiabatic conditions is denoted by dT/dt\mathrm{d}T/\mathrm{d}t, in kelvin per second (K s−1\text{K s}^{-1}), where TT is the reaction-mass temperature, in kelvin (K), and tt is time, in seconds (s). If the heat release rate stayed at its stated value,

(dTdt)ad=Qm cp=500 kJ s−1m cp.\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)_{\text{ad}} = \frac{Q}{m\, c_{p}} = \frac{500\ \text{kJ s}^{-1}}{m\, c_{p}}.

The denominator mcpm c_{p}, in kilojoules per kelvin (kJ K−1\text{kJ K}^{-1}), is not given, so even this rate has no numerical value here. It is in any case only an initial rate: as TT rises the reaction rate, and hence QQ, normally increases strongly with temperature (Section 3), while as reactant is consumed QQ eventually falls; ΔTad\Delta T_{\text{ad}} is set by the integral of that behaviour, which is exactly Etot/(mcp)E_{\text{tot}}/(m c_{p}).

The quantity normally carried into relief and emergency-response design is the maximum temperature of the synthesis reaction, denoted by MTSR\text{MTSR}, in kelvin (K), defined as the process temperature plus ΔTad\Delta T_{\text{ad}} for the accumulated (worst-case) charge. Neither the absolute process temperature nor ΔTad\Delta T_{\text{ad}} is given, so MTSR\text{MTSR} also cannot be stated, and it cannot be checked against the onset temperature of any decomposition reaction or against the boiling point of the contents.

3. Temperature at which heat generation exceeds maximum heat removal — not determinable from the given data

The coolant temperature is denoted by TcT_{\text{c}}, in kelvin (K). The heat removal rate at reaction-mass temperature TT is denoted by QremQ_{\text{rem}}, in kilowatts (kW). The heat generation rate at temperature TT is denoted by QgenQ_{\text{gen}}, in kilowatts (kW). With a fixed coolant temperature and a constant UAU A,

Qrem(T)=UA (T−Tc),Q_{\text{rem}}(T) = U A\,(T - T_{\text{c}}),

which is a straight line in TT with slope UA=20 kW K−1U A = 20\ \text{kW K}^{-1} (Section 1). Heat generation, by contrast, follows the reaction kinetics: for a single reaction step its temperature dependence is dominated by an Arrhenius factor containing the activation energy, denoted by EaE_{\text{a}}, in joules per mole (J mol−1\text{J mol}^{-1}), and the gas constant, denoted by RR, in joules per mole per kelvin (J mol−1 K−1\text{J mol}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}), so that QgenQ_{\text{gen}} rises approximately exponentially with TT, in proportion to exp⁡(−Ea/(RT))\exp(-E_{\text{a}}/(R T)).

Heat generation exceeds heat removal above the upper intersection of the generation curve with the removal line. At the critical (tangency, Semenov) condition the two rates and their temperature derivatives are simultaneously equal:

Qgen(T)=Qrem(T),dQgendT=UA.Q_{\text{gen}}(T) = Q_{\text{rem}}(T), \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}Q_{\text{gen}}}{\mathrm{d}T} = U A.

Solving for that temperature requires all of the following, none of which is given:

  • EaE_{\text{a}}, and the reaction rate (or QgenQ_{\text{gen}}) at a stated absolute reference temperature — only a temperature difference of 25 K25\ \text{K} is supplied, and the Arrhenius factor depends on the absolute TT, so the generation curve cannot even be anchored;
  • the absolute process temperature and TcT_{\text{c}} separately (only their difference is known);
  • the reaction order and reactant concentrations, which set how QgenQ_{\text{gen}} changes as reactant is consumed;
  • confirmation of what "maximum" removal means — coolant at its lowest available temperature and flow, and whether the installed AA is the 33.3 m233.3\ \text{m}^{2} or the 100 m2100\ \text{m}^{2} figure, since over-installing area raises UAU A and moves the intersection to a higher temperature.

One stability check can be made at the stated operating point, where generation and removal are equal at 500 kW500\ \text{kW} by construction. The operating point is thermally stable only if generation rises more slowly with temperature than removal does:

dQgendT≈Q⋅EaRT2<UA=20 kW K−1,i.e.EaRT2<0.04 K−1.\frac{\mathrm{d}Q_{\text{gen}}}{\mathrm{d}T} \approx Q \cdot \frac{E_{\text{a}}}{R T^{2}} < U A = 20\ \text{kW K}^{-1}, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \frac{E_{\text{a}}}{R T^{2}} < 0.04\ \text{K}^{-1}.

Whether this inequality holds cannot be tested without EaE_{\text{a}} and the absolute TT. If it fails, the stated operating point is already unstable and any small upward temperature disturbance grows without any loss of cooling. If it holds, the margin in temperature before the tangency point is reached still requires the full generation curve.

4. Consequence of loss of cooling

On loss of cooling (coolant flow stopped, coolant supply lost, or UAU A otherwise collapsing), QremQ_{\text{rem}} falls to approximately zero apart from heat losses through the vessel wall and to the surroundings, which are small for a large vessel relative to 500 kW500\ \text{kW}. The consequences then follow in sequence:

  1. Self-heating. The 500 kW500\ \text{kW} released is retained in the charge, which heats at the initial rate Q/(mcp)Q/(m c_{p}) of Section 2. The time available for detection and response is set by mcpm c_{p} and by the kinetics; it cannot be quoted in minutes from the given data, and it shortens rapidly as the temperature rises.
  2. Acceleration (potential thermal runaway). Because QgenQ_{\text{gen}} increases approximately exponentially with TT while there is no longer a removal line to intersect it, the self-heating accelerates. The temperature tends toward the maximum temperature of the synthesis reaction (MTSR\text{MTSR}, Section 2), unless reactant exhaustion stops the reaction first. Whether a true runaway occurs, and how violent it is, depends on ΔTad\Delta T_{\text{ad}}, EaE_{\text{a}}, and the inventory — the quantities missing above — so a runaway cannot be asserted as certain, but it also cannot be excluded, and the case must be treated as a potential runaway until calorimetric data (reaction enthalpy, ΔTad\Delta T_{\text{ad}}, decomposition onset, gas generation) show otherwise.
  3. Pressure rise. Rising temperature raises the vapour pressure of the contents; at the boiling point the temperature is temporarily held by vaporisation while pressure climbs, and any secondary decomposition reaction reached at the elevated temperature may generate permanent gas and a second, often larger, temperature and pressure rise.
  4. Relief and failure. If a relief system is present and sized for the runaway case (including possible two-phase, vapour-plus-liquid discharge, which greatly increases the required relief area), the contents are discharged to a safe location and the vessel survives, with loss of the batch and a hazardous release to the relief system. If relief is absent, blocked, or sized only for a single-phase or non-runaway case, pressure can exceed the vessel design pressure and the vessel can rupture, releasing flammable and/or toxic contents with the potential for fire, vapour-cloud explosion, and injury. Loss of cooling is therefore a loss-of-containment hazard, not merely a loss of temperature control.
  5. Required safeguards implied by the duty. A 500 kW500\ \text{kW} exothermic duty of this kind normally requires, as a minimum, high-temperature alarm and trip that stop reagent addition and heating, an independent emergency cooling or quench/dump provision, and relief sizing based on measured runaway calorimetry. None of these can be specified numerically from QQ and ΔT\Delta T alone.

B4. Mixing in a Larger Vessel

Response without defensive prompt

Scale-up of a stirred vessel from 0.1 m³ to 10 m³

Given data and definitions
  • V1V_1 = volume of the laboratory vessel = 0.1 m³
  • V2V_2 = volume of the large vessel = 10 m³
  • N1N_1 = laboratory agitator speed = 300 revolutions per minute (rpm)
  • P1P_1 = laboratory power input = 50 W, where W denotes the watt
  • N2N_2 = agitator speed of the large vessel, in rpm, to be found
  • P2P_2 = power input of the large vessel, in W, to be found
  • D1D_1 = impeller diameter in the laboratory vessel, in metres (m)
  • D2D_2 = impeller diameter in the large vessel, in m
  • λ\lambda = linear scale ratio, defined as λ=D2/D1\lambda = D_2/D_1, dimensionless; under geometric similarity the same ratio applies to every linear dimension of the vessel and the impeller
  • ρ\rho = fluid density, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg m⁻³)
  • μ\mu = fluid dynamic viscosity, in pascal seconds (Pa s)
  • NPN_{\mathrm{P}} = power number, dimensionless, defined by P=NPρN3D5P = N_{\mathrm{P}} \rho N^{3} D^{5}, where in that definition NN is the agitator speed in revolutions per second and DD is the impeller diameter in m, so that PP is in W
  • ReRe = impeller Reynolds number, dimensionless, defined as Re=ρND2/μRe = \rho N D^{2}/\mu, with NN in revolutions per second
  • utipu_{\mathrm{tip}} = impeller tip speed, in metres per second (m s⁻¹), defined as utip=πDNu_{\mathrm{tip}} = \pi D N, with NN in revolutions per second

No value of D1D_1, ρ\rho or μ\mu is supplied, so ReRe itself and the flow regime cannot be evaluated numerically. The main calculation below is conditional on the standard scale-up assumption stated in the next section.

1. Linear scale ratio

Under geometric similarity, volume is proportional to the cube of any linear dimension, so:

V2V1=λ3\frac{V_2}{V_1} = \lambda^{3}

V2V1=10 m30.1 m3=100\frac{V_2}{V_1} = \frac{10\ \mathrm{m^3}}{0.1\ \mathrm{m^3}} = 100

λ=1001/3=4.64\lambda = 100^{1/3} = 4.64

That is, every linear dimension of the large vessel and of its impeller is 4.64 times the corresponding laboratory dimension: D2=4.64 D1D_2 = 4.64\,D_1, and likewise for the vessel diameter, the liquid depth and the impeller clearance.

2. Why a scale-up criterion must be stated

Geometric similarity alone does not fix N2N_2. With geometric similarity, and with the same fluid in both vessels, the quantities P/VP/V (power input per unit volume, in watts per cubic metre, W m⁻³, where VV is the vessel volume in m³), utipu_{\mathrm{tip}}, ReRe and the mixing time cannot all be held constant at once, because each one depends on a different combination of NN and DD. A numerical answer for N2N_2 and P2P_2 therefore requires one stated criterion.

The criterion most used for stirred-vessel scale-up, and the one adopted as the main result here, is constant power input per unit volume, P/VP/V. Results for the other common criteria are given in Section 5, so that the dependence on the choice is explicit.

3. Power relation used

For a fully baffled vessel in turbulent flow, NPN_{\mathrm{P}} is approximately constant, independent of ReRe. With the same fluid (ρ\rho unchanged) and geometric similarity (NPN_{\mathrm{P}} unchanged) in both vessels, the definition of NPN_{\mathrm{P}} gives:

P2P1=(N2N1)3(D2D1)5=(N2N1)3λ5\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{N_2}{N_1}\right)^{3} \left(\frac{D_2}{D_1}\right)^{5} = \left(\frac{N_2}{N_1}\right)^{3} \lambda^{5}

Speeds may be inserted in rpm in this ratio and in every ratio below, because the conversion factor between rpm and revolutions per second cancels between the two vessels.

Dividing by the volumes and using V2/V1=λ3V_2/V_1 = \lambda^{3}:

P2/V2P1/V1=(N2N1)3λ2\frac{P_2/V_2}{P_1/V_1} = \left(\frac{N_2}{N_1}\right)^{3} \lambda^{2}

so that power input per unit volume is proportional to N3D2N^{3}D^{2}.

4. Main result: constant power input per unit volume

Laboratory power input per unit volume:

P1V1=50 W0.1 m3=500 W m−3\frac{P_1}{V_1} = \frac{50\ \mathrm{W}}{0.1\ \mathrm{m^3}} = 500\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}

Setting P2/V2=P1/V1P_2/V_2 = P_1/V_1 in the relation of Section 3:

(N2N1)3λ2=1\left(\frac{N_2}{N_1}\right)^{3} \lambda^{2} = 1

N2N1=λ−2/3=4.6416−2/3=0.359\frac{N_2}{N_1} = \lambda^{-2/3} = 4.6416^{-2/3} = 0.359

N2=0.359×300 rpm=108 rpmN_2 = 0.359 \times 300\ \mathrm{rpm} = 108\ \mathrm{rpm}

The large-vessel power input then follows directly from the criterion itself:

P2=(P1V1)V2=500 W m−3×10 m3=5000 W=5.0 kWP_2 = \left(\frac{P_1}{V_1}\right) V_2 = 500\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-3}} \times 10\ \mathrm{m^3} = 5000\ \mathrm{W} = 5.0\ \mathrm{kW}

where kW denotes the kilowatt, 1 kW = 1000 W. Equivalently, P2/P1=V2/V1=100P_2/P_1 = V_2/V_1 = 100, and 100×50 W=5000 W100 \times 50\ \mathrm{W} = 5000\ \mathrm{W}, in agreement with the power relation of Section 3: 0.3593×4.64165=1000.359^{3} \times 4.6416^{5} = 100.

Result at constant P/VP/V: N2≈108N_2 \approx 108 rpm and P2≈5.0P_2 \approx 5.0 kW.

Consequences of this choice, obtained from the definitions of utipu_{\mathrm{tip}} and ReRe:

  • Tip-speed ratio: (N2/N1)λ=0.359×4.6416=1.67(N_2/N_1)\lambda = 0.359 \times 4.6416 = 1.67. The tip speed rises by a factor of 1.67, so shear at the impeller tip is not preserved.
  • Reynolds-number ratio: (N2/N1)λ2=0.359×21.54=7.74(N_2/N_1)\lambda^{2} = 0.359 \times 21.54 = 7.74. The large vessel operates at a Reynolds number 7.74 times the laboratory value; it is therefore deeper into the turbulent regime, which is consistent with the constant-NPN_{\mathrm{P}} assumption if the laboratory vessel was already turbulent.

Each row applies the same power relation, P2/P1=(N2/N1)3λ5P_2/P_1 = (N_2/N_1)^{3}\lambda^{5} with λ5=2154.4\lambda^{5} = 2154.4, together with the stated criterion.

6. Assumptions and limits
  1. Geometric similarity: all linear dimensions scale by λ=4.64\lambda = 4.64, including the impeller diameter, so D2/D1=λD_2/D_1 = \lambda.
  2. Same fluid in both vessels: ρ\rho and μ\mu unchanged.
  3. Fully baffled, turbulent operation in both vessels, so that NPN_{\mathrm{P}} is the same in both and P=NPρN3D5P = N_{\mathrm{P}}\rho N^{3}D^{5} applies. This cannot be verified from the data supplied, because D1D_1, ρ\rho and μ\mu are not given and ReRe therefore cannot be computed. If the laboratory vessel were in laminar flow instead, where NPN_{\mathrm{P}} is proportional to Re−1Re^{-1} and PP is proportional to μN2D3\mu N^{2}D^{3}, the exponents would differ and the numbers above would not apply.
  4. P1=50P_1 = 50 W is taken as the power actually delivered to the fluid (the drawn, unaerated power), with no allowance for motor, gearbox or seal losses; the installed motor rating for the large vessel must exceed the 5.0 kW fluid power of the main result by the drive efficiency and a service margin.
  5. No allowance is made for non-geometric practical effects that commonly limit scale-up at constant P/VP/V: the 1.67-fold rise in tip speed noted in Section 4, longer blending time in the large vessel, heat-removal area per unit volume falling by a factor of λ\lambda (surface area scales as λ2\lambda^{2} while volume scales as λ3\lambda^{3}), and mechanical limits on shaft torque, where torque, defined as P/(2πN)P/(2\pi N) with PP in W and NN in revolutions per second, rises by a factor of (P2/P1)/(N2/N1)=100/0.359=278(P_2/P_1)/(N_2/N_1) = 100/0.359 = 278 at constant P/VP/V.
Answer
  • Linear scale ratio: λ=(V2/V1)1/3=1001/3=4.64\lambda = (V_2/V_1)^{1/3} = 100^{1/3} = 4.64.
  • On the standard criterion of constant power input per unit volume (500 W m⁻³ in both vessels): the agitator speed falls from 300 rpm to approximately 108 rpm, and the power input rises from 50 W to approximately 5.0 kW, a 100-fold increase in power in proportion to the 100-fold increase in volume.
  • No unique scaled speed and power exist without a criterion; the values under constant tip speed, constant Reynolds number and constant speed are 64.6 rpm and 1.08 kW, 13.9 rpm and 10.8 W, and 300 rpm and 108 kW respectively.
Response with defensive prompt

Stirred-Vessel Scale-Up from 0.1 m³ to 10 m³

Symbols and given data

All symbols are defined here before use.

  • V1V_1 is the laboratory vessel volume, in cubic metres (m3\mathrm{m^3}): V1=0.1 m3V_1 = 0.1\ \mathrm{m^3}.
  • V2V_2 is the plant vessel volume, in cubic metres (m3\mathrm{m^3}): V2=10 m3V_2 = 10\ \mathrm{m^3}.
  • N1N_1 is the laboratory agitator speed, in revolutions per minute (rpm\mathrm{rpm}): N1=300 rpmN_1 = 300\ \mathrm{rpm}.
  • N2N_2 is the plant agitator speed, in revolutions per minute (rpm\mathrm{rpm}): to be found.
  • P1P_1 is the laboratory power input, in watts (W\mathrm{W}): P1=50 WP_1 = 50\ \mathrm{W}.
  • P2P_2 is the plant power input, in watts (W\mathrm{W}): to be found.
  • D1D_1 is the laboratory impeller diameter, in metres (m\mathrm{m}).
  • D2D_2 is the plant impeller diameter, in metres (m\mathrm{m}).
  • λ\lambda is the linear scale ratio, dimensionless: λ=D2/D1\lambda = D_2/D_1.
  • ρ\rho is the liquid density, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg m−3\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}), taken as the same in both vessels.
  • μ\mu is the liquid dynamic viscosity, in pascal-seconds (Pa s\mathrm{Pa\,s}), taken as the same in both vessels.
  • NPN_{\mathrm{P}} is the power number, dimensionless.
  • ReRe is the impeller Reynolds number, dimensionless.
  • utipu_{\mathrm{tip}} is the impeller tip speed, in metres per second (m s−1\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}).
  • T\mathcal{T} is the shaft torque, in newton-metres (N m\mathrm{N\,m}).

Numerical values of ρ\rho, μ\mu, D1D_1 and D2D_2 are not supplied. The scale-up ratios below do not need those values provided that geometric similarity holds, the liquid is unchanged, and NPN_{\mathrm{P}} is unchanged between the two vessels. The last condition is examined in §5.

1. Linear scale ratio

Geometric similarity means that every linear dimension scales by the same factor λ\lambda, so volume scales as λ3\lambda^3:

V2V1=λ3\frac{V_2}{V_1} = \lambda^3

λ=(V2V1)1/3=(100.1)1/3=1001/3=4.64\lambda = \left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\frac{10}{0.1}\right)^{1/3} = 100^{1/3} = 4.64

That is, λ=4.64\lambda = 4.64 (dimensionless), and consequently λ2=21.5\lambda^2 = 21.5 and λ5=2.15×103\lambda^5 = 2.15\times10^{3}.

2. Governing relations

For a stirred vessel, the power number NPN_{\mathrm{P}} is defined by

P=NP ρ n3D5P = N_{\mathrm{P}}\,\rho\,n^3 D^5

where, in this defining equation only, nn is the agitator speed in revolutions per second (s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}}) and DD is the impeller diameter in metres (m\mathrm{m}), so that PP is in watts (W\mathrm{W}). Because the same conversion between revolutions per minute and revolutions per second applies to both vessels, speed ratios may be taken directly in revolutions per minute.

With NPN_{\mathrm{P}} and ρ\rho unchanged, the power ratio is therefore

P2P1=(N2N1)3(D2D1)5=(N2N1)3λ5(1)\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \left(\frac{N_2}{N_1}\right)^{3}\left(\frac{D_2}{D_1}\right)^{5} = \left(\frac{N_2}{N_1}\right)^{3}\lambda^{5} \tag{1}

The impeller Reynolds number ReRe and the tip speed utipu_{\mathrm{tip}} are

Re=ρ nD2μ,utip=πDn(2)Re = \frac{\rho\,n D^{2}}{\mu}, \qquad u_{\mathrm{tip}} = \pi D n \tag{2}

where nn is again in revolutions per second (s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}}) in these defining equations, and the ratios used below are unaffected by that choice of unit.

Dividing the power relation by volume, and using V∝D3V \propto D^{3} under geometric similarity, gives the specific power scaling

PV∝N3D2(3)\frac{P}{V} \propto N^{3} D^{2} \tag{3}

where P/VP/V is the power per unit volume, in watts per cubic metre (W m−3\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}).

3. Three scale-up criteria
3.1 Constant power per unit volume

Setting P2/V2=P1/V1P_2/V_2 = P_1/V_1 gives the power directly:

P2=P1 V2V1=50 W×100.1=5.00×103 W=5.00 kWP_2 = P_1\,\frac{V_2}{V_1} = 50\ \mathrm{W} \times \frac{10}{0.1} = 5.00\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{W} = 5.00\ \mathrm{kW}

The three criteria are mutually incompatible. No choice of N2N_2 satisfies more than one of them at λ=4.64\lambda = 4.64, and the predicted plant power spans a factor of 464464 between the largest value (5.00 kW5.00\ \mathrm{kW}) and the smallest value (10.8 W10.8\ \mathrm{W}).

For mechanical scale, the torque T=P/(2πn)\mathcal{T} = P/(2\pi n), with nn in revolutions per second (s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}}), is 1.59 N m1.59\ \mathrm{N\,m} in the laboratory vessel and becomes 443 N m443\ \mathrm{N\,m} at constant power per unit volume, 159 N m159\ \mathrm{N\,m} at constant tip speed, and 7.39 N m7.39\ \mathrm{N\,m} at constant Reynolds number. Shaft and drive sizing therefore differ as strongly as the power figures.

5. Validity of the constant power number assumption

Equations (1)–(3) assume that NPN_{\mathrm{P}} is the same in both vessels. NPN_{\mathrm{P}} is approximately constant only in fully turbulent, baffled operation, where ReRe is large (of order 10410^{4} or above); in laminar and transitional operation NPN_{\mathrm{P}} depends on ReRe.

  • Under constant Reynolds number, Re2=Re1Re_2 = Re_1 by construction, so NPN_{\mathrm{P}} is unchanged and the result in §3.3 is self-consistent.
  • Under constant power per unit volume and under constant tip speed, ReRe rises by a factor of 7.747.74 and 4.644.64 respectively. If the laboratory vessel is already fully turbulent, NPN_{\mathrm{P}} remains approximately constant and the results in §3.1 and §3.2 hold. If the laboratory vessel is transitional, NPN_{\mathrm{P}} changes on scale-up and the powers in §3.1 and §3.2 require correction with the actual NPN_{\mathrm{P}}–ReRe curve for the impeller.

The absolute value of Re1Re_1 cannot be calculated from the data supplied, because ρ\rho, μ\mu and D1D_1 are not given. The flow regime of either vessel is therefore not established by the problem data.

6. Which phenomenon limits the process, and which criterion follows

No limiting phenomenon is stated in the problem, and none can be deduced from V1V_1, V2V_2, N1N_1 and P1P_1. Those four numbers determine the three operating points in §4; they carry no information about what the vessel is required to do. A single criterion selected from the data alone would be an unsupported assumption, not a result.

The criterion follows from the phenomenon that limits the process, as follows.

Limiting phenomenon Physical quantity that must be preserved Criterion that follows
Turbulent transfer limited by mean energy dissipation: gas–liquid or liquid–liquid dispersion, drop breakup, micromixing-limited reaction, turbulent heat and mass transfer correlated against specific power Mean power dissipated per unit volume (equivalently, per unit mass at fixed ρ\rho) Constant P/VP/V: 108 rpm108\ \mathrm{rpm}, 5.00 kW5.00\ \mathrm{kW}
Damage or breakage set by the maximum shear at the impeller: shear-sensitive cells, flocs, fragile crystals, shear-limited emulsions Maximum local shear, for which utipu_{\mathrm{tip}} is the standard scale-up proxy Constant tip speed: 64.6 rpm64.6\ \mathrm{rpm}, 1.08 kW1.08\ \mathrm{kW}
Flow pattern and regime set by the balance of inertial and viscous forces, as in laminar or high-viscosity blending Dynamic similarity, i.e. equal ReRe Constant ReRe: 13.9 rpm13.9\ \mathrm{rpm}, 10.8 W10.8\ \mathrm{W}

Further limitations fall outside all three criteria and would need their own relations: just-suspended speed for solids suspension, blend time for bulk blending, flooding and gas hold-up for aerated operation, and heat removal, for which the jacket area per unit volume falls as 1/λ1/\lambda on scale-up, so none of the three criteria preserves the laboratory heat-removal capability.

Two consequences follow for any selection made without that information:

  1. Constant ReRe is the criterion of dynamic similarity, not of equal mixing performance. Applied to a vessel that operates turbulently, it reduces the specific power by a factor of 464464 and leaves the plant vessel severely under-agitated relative to the laboratory vessel.
  2. Constant P/VP/V is the criterion most often adopted for dissipation-controlled turbulent duties, and constant tip speed for shear-limited duties. Neither status is established here, because the duty is not specified.

Answer. Plant conditions are 108 rpm108\ \mathrm{rpm} and 5.00 kW5.00\ \mathrm{kW} at constant power per unit volume; 64.6 rpm64.6\ \mathrm{rpm} and 1.08 kW1.08\ \mathrm{kW} at constant tip speed; and 13.9 rpm13.9\ \mathrm{rpm} and 10.8 W10.8\ \mathrm{W} at constant Reynolds number. The limiting phenomenon is not specified in the problem and cannot be inferred from the given data, so no one of the three criteria is determined: the criterion must be selected from the process duty using the correspondence in the table above — constant power per unit volume for a dissipation-limited turbulent duty, constant tip speed for a maximum-shear-limited duty, and constant Reynolds number for a viscous-regime-limited duty.

Response with defensive prompt

First-Order Conversion with Bypass

Symbols
  • kk = first-order rate constant, in reciprocal time (time−1^{-1})
  • VV = active reactor volume, in volume units (for example m3^{3})
  • QQ = total volumetric feed rate, in volume per time (for example m3^{3} s−1^{-1})
  • τ\tau = nominal residence time, τ=V/Q\tau = V/Q, in time units
  • DaDa = dimensionless product kτk\tau, here Da=kτ=2.0Da = k\tau = 2.0
  • XX = fractional conversion of the limiting reactant, dimensionless
  • XaX_{\mathrm{a}} = fractional conversion of the portion of feed that passes through the active reactor volume, dimensionless
  • bb = bypass fraction, the fraction of the total feed that bypasses the active volume and undergoes no reaction, dimensionless
  • QaQ_{\mathrm{a}} = volumetric rate through the active volume, Qa=(1−b)QQ_{\mathrm{a}} = (1-b)Q
  • τa\tau_{\mathrm{a}} = residence time of the active stream, τa=V/Qa\tau_{\mathrm{a}} = V/Q_{\mathrm{a}}
  • DaaDa_{\mathrm{a}} = dimensionless product for the active stream, Daa=kτaDa_{\mathrm{a}} = k\tau_{\mathrm{a}}

The reaction is first order, isothermal, and at constant density. The active volume is treated as plug flow, which is the flow pattern consistent with the ideal-flow expression stated in the problem.

1. Ideal flow, full volume active

For plug flow with a first-order reaction, the outlet conversion is

X=1−exp⁡(−kτ)=1−exp⁡(−Da)X = 1 - \exp(-k\tau) = 1 - \exp(-Da)

With Da=2.0Da = 2.0:

X=1−exp⁡(−2.0)=1−0.1353=0.8647X = 1 - \exp(-2.0) = 1 - 0.1353 = 0.8647

Ideal-flow conversion: X=0.865X = 0.865, i.e. 86.5 %.

For reference, this is a plug-flow result. A perfectly mixed continuous stirred-tank reactor at the same value of DaDa would give X=Da/(1+Da)=2.0/3.0=0.667X = Da/(1+Da) = 2.0/3.0 = 0.667. A measured conversion alone therefore does not identify the flow pattern.

2. Bypass model

The feed is split into two parts:

  1. A fraction bb bypasses the active volume, leaves with zero conversion, and rejoins the treated stream at the outlet.
  2. A fraction (1−b)(1-b) passes through the active volume as plug flow.

Because the active volume receives only Qa=(1−b)QQ_{\mathrm{a}} = (1-b)Q, its residence time is longer than the nominal residence time:

τa=V(1−b)Q=τ1−b,Daa=Da1−b=2.01−b\tau_{\mathrm{a}} = \frac{V}{(1-b)Q} = \frac{\tau}{1-b}, \qquad Da_{\mathrm{a}} = \frac{Da}{1-b} = \frac{2.0}{1-b}

The conversion of the active stream is

Xa=1−exp⁡(−Daa)=1−exp⁡ ⁣(−2.01−b)X_{\mathrm{a}} = 1 - \exp(-Da_{\mathrm{a}}) = 1 - \exp\!\left(\frac{-2.0}{1-b}\right)

Mixing the untreated bypass stream with the treated stream at the outlet gives the overall conversion:

X=(1−b) Xa+b×0=(1−b)[1−exp⁡ ⁣(−2.01−b)]X = (1-b)\,X_{\mathrm{a}} + b \times 0 = (1-b)\left[1 - \exp\!\left(\frac{-2.0}{1-b}\right)\right]

Numerical results:

Bypass fraction bb Daa=2.0/(1−b)Da_{\mathrm{a}} = 2.0/(1-b) Active-stream conversion XaX_{\mathrm{a}} Overall conversion XX
0 (ideal) 2.000 0.865 0.865 (86.5 %)
0.05 2.105 0.878 0.834 (83.4 %)
0.15 2.353 0.905 0.769 (76.9 %)
0.30 2.857 0.943 0.660 (66.0 %)

The active-stream conversion rises as bb rises, because the flow through the active volume falls and its residence time rises. The overall conversion still falls, because a growing share of the feed receives no treatment at all, and that loss outweighs the gain in the treated share.

Note on a common simplified convention

Some simplified treatments define the bypass fraction after the fact, as the untreated share of the outlet stream, while holding the treated stream at the nominal residence time τ\tau. Under that lumped convention the overall conversion is X=(1−b)[1−exp⁡(−2.0)]X = (1-b)[1-\exp(-2.0)], giving 0.821 at b=0.05b = 0.05, 0.735 at b=0.15b = 0.15, and 0.605 at b=0.30b = 0.30. The table above is the flow-split result, in which the reduced flow through the active volume is accounted for in τa\tau_{\mathrm{a}}. The two sets of numbers differ only in that residence-time correction; they agree at b=0b = 0.

3. Evidence that would establish the flow pattern

A single steady-state conversion measurement cannot establish bypassing. The same overall conversion can be produced by axial dispersion, by partial mixing toward stirred-tank behaviour, by dead (stagnant) volume, by a lower effective value of kk than the value measured in a batch or laboratory reactor, or by a combination of these. Independent, non-reacting hydrodynamic evidence is required:

  1. Residence-time distribution (RTD) from an inert tracer test. Inject a pulse or step of a non-reacting, non-adsorbing tracer at conditions matching the operating flow, density, and viscosity, and measure the outlet tracer concentration against time. - Pulse input: bypassing gives tracer appearing at the outlet at essentially zero time — an early spike or a distinct early peak, well before the breakthrough time expected for plug flow — followed by the main response from the active volume. The area under the early spike, as a fraction of the total recovered tracer area, estimates bb. - Step input: bypassing gives an immediate jump in the cumulative tracer response at zero time, to a level approximately equal to bb, before the active-volume response arrives. Plug flow without bypass gives no outlet response until one active-volume residence time has elapsed; a stirred tank gives a smooth exponential rise from zero with no initial jump.
  2. Tracer mass recovery and mean residence time. Full tracer recovery confirms the test is quantitative. The mean of the residence-time distribution gives the hydrodynamically active volume. A mean residence time below V/QV/Q indicates dead volume in addition to, or instead of, bypass; the early-time response separates the two, since dead volume alone delays and spreads the response but does not produce a zero-time breakthrough.
  3. Conversion measured at several flow rates. Values of XX measured as QQ (and hence DaDa) is varied can be tested against the bypass equation above, with bb held fixed, against the dispersion and tanks-in-series alternatives. A model that fits one flow rate but not the trend has not been established.
  4. Direct internal evidence, where accessible. Dye or tracer visualisation, local sampling of concentration or tracer at several positions inside the vessel, local velocity measurement, or temperature mapping under reaction (a cold, unreacted short-circuit path) can locate the bypass path directly and show whether the remainder of the volume is near plug flow, mixed, or stagnant.
  5. Checks against artefacts. The tracer result should be repeated, checked with a second tracer, and checked for tracer adsorption, reaction, and density-driven flow, and the sampling and injection lines should be shown not to create the early response themselves.

In summary: the diagnostic signature of bypass is tracer (and, under reaction, unconverted feed) appearing at the outlet at near-zero residence time, quantified by the initial jump in a step-tracer response or the early area in a pulse-tracer response, combined with a flow-rate series of conversions consistent with the bypass model.

Response with defensive prompt

Minimum Number of Theoretical Stages

Definitions

The following symbols are defined before use:

  • Nmin⁡N_{\min}: minimum number of theoretical (equilibrium) stages at total reflux, dimensionless count.
  • α\alpha: relative volatility of the light key component with respect to the heavy key component, dimensionless.
  • SS: product of the distillate and bottoms composition ratios appearing in the Fenske equation, dimensionless. Its stated value is S=9801S = 9801.
  • ln⁡\ln: natural logarithm, dimensionless.

For a binary separation, the product SS is written in component terms as follows, where the light key component is denoted LK, the heavy key component is denoted HK, the distillate stream is denoted D, the bottoms stream is denoted B, and xi,jx_{i,j} denotes the mole fraction, dimensionless, of component ii in stream jj:

S=(xLK,DxHK,D)(xHK,BxLK,B)=9801S = \left(\frac{x_{\mathrm{LK,D}}}{x_{\mathrm{HK,D}}}\right) \left(\frac{x_{\mathrm{HK,B}}}{x_{\mathrm{LK,B}}}\right) = 9801

Calculation

The Fenske equation for the minimum number of theoretical stages at total reflux, for constant relative volatility, is:

Nmin⁡=ln⁡Sln⁡αN_{\min} = \frac{\ln S}{\ln \alpha}

The stated relative volatility is α=1.30\alpha = 1.30. Substitution gives:

Nmin⁡=ln⁡(9801)ln⁡(1.30)=9.19020.26236=35.03N_{\min} = \frac{\ln(9801)}{\ln(1.30)} = \frac{9.1902}{0.26236} = 35.03

The same result is obtained with logarithms to base 10, because the change of logarithm base cancels between the numerator and the denominator.

Result

The calculated value is 35.03 theoretical stages. A stage count must be a whole number, so the minimum whole number is:

36 theoretical stages

Under the usual Fenske convention, this count includes a partial reboiler counted as one theoretical stage. On that convention, 36 total theoretical stages correspond to 35 trays plus the reboiler.

The calculation assumes total reflux, equilibrium stages, and a relative volatility represented by the single stated value of 1.30. If the relative volatility varies through the column, the value used in the Fenske equation must be a suitable average (conventionally a geometric mean of the end values); no such averaging can be performed from the data given here, for the reason stated in the next section.

Relative Volatility Across the Composition Range, Azeotrope, and Range of Stage Counts

No value other than the single stated value, α=1.30\alpha = 1.30, can be reported from the problem statement.

  • Variation across the composition range: Not determinable. The problem identifies no binary pair, states no temperature or pressure, and supplies no vapour–liquid equilibrium data and no table or function of relative volatility against composition. A variation across the range therefore cannot be reported without inventing data.
  • Azeotrope: Neither the presence nor the absence of an intervening azeotrope can be established. For a binary system at fixed pressure, an azeotrope occurs at a composition where the vapour and liquid compositions are equal, which corresponds to a relative volatility of 1 at that composition. The single stated value of 1.30 is not 1, but it describes only the condition to which it applies; it gives no information about the relative volatility at other compositions, where an azeotrope could or could not occur.
  • Count at the lowest and highest plausible relative volatility: Not calculable. No lowest value and no highest value, and no basis for setting plausible bounds, are given or derivable from the single stated value. Assigning numerical bounds would be an unsupported assumption, so no such counts are reported.

If end values or bounds for the relative volatility are later supplied from vapour–liquid equilibrium data for a named binary pair at a stated pressure, each corresponding count follows from the same equation, Nmin⁡=ln⁡S/ln⁡αN_{\min} = \ln S / \ln \alpha, with S=9801S = 9801 held fixed. Given data
  • QQ, the vapour volumetric flow rate at the flooding-limited section, expressed in cubic metres per second (m3/s\mathrm{m^3/s}): Q=3.0 m3/sQ = 3.0\ \mathrm{m^3/s}

  • DD, the required column (inside) diameter, expressed in metres (m\mathrm{m})

Calculation

The superficial vapour velocity uu (in m/s\mathrm{m/s}) is defined as the vapour volumetric flow rate QQ (in m3/s\mathrm{m^3/s}) divided by the column cross-sectional area AA (in m2\mathrm{m^2}):

The number of equilibrium stages is denoted by the symbol NN, which is dimensionless. The fraction of the feed solute remaining in the raffinate is denoted by the symbol φ\varphi, which is dimensionless. The solute concentration in the feed, expressed in moles per cubic metre (mol m−3\mathrm{mol\,m^{-3}}), is denoted by the symbol xFx_F. The solute concentration in the raffinate leaving the final stage, expressed in mol m−3\mathrm{mol\,m^{-3}}, is denoted by the symbol xNx_N. The fraction remaining is defined by

φ=xNxF.\varphi = \frac{x_N}{x_F}.

The required value is φ=0.02\varphi = 0.02.

Model and assumptions

The cascade is countercurrent. The stage index is denoted by the symbol ii, which is a dimensionless integer running from 1 to NN: the feed enters stage 1 and the fresh solvent enters stage NN. The solute concentration in the raffinate phase leaving stage ii, expressed in mol m−3\mathrm{mol\,m^{-3}}, is denoted by the symbol xix_i. The solute concentration in the extract phase leaving stage ii, expressed in mol m−3\mathrm{mol\,m^{-3}}, is denoted by the symbol yiy_i.

The constant flow rate of the raffinate (feed-carrier) phase, expressed in cubic metres per second (m3 s−1\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}), is denoted by the symbol FF. The constant flow rate of the extract (solvent) phase, expressed in m3 s−1\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}, is denoted by the symbol SS. The given solvent-to-feed ratio is S/F=1.0S/F = 1.0, which is dimensionless. The two phases are taken as immiscible, so that FF and SS do not change from stage to stage. The entering solvent is taken as solute-free. Any change of FF or SS by solute transfer is neglected.

The distribution coefficient is denoted by the symbol DD, which is dimensionless and is defined as the solute concentration in the extract phase divided by the solute concentration in the raffinate phase at equilibrium:

D=yixi.D = \frac{y_i}{x_i}.

The extraction factor is denoted by the symbol EE, which is dimensionless and is defined by

For a countercurrent cascade of equilibrium stages with solute-free entering solvent, constant phase flow rates, and a constant distribution coefficient, the Kremser relation gives the fraction remaining as

φ=11+E+E2+⋯+EN,\varphi = \frac{1}{1 + E + E^{2} + \dots + E^{N}},

in which the summation index is denoted by the symbol kk, a dimensionless integer running from 0 to NN, so that the denominator is the sum of EkE^{k} over that range. The geometric-sum identity, valid here because E≠1E \neq 1,

1+E+E2+⋯+EN=EN+1−1E−1,1 + E + E^{2} + \dots + E^{N} = \frac{E^{N+1} - 1}{E - 1},

φ=E−1EN+1−1.\varphi = \frac{E - 1}{E^{N+1} - 1}.

Setting φ=0.02\varphi = 0.02 and E=2.0E = 2.0:

2.0−12.0 N+1−1=0.02,\frac{2.0 - 1}{2.0^{\,N+1} - 1} = 0.02,

2.0 N+1−1=10.02=50,2.0^{\,N+1} - 1 = \frac{1}{0.02} = 50,

2.0 N+1=51.2.0^{\,N+1} = 51.

The natural logarithm is denoted by the symbol ln⁡\ln. Taking ln⁡\ln of both sides and solving for NN:

N+1=ln⁡51ln⁡2.0=3.93180.6931=5.672,N + 1 = \frac{\ln 51}{\ln 2.0} = \frac{3.9318}{0.6931} = 5.672,

N=5.672−1=4.672.N = 5.672 - 1 = 4.672.

The calculated requirement is therefore 4.67 equilibrium stages. A stage count must be a whole number, and rounding down would not reach the target, so the count is rounded up.

With N=4N = 4:

φ=2.0−12.05−1=131=0.0323,\varphi = \frac{2.0 - 1}{2.0^{5} - 1} = \frac{1}{31} = 0.0323,

which corresponds to 3.23% remaining, above the 2% limit.

With N=5N = 5:

φ=2.0−12.06−1=163=0.0159,\varphi = \frac{2.0 - 1}{2.0^{6} - 1} = \frac{1}{63} = 0.0159,

The requirement is 4.67 equilibrium stages in continuous terms, so 5 equilibrium stages are required. This count assumes ideal equilibrium stages; a real cascade with stage efficiency below 100% would require more physical stages, by an amount that cannot be fixed from the data given.

C4. Adsorption Breakthrough

Response without defensive prompt

Time to Breakthrough for a Fixed Adsorbent Bed

Result

The stoichiometric (ideal, sharp-front) time is 160 h. This is the time to saturate the whole bed at the stated equilibrium capacity and is therefore an upper bound on the practical breakthrough time. Breakthrough in a real bed occurs earlier, by an amount that cannot be calculated from the data given, because no mass-transfer, bed-geometry, or breakthrough-concentration data are supplied.

Symbols

All symbols are defined here, before first use in the calculation.

  • MM, in kilograms (kg): mass of adsorbent in the bed.
  • qq, in kilograms of solute per kilogram of adsorbent (kg/kg): equilibrium adsorbent capacity at the feed concentration, i.e. the mass of solute held per unit mass of adsorbent when the adsorbent is in equilibrium with the feed.
  • QQ, in kilograms (kg): total mass of solute the bed can hold at equilibrium with the feed.
  • m˙\dot m, in kilograms per hour (kg/h): mass rate at which solute enters the bed in the feed stream.
  • tstt_{\mathrm{st}}, in hours (h): stoichiometric time, i.e. the time to supply an amount of solute equal to QQ at the rate m˙\dot m, and, under the ideal assumptions below, the time to breakthrough.
  • tbt_{\mathrm{b}}, in hours (h): practical breakthrough time, i.e. the operating time at which the outlet solute concentration first reaches the specified allowable (breakthrough) concentration.
  • ff, dimensionless: usable fraction of the equilibrium capacity attained at breakthrough, i.e. the capacity actually used up to tbt_{\mathrm{b}} divided by QQ.
Data
  • M=1,000 kgM = 1{,}000\ \mathrm{kg}
  • q=0.08 kg/kgq = 0.08\ \mathrm{kg/kg}, from a fitted isotherm evaluated at the feed concentration
  • m˙=0.5 kg/h\dot m = 0.5\ \mathrm{kg/h}

No other data are given: there is no bed length, diameter, or void fraction; no particle size; no volumetric flow rate or feed concentration separately (only their product, the solute mass rate m˙\dot m, is given); no mass-transfer coefficient, diffusivity, or mass-transfer-zone length; no isotherm shape away from the feed concentration; and no definition of the breakthrough concentration.

Assumptions for the Ideal Estimate
  1. Before breakthrough the outlet solute concentration is negligible, so essentially all solute entering the bed is adsorbed.
  2. The adsorption front is sharp: the bed behind the front is fully saturated at the capacity qq, and the bed ahead of the front is unused. There is no mass-transfer zone of finite width.
  3. The capacity qq applies uniformly to the whole bed, there is no channelling or bypassing, and the adsorbent is fresh (initially solute-free) at the start.
  4. The feed solute rate m˙\dot m is constant in time.

Under assumptions 1–4, tb=tstt_{\mathrm{b}} = t_{\mathrm{st}}.

Calculation

Total equilibrium capacity of the bed:

Q=Mq=(1,000 kg)(0.08 kg/kg)=80 kg of soluteQ = M q = (1{,}000\ \mathrm{kg})(0.08\ \mathrm{kg/kg}) = 80\ \mathrm{kg\ of\ solute}

Overall solute balance up to saturation, with negligible solute leaving before breakthrough (assumption 1):

m˙ tst=Q\dot m \, t_{\mathrm{st}} = Q

Hence:

tst=Qm˙=80 kg0.5 kg/h=160 ht_{\mathrm{st}} = \frac{Q}{\dot m} = \frac{80\ \mathrm{kg}}{0.5\ \mathrm{kg/h}} = 160\ \mathrm{h}

Unit check: kilograms divided by kilograms per hour gives hours, as required.

Arithmetic check: 0.5 kg/h×160 h=80 kg0.5\ \mathrm{kg/h} \times 160\ \mathrm{h} = 80\ \mathrm{kg}, which equals QQ, so the balance closes exactly.

In days, 160 h160\ \mathrm{h} is 160/24=6.7160 / 24 = 6.7 days of continuous operation.

Interpretation and Limits of the Estimate

160 h160\ \mathrm{h} is the answer obtainable from the stated data, and it must be reported as the stoichiometric / ideal-saturation time, not as an exact practical breakthrough time.

In a real bed the front is spread into a mass-transfer zone of finite length. Breakthrough (at any low, non-zero allowable outlet concentration) occurs when the leading edge of that zone reaches the bed outlet, while part of the bed in the zone is still only partly saturated. Therefore:

tb=f tst,f<1t_{\mathrm{b}} = f \, t_{\mathrm{st}}, \qquad f < 1

so tb<160 ht_{\mathrm{b}} < 160\ \mathrm{h}. The value of ff (equivalently, the length of unused bed) depends on the mass-transfer rate, the isotherm shape, the particle size, the fluid velocity, and the chosen breakthrough concentration, none of which are supplied. No defensible numerical correction can be made without at least one of: a measured breakthrough curve for this system, a mass-transfer-zone length or length of unused bed, or kinetic / mass-transfer data together with bed dimensions.

For illustration only (not a prediction), the sensitivity to ff is linear:

ff, dimensionless tb=f×160 ht_{\mathrm{b}} = f \times 160\ \mathrm{h}, in h
1.00 (ideal sharp front) 160
0.90 144
0.80 128
0.50 80

A design or scheduling decision should therefore treat 160 h as a non-conservative upper bound and allow a margin, or obtain breakthrough-curve / mass-transfer data to fix ff.

  • Stoichiometric (ideal breakthrough) time: 160 h160\ \mathrm{h} (about 6.7 days) at a solute feed rate of 0.5 kg/h0.5\ \mathrm{kg/h}.
