16 Power failure, steam, electric, or other Not quantifiable. No driven equipment, utility system, or resulting process response is given.
Governing scenario

The governing scenario in relief sizing is the applicable scenario that requires the largest orifice area, where required orifice area, denoted AA, in square metres (m²), increases with WW and decreases with GG.

  • Provisional governing case: the single quantified case, W=2 kg/sW = 2\ \text{kg/s} at G=1,200 kg/(m2⋅s)G = 1{,}200\ \text{kg/(m}^2\text{·s)}. It governs by default because it is the only case with a numerical rate.
  • Not established: that this case is the governing case for an actual item of equipment. None of the 16 scenarios in the table can be ruled in, ruled out, or assigned a rate from the data supplied. Any applicable scenario with a rate above 2 kg/s2\ \text{kg/s} at the same GG, or with a lower GG at the same rate, would require a larger area and would displace it. A final governing-case determination requires the protected system, its operating and design conditions, and a rate calculation for each applicable scenario.
Phase of the relieving stream

Classification used in the calculation: vapour.

Reason: the supplied value of GG is stated to rest on a vapour-only assumption. Under that assumption the stream at the orifice is a single vapour (gas) phase, so the mass rate is the product of a vapour mass flux and the orifice area, and no liquid-phase or two-phase term enters.

Limits of that classification:

  • It is an assumption adopted from the stated basis, not a result checked from fluid data. No relieving pressure, relieving temperature, saturation condition, composition, liquid level, or liquid inventory is supplied, so flashing, liquid swell, and entrainment cannot be assessed.
  • It is not classified as liquid: no liquid density, pressure drop, or liquid sizing basis is supplied, and the stated basis is vapour-only.
  • It is not classified as two-phase: no liquid mass fraction, void fraction, or two-phase sizing method (for example a homogeneous-equilibrium or omega-method calculation under API Standard 520, Part I) is supplied or applied.
  • If the protected equipment contains liquid at or near its saturation condition, the actual relief could be two-phase, the applicable flux would differ from 1,200 kg/(m2⋅s)1{,}200\ \text{kg/(m}^2\text{·s)}, and the area computed below would not apply. Confirmation of the vapour-only basis requires the relieving fluid state at the relieving pressure and temperature.
Calculation

By definition of mass flux, the rate through an orifice is the product of the mass flux and the area:

W=G⋅AW = G \cdot A

Solving for AA:

A=WG=2 kg/s1,200 kg/(m2⋅s)=1.67×10−3 m2A = \frac{W}{G} = \frac{2\ \text{kg/s}}{1{,}200\ \text{kg/(m}^2\text{·s)}} = 1.67 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2

Unit check: (kg/s) divided by (kg/(m²·s)) gives m², as required for an area.

Conversions of the required area, denoted AreqA_{\text{req}}:

  • Areq=1.67×10−3 m2A_{\text{req}} = 1.67 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2
  • Areq=16.7 cm2A_{\text{req}} = 16.7\ \text{cm}^2
  • Areq=1,667 mm2A_{\text{req}} = 1{,}667\ \text{mm}^2
  • Areq=2.58 in2A_{\text{req}} = 2.58\ \text{in}^2

Equivalent circular diameter, denoted dd, in metres (m), for a round bore of the same area, from A=πd2/4A = \pi d^{2} / 4, where π\pi is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter:

d=4Aπ=4×1.67×10−3π=0.0461 m=46.1 mmd = \sqrt{\frac{4 A}{\pi}} = \sqrt{\frac{4 \times 1.67 \times 10^{-3}}{\pi}} = 0.0461\ \text{m} = 46.1\ \text{mm}

Back-check: G⋅A=1,200×1.6667×10−3=2.0 kg/sG \cdot A = 1{,}200 \times 1.6667 \times 10^{-3} = 2.0\ \text{kg/s}, which returns the supplied value of WW.

No discharge coefficient, back-pressure correction, or viscosity correction is applied separately: any such factor would belong inside the supplied value of GG. If GG were instead an uncorrected theoretical flux, those factors would be required and the area would increase; the problem states GG as the orifice mass flux to be used, so it is used as given.

Standard orifice selection

Comparison with the standard effective orifice areas of API Standard 526:

  • "K" orifice: 1.838 in2=11.86 cm21.838\ \text{in}^2 = 11.86\ \text{cm}^2 — smaller than 16.7 cm216.7\ \text{cm}^2; insufficient.
  • "L" orifice: 2.853 in2=18.41 cm22.853\ \text{in}^2 = 18.41\ \text{cm}^2 — the smallest standard letter area that is equal to or greater than AreqA_{\text{req}}.

At the same GG, an "L" orifice passes 1,200×1.841×10−3=2.21 kg/s1{,}200 \times 1.841 \times 10^{-3} = 2.21\ \text{kg/s}, an area margin of about 10 % over the required 16.7 cm216.7\ \text{cm}^2.

This letter selection is a screening result based on effective areas. Final device selection requires the manufacturer's certified capacity and effective area, the set pressure, the total back pressure, inlet pressure loss, and the pressure–temperature limits of the valve, none of which are supplied here.

Result
  • Required orifice area: Areq=1.67×10−3 m2A_{\text{req}} = 1.67 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2 (16.7 cm²; 1,667 mm²; 2.58 in²), for W=2 kg/sW = 2\ \text{kg/s} at G=1,200 kg/(m2⋅s)G = 1{,}200\ \text{kg/(m}^2\text{·s)}.
  • Phase basis: vapour only, as stated for GG; not independently verified from fluid data, and not valid if the actual relief is liquid or two-phase.
  • Governing scenario: provisional only — the single quantified case. A design governing case cannot be named until each applicable scenario in the API Standard 521 checklist has been assigned a relieving rate for the specific protected system.
  • Smallest standard API Standard 526 letter meeting the required area: "L" (18.41 cm218.41\ \text{cm}^2).
  • Editions used: API Standard 520, Part I, 10th edition (2020, Errata 1, 2023); API Standard 521, 7th edition (2020, Errata 1, 2022); API Standard 526, 8th edition (2023).

E2. Thermal Runaway Time

Response without defensive prompt

Response Time under Adiabatic Self-Heating

Given data and symbols
  • TT (kelvin, K): the absolute temperature already reached, T=393 KT = 393\ \mathrm{K} (120 ∘C120\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}).
  • RR (joules per mole per kelvin, J/(mol·K)): the universal gas constant, R=8.314 J/(mol⋅K)R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}.
  • qq (watts per kilogram, W/kg): the specific self-heating power, that is, heat generated by reaction per unit mass per unit time, at TT, q=5 W/kgq = 5\ \mathrm{W/kg}.
  • cpc_p (joules per kilogram per kelvin, J/(kg·K)): the specific heat capacity at constant pressure, cp=2,000 J/(kg⋅K)c_p = 2{,}000\ \mathrm{J/(kg\cdot K)}.
  • EaE_a (joules per mole, J/mol): the activation energy, Ea=100 kJ/mol=100,000 J/molE_a = 100\ \mathrm{kJ/mol} = 100{,}000\ \mathrm{J/mol}.
  • tt (seconds, s): time measured from the instant at which the temperature is TT.
  • trespt_{\mathrm{resp}} (seconds, s): the estimated response time sought, namely the time remaining from reaching TT until thermal runaway, taken here as the adiabatic time to maximum rate.
  • T′T' (kelvin, K): a variable absolute temperature during the subsequent self-heating, used as the integration variable.
  • q(T′)q(T') (watts per kilogram, W/kg): the specific self-heating power at T′T'.
  • dT′/dt\mathrm{d}T'/\mathrm{d}t (kelvin per second, K/s): the rate of temperature rise at T′T'.
  • ΔTc\Delta T_c (kelvin, K): the characteristic temperature rise defined in the derivation below.

The estimate rests on the following stated assumptions: adiabatic conditions (no heat loss to the surroundings), constant cpc_p, constant EaE_a, heat generation following an Arrhenius temperature dependence, and negligible consumption of reactant before runaway, so that temperature alone controls the rate in the interval considered.

Energy balance at TT

Under adiabatic conditions all heat generated is retained as sensible heat. Per unit mass,

cpdT′dt=q(T′).c_p \frac{\mathrm{d}T'}{\mathrm{d}t} = q(T').

At the starting temperature TT this gives

dT′dt∣T=qcp=5 W/kg2,000 J/(kg⋅K)=2.5×10−3 K/s=0.15 K/min.\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}T'}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|_{T} = \frac{q}{c_p} = \frac{5\ \mathrm{W/kg}}{2{,}000\ \mathrm{J/(kg\cdot K)}} = 2.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K/s} = 0.15\ \mathrm{K/min}.

Used alone, this initial rate would greatly overstate the time available, because q(T′)q(T') rises steeply with T′T'. The accelerating rate must be included.

Arrhenius acceleration

With the Arrhenius temperature dependence anchored at the known value at TT,

q(T′)=qexp⁡[−EaR(1T′−1T)].q(T') = q \exp\left[-\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T'} - \frac{1}{T}\right)\right].

The time to pass from TT to a much higher temperature, at which the rate is at its maximum in this no-consumption model, is therefore

tresp=∫T∞cpq(T′) dT′.t_{\mathrm{resp}} = \int_{T}^{\infty} \frac{c_p}{q(T')}\,\mathrm{d}T'.

For the temperatures that dominate this integral, T′T' is close to TT, and

1T′−1T≈−T′−TT2.\frac{1}{T'} - \frac{1}{T} \approx -\frac{T' - T}{T^{2}}.

Substitution in the integral, followed by evaluation of the resulting exponential integral, gives the standard adiabatic time-to-maximum-rate estimate

tresp≈cpRT2qEa.t_{\mathrm{resp}} \approx \frac{c_p R T^{2}}{q E_a}.

The same result follows from a characteristic-rise form. Define

ΔTc=RT2Ea.\Delta T_c = \frac{R T^{2}}{E_a}.

ΔTc\Delta T_c (kelvin, K) is the temperature rise over which the Arrhenius factor changes by a factor of ee, where ee is the base of natural logarithms (dimensionless). Over one such rise the heating rate grows ee-fold, successive rises take ee times less time, and the total time is the time to cross the first characteristic rise:

tresp≈ΔTcdT′/dt∣T=RT2/Eaq/cp=cpRT2qEa.t_{\mathrm{resp}} \approx \frac{\Delta T_c}{\left.\mathrm{d}T'/\mathrm{d}t\right|_{T}} = \frac{R T^{2}/E_a}{q/c_p} = \frac{c_p R T^{2}}{q E_a}.

Numerical evaluation

First, the characteristic temperature rise:

ΔTc=RT2Ea=8.314 J/(mol⋅K)×(393 K)2100,000 J/mol=8.314×154,449100,000 K=12.8 K.\Delta T_c = \frac{R T^{2}}{E_a} = \frac{8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)} \times (393\ \mathrm{K})^{2}}{100{,}000\ \mathrm{J/mol}} = \frac{8.314 \times 154{,}449}{100{,}000}\ \mathrm{K} = 12.8\ \mathrm{K}.

Next, the response time:

tresp≈cpRT2qEa=2,000 J/(kg⋅K)×8.314 J/(mol⋅K)×(393 K)25 W/kg×100,000 J/molt_{\mathrm{resp}} \approx \frac{c_p R T^{2}}{q E_a} = \frac{2{,}000\ \mathrm{J/(kg\cdot K)} \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)} \times (393\ \mathrm{K})^{2}}{5\ \mathrm{W/kg} \times 100{,}000\ \mathrm{J/mol}}

=2.568×1095.00×105 s=5,136 s.= \frac{2.568\times10^{9}}{5.00\times10^{5}}\ \mathrm{s} = 5{,}136\ \mathrm{s}.

Equivalently,

tresp≈ΔTcq/cp=12.8 K2.5×10−3 K/s=5,136 s.t_{\mathrm{resp}} \approx \frac{\Delta T_c}{q/c_p} = \frac{12.8\ \mathrm{K}}{2.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K/s}} = 5{,}136\ \mathrm{s}.

Conversion to other units:

5,136 s÷60 s/min=85.6 min,85.6 min÷60 min/h=1.43 h.5{,}136\ \mathrm{s} \div 60\ \mathrm{s/min} = 85.6\ \mathrm{min}, \qquad 85.6\ \mathrm{min} \div 60\ \mathrm{min/h} = 1.43\ \mathrm{h}.

Check

Direct numerical integration of the unapproximated Arrhenius integral above, from 393 K393\ \mathrm{K} to a temperature far above TT, gives 5,510 s5{,}510\ \mathrm{s} (1.53 h1.53\ \mathrm{h}). The closed-form estimate, 5,136 s5{,}136\ \mathrm{s}, is about 7%7\% below the unapproximated value: the same order of magnitude, and slightly conservative, that is, slightly short, for response planning. Dimensional check: cpRT2/(qEa)c_p R T^{2} / (q E_a) has units [J/(kg⋅K)] [J/(mol⋅K)] [K2]/([J/(s⋅kg)] [J/mol])=s\mathrm{[J/(kg\cdot K)]\,[J/(mol\cdot K)]\,[K^{2}] / ([J/(s\cdot kg)]\,[J/mol]) = s}, as required for a time.

Result

The estimated response time after the reacting mass reaches 393 K393\ \mathrm{K} (120 ∘C120\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}) under adiabatic conditions is

tresp≈5.1×103 s≈86 min≈1.4 h.t_{\mathrm{resp}} \approx 5.1\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{s} \approx 86\ \mathrm{min} \approx 1.4\ \mathrm{h}.

Approximately one and a half hours are therefore available for response from the point at which 393 K393\ \mathrm{K} is reached, before thermal runaway under the stated adiabatic, no-consumption assumptions. Heat loss would lengthen the time; reactant consumption, neglected here, would also lengthen it or prevent runaway if the reactant were exhausted first.

Response time at 393 K under adiabatic conditions

Symbols
  • Absolute temperature at the stated starting point, denoted T0T_0 (kelvin, K): T0=393 KT_0 = 393\ \mathrm{K}.

  • Thermal inertia factor, denoted ϕ\phi (dimensionless), defined in Section 4.

All quantities above are the quantities supplied in the problem. No other measured quantity is supplied.

1. Quantity that can be calculated from the supplied values
1.1 Initial self-heating rate

Under adiabatic conditions, with no heat loss and with cpc_p treated as constant, the initial rate of temperature rise, denoted dT/dt∣0\left.\mathrm{d}T/\mathrm{d}t\right|_0 (kelvin per second, K/s), is

dTdt∣0=q0cp=5 J/(s⋅kg)2,000 J/(kg⋅K)=0.0025 K/s=0.15 K/min=9.0 K/h.(1)\left.\frac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|_0 = \frac{q_0}{c_p} = \frac{5\ \mathrm{J/(s\cdot kg)}}{2{,}000\ \mathrm{J/(kg\cdot K)}} = 0.0025\ \mathrm{K/s} = 0.15\ \mathrm{K/min} = 9.0\ \mathrm{K/h}. \tag{1}

1.2 Temperature acceleration

For a single reaction whose rate follows the Arrhenius temperature dependence, and with reactant depletion neglected up to the maximum rate, the specific thermal power near T0T_0 is approximated by

q(T)≈q0exp⁡ ⁣[β (T−T0)],β=EaRT02.(2)q(T) \approx q_0 \exp\!\left[\beta\,(T - T_0)\right], \qquad \beta = \frac{E_a}{R T_0^{2}}. \tag{2}

Substitution gives

β=100,000 J/mol8.314 J/(mol⋅K)×(393 K)2=0.0779 K−1,1β=12.8 K.\beta = \frac{100{,}000\ \mathrm{J/mol}} {8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)} \times (393\ \mathrm{K})^{2}} = 0.0779\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}, \qquad \frac{1}{\beta} = 12.8\ \mathrm{K}.

The quantity 1/β=12.8 K1/\beta = 12.8\ \mathrm{K} is the temperature rise over which the thermal power increases by a factor of ee (approximately 2.72) in this approximation.

1.3 Time to maximum rate, nominal values

Integration of dT/dt=(q0/cp)exp⁡[β(T−T0)]\mathrm{d}T/\mathrm{d}t = (q_0/c_p)\exp[\beta (T-T_0)] from T0T_0 to the runaway limit gives the standard adiabatic approximation

TMRad≈1(q0/cp) β=cp R T02q0 Ea.(3)\mathrm{TMR_{ad}} \approx \frac{1}{(q_0/c_p)\,\beta} = \frac{c_p\,R\,T_0^{2}}{q_0\,E_a}. \tag{3}

Dimensional check: [J/(kg⋅K)][J/(mol⋅K)][K2][\mathrm{J/(kg\cdot K)}][\mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}][\mathrm{K^2}] divided by [J/(s⋅kg)][J/mol][\mathrm{J/(s\cdot kg)}][\mathrm{J/mol}] gives seconds, s.

Numerical substitution gives

TMRad≈2,000×8.314×39325×100,000 s=5,136 s≈85.6 min≈1.43 h.\mathrm{TMR_{ad}} \approx \frac{2{,}000 \times 8.314 \times 393^{2}} {5 \times 100{,}000}\ \mathrm{s} = 5{,}136\ \mathrm{s} \approx 85.6\ \mathrm{min} \approx 1.43\ \mathrm{h}.

This is the response time after the reacting mass reaches 393 K that follows from the supplied nominal values: approximately 1.4 h, on the assumptions in Section 5. It is the time scale for thermal acceleration, not a guaranteed safe handling time; a usable response time in practice must be shorter, by a margin set by the application.

2. Combined worst case: not calculable from the supplied data

A combined worst-case value cannot be given numerically, and no numerical worst-case value is stated here, for a stated reason: the problem supplies one value for each of q0q_0, cpc_p, EaE_a and T0T_0 and supplies no range, tolerance, uncertainty, detection limit, or replicate scatter for any of them. A combined worst case is a combination of the adverse ends of those ranges. With no ranges, the adverse ends do not exist in the data, and assigning any (for example a percentage allowance on any input) would be an invented input, not a calculation from the data.

The direction of the adverse end of each input, and the way the inputs combine, do follow from Eq. (3). The shortest TMRad\mathrm{TMR_{ad}}, which is the adverse direction for response time, results from:

  • the highest q0q_0 (thermal power at 393 K);
  • the lowest cpc_p;
  • the highest EaE_a, at the stated fixed q0q_0 at 393 K, because a higher EaE_a gives a steeper temperature acceleration, i.e. a larger β\beta in Eq. (2);
  • the lowest T0T_0 in the factor T02T_0^{2} in Eq. (3), for a mass whose thermal power at its own starting temperature is the stated q0q_0.

In fractional form, for adverse-end values denoted by the subscripts max and min,

TMRad,worst=TMRad,nominal×cp,min⁡cp,nominal×q0,nominalq0,max⁡×Ea,nominalEa,max⁡×(T0,min⁡T0,nominal)2,\mathrm{TMR_{ad,worst}} = \mathrm{TMR_{ad,nominal}} \times \frac{c_{p,\min}}{c_{p,\mathrm{nominal}}} \times \frac{q_{0,\mathrm{nominal}}}{q_{0,\max}} \times \frac{E_{a,\mathrm{nominal}}}{E_{a,\max}} \times \left(\frac{T_{0,\min}}{T_{0,\mathrm{nominal}}}\right)^{2},

subject also to the thermal inertia correction in Section 4, which can only shorten the value further. Each adverse factor is at or below 1, so the combined worst case is at or below 1.43 h. Its numerical value requires the missing input ranges. Until those ranges are supplied, 1.43 h must be reported as a nominal estimate, not as a worst case and not as a conservative bound.

3. Calorimetric basis

The calorimetric basis is not stated in the supplied data, and none is claimed here.

The supplied data do not state:

  • the instrument or method (for example differential scanning calorimetry, accelerating rate calorimetry, or another calorimeter);
  • the sample mass, the sample composition, or the mass to which the unit kilogram in q0q_0 refers (reacting mass, total contents, or sample as loaded);
  • whether q0q_0 at 393 K was measured directly at 393 K, interpolated, or extrapolated from measurements at other temperatures;
  • the temperature, conversion, or ageing state of the sample when q0q_0 was obtained.

Accordingly q0=5 W/kgq_0 = 5\ \mathrm{W/kg} is used here exactly as given — a specific thermal power at 393 K — with no instrument, sample, or measurement basis attributed to it.

4. Thermal inertia correction

No numerical thermal inertia correction can be applied, because no value of ϕ\phi is supplied and none of the quantities needed to calculate ϕ\phi (container mass, container specific heat capacity, sample mass, sample specific heat capacity) is supplied.

The definition and the direction of the correction are as follows. The factor ϕ\phi is the ratio of the total heat capacity of sample plus container to the heat capacity of the sample alone; ϕ=1\phi = 1 is the ideal adiabatic limit for the sample alone, and ϕ>1\phi > 1 for a real container that absorbs part of the heat released. Heat absorbed by a container lowers the temperature rise observed in a calorimeter, so:

  • if the stated q0q_0 is an uncorrected value observed in a container, the sample-only adiabatic thermal power is ϕ q0\phi\, q_0, and the sample-only time to maximum rate is TMRad\mathrm{TMR_{ad}} from Eq. (3) divided by ϕ\phi, i.e. shorter than 1.43 h;
  • if the stated q0q_0 has already been corrected to ϕ=1\phi = 1, no further division applies, and applying one would double-count the correction.

The supplied data do not state which of these two cases holds. The value 1.43 h is therefore the value for the data as stated, with the thermal inertia status unresolved; it is not a ϕ\phi-corrected value and it is not presented as one.

5. Gas generation

Gas generation was not reported in the supplied data, and no gas generation result is stated here.

No pressure, rate of pressure rise, gas volume, amount of gas per kilogram, or gas composition is supplied. The calculation in Section 1 is thermal only: it uses a thermal power, a heat capacity, and an activation energy. It gives a time to maximum temperature rate. It gives no time to maximum pressure rate, no maximum pressure, and no venting or containment load. A system that generates gas can reach a pressure limit before, or independently of, the thermal maximum rate, so the thermal value above does not by itself characterise the hazard of a closed or vented system.

6. Assumptions behind the nominal value

The nominal value in Section 1 rests on all of the following. Where an assumption is not supported by the supplied data, that is stated.

  1. Adiabatic conditions: no heat loss to the surroundings over the interval calculated.
  2. One reaction with Arrhenius temperature dependence over the interval from 393 K to the maximum rate.
  3. Reactant depletion neglected up to the maximum rate (the exponential approximation of Eq. (2)); appreciable depletion lengthens the time to a finite maximum rate.
  4. cpc_p constant at 2,000 J/(kg·K) over the interval, and no heat absorbed by a phase change.
  5. Uniform temperature throughout the reacting mass; no internal temperature gradient or heat-transfer limit.
  6. q0q_0 applies to the same mass, composition, and conversion state whose response time is required, at 393 K.
7. Result
  • Nominal time to maximum rate from 393 K, from the supplied values: TMRad≈5.1×103 s≈86 min≈1.43 h\mathrm{TMR_{ad}} \approx 5.1\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{s} \approx 86\ \mathrm{min} \approx 1.43\ \mathrm{h}.
  • Combined worst case: not numerically determinable from the supplied data, because no input ranges are given; it is at or below 1.43 h, by the factor expression in Section 2 and, if applicable, division by ϕ\phi as in Section 4.
  • Calorimetric basis: not stated in the supplied data; none claimed.
  • Thermal inertia correction: not applicable numerically; no ϕ\phi value or container data supplied, and the correction status of q0q_0 is not stated.

Response without defensive prompt

Ground-Level Centreline Concentration at 500 m Downwind — Gaussian Plume Estimate

Symbols and given values
  • CC is the ground-level centreline concentration, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg m−3\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}).
  • QQ is the continuous release rate, in kilograms per second (kg s−1\mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}); Q=1 kg s−1Q = 1\ \mathrm{kg\,s^{-1}}.
  • uu is the wind speed, in metres per second (m s−1\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}); u=3 m s−1u = 3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.
  • xx is the downwind distance from the source, in metres (m\mathrm{m}); x=500 mx = 500\ \mathrm{m}.
  • π\pi is the mathematical constant pi; π≈3.1416\pi \approx 3.1416.
  • σy\sigma_y is the lateral (crosswind) dispersion coefficient at distance xx, in metres (m\mathrm{m}).
  • σz\sigma_z is the vertical dispersion coefficient at distance xx, in metres (m\mathrm{m}).

The relation supplied in the problem is

C=Qπ u σy σz.C = \frac{Q}{\pi\, u\, \sigma_y\, \sigma_z}.

This form corresponds to a release at ground level, or to a release whose effective height is neglected, with total reflection at the ground. No exponential term for an elevated source appears in the supplied relation.

Information not supplied, and the assumption adopted

Neither σy\sigma_y nor σz\sigma_z is given, and no atmospheric stability class, surface type, or averaging time is stated. The concentration therefore has no unique numerical value from the stated data alone: σy\sigma_y and σz\sigma_z at a given xx depend principally on atmospheric stability.

A conventional baseline estimate is made under the following stated assumptions:

  1. Pasquill stability class D (neutral stability), the standard default in the absence of insolation or night-time cloud information.
  2. Open-country terrain.
  3. σy\sigma_y and σz\sigma_z evaluated from the Briggs (1973) dispersion formulae, which are algebraic fits to the Pasquill–Gifford dispersion curves.
  4. Steady, continuous release, flat terrain, no chemical reaction, deposition, plume rise, or building effects, and a wind direction that carries the plume centreline over the receptor.

The sensitivity of the result to the stability assumption is quantified in the final section.

Dispersion coefficients at x=500 mx = 500\ \mathrm{m}, class D

For stability class D over open country, the Briggs formulae are

σy=0.08 x(1+0.0001 x)1/2,σz=0.06 x(1+0.0015 x)1/2,\sigma_y = \frac{0.08\,x}{\left(1 + 0.0001\,x\right)^{1/2}}, \qquad \sigma_z = \frac{0.06\,x}{\left(1 + 0.0015\,x\right)^{1/2}},

where xx, σy\sigma_y, and σz\sigma_z are all in metres (m\mathrm{m}), and the numerical coefficients and the coefficients 0.0001 m−10.0001\ \mathrm{m^{-1}} and 0.0015 m−10.0015\ \mathrm{m^{-1}} inside the parentheses are the empirical constants of those formulae.

Substitution of x=500 mx = 500\ \mathrm{m} gives

σy=0.08×500(1+0.0001×500)1/2=40(1.05)1/2=401.025≈39 m,\sigma_y = \frac{0.08 \times 500}{\left(1 + 0.0001 \times 500\right)^{1/2}} = \frac{40}{(1.05)^{1/2}} = \frac{40}{1.025} \approx 39\ \mathrm{m},

σz=0.06×500(1+0.0015×500)1/2=30(1.75)1/2=301.323≈23 m.\sigma_z = \frac{0.06 \times 500}{\left(1 + 0.0015 \times 500\right)^{1/2}} = \frac{30}{(1.75)^{1/2}} = \frac{30}{1.323} \approx 23\ \mathrm{m}.

Result

Under neutral (class D) stability over open country, the estimated ground-level centreline concentration at 500 m500\ \mathrm{m} downwind is approximately

Sensitivity to atmospheric stability

Repeating the same calculation with the Briggs open-country formulae for the other Pasquill stability classes, with QQ, uu, and xx unchanged, gives:

Pasquill stability class σy\sigma_y (m) σz\sigma_z (m) CC (mg m−3\mathrm{mg\,m^{-3}})
A (very unstable) 107 100 9.9
B (unstable) 78 60 23
C (slightly unstable) 54 38 52
D (neutral) 39 23 120
E (stable) 29 13 280
F (very stable) 20 7.0 780

The concentration varies by a factor of about 80 across the stability range, principally because σz\sigma_z is strongly suppressed under stable conditions. The class D value of about 120 mg m−3120\ \mathrm{mg\,m^{-3}} is therefore a conditional estimate, not a value determined by QQ, uu, and xx alone. If a stability class, measured values of σy\sigma_y and σz\sigma_z, an urban surface, or a non-zero effective release height were specified, the estimate would change accordingly; an elevated release in particular would reduce the ground-level value through the exponential height term absent from the supplied relation.

Such extrapolated distances must not be used without a model that includes the mixing layer.

Governing case

Class F at u=1 m s−1u = 1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} governs. It gives both the highest concentration at 500 m500\ \mathrm{m}, 2.3×10−3 kg m−32.3 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}} (2,300 mg m−32{,}300\ \mathrm{mg\,m^{-3}}), about 100 times the class B value at u=3 m s−1u = 3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}, and the longest distance to the reference concentration, about 3.4 km3.4\ \mathrm{km}.

The reason is in the relation itself. Stable stratification (class F) suppresses vertical and crosswind turbulence, so σy\sigma_y and σz\sigma_z are the smallest of the three classes (20 m20\ \mathrm{m} and 7.0 m7.0\ \mathrm{m} at 500 m500\ \mathrm{m}, against 78 m78\ \mathrm{m} and 60 m60\ \mathrm{m} for class B); the released material is diluted into a much smaller plume cross-section. Low wind speed acts in the same direction through the 1/u1/u factor, giving a further factor of 3 relative to u=3 m s−1u = 3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}, and also generates less mechanical turbulence. The two effects multiply.

Two qualifications apply to the governing case. First, class F at low wind speed is a meteorologically consistent combination (clear night, weak wind), whereas class B at u=1 m s−1u = 1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} is rarely consistent, because class B requires strong solar heating, which is normally accompanied by more wind and mixing; the B, u=1 m s−1u = 1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} entry is a sensitivity case, not a likely weather state. Second, the steady Gaussian plume model is least reliable exactly in the governing conditions: at u=1 m s−1u = 1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} in stable air the plume meanders, wind direction is poorly defined, and short-term centreline concentrations vary widely about the calculated mean. Class F at u=1 m s−1u = 1\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} is therefore the correct screening and design case, with an uncertainty of at least a factor of 2 to 3 on concentration and a correspondingly large uncertainty on distance.

Process model

The process is self-regulating and is represented by a first-order-plus-dead-time model:

Internal-model-control tuning for a proportional–integral controller

For a first-order-plus-dead-time process, the internal-model-control proportional–integral tuning used here is:

Kc=1Kp×τθ+θcK_c = \frac{1}{K_p} \times \frac{\tau}{\theta + \theta_c}

τI=τ\tau_I = \tau

The first relation is the internal-model-control gain stated in the problem. The second relation sets the integral time equal to the process time constant, so that the controller integral term cancels the process lag in the internal-model-control design.

θ+θc=5 s+5 s=10 s\theta + \theta_c = 5\ \mathrm{s} + 5\ \mathrm{s} = 10\ \mathrm{s}

F2. Meter Readings That Do Not Add Up

Response without defensive prompt

Data reconciliation and gross-error test for a two-feed, one-product unit

1. Data and definitions

All flows are in the same flow units.

The measured feed flows are denoted F1,mF_{1,m} and F2,mF_{2,m} (flow units), the measured product flow is denoted PmP_m (flow units), and the reconciled (balance-satisfying) values are denoted F1F_1, F2F_2, and PP (flow units):

  • F1,m=100F_{1,m} = 100
  • F2,m=50F_{2,m} = 50
  • Pm=140P_m = 140

Each meter standard deviation is denoted σ\sigma (flow units) and is given as 2%2\% of that meter's reading. The individual standard deviations are denoted σ1\sigma_1, σ2\sigma_2, and σP\sigma_P (flow units) for feed meter 1, feed meter 2, and the product meter respectively:

  • σ1=0.02×100=2.00\sigma_1 = 0.02 \times 100 = 2.00
  • σ2=0.02×50=1.00\sigma_2 = 0.02 \times 50 = 1.00
  • σP=0.02×140=2.80\sigma_P = 0.02 \times 140 = 2.80

The meter errors are taken as independent and normally distributed, which is the standard assumption behind the 2%2\% figures. No other error source (a leak, an unmeasured stream, or a biased meter) is included at this stage; Section 4 tests whether that assumption is tenable.

2. The imbalance and its own uncertainty

At steady state with no inventory change, the overall balance is

F1+F2−P=0F_1 + F_2 - P = 0

The measured imbalance, denoted rr (flow units), is

r=F1,m+F2,m−Pm=100+50−140=10r = F_{1,m} + F_{2,m} - P_m = 100 + 50 - 140 = 10

The feeds read 10 flow units high relative to the product — that is, 6.7%6.7\% of the total measured feed of 150 flow units, or 7.1%7.1\% of the measured product.

Because the three meter errors are independent, the variance of a sum or difference is the sum of the variances. The variance of the imbalance is denoted σr2\sigma_r^{2} (flow units squared), and its standard deviation is denoted σr\sigma_r (flow units):

σr2=σ12+σ22+σP2=2.002+1.002+2.802=4.00+1.00+7.84=12.84\sigma_r^{2} = \sigma_1^{2} + \sigma_2^{2} + \sigma_P^{2} = 2.00^{2} + 1.00^{2} + 2.80^{2} = 4.00 + 1.00 + 7.84 = 12.84

σr=12.84=3.58\sigma_r = \sqrt{12.84} = 3.58

So random meter error alone would be expected to produce an imbalance of roughly ±3.6\pm 3.6 flow units (1σr1\sigma_r), and about ±7.0\pm 7.0 flow units at the 95%95\% level (1.96 σr=7.021.96\,\sigma_r = 7.02). The observed imbalance of 1010 flow units is larger than that.

3. Significance test: is the imbalance only random error?

The standardised imbalance, denoted zz (dimensionless), is

z=rσr=103.58=2.79z = \frac{r}{\sigma_r} = \frac{10}{3.58} = 2.79

Equivalently, the chi-squared statistic with one degree of freedom, denoted χ2\chi^{2} (dimensionless), is

χ2=z2=r2σr2=10012.84=7.79\chi^{2} = z^{2} = \frac{r^{2}}{\sigma_r^{2}} = \frac{100}{12.84} = 7.79

The 95%95\% critical values are 1.961.96 for ∣z∣|z| and 3.843.84 for χ2\chi^{2} with one degree of freedom. The observed values, 2.792.79 and 7.797.79, exceed both. The two-sided probability of a value at least this large under purely random error is about 0.0050.005.

Result of the test: the imbalance is statistically significant. An imbalance of 10 flow units is not plausibly explained by the stated 2%2\% random meter errors alone. At least one of the following holds:

  1. one (or more) of the meters carries a systematic (gross) error larger than its stated random precision;
  2. the true meter standard deviations are larger than 2%2\% of reading;
  3. the flowsheet is incomplete — for example a leak, a vent, a bypass, or another unmeasured stream of about 10 flow units; or
  4. the unit was not exactly at steady state, so inventory changed during the measurement period.

Reconciliation (Section 4) is still carried out, because it gives the balance-consistent flows under the stated error model, but its output must be read with the finding above in mind: if a gross error or a missing stream is present, the reconciled values spread that error over all three meters and do not identify the true flows.

4. Reconciliation: weighted least squares
4.1 Method

Reconciliation chooses F1F_1, F2F_2, and PP to satisfy the balance exactly while moving each measurement as little as possible in units of its own standard deviation. The objective function, denoted JJ (dimensionless), is

J=(F1−F1,mσ1)2+(F2−F2,mσ2)2+(P−PmσP)2J = \left(\frac{F_1 - F_{1,m}}{\sigma_1}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{F_2 - F_{2,m}}{\sigma_2}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{P - P_m}{\sigma_P}\right)^{2}

minimised subject to F1+F2−P=0F_1 + F_2 - P = 0.

For a single linear balance, minimisation with a Lagrange multiplier gives a closed form. The correction applied to each measurement is proportional to that meter's variance times the sign with which the stream enters the balance (+1+1 for a feed, −1-1 for the product), scaled by the common factor r/σr2r / \sigma_r^{2}:

  • F1=F1,m−σ12 r/σr2F_1 = F_{1,m} - \sigma_1^{2}\, r / \sigma_r^{2}
  • F2=F2,m−σ22 r/σr2F_2 = F_{2,m} - \sigma_2^{2}\, r / \sigma_r^{2}
  • P=Pm+σP2 r/σr2P = P_m + \sigma_P^{2}\, r / \sigma_r^{2}

The common factor is r/σr2=10/12.84=0.7788r / \sigma_r^{2} = 10 / 12.84 = 0.7788 (per flow unit). The imprecise (high-variance) meters are moved the most; the precise meters are moved the least.

4.2 Calculation
  • F1=100−4.00×0.7788=100−3.12=96.88F_1 = 100 - 4.00 \times 0.7788 = 100 - 3.12 = 96.88
  • F2=50−1.00×0.7788=50−0.78=49.22F_2 = 50 - 1.00 \times 0.7788 = 50 - 0.78 = 49.22
  • P=140+7.84×0.7788=140+6.11=146.11P = 140 + 7.84 \times 0.7788 = 140 + 6.11 = 146.11
Stream Measured (flow units) Meter σ\sigma (flow units) Correction (flow units) Correction in σ\sigma units Reconciled (flow units)
Feed 1 100 2.00 −3.12-3.12 −1.56-1.56 96.88
Feed 2 50 1.00 −0.78-0.78 −0.78-0.78 49.22
Product 140 2.80 +6.11+6.11 +2.18+2.18 146.11

Balance check: 96.88+49.22−146.11=0.0096.88 + 49.22 - 146.11 = 0.00. The balance closes exactly, as required.

The corrections are also distributed in proportion to the variance shares of the imbalance: feed 1 contributes 4.00/12.84=31%4.00/12.84 = 31\%, feed 2 contributes 1.00/12.84=8%1.00/12.84 = 8\%, and the product contributes 7.84/12.84=61%7.84/12.84 = 61\% of σr2\sigma_r^{2}, so the product meter absorbs 61%61\% of the imbalance.

4.3 Uncertainty of the reconciled values

Imposing the balance reduces the uncertainty of each flow. The standard deviations of the reconciled values, computed from the reconciled variance–covariance matrix (the measurement variance matrix minus the part removed by the constraint), are approximately:

  • F1=96.9±1.7F_1 = 96.9 \pm 1.7 flow units
  • F2=49.2±1.0F_2 = 49.2 \pm 1.0 flow units
  • P=146.1±1.7P = 146.1 \pm 1.7 flow units

(each ±\pm figure is one standard deviation). The product standard deviation falls the most, from 2.802.80 to 1.751.75, because the balance ties it to the two more precise feed meters.

5. Interpretation
  1. The data are internally inconsistent at the stated precision. The imbalance of 10 flow units is 2.792.79 times its own standard deviation of 3.583.58 flow units (χ2=7.79\chi^{2} = 7.79 with one degree of freedom, probability about 0.0050.005 under random error alone). The 2%2\% random-error model by itself does not account for the data; a gross error, an unmeasured stream of about 10 flow units, or non-steady operation should be investigated before the meters are trusted individually.
  2. Balance-consistent flows, if the error model is accepted, are F1=96.9F_1 = 96.9, F2=49.2F_2 = 49.2, and P=146.1P = 146.1 flow units. Both feeds are adjusted downward and the product upward, with the largest adjustment (+6.1+6.1 flow units, +2.18σP+2.18\sigma_P) falling on the product meter, the least precise of the three.
  3. The product meter is the prime suspect, but is not proven to be at fault. Its standardised adjustment, 2.182.18, is the largest of the three, and it carries 61%61\% of the imbalance variance, so a single gross error in the product meter is the most economical single-meter explanation. With only one balance equation, however, the test cannot separate a product-meter bias from a feed-meter bias or from a real unmeasured loss; that requires independent information (meter calibration, a check meter, or a component balance).

F3. Corrosion and Remaining Life

Response without defensive prompt

Remaining Life of a Corroding Vessel

Given data
  • tmeasuredt_{\mathrm{measured}}, the measured wall thickness, in millimetres (mm): tmeasured=12 mmt_{\mathrm{measured}} = 12\ \mathrm{mm}
  • tmint_{\mathrm{min}}, the minimum required wall thickness, in millimetres (mm): tmin=8 mmt_{\mathrm{min}} = 8\ \mathrm{mm}
  • rr, the general corrosion rate, in millimetres per year (mm/year): r=0.15 mm/yearr = 0.15\ \mathrm{mm/year}
Quantities to be determined
  • Δt\Delta t, the available metal loss, in millimetres (mm): the amount of wall thickness that can be lost by corrosion before the minimum required wall thickness is reached.
  • LL, the remaining life, in years (year): the time for corrosion at the rate rr to consume the available metal loss Δt\Delta t.
Method

The available metal loss Δt\Delta t is the difference between the measured wall thickness tmeasuredt_{\mathrm{measured}} and the minimum required wall thickness tmint_{\mathrm{min}}:

Δt=tmeasured−tmin\Delta t = t_{\mathrm{measured}} - t_{\mathrm{min}}

At a constant general corrosion rate rr, the wall thickness decreases linearly with time. The remaining life LL is therefore the available metal loss Δt\Delta t divided by the corrosion rate rr:

L=ΔtrL = \frac{\Delta t}{r}

Calculation

Available metal loss Δt\Delta t:

Δt=12 mm−8 mm=4 mm\Delta t = 12\ \mathrm{mm} - 8\ \mathrm{mm} = 4\ \mathrm{mm}

Remaining life LL:

L=4 mm0.15 mm/year=26.666… yearL = \frac{4\ \mathrm{mm}}{0.15\ \mathrm{mm/year}} = 26.666\ldots\ \mathrm{year}

Dimensional check: millimetres (mm) divided by millimetres per year (mm/year) gives years (year), as required for LL.

Result

The remaining life LL is approximately 26.726.7 years, i.e. about 2727 years if rounded to the nearest whole year, and 2626 years if rounded down conservatively to a whole number of years.

Scope and assumptions
  1. The corrosion is general (uniform) corrosion, so a single rate rr describes metal loss over the vessel wall. Localised corrosion, pitting, cracking, erosion, or other damage mechanisms are not included.
  2. The corrosion rate rr remains constant at 0.15 mm/year0.15\ \mathrm{mm/year} over the remaining life LL.
  3. The minimum required wall thickness tmin=8 mmt_{\mathrm{min}} = 8\ \mathrm{mm} is taken as given; no additional corrosion allowance is added to it.
  4. The measured wall thickness tmeasured=12 mmt_{\mathrm{measured}} = 12\ \mathrm{mm} is taken as the current, representative thickness at the location governing the remaining life.
Response with defensive prompt

Remaining Life of a Vessel with General Corrosion

Symbols and given data
  • tmeast_{\mathrm{meas}} (millimetres, mm): measured wall thickness = 12 mm12\ \mathrm{mm}
  • tmint_{\mathrm{min}} (millimetres, mm): minimum required thickness = 8 mm8\ \mathrm{mm}
  • Δt\Delta t (millimetres, mm): available metal loss, defined as tmeas−tmint_{\mathrm{meas}} - t_{\mathrm{min}}
  • rr (millimetres per year, mm/year): general (uniform) corrosion rate = 0.15 mm/year0.15\ \mathrm{mm/year}
  • RLRL (years): remaining life
Nominal calculation

Available metal loss:

Δt=tmeas−tmin=12 mm−8 mm=4 mm\Delta t = t_{\mathrm{meas}} - t_{\mathrm{min}} = 12\ \mathrm{mm} - 8\ \mathrm{mm} = 4\ \mathrm{mm}

Remaining life for uniform loss at a constant rate:

RL=Δtr=4 mm0.15 mm/year=26.7 yearsRL = \frac{\Delta t}{r} = \frac{4\ \mathrm{mm}}{0.15\ \mathrm{mm/year}} = 26.7\ \mathrm{years}

Nominal remaining life: approximately 27 years, under the assumptions stated below.

Assumptions in this calculation:

  1. Loss is uniform over the governing area of wall.
  2. rr stays constant at 0.15 mm/year0.15\ \mathrm{mm/year} — no change in fluid, temperature, flow, coating, inhibition, or operating regime.
  3. The measured 12 mm12\ \mathrm{mm} is accurate and representative of the thinnest governing location.
  4. tmin=8 mmt_{\mathrm{min}} = 8\ \mathrm{mm} is correct for the design pressure, temperature, diameter, material allowable stress, weld joint efficiency, and any structural loads.
  5. Retirement or repair occurs at tmint_{\mathrm{min}}.
Remaining life at both ends of the rate range

No rate range is supplied in the problem. Only a single value, r=0.15 mm/yearr = 0.15\ \mathrm{mm/year}, is given. A numerical range for RLRL therefore cannot be derived from the given data without inventing rates.

With the single supplied rate, the two ends coincide:

Case Rate rr (mm/year) RL=Δt/rRL = \Delta t / r (years)
Low-rate end 0.15 26.7
High-rate end 0.15 26.7

Once an item-specific rate interval is measured, with rlowr_{\mathrm{low}} (mm/year) defined as the lowest credible rate and rhighr_{\mathrm{high}} (mm/year) defined as the highest credible rate at the governing location, the ends are:

RLmax=4 mmrlow,RLmin=4 mmrhighRL_{\mathrm{max}} = \frac{4\ \mathrm{mm}}{r_{\mathrm{low}}}, \qquad RL_{\mathrm{min}} = \frac{4\ \mathrm{mm}}{r_{\mathrm{high}}}

RLRL falls as rr rises, so the high-rate end controls planning.

Sensitivity only — the following values are arithmetic illustrations, not estimates for this vessel:

Illustrative rr (mm/year) 0.075 0.15 0.30
RLRL (years) 53.3 26.7 13.3

A factor of two error or change in rr changes RLRL by a factor of two. This is why a single quoted general rate, with no history or scatter, does not support a narrow remaining-life range.

Damage mechanisms

The 26.726.7-year result covers uniform thinning only. Other mechanisms can end service life earlier, and localised attack in particular is not described by a general rate: a pit or groove can penetrate the 4 mm4\ \mathrm{mm} of available metal while the average wall loss is small.

Mechanisms to screen, according to material, fluid, temperature, and geometry:

  • Uniform thinning: carbon dioxide corrosion, hydrogen sulfide corrosion, oxygen corrosion, acid corrosion, atmospheric corrosion, galvanic corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and sulfidation.
  • Localised attack: chloride pitting; crevice corrosion; under-deposit corrosion; microbiologically influenced corrosion; galvanic attack at dissimilar-metal joints; preferential weld and heat-affected-zone attack; corrosion under insulation; corrosion at supports, dead legs, injection points, and liquid-level lines.
  • Flow-related thinning: erosion–corrosion and flow-accelerated corrosion, concentrated at bends, tees, reducers, inlets, and downstream of control valves or other restrictions.
  • Cracking, which can cause failure with little or no wall loss: chloride stress corrosion cracking, caustic stress corrosion cracking, amine stress corrosion cracking, hydrogen-induced cracking and stress-oriented hydrogen-induced cracking, hydrogen embrittlement, and corrosion fatigue.
  • Service-specific attack, if the conditions occur: naphthenic acid corrosion, dew-point corrosion, ammonium bisulfide corrosion, and soil-side corrosion for buried or partly buried parts.

For localised loss, remaining life is governed by the deepest or fastest-growing feature, not by rr. The corresponding quantities are tpitt_{\mathrm{pit}} (mm), defined as the remaining thickness at the deepest measured feature, and rpitr_{\mathrm{pit}} (mm/year), defined as the penetration rate of that feature. Where those are measured:

RLlocal=tpit−tminrpitRL_{\mathrm{local}} = \frac{t_{\mathrm{pit}} - t_{\mathrm{min}}}{r_{\mathrm{pit}}}

Local metal loss also reduces load-bearing area, so a fitness-for-service assessment of the affected area (for example to API 579-1/ASME FFS-1) may set a limit below the simple thickness criterion. No value of RLlocalRL_{\mathrm{local}} can be computed from the data given.

Item-specific inspection data required to narrow the range
  1. Thickness history at fixed locations: dated ultrasonic thickness readings at marked thickness monitoring locations, with the original nominal thickness, so that a long-term rate (from the earliest reading) and a short-term rate (from the last two readings) can both be calculated for each location. The highest credible location rate, not the vessel average, sets the high-rate end.
  2. Thickness coverage, not a single point: a grid or scan (manual ultrasonic grid, encoded ultrasonic C-scan, or phased-array ultrasonic testing) covering shell courses, heads, nozzles, welds, bends, dead legs, injection and mixing points, liquid-level lines, and low points, with the minimum reading and its location in each zone.
  3. Measurement quality: instrument and probe, calibration record, surface condition and temperature, reading repeatability, and the stated measurement uncertainty in mm, so that uncertainty can be carried into Δt\Delta t.
  4. Localised-attack data: maximum pit depth, pit diameter and density, remaining thickness at the deepest pits, groove length and depth at welds, and profile or scan records that distinguish pitting, grooving, and general roughening from uniform loss.
  5. Cracking inspection where the material and fluid make cracking credible: wet fluorescent magnetic particle, liquid penetrant, alternating current field measurement, phased-array ultrasonic testing, or time-of-flight diffraction results for welds and high-stress areas, with any crack length and depth recorded.
  6. Basis of tmint_{\mathrm{min}}: design code and edition, design pressure and temperature, internal diameter, material specification and allowable stress, weld joint efficiency, corrosion allowance in the original design, and whether structural, wind, seismic, nozzle, or support loads add to the required thickness.
  7. Process data for the period covered by the thickness history: fluid composition (chloride, pH, dissolved oxygen, carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulfide, water fraction, sulfur, total acid number), operating temperature and pressure, flow velocity and solids content, coating and insulation condition, corrosion inhibitor and biocide dosing records, and any process changes or excursions.
  8. Corrosion monitoring records: coupon mass-loss results, electrical resistance or linear polarisation resistance probe trends, and process iron counts, each with location and exposure period, as an independent check on rr.
  9. History of the item and of similar items: previous inspection reports, repairs and alterations, leaks or failures, and rates measured on vessels in the same service, which show whether 0.15 mm/year0.15\ \mathrm{mm/year} is typical, low, or high for this duty.
  10. Access and internal condition: internal visual inspection findings, deposit and scale samples, coating breakdown area, and the state of insulation and its cladding where corrosion under insulation is possible.

With items 1–4, a defensible rlowr_{\mathrm{low}} and rhighr_{\mathrm{high}} and a localised remaining life can be stated. Without them, only the nominal uniform-loss value can be stated.

Conclusion

Remaining life on general corrosion alone is 4 mm/0.15 mm/year=26.74\ \mathrm{mm} / 0.15\ \mathrm{mm/year} = 26.7 years. No wider numerical range is supported by the data supplied: the low-rate and high-rate ends are both 26.726.7 years until item-specific thickness history, localised-attack measurements, and process records provide a measured rate range. That figure is not a safe inspection interval; the next inspection must be set well before tmint_{\mathrm{min}} is approached, using the governing local rate and the applicable inspection code, and localised attack or cracking can require action much sooner.

G1. Cost of Building a Plant

Response without defensive prompt

Capital Cost Estimate by Capacity Scaling

Given data
  • Known capital cost, denoted C1C_1 (unit: million United States dollars, USD): C1=10C_1 = 10 million USD.
  • Known capacity, denoted Q1Q_1 (unit: kilotonnes per year, kt yr−1^{-1}; 1 kilotonne, kt, equals 1,000 tonnes): Q1=50Q_1 = 50 kt yr−1^{-1}.
  • Required capacity, denoted Q2Q_2 (unit: kt yr−1^{-1}): Q2=100Q_2 = 100 kt yr−1^{-1}.
  • Capacity exponent, denoted nn (dimensionless): n=0.6n = 0.6.

No numerical value is given for a cost index at either date, and no numerical value is given for a location factor at either location. The numerical result below is therefore the capacity-scaled cost on the same year and location basis as C1C_1. The form of the year and location correction is stated in the section "Year and location correction" so that the correction can be applied when those values are supplied.

Method

The capacity-scaling relation, commonly called the six-tenths rule when the exponent nn defined above is 0.6, is

C2=C1(Q2Q1)nC_2 = C_1 \left(\frac{Q_2}{Q_1}\right)^{n}

where C2C_2 denotes the estimated capital cost of the required unit (unit: million USD), and C1C_1, Q1Q_1, Q2Q_2, and nn are as defined above.

The relation applies to the same process and to a comparable scope of supply, technology, and design. An exponent nn less than 1 represents economy of scale: cost rises less than in direct proportion to capacity.

Calculation

The capacity ratio, denoted RR (dimensionless), is

R=Q2Q1=100 kt yr−150 kt yr−1=2.00R = \frac{Q_2}{Q_1} = \frac{100\ \text{kt yr}^{-1}}{50\ \text{kt yr}^{-1}} = 2.00

The capacity factor obtained from RR and nn is

Rn=2.000.6=1.516R^{n} = 2.00^{0.6} = 1.516

Hence

C2=10 million USD×1.516=15.16 million USDC_2 = 10\ \text{million USD} \times 1.516 = 15.16\ \text{million USD}

Rounded to three significant figures, consistent with the precision of the given cost and exponent:

C2≈15.2 million USDC_2 \approx 15.2\ \text{million USD}

Year and location correction

In general, a cost transferred to a different year is multiplied by a cost-index ratio, and a cost transferred to a different location is multiplied by a location-factor ratio. The full form is

C2,corrected=C1(Q2Q1)n(I2I1)(F2F1)C_{2,\text{corrected}} = C_1 \left(\frac{Q_2}{Q_1}\right)^{n} \left(\frac{I_2}{I_1}\right) \left(\frac{F_2}{F_1}\right)

where:

  • C2,correctedC_{2,\text{corrected}} denotes the capacity-, year-, and location-corrected capital cost (unit: million USD);
  • I1I_1 denotes a cost index, dimensionless, at the year and for the cost basis of the known unit;
  • I2I_2 denotes the same cost index, dimensionless, at the year required for the estimate;
  • F1F_1 denotes a location factor, dimensionless, for the location of the known unit, expressed relative to a stated reference location;
  • F2F_2 denotes the same location factor, dimensionless, for the location of the required unit, expressed relative to the same reference location as F1F_1.

Because no values of I1I_1, I2I_2, F1F_1, or F2F_2 are supplied in the problem statement, the ratios I2/I1I_2/I_1 and F2/F1F_2/F_1 cannot be evaluated numerically. Setting both ratios to 1 recovers the result above. Any reported final cost for a specific later year and a specific different location must include those two ratios once their values are known; omitting them understates or overstates the transferred cost by the product of the two ratios.

Checks
  • Limiting case: if Q2=Q1Q_2 = Q_1, then R=1R = 1, Rn=1R^{n} = 1, and C2=C1C_2 = C_1, as required.
  • Economy of scale: doubling capacity (R=2R = 2) increases cost by a factor of 1.516, which is less than 2. This is consistent with n=0.6<1n = 0.6 < 1.
  • Units: RR, nn, I2/I1I_2/I_1, and F2/F1F_2/F_1 are dimensionless, so C2C_2 and C2,correctedC_{2,\text{corrected}} carry the same unit as C1C_1, million USD.
Result

The estimated capital cost of the 100 kt yr−1^{-1} unit is approximately 15.2 million USD, on the same year and location basis as the known 10 million USD cost for the 50 kt yr−1^{-1} unit. A cost stated for a different year and location requires multiplication by the cost-index ratio I2/I1I_2/I_1 and the location-factor ratio F2/F1F_2/F_1 defined above, for which no numerical values were given.

  1. Reference year and target year. Neither calendar year is named, and no values of IrefI_{\mathrm{ref}} or ItargetI_{\mathrm{target}} are supplied. No escalation (cost-index) adjustment can be calculated.
  2. Reference location and target location. Neither place is named, and no value of FlocF_{\mathrm{loc}}, and no range Floc,lowF_{\mathrm{loc,low}} to Floc,highF_{\mathrm{loc,high}}, is supplied. No location adjustment can be calculated.
  3. Exponent range. Only the single value n=0.6n = 0.6 is supplied. No process-specific range for nn is supplied. Section 6.1 therefore reports the ends of a published generic range, clearly labelled as generic, and gives the formula for any process-specific range supplied later.
  4. Scope and battery limits of the reference cost. The problem does not state what the 10 million USD covers. Section 7 sets out what can and cannot be said.
  5. Design basis. Feed, product slate, number of trains, maximum single-train or single-item equipment size, materials of construction, design pressure and temperature, and applicable codes are not stated. The scaling result holds only if all of these are the same as for the reference unit and if the 100 kt/y duty is met by one train of the same design rather than by two parallel 50 kt/y trains.
4. Capacity scaling calculation

The capacity-factored ("six-tenths rule") relation is

Cnew=Cref(QnewQref)nFlocItargetIrefC_{\mathrm{new}} = C_{\mathrm{ref}} \left( \frac{Q_{\mathrm{new}}}{Q_{\mathrm{ref}}} \right)^{n} F_{\mathrm{loc}} \frac{I_{\mathrm{target}}}{I_{\mathrm{ref}}}

Because no location factor and no cost-index values were supplied, the only factor that can be evaluated numerically is the capacity factor. Setting Floc=1F_{\mathrm{loc}} = 1 and Itarget/Iref=1I_{\mathrm{target}} / I_{\mathrm{ref}} = 1 in the equation above means "no location or date adjustment applied"; it does not mean the target location and year are in fact the same as the reference location and year.

Step 1 — capacity ratio:

R=QnewQref=100 kt/y50 kt/y=2.00(dimensionless)R = \frac{Q_{\mathrm{new}}}{Q_{\mathrm{ref}}} = \frac{100\ \mathrm{kt/y}}{50\ \mathrm{kt/y}} = 2.00 \quad \text{(dimensionless)}

Step 2 — capacity factor at the given exponent:

Rn=2.000.6=1.516R^{n} = 2.00^{0.6} = 1.516

Step 3 — intermediate scaled cost (reference year, reference location, reference scope):

Cnew=10 million USD×1.516=15.16 million USDC_{\mathrm{new}} = 10\ \text{million USD} \times 1.516 = 15.16\ \text{million USD}

This intermediate value is not the reported result. Section 5 assigns the estimate class and converts this value into the reported range.

A capacity ratio of 2.00 is within the range over which capacity factoring is normally applied, provided the conditions in item 5 of Section 3 hold. If the larger unit needs two parallel trains, the exponent does not apply in this form and the cost would move toward twice the reference cost, i.e. toward 20 million USD on the reference basis, before any other adjustment.

5. Estimate class, standard accuracy range, and base date
5.1 Estimate class

AACE Class 5 (concept screening), under AACE International Recommended Practice 18R-97, Cost Estimate Classification System — As Applied in Engineering, Procurement and Construction for the Process Industries.

Reasons: the level of project definition is effectively 0 % to 2 % (no design information beyond a capacity and a statement that the process is the same), and the method used — capacity factoring from one similar plant — is the method that Recommended Practice 18R-97 lists for Class 5. This estimate is suitable for screening only. It is not suitable for budget authorisation, financing, or a funding decision; those require a Class 3 estimate or better.

5.2 Standard accuracy range

The standard accuracy range for a Class 5 estimate in the process industries is commonly summarised as −50 % to +100 %. In the fuller form given in Recommended Practice 18R-97, the low side varies from −20 % to −50 % and the high side from +30 % to +100 %, depending on project-specific risk. These ranges are typical values, not guarantees, and a project-specific range should come from a risk analysis of the actual project.

The reported range uses the widest standard ends, −50 % and +100 %, applied to the intermediate value of 15.16 million USD from Section 4:

  • Low end: 15.16×(1−0.50)=15.16×0.50=7.5815.16 \times (1 - 0.50) = 15.16 \times 0.50 = 7.58 million USD, reported as 7.6 million USD.
  • High end: 15.16×(1+1.00)=15.16×2.00=30.3115.16 \times (1 + 1.00) = 15.16 \times 2.00 = 30.31 million USD, reported as 30.3 million USD.

Reported range: USD 7.6 million to USD 30.3 million, on the reference basis defined in Section 5.3.

5.3 Base date

The base date of this estimate is the cost date of the reference unit, and that date is not stated in the problem. The range above is therefore expressed in "reference-year USD": dollars of whatever year the 10 million USD reference cost belongs to. No calendar base date can be stated, and no figure in this solution is expressed in dollars of the target year.

To restate the estimate at a target date, the following are required: the reference year, the target year, and values of one named plant cost index at both dates, applied as the ratio Itarget/IrefI_{\mathrm{target}} / I_{\mathrm{ref}}. Until those are supplied, any figure presented as a target-year cost would require an invented escalation factor.

6. Results at both ends of the exponent range and of the location-factor range
6.1 Exponent range

The problem supplies only the single value n=0.6n = 0.6. Published surveys of the capacity exponent for process plant report that nn usually lies between 0.4 and 0.8, with 0.6 as the average value across the chemical industry; the value for a specific process can fall outside that band (values from about 0.4–0.5 are reported for small, highly instrumented plants, and 0.8–0.9 for plants with a large amount of mechanical work or gas compression). The table below therefore uses nlow=0.4n_{\mathrm{low}} = 0.4 and nhigh=0.8n_{\mathrm{high}} = 0.8 as a generic literature range, not a range supplied with the problem and not a range measured for this process. All values are on the reference basis (Floc=1F_{\mathrm{loc}} = 1, Itarget/Iref=1I_{\mathrm{target}} / I_{\mathrm{ref}} = 1), before the Class 5 accuracy range is applied.

Note on combination: the spread from the exponent alone (13.20 to 17.41 million USD) is much narrower than the Class 5 accuracy range (7.6 to 30.3 million USD). The accuracy range is the range to report. The exponent ends and the accuracy ends should not be multiplied together to form a still wider range, because the Class 5 accuracy range already reflects, in part, uncertainty of exactly this kind; multiplying them double-counts it.

6.2 Location-factor range

No location factor, and no location-factor range, was supplied, and neither location was named. There is no standard universal location-factor range that can be substituted: location factors are published for named locations relative to a named base location, for a stated year. End values for a location adjustment therefore cannot be reported as numbers belonging to this estimate. What can be reported is the result at both ends of any range, in a form that gives the number as soon as a range is provided:

  • Lower end: Cnew=15.16×Floc,lowC_{\mathrm{new}} = 15.16 \times F_{\mathrm{loc,low}} million USD.
  • Upper end: Cnew=15.16×Floc,highC_{\mathrm{new}} = 15.16 \times F_{\mathrm{loc,high}} million USD.

with both values still on the reference cost date and still to be combined with the escalation ratio Itarget/IrefI_{\mathrm{target}} / I_{\mathrm{ref}} and the Class 5 accuracy range. For direct use, the table below gives the scaled cost, before the accuracy range is applied, at the given exponent n=0.6n = 0.6 and at the two generic exponent ends of Section 6.1, for a set of location-factor values spanning the values commonly encountered between established industrial locations. 7. Scope and battery limits

The scope of the reference cost is not stated, so the scope of this estimate can only be defined by inheritance: the estimate covers exactly what the reference unit's 10 million USD covered, and excludes exactly what that cost excluded, with the same battery limits. Nothing more specific can be stated without inventing scope.

Concretely, the following are unknown and must be confirmed before this range is used for any decision:

  • Whether the reference cost is an ISBL cost only, or a total installed cost, or a total capital investment including OSBL.
  • Whether it includes offsites and utilities (steam, cooling water, power, water treatment, effluent treatment), tankage and storage, loading facilities, buildings, and site development.
  • Whether it includes engineering, procurement and construction management, construction indirects, spares, catalyst and first chemical fills, commissioning and start-up, owner's costs, land, permits, escalation during construction, interest during construction, working capital, and contingency — and, if contingency is included, at what level.
  • The battery-limit tie-in points: where feed, product, and utility streams cross the unit boundary, and whether the reference unit relied on utilities or storage supplied by an existing site (a common reason a scaled estimate understates a stand-alone unit).
  • Whether the two capacities are stated on the same basis (nameplate or demonstrated rate, feed basis or product basis, and the same operating hours per year). The ratio R=2.00R = 2.00 is valid only if both capacities use the same basis.

Until the reference scope is documented, the range in Section 5.2 must not be compared with estimates of a different scope, and must not be described as a total project cost.

8. What is needed to convert this screening range into a target-year, target-location estimate
  1. The reference year and the target year, with values of a named plant cost index at both dates, giving Itarget/IrefI_{\mathrm{target}} / I_{\mathrm{ref}}.
  2. The reference location and the target location, with a location factor FlocF_{\mathrm{loc}} (or a stated range for it) for the target location relative to the reference location, from a source that states its own base location and year.
  3. A written scope and battery-limit definition for the reference cost (Section 7).
  4. Confirmation of a single train at 100 kt/y, and a process-specific value or range for nn.
  5. Confirmation that technology, feed, product slate, materials of construction, and design standards are unchanged.

With items 1 and 2 supplied, the adjusted intermediate value is 15.16×Floc×(Itarget/Iref)15.16 \times F_{\mathrm{loc}} \times (I_{\mathrm{target}} / I_{\mathrm{ref}}) million USD, and the Class 5 range of −50 % to +100 % is applied to that adjusted value. Supplying those items does not raise the estimate class; only added project definition does that.

9. Summary
  • Method: capacity factoring, Cnew=Cref (Qnew/Qref)nC_{\mathrm{new}} = C_{\mathrm{ref}} \, (Q_{\mathrm{new}}/Q_{\mathrm{ref}})^{n}, with Cref=10C_{\mathrm{ref}} = 10 million USD, Qnew/Qref=2.00Q_{\mathrm{new}}/Q_{\mathrm{ref}} = 2.00, and n=0.6n = 0.6, giving an intermediate value of 15.16 million USD.
  • Estimate class: AACE Class 5, concept screening (Recommended Practice 18R-97); standard accuracy range −50 % to +100 %.
  • Reported result: USD 7.6 million to USD 30.3 million.
  • Base date: the unstated cost date of the reference unit; the result is in reference-year USD, not target-year USD.
  • Location: no adjustment applied, because no location factor or range and no locations were supplied; results at both ends of a location-factor range are given as 15.16×Floc,low15.16 \times F_{\mathrm{loc,low}} and 15.16×Floc,high15.16 \times F_{\mathrm{loc,high}} million USD, with a reading table in Section 6.2.
  • Exponent ends: at the generic literature ends nlow=0.4n_{\mathrm{low}} = 0.4 and nhigh=0.8n_{\mathrm{high}} = 0.8, the scaled cost on the reference basis is 13.20 million USD and 17.41 million USD respectively, before the accuracy range is applied.
  • Scope and battery limits: inherited unchanged from the reference cost, whose scope is not stated in the problem and must be documented before use.

  • Williams, R., Jr. (1947), "Six-tenths factor aids in approximating costs", Chemical Engineering — origin of the capacity exponent relation used in Section 4.

Annual Hot-Utility Cost at a Minimum Temperature Approach of 10 K

Symbols
  • ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (kelvin, K): the minimum temperature approach in heat recovery.
  • QHQ_H (megawatt, MW): the hot-utility duty.

  • topt_{\mathrm{op}} (hours per year, h/year): the annual operating time.
  • EHE_H (megawatt hours per year, MWh/year): the annual hot-utility energy consumption.

Given data
  • ΔTmin⁡=10 K\Delta T_{\min} = 10\ \mathrm{K}
  • QH=20 MWQ_H = 20\ \mathrm{MW}

The value of ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} identifies the heat-recovery condition at which QHQ_H applies. No additional relation between ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} and QHQ_H is needed, because QHQ_H is given directly for that condition.

Calculation
Annual hot-utility energy consumption

EHE_H is QHQ_H multiplied by topt_{\mathrm{op}}:

EH=QH topE_H = Q_H \, t_{\mathrm{op}}

EH=(20 MW)(8,000 h/year)=160,000 MWh/yearE_H = (20\ \mathrm{MW})(8{,}000\ \mathrm{h/year}) = 160{,}000\ \mathrm{MWh/year}

CH=EH pC_H = E_H \, p

CH=(160,000 MWh/year)(25 USD/MWh)=4,000,000 USD/yearC_H = (160{,}000\ \mathrm{MWh/year})(25\ \mathrm{USD/MWh}) = 4{,}000{,}000\ \mathrm{USD/year}
