The annual hot-utility cost at ΔTmin⁡=10 K\Delta T_{\min} = 10\ \mathrm{K} is

CH=4,000,000 USD/yearC_H = 4{,}000{,}000\ \mathrm{USD/year}, i.e. 4.0 million USD per year.

Response with defensive prompt

Annual Hot-Utility Cost at a Minimum Temperature Approach of 10 K

Given data and symbol definitions

Each symbol is defined here, before its first use in a calculation.

  • Minimum temperature approach in heat recovery, ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (kelvin, K): 10 K10\ \mathrm{K} for the case to be costed.
  • Hot-utility duty, QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (megawatt, MW): 20 MW20\ \mathrm{MW} at ΔTmin⁡=10 K\Delta T_{\min} = 10\ \mathrm{K}.
  • Utility price, pp (United States dollars per megawatt hour, USD/MWh): 25 USD/MWh25\ \mathrm{USD/MWh}.
  • Operating time per year, topt_{\mathrm{op}} (hour per year, h/year): 8,000 h/year8{,}000\ \mathrm{h/year}.
  • Annual hot-utility energy consumption, EHE_{\mathrm{H}} (megawatt hour per year, MWh/year): to be calculated.
  • Annual hot-utility cost, CHC_{\mathrm{H}} (United States dollars per year, USD/year): to be calculated.

No other process data are given. In particular, no hot-stream or cold-stream temperatures, flow rates, or heat-capacity flow rates are given; no hot and cold composite curves are given; no heat-exchanger overall heat-transfer coefficient, capital cost, or capital-annualisation factor is given; and no source or date for pp is given beyond the statement of pp itself in the problem.

Calculation

The annual hot-utility energy consumption EHE_{\mathrm{H}} is the hot-utility duty QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} multiplied by the operating time per year topt_{\mathrm{op}}:

EH=QH top=20 MW×8,000 h/year=160,000 MWh/year.E_{\mathrm{H}} = Q_{\mathrm{H}} \, t_{\mathrm{op}} = 20\ \mathrm{MW} \times 8{,}000\ \mathrm{h/year} = 160{,}000\ \mathrm{MWh/year}.

Unit check for EHE_{\mathrm{H}}: MW×h/year=MWh/year\mathrm{MW} \times \mathrm{h/year} = \mathrm{MWh/year}, as required.

The annual hot-utility cost CHC_{\mathrm{H}} is the annual hot-utility energy consumption EHE_{\mathrm{H}} multiplied by the utility price pp:

CH=EH p=160,000 MWh/year×25 USD/MWh=4,000,000 USD/year.C_{\mathrm{H}} = E_{\mathrm{H}} \, p = 160{,}000\ \mathrm{MWh/year} \times 25\ \mathrm{USD/MWh} = 4{,}000{,}000\ \mathrm{USD/year}.

Unit check for CHC_{\mathrm{H}}: MWh/year×USD/MWh=USD/year\mathrm{MWh/year} \times \mathrm{USD/MWh} = \mathrm{USD/year}, as required.

Equivalently, in one step:

CH=QH top p=20×8,000×25=4,000,000 USD/year.C_{\mathrm{H}} = Q_{\mathrm{H}} \, t_{\mathrm{op}} \, p = 20 \times 8{,}000 \times 25 = 4{,}000{,}000\ \mathrm{USD/year}.

Result

At ΔTmin⁡=10 K\Delta T_{\min} = 10\ \mathrm{K}, with QH=20 MWQ_{\mathrm{H}} = 20\ \mathrm{MW}, p=25 USD/MWhp = 25\ \mathrm{USD/MWh}, and top=8,000 h/yeart_{\mathrm{op}} = 8{,}000\ \mathrm{h/year}:

Annual hot-utility cost CH=4.0×106C_{\mathrm{H}} = 4.0 \times 10^{6} USD/year, i.e. USD 4.0 million per year.

This result uses only the data given. It assumes QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} is sustained at 20 MW20\ \mathrm{MW} over the full topt_{\mathrm{op}}, and that pp applies uniformly to all hot-utility energy consumed. No other assumption is made.

Approaches of 5 K and 20 K: what can and cannot be stated

The additional request was for duty, cost, and relative area at ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} values of 5 K5\ \mathrm{K}, 10 K10\ \mathrm{K}, and 20 K20\ \mathrm{K}. The table below states exactly what the given data support.

ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} (K) QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} (MW) CHC_{\mathrm{H}} (USD/year) Relative heat-transfer area
5 Not determinable from the data given Not determinable; CH=QH(5 K)×8,000×25C_{\mathrm{H}} = Q_{\mathrm{H}}(5\ \mathrm{K}) \times 8{,}000 \times 25 once QH(5 K)Q_{\mathrm{H}}(5\ \mathrm{K}) is known Greater than at 10 K, qualitatively; no numerical value determinable
10 20 (given) 4,000,000 (calculated above) 1.00, by definition as the reference case
20 Not determinable from the data given Not determinable; CH=QH(20 K)×8,000×25C_{\mathrm{H}} = Q_{\mathrm{H}}(20\ \mathrm{K}) \times 8{,}000 \times 25 once QH(20 K)Q_{\mathrm{H}}(20\ \mathrm{K}) is known Less than at 10 K, qualitatively; no numerical value determinable

Reasons, stated plainly:

  1. Duty at another approach. QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} as a function of ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} is set by the process hot and cold composite curves, i.e. by the stream temperatures, flow rates, and heat-capacity flow rates, through a pinch (heat-cascade) calculation. One point on that function, QH=20 MWQ_{\mathrm{H}} = 20\ \mathrm{MW} at ΔTmin⁡=10 K\Delta T_{\min} = 10\ \mathrm{K}, does not determine the function at any other ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min}. No linear, proportional, or other interpolation or extrapolation from a single point is justified, so no numerical duty at 5 K5\ \mathrm{K} or 20 K20\ \mathrm{K} is reported. Reporting one would be an invented value, not an estimate from the data given. Qualitatively only, for a fixed process, reducing ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} permits more heat recovery and therefore does not increase QHQ_{\mathrm{H}}, and increasing ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} permits less heat recovery and therefore does not decrease QHQ_{\mathrm{H}}. No magnitude follows from the data given.

  2. Cost at another approach. Cost follows duty through CH=QH top pC_{\mathrm{H}} = Q_{\mathrm{H}} \, t_{\mathrm{op}} \, p. With QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} unknown at 5 K5\ \mathrm{K} and 20 K20\ \mathrm{K}, CHC_{\mathrm{H}} is likewise unknown there. The formula in the table is the complete statement possible.

  3. Relative area. Heat-transfer area depends on the duties of the individual exchangers in the network, on the overall heat-transfer coefficient in each exchanger, and on the logarithmic mean temperature difference in each exchanger. None of these is given, and the network structure itself changes with ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min}. A ratio such as area proportional to 1/ΔTmin⁡1/\Delta T_{\min} would hold only under added assumptions (a single exchanger, constant duty, constant overall coefficient, and a logarithmic mean temperature difference equal to ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min}) that are not stated and do not describe a heat-recovery network. No such numerical ratio is therefore reported. Qualitatively only, a smaller ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} gives smaller driving temperature differences and hence larger area for a given recovered duty, and a larger ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} gives the reverse.

Recommended approach

No ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} is recommended. A recommendation requires a total annual cost comparison: annual utility cost (calculated here for 10 K10\ \mathrm{K} only) plus annualised capital cost of the heat-exchanger network at each candidate ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min}. The capital cost, the annualisation basis, the exchanger costing correlation, and the duties at 5 K5\ \mathrm{K} and 20 K20\ \mathrm{K} are all absent, so the total-cost minimum cannot be located.

On price basis: p=25 USD/MWhp = 25\ \mathrm{USD/MWh} is a value stated in the problem. No source, price date, contract basis, or cost date accompanies it in the problem, so no cost date can be attached to it here, and it must not be presented as a verified current market price. Any later recommendation must state the price actually used, its source, and its date, together with the date basis of the capital costs used with it.

Data required to complete the 5 K and 20 K cases
  • Hot-stream and cold-stream supply and target temperatures, flow rates, and heat-capacity flow rates (or, equivalently, the hot and cold composite curves).
  • A pinch calculation at each candidate ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} to obtain QHQ_{\mathrm{H}} at that approach.
  • Exchanger overall heat-transfer coefficients and a network area calculation at each candidate ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min} for relative area.
  • Exchanger capital costs, an annualisation factor or plant life and discount rate, and a dated utility price, for a total annual cost and hence for any recommended ΔTmin⁡\Delta T_{\min}.

G3. Carbon Emissions per Tonne

Response without defensive prompt

Annual Emissions and Product Carbon Intensity

1. Given data and scope

The following symbols are defined at first use, with units:

  • mCO2m_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = direct carbon dioxide (CO2_2) emission rate of the plant = 100 kt yr−1^{-1}, where kt means kilotonne, 1 kt = 1,000 t and 1 t = 1,000 kg.
  • mCH4m_{\mathrm{CH_4}} = methane (CH4_4) leak rate = 2 kt yr−1^{-1}.
  • mPm_P = production rate of the principal product = 80 kt yr−1^{-1}.
  • GWPH_H = global warming potential over a time horizon HH, in years: the integrated radiative forcing from 1 kg of a gas divided by the integrated radiative forcing from 1 kg of CO2_2 over the same horizon. GWP is dimensionless (kg CO2_2-equivalent per kg of gas, written kg CO2_2e kg−1^{-1}).
  • EE = total annual emission rate, in kt CO2_2e yr−1^{-1}.
  • IPI_P = carbon intensity of the principal product, in t CO2_2e per t of product (numerically equal to kg CO2_2e per kg of product).

Scope limits that the problem statement imposes, and that no calculation can remove:

  1. Only two emission streams are given. No nitrous oxide (N2_2O), fluorinated gases, purchased electricity, purchased heat, upstream fuel and feedstock emissions, downstream transport, or end-of-life emissions are given. The result below is therefore a direct (gate-to-gate, Scope 1) inventory only, not a full life-cycle (cradle-to-grave) footprint. A product footprint reported under ISO 14067 or the GHG Protocol Product Standard would normally add Scope 2 and relevant Scope 3 terms and would be larger.
  2. It is not stated whether the 100 kt CO2_2 is fossil, biogenic, or a mixture, and whether the leaked CH4_4 is fossil (for example natural-gas leakage) or non-fossil (biogenic). That distinction changes the methane GWP100_{100} value (Section 2).
  3. No quantity, mass, energy content, or sales value is given for the co-product. The split of plant emissions between the principal product and the co-product is therefore not uniquely determined by the data. Section 4 gives the unallocated value, the bounding values, and worked allocation examples with the extra data each method requires stated explicitly.
  4. No uncertainty is given for either emission rate. Leaked (fugitive) CH4_4 is in practice the least certain term in such an inventory, because it is usually estimated from emission factors or intermittent surveys rather than measured continuously.
2. Conversion of methane to CO2_2-equivalent emissions

Methane and carbon dioxide are added only after conversion to a common metric. The standard metric in national inventories and corporate reporting is GWP100_{100}, the 100-year GWP.

Values from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Sixth Assessment Report (AR6, 2021, Working Group I, Chapter 7, Table 7.15):

Gas and origin GWP20_{20} GWP100_{100}
CO2_2, any origin 1 1
CH4_4, fossil 82.5 29.8
CH4_4, non-fossil (biogenic) 80.8 27.2

Older values still used in some reporting schemes: GWP100_{100} for CH4_4 = 28 (IPCC Fifth Assessment Report, AR5, without climate–carbon feedbacks for non-fossil CH4_4) and 25 (IPCC Fourth Assessment Report, AR4, used in earlier Kyoto Protocol reporting). The choice of assessment report and of time horizon must be stated with any result, because the total changes materially with that choice (Section 5).

The methane term, ECH4E_{\mathrm{CH_4}}, in kt CO2_2e yr−1^{-1}, is

ECH4=mCH4×GWPHE_{\mathrm{CH_4}} = m_{\mathrm{CH_4}} \times \mathrm{GWP}_H

and the total is

E=mCO2×1  +  ECH4E = m_{\mathrm{CO_2}} \times 1 \;+\; E_{\mathrm{CH_4}}

because GWP for CO2_2 is 1 by definition.

3. Annual emissions: result
3.1 Base case

Base-case conventions, stated so the result can be reproduced or restated on another basis: GWP100_{100} from IPCC AR6, and fossil CH4_4 with GWP100_{100} = 29.8, on the ground that a leak from an industrial plant handling 100 kt yr−1^{-1} of direct CO2_2 emissions is most commonly a fossil-fuel or fossil-feedstock leak. This is an assumption, not a fact in the problem statement; the non-fossil alternative is carried through Section 5.

  • CO2_2 term: 100 kt yr−1^{-1} × 1 = 100 kt CO2_2e yr−1^{-1}
  • CH4_4 term: 2 kt yr−1^{-1} × 29.8 = 59.6 kt CO2_2e yr−1^{-1}
  • Total: EE = 100 + 59.6 = 159.6 kt CO2_2e yr−1^{-1}, reported to the precision the inputs support as about 160 kt CO2_2e yr−1^{-1}.

The methane leak is 2 % of the emitted mass (2 kt out of 102 kt of gas) but 59.6 / 159.6 = 37 % of the GWP100_{100}-weighted total. Stated the other way: cutting the leak to zero would cut the weighted total by more than one third, while a 37 % cut in direct CO2_2 would be needed for the same weighted reduction. Per unit mass, leak reduction is therefore the higher-leverage abatement target in this plant on a GWP100_{100} basis, and more so on a short horizon (Section 5).

3.2 What the number is not
  • 160 kt CO2_2e yr−1^{-1} is not 160 kt of gas. The physical gas total is 102 kt yr−1^{-1} (100 kt CO2_2 + 2 kt CH4_4).
  • It is not a warming prediction. GWP is an index of integrated forcing relative to CO2_2; CH4_4 has an atmospheric lifetime of about 12 years, so a constant CH4_4 leak rate sustains a roughly constant added forcing after the first decades, whereas constant CO2_2 emissions accumulate. Metrics designed for that distinction (for example GWP*, the warming-equivalent form of GWP) would treat a stable long-running leak differently from a new or growing leak. No leak history is given, so no such correction is applied here.
  • If any part of the 100 kt CO2_2 is biogenic and is reported as a memo item (zero-rated in some inventory conventions, with the carbon uptake accounted in land use), the reported total would fall by that part. The problem statement gives no split, so all 100 kt is counted.
4. Carbon intensity of the principal product
4.1 Definition and the allocation problem

The carbon intensity of the principal product is

IP=fP EmPI_P = \frac{f_P \, E}{m_P}

where fPf_P is the allocation fraction: the dimensionless fraction of plant emissions assigned to the principal product, between 0 and 1. The remaining fraction, 1−fP1 - f_P, is assigned to the co-product.

The plant makes two outputs from shared equipment and shared emission sources. The emission streams given are plant totals, not product-specific measurements, so fPf_P cannot be read from the data. ISO 14044 gives a hierarchy for choosing it: first avoid allocation by subdividing the process or by system expansion (crediting the co-product with the emissions of the production it displaces); if allocation cannot be avoided, use a physical relationship (mass, energy content, or another causal physical quantity); if no physical relationship can be established, use another relationship, in practice economic value. Each choice gives a different, defensible IPI_P. Any single quoted intensity that does not state its allocation method and its fPf_P is incomplete.

4.2 Unallocated (all emissions to the principal product) value

Setting fP=1f_P = 1 gives an upper bound for the principal product and is the value obtained when the co-product is treated as a waste or as having no allocated burden:

IP=159.6 kt CO2e yr−180 kt yr−1=1.995 t CO2e t−1≈2.0 t CO2e per t of principal productI_P = \frac{159.6\ \mathrm{kt\ CO_2e\ yr^{-1}}}{80\ \mathrm{kt\ yr^{-1}}} = 1.995\ \mathrm{t\ CO_2e\ t^{-1}} \approx \mathbf{2.0\ t\ CO_2e\ per\ t\ of\ principal\ product}

Components, on the same basis:

  • Direct CO2_2 only: 100 / 80 = 1.25 t CO2_2 per t of product.
  • CH4_4 leak only: 59.6 / 80 = 0.75 t CO2_2e per t of product.
  • Sum: 2.00 t CO2_2e per t of product (1.995 before rounding).

On the AR5 GWP100_{100} = 28 basis the corresponding total intensity is 156.0 / 80 = 1.95 t CO2_2e t−1^{-1}; on an AR6 non-fossil CH4_4 basis it is 154.4 / 80 = 1.93 t CO2_2e t−1^{-1}.

4.3 Worked allocation examples

The examples below use stated, illustrative co-product data because the problem statement supplies none. They show the size of the allocation effect; they are not additional results for this plant. In each case EE = 159.6 kt CO2_2e yr−1^{-1} (base case, Section 3.1) and mPm_P = 80 kt yr−1^{-1}.

(a) Mass allocation. Requires the co-product production rate, mCm_C, in kt yr−1^{-1}. The allocation fraction is fP=mP/(mP+mC)f_P = m_P / (m_P + m_C).

  • If mCm_C = 40 kt yr−1^{-1}: fPf_P = 80 / 120 = 0.667; allocated emissions = 0.667 × 159.6 = 106.4 kt CO2_2e yr−1^{-1}; IPI_P = 106.4 / 80 = 1.33 t CO2_2e t−1^{-1}. The co-product carries 53.2 kt CO2_2e yr−1^{-1}, also 1.33 t CO2_2e t−1^{-1}, because mass allocation assigns the same intensity to every kilogram of output.
  • If mCm_C = 80 kt yr−1^{-1}: fPf_P = 0.500; IPI_P = 1.00 t CO2_2e t−1^{-1}.

(b) Economic allocation. Requires the unit prices (or annual sales values) of both products. The allocation fraction is the principal product share of total sales value. If, for illustration, the principal product accounts for 80 % of sales value, fPf_P = 0.80; allocated emissions = 127.7 kt CO2_2e yr−1^{-1}; IPI_P = 1.60 t CO2_2e t−1^{-1}. Economic allocation moves with prices, so an intensity reported on this basis must state the price period used.

(c) Energy allocation. If both products are fuels or are used for their energy content, allocation by lower heating value output is used in place of mass in item (a). It cannot be computed here: no heating values are given.

(d) System expansion (no allocation). The co-product is credited with the emissions of the conventional production route it displaces, and that credit is subtracted from EE before division by mPm_P. It cannot be computed here: neither the identity of the co-product nor the displaced route and its emission intensity are given. This method can give an IPI_P below every allocation result in items (a)–(b), and can in principle give a negative value if the credit exceeds EE; that is a property of the method, not an error.

4.4 Range statement

From the data given, the defensible statement is:

  • Upper bound (fPf_P = 1, no credit to the co-product): IPI_P ≈ 2.0 t CO2_2e t−1^{-1} on the base-case (AR6, fossil CH4_4, GWP100_{100}) basis.
  • IPI_P decreases in direct proportion to fPf_P: IPI_P = 2.0 × fPf_P t CO2_2e t−1^{-1} on that basis, to first order in the rounding used here. For example, fPf_P = 0.667 gives 1.33 and fPf_P = 0.50 gives 1.00 t CO2_2e t−1^{-1}.
  • A point value below 2.0 requires one named extra input: the co-product rate for mass allocation, the sales-value split for economic allocation, the heating-value split for energy allocation, or the displaced-production credit for system expansion.
5. Sensitivity to the methane metric

Total emissions, EE, and the unallocated intensity (fPf_P = 1) for each metric choice, with mCO2m_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 100 kt yr−1^{-1}, mCH4m_{\mathrm{CH_4}} = 2 kt yr−1^{-1}, and mPm_P = 80 kt yr−1^{-1} throughout:

Metric basis GWP for CH4_4 CH4_4 term (kt CO2_2e yr−1^{-1}) EE (kt CO2_2e yr−1^{-1}) CH4_4 share of EE IPI_P at fPf_P = 1 (t CO2_2e t−1^{-1})
IPCC AR4, GWP100_{100} 25 50.0 150.0 33 % 1.88

Reading of the table:

  1. Among GWP100_{100} choices, the total moves only between 150 and 160 kt CO2_2e yr−1^{-1} (about ±3 % around the base case). The headline annual figure is therefore robust to the assessment-report choice, provided the horizon is 100 years and the basis is stated.
  2. The horizon is not a minor choice. On a 20-year horizon the same physical plant reports about 262–265 kt CO2_2e yr−1^{-1}, about 1.7 times the GWP100_{100} figure, and methane becomes the larger term. GWP20_{20} is not the convention for inventory reporting, but it is the relevant sensitivity for near-term climate effect, and the two figures must never be mixed or quoted without the horizon.
  3. Uncertainty in the leak rate itself acts linearly and is likely larger than the spread in item 1. If the true leak is 3 kt yr−1^{-1} rather than 2 kt yr−1^{-1} (a 50 % underestimate, within the range found when top-down atmospheric measurements are compared with bottom-up fugitive inventories at oil, gas, and chemical sites), the base-case total becomes 100 + 3 × 29.8 = 189.4 kt CO2_2e yr−1^{-1}, and the unallocated intensity becomes 2.37 t CO2_2e t−1^{-1}. A leak figure should therefore carry its measurement method (emission-factor estimate, component survey, or continuous/top-down measurement) with it.

Response with defensive prompt

Annual Emissions and Product Carbon Intensity

Declared basis
Item Declaration
Standards Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard for the plant total; GHG Protocol Product Life Cycle Accounting and Reporting Standard and International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 14044 allocation hierarchy for the product intensity
Boundary Plant fence line, one operating year, direct emissions only (Scope 1 under the GHG Protocol). Included: direct carbon dioxide (CO₂) emission and fugitive methane (CH₄) leak. Excluded, for lack of data: purchased-energy emissions (Scope 2), upstream and downstream value-chain emissions (Scope 3), and all other greenhouse gases. No offsets or removals are deducted.
Consolidation approach Operational control is assumed; the problem states no equity share or financial-control boundary.
Allocation rule ISO 14044 hierarchy: allocation is avoided first by subdivision or system expansion; neither is possible with the data given, so allocation is used, as instructed. Two allocation bases are reported: mass (a physical relationship, preferred under the hierarchy) and economic value.
Horizons 100-year global warming potential (GWP100) as the primary reporting horizon, consistent with United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and Paris Agreement practice, and 20-year global warming potential (GWP20) as a sensitivity. Both horizons are reported throughout.
GWP values Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Sixth Assessment Report (AR6), fossil methane: GWP100 = 29.8 and GWP20 = 82.5, both dimensionless (kilogrammes of CO₂ equivalent per kilogramme of CH₄, kg CO₂e/kg CH₄). Carbon dioxide has GWP = 1 at every horizon by definition. The fossil values are used because a plant leak is treated here as fossil-origin methane; the non-fossil sensitivity is given in Section 3. If a reporting programme mandates AR5 or another GWP set, the totals change and must be restated.

This is therefore a direct-emissions (gate-to-gate, Scope 1 only) intensity. It is not a full cradle-to-gate or cradle-to-grave product carbon footprint, and it must not be reported as one.

Symbols and given data
  • ECO₂ = direct CO₂ emission rate = 100 kilotonnes per year (kt/yr), where 1 kt = 10⁶ kilogrammes (kg).
  • mCH₄ = methane leak rate = 2 kt CH₄/yr.
  • EH = total annual emission rate at horizon H, in kt of CO₂ equivalent per year (kt CO₂e/yr), where H is the GWP time horizon in years (yr), either 20 yr or 100 yr.
  • GWPH,CH₄ = global warming potential of methane at horizon H, dimensionless.
  • mp = principal product production rate = 80 kt/yr.
  • mc = co-product production rate, in kt/yr — not given.
  • pp = price of the principal product, in currency per tonne (t), and pc = price of the co-product, in currency per tonne — neither is given, and neither are the revenues.
  • f = allocation fraction, dimensionless: the share of EH assigned to the principal product.
  • IH = carbon intensity of the principal product at horizon H, in tonnes of CO₂ equivalent per tonne of principal product (t CO₂e/t), numerically equal to kilogrammes of CO₂ equivalent per kilogramme (kg CO₂e/kg).
1. Plant total annual emissions

The total at horizon H is

EH = ECO₂ + mCH₄ × GWPH,CH₄.

100-year horizon

  • Methane term: 2 kt CH₄/yr × 29.8 kg CO₂e/kg CH₄ = 59.6 kt CO₂e/yr.
  • Total: E₁₀₀ = 100 + 59.6 = 159.6 kt CO₂e/yr, reported as 160 kt CO₂e/yr at three significant figures.

20-year horizon

  • Methane term: 2 kt CH₄/yr × 82.5 kg CO₂e/kg CH₄ = 165.0 kt CO₂e/yr.
  • Total: E₂₀ = 100 + 165.0 = 265.0 kt CO₂e/yr, reported as 265 kt CO₂e/yr.
Horizon H CO₂ term (kt CO₂e/yr) CH₄ term (kt CO₂e/yr) Total EH (kt CO₂e/yr) CH₄ share of total
100 yr 100 59.6 159.6 37 %
20 yr 100 165.0 265.0 62 %

The mass emitted does not change with horizon; only the weighting of methane changes. Methane is 2 % of the emitted mass but 37 % of the GWP100 total and 62 % of the GWP20 total, so leak control is the largest single reduction lever at either horizon, and especially on a 20-year view.

2. Sensitivity to methane origin

If the leaked methane were non-fossil (biogenic) rather than fossil, the AR6 values would be GWP100 = 27.0 and GWP20 = 79.7, giving E₁₀₀ = 100 + 2 × 27.0 = 154.0 kt CO₂e/yr and E₂₀ = 100 + 2 × 79.7 = 259.4 kt CO₂e/yr. The origin of the methane is not stated in the problem; the fossil values in Section 1 are the stated basis, and this sensitivity bounds the effect of that choice (about 4 % at GWP100 and about 2 % at GWP20).

3. Carbon intensity of the principal product
3.1 Data limitation

A unique allocated intensity cannot be computed from the data given. Mass allocation requires mc, which is not given. Economic allocation requires pp, pc, and mc (or, equivalently, the two product revenues), none of which is given. Any single numerical allocated intensity would require inventing those values, so none is presented as a result. The exact results obtainable from the given data are (a) the unallocated intensity, which is the upper bound for the principal product, and (b) closed-form allocated intensities into which mc and the prices are inserted when known.

3.2 Unallocated intensity (all emissions to the principal product, f = 1)

IH = EH / mp.

  • GWP100: I₁₀₀ = 159.6 kt CO₂e/yr ÷ 80 kt/yr = 1.995 t CO₂e/t ≈ 2.00 t CO₂e/t (2.00 kg CO₂e/kg).
  • GWP20: I₂₀ = 265.0 kt CO₂e/yr ÷ 80 kt/yr = 3.3125 t CO₂e/t ≈ 3.31 t CO₂e/t (3.31 kg CO₂e/kg).
3.3 Mass allocation

The mass allocation fraction for the principal product is

fmass = mp / (mp + mc) = 80 / (80 + mc),

with mc in kt/yr. The allocated intensity is

IH,mass = EH × fmass / mp = EH / (80 + mc),

with EH in kt CO₂e/yr and the denominator in kt/yr, giving t CO₂e/t. That is:

  • GWP100: I₁₀₀,mass = 159.6 / (80 + mc) t CO₂e/t.
  • GWP20: I₂₀,mass = 265.0 / (80 + mc) t CO₂e/t.
3.4 Economic allocation

The economic allocation fraction for the principal product is the principal product's share of total product revenue:

fecon = (mp × pp) / (mp × pp + mc × pc) = (80 × pp) / (80 × pp + mc × pc).

The allocated intensity is

IH,econ = EH × fecon / mp = EH × fecon / 80,

giving:

  • GWP100: I₁₀₀,econ = 1.995 × fecon t CO₂e/t.
  • GWP20: I₂₀,econ = 3.3125 × fecon t CO₂e/t.
3.5 How any allocation result is read off

For either allocation basis, once its fraction f is known, the intensity is f times the unallocated value in Section 3.2. The table below is an arithmetic sensitivity only; the fractions shown are illustrative and are not data for this plant.

Allocation fraction f assigned to principal product I₁₀₀ (t CO₂e/t) I₂₀ (t CO₂e/t)
1.00 (no allocation; co-product assigned nothing) 2.00 3.31
0.80 (for example, mass allocation if mc were 20 kt/yr) 1.60 2.65
0.50 1.00 1.66

Mass and economic allocation give the same intensity only if the mass share and the revenue share happen to be equal. In general they differ: economic allocation shifts burden toward the higher-value product, so a high-priced principal product with a low-priced, heavy co-product receives a larger share under economic allocation than under mass allocation, and the reverse when the co-product carries most of the value.

4. Limitations and data required to complete the estimate
  1. Missing allocation data. mc, pp, and pc (or both revenues) are required before a single allocated intensity can be reported. Prices should be stated for a defined period (for example, a multi-year average), because economic allocation moves with market prices even when the process does not change.
  2. Partial boundary. Scope 2 and Scope 3 emissions are excluded only because no data were supplied. A product carbon footprint under ISO 14067 or the GHG Protocol Product Standard requires the upstream (cradle-to-gate at minimum) inventory; the intensities here would rise if those emissions were included.
  3. Other gases and sources. Only CO₂ and CH₄ are included. Any nitrous oxide, fluorinated gases, or additional fugitive and process sources at the plant would add to EH.
  4. Uncertainty. No measurement uncertainty was supplied. Fugitive methane rates are typically the least certain term in such an inventory (often estimated from emission factors rather than measured), and the results are stated to three significant figures on the arithmetic only; that precision is not a statement of accuracy.
  5. GWP set. Results use IPCC AR6 fossil-methane values, as declared. A programme mandating a different assessment-report vintage changes the methane terms in Section 1 and every intensity in proportion.

Third test: the held-out problems

The 64 responses of the third test, on the 32 new problems written for that test.

A1. Henry's Law Conventions — Carbon Dioxide in Water

Response without defensive prompt

Dissolved carbon dioxide in water in equilibrium with air at 25 °C

Result

The saturation concentration of physically dissolved carbon dioxide, chemical formula CO₂, in water at 25 °C in equilibrium with air at 1 atm is approximately

1.4 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L,

i.e. approximately 0.63 mg/L, corresponding to a liquid-phase mole fraction of approximately 2.6 × 10⁻⁷.

Definitions
  • Temperature, symbol T: 25 °C, given.
  • Total pressure of the gas, symbol P, in atmosphere (atm): 1 atm, given.
  • Mole fraction of CO₂ in the gas (air), symbol y, dimensionless: 0.00042, given.
  • Partial pressure of CO₂ in the gas, symbol p, in atm: defined below.
  • Molar concentration of dissolved CO₂ in the liquid at saturation, symbol C, in mole per litre (mol/L): the quantity sought.
  • Henry's law constant in the pressure–concentration form, symbol H, in litre atmosphere per mole (L·atm/mol): 29.4 L·atm/mol, given.
  • Molar mass of CO₂, symbol M, in gram per mole (g/mol): 44.01 g/mol, used only for the optional mass concentration.
  • Molar concentration of water in (nearly pure) liquid water, symbol C_w, in mol/L: approximately 55.5 mol/L, used only for the optional mole-fraction conversion.

The state "where no more will dissolve" is gas–liquid equilibrium (saturation). At equilibrium, for a dilute dissolved gas, Henry's law relates p and C.

Resolution of the convention of the quoted constant

Henry's law is quoted in several reciprocal forms, so the convention must be identified before a numerical value is used. The units given determine the form here.

The quoted unit for H is L·atm/mol, which is pressure divided by molar concentration:

atm / (mol/L) = L·atm/mol.

Hence the consistent form is

p = H C,

i.e. partial pressure equals the constant multiplied by the liquid molar concentration. Equivalently, C = p / H.

This is consistent with the known magnitude for this system: for pure CO₂ at p = 1 atm, this form gives C = 1 / 29.4 mol/L = 0.034 mol/L, the accepted order for CO₂ solubility in water at 25 °C. The other common forms would carry different units and different numerical values — for example a pressure–mole-fraction constant would be in atm (approximately 1.6 × 10³ atm for CO₂ in water at 25 °C), and a solubility constant defined as C / p would be in mol/(L·atm) (approximately 0.034 mol/(L·atm)) — so neither matches a value of 29.4 L·atm/mol.

Calculation

For an (approximately) ideal gas mixture, the partial pressure is the mole fraction multiplied by the total pressure:

p = y P = 0.00042 × 1 atm = 4.2 × 10⁻⁴ atm.

Applying Henry's law in the form identified above:

C = p / H = (4.2 × 10⁻⁴ atm) / (29.4 L·atm/mol) = 1.43 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L.

The units cancel as atm / (L·atm/mol) = mol/L, as required.

Optional conversions, from C:

  • Mass concentration: C × M = (1.43 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L) × (44.01 g/mol) = 6.3 × 10⁻⁴ g/L = 0.63 mg/L.
  • Liquid mole fraction, symbol x, dimensionless: for a dilute solution, x ≈ C / (C + C_w) ≈ (1.43 × 10⁻⁵) / (55.5) ≈ 2.6 × 10⁻⁷.
Scope and assumptions
  • Ideal-gas behaviour for the air, and a dilute liquid solution, so Henry's law in the linear form above applies.
  • The value is the physically dissolved CO₂ given by Henry's law. A small additional amount of inorganic carbon can be present as carbonic acid, bicarbonate, and carbonate formed by reaction with water; that reactive speciation depends on pH (the negative base-10 logarithm of the hydrogen-ion activity) and is not included in the Henry's-law figure above.
  • Water vapour in the gas and the small change in liquid volume on dissolution are neglected; both are negligible at this precision (two to three significant figures).
Response with defensive prompt

Dissolved Carbon Dioxide in Water in Equilibrium with Air at 25 °C

Symbols and given data

  • yCO2y_{\mathrm{CO_2}} is the mole fraction of carbon dioxide (CO2\mathrm{CO_2}) in the gas (air), dimensionless: yCO2=0.00042y_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 0.00042.

  • cCO2c_{\mathrm{CO_2}} is the concentration of physically dissolved carbon dioxide in the liquid water at saturation (no more will dissolve), in moles per litre (mol/L).
  • xCO2x_{\mathrm{CO_2}} is the mole fraction of dissolved carbon dioxide in the liquid water, dimensionless.
  • cH2Oc_{\mathrm{H_2O}} is the molar concentration of water itself in liquid water, in moles per litre (mol/L).
  • MCO2M_{\mathrm{CO_2}} is the molar mass of carbon dioxide, in grams per mole (g/mol): MCO2=44.01 g/molM_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 44.01\ \text{g/mol}.

Given quoted value, with its convention to be identified:

H=29.4 L⋅atm/molH = 29.4\ \text{L·atm/mol}

where HH is the quoted Henry's law constant for carbon dioxide in water at 25 °C25\ \text{°C}.

The state considered is gas–liquid equilibrium (saturation). Henry's law applies because the dissolved concentration is very dilute, as the result confirms.

1. Partial pressure of carbon dioxide in air

For an ideal-gas mixture, the partial pressure is the mole fraction multiplied by the total pressure:

pCO2=yCO2 Pp_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = y_{\mathrm{CO_2}}\, P

pCO2=(0.00042)(1 atm)=4.2×10−4 atmp_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = (0.00042)(1\ \text{atm}) = 4.2 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{atm}

That is, the driving pressure for dissolution is not 1 atm1\ \text{atm}, but only 0.00042 atm0.00042\ \text{atm}, corresponding to 420420 parts per million by mole in air.

2. Which Henry's law convention the quoted constant uses

Two common conventions are in use for a solute gas at dilute concentration.

Convention A — pressure proportional to liquid concentration:

pCO2=Hpc  cCO2p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = H_{p c}\; c_{\mathrm{CO_2}}

In Convention A, HpcH_{p c} must have units of pressure divided by concentration:

atmmol/L=L⋅atm/mol\frac{\text{atm}}{\text{mol/L}} = \text{L·atm/mol}

Convention B — pressure proportional to liquid mole fraction:

pCO2=Hpx  xCO2p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = H_{p x}\; x_{\mathrm{CO_2}}

In Convention B, xCO2x_{\mathrm{CO_2}} is dimensionless, so HpxH_{p x} must have units of pressure alone, atm.

The quoted constant has units L·atm/mol. Those units match Convention A and do not match Convention B. Therefore:

The quoted value 29.4 L⋅atm/mol29.4\ \text{L·atm/mol} is HpcH_{p c}, the pressure–concentration constant:

Hpc=29.4 L⋅atm/mol,pCO2=Hpc cCO2H_{p c} = 29.4\ \text{L·atm/mol}, \qquad p_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = H_{p c}\, c_{\mathrm{CO_2}}

The units alone settle the convention. Treating 29.429.4 as if it were HpxH_{p x} in atm would be a unit error and, as shown in Section 5, would overstate the concentration by a factor of about 55.555.5.

3. Saturated concentration in air

Rearranging Convention A:

cCO2=pCO2Hpc=4.2×10−4 atm29.4 L⋅atm/molc_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = \frac{p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{H_{p c}} = \frac{4.2 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{atm}}{29.4\ \text{L·atm/mol}}

cCO2=1.43×10−5 mol/Lc_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 1.43 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{mol/L}

Equivalent forms of the same result:

  • In micromoles per litre (μ\mumol/L), where 1 μmol=10−6 mol1\ \mu\text{mol} = 10^{-6}\ \text{mol}:

cCO2=14.3 μmol/Lc_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 14.3\ \mu\text{mol/L}

  • As a mass concentration, obtained by multiplying by MCO2M_{\mathrm{CO_2}}:

cCO2 MCO2=(1.43×10−5 mol/L)(44.01 g/mol)=6.3×10−4 g/L=0.63 mg/Lc_{\mathrm{CO_2}}\, M_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = (1.43 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{mol/L})(44.01\ \text{g/mol}) = 6.3 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{g/L} = 0.63\ \text{mg/L}

where mg is milligram, 1 mg=10−3 g1\ \text{mg} = 10^{-3}\ \text{g}.

  • As a liquid mole fraction. First, the molar concentration of water is

cH2O=ρH2OMH2O=1000 g/L18.015 g/mol=55.5 mol/Lc_{\mathrm{H_2O}} = \frac{\rho_{\mathrm{H_2O}}}{M_{\mathrm{H_2O}}} = \frac{1000\ \text{g/L}}{18.015\ \text{g/mol}} = 55.5\ \text{mol/L}

Then, for a dilute solution in which cCO2≪cH2Oc_{\mathrm{CO_2}} \ll c_{\mathrm{H_2O}},

xCO2=cCO2cCO2+cH2O≈cCO2cH2O=1.43×10−5 mol/L55.5 mol/L=2.6×10−7x_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = \frac{c_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{c_{\mathrm{CO_2}} + c_{\mathrm{H_2O}}} \approx \frac{c_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{c_{\mathrm{H_2O}}} = \frac{1.43 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{mol/L}}{55.5\ \text{mol/L}} = 2.6 \times 10^{-7}

dimensionless, as required for a mole fraction.

4. Conversion to the other convention

From the definitions in Section 2,

Hpx=pCO2xCO2,Hpc=pCO2cCO2,xCO2≈cCO2cH2OH_{p x} = \frac{p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{x_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}, \qquad H_{p c} = \frac{p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{c_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}, \qquad x_{\mathrm{CO_2}} \approx \frac{c_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{c_{\mathrm{H_2O}}}

Substitution gives the conversion, valid for a dilute solution:

Hpx≈Hpc  cH2OH_{p x} \approx H_{p c}\; c_{\mathrm{H_2O}}

Hpx≈(29.4 L⋅atm/mol)(55.5 mol/L)=1.63×103 atmH_{p x} \approx (29.4\ \text{L·atm/mol})(55.5\ \text{mol/L}) = 1.63 \times 10^{3}\ \text{atm}

So the same physical constant is quoted in the two conventions as

Hpc=29.4 L⋅atm/mol⟺Hpx≈1630 atmH_{p c} = 29.4\ \text{L·atm/mol} \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad H_{p x} \approx 1630\ \text{atm}

Check using Convention B directly:

xCO2=pCO2Hpx=4.2×10−4 atm1.63×103 atm=2.6×10−7x_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = \frac{p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{H_{p x}} = \frac{4.2 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{atm}}{1.63 \times 10^{3}\ \text{atm}} = 2.6 \times 10^{-7}

which is the same liquid mole fraction as in Section 3, and multiplying by cH2O=55.5 mol/Lc_{\mathrm{H_2O}} = 55.5\ \text{mol/L} returns cCO2=1.43×10−5 mol/Lc_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 1.43 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{mol/L}.

A third, reciprocal, form is also in common use, the solubility form:

KH=cCO2pCO2=1Hpc=129.4 L⋅atm/mol=3.4×10−2 mol/(L⋅atm)K_{H} = \frac{c_{\mathrm{CO_2}}}{p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}} = \frac{1}{H_{p c}} = \frac{1}{29.4\ \text{L·atm/mol}} = 3.4 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{mol/(L·atm)}

with cCO2=KH pCO2c_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = K_{H}\, p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}.

5. Check against the known solubility of carbon dioxide in water

Pure carbon dioxide at 1 atm1\ \text{atm}. Setting pCO2=1 atmp_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 1\ \text{atm} in Convention A:

cCO2=1 atm29.4 L⋅atm/mol=3.4×10−2 mol/Lc_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = \frac{1\ \text{atm}}{29.4\ \text{L·atm/mol}} = 3.4 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{mol/L}

As a mass concentration: (3.4×10−2 mol/L)(44.01 g/mol)=1.5 g/L(3.4 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{mol/L})(44.01\ \text{g/mol}) = 1.5\ \text{g/L}.

This matches the tabulated solubility of carbon dioxide in water at 25 °C25\ \text{°C} under 1 atm1\ \text{atm} of carbon dioxide, about 1.451.45–1.5 g/L1.5\ \text{g/L} (about 0.034 mol/L0.034\ \text{mol/L}). The quoted constant therefore reproduces the known pure-gas solubility.

In air. Air contains only the fraction yCO2=0.00042y_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 0.00042 of carbon dioxide, so by the linearity of Henry's law the saturated concentration in contact with air is that same pure-gas value scaled by 0.000420.00042:

(3.4×10−2 mol/L)(0.00042)=1.43×10−5 mol/L(3.4 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{mol/L})(0.00042) = 1.43 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{mol/L}

This is the accepted order for water in equilibrium with present-day air at 25 °C25\ \text{°C}: about 14 μmol/L14\ \mu\text{mol/L} of physically dissolved carbon dioxide, about 0.6 mg/L0.6\ \text{mg/L}, liquid mole fraction about 2.6×10−72.6 \times 10^{-7}. Tabulated mole-fraction Henry constants for carbon dioxide in water at 25 °C25\ \text{°C} are likewise about 1630 atm1630\ \text{atm}, confirming the conversion in Section 4.

Error that the unit check prevents. If 29.429.4 were incorrectly used as HpxH_{p x} in atm, the result would be xCO2=(4.2×10−4)/(29.4)=1.43×10−5x_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = (4.2 \times 10^{-4})/(29.4) = 1.43 \times 10^{-5} and cCO2=xCO2 cH2O=7.9×10−4 mol/Lc_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = x_{\mathrm{CO_2}}\, c_{\mathrm{H_2O}} = 7.9 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol/L}, a factor of 55.555.5 too high and inconsistent with the known solubility above.

Scope. The values above are for physically dissolved carbon dioxide, CO2(aq)\mathrm{CO_2(aq)} (conventionally reported together with the small amount of undissociated carbonic acid formed from it). Total dissolved inorganic carbon in a real water also includes bicarbonate and carbonate ions formed by subsequent acid–base reactions; that total depends on the pH of the water and is not given by Henry's law alone.

A2. Non-Ideal Vapour–Liquid Equilibrium — Bubble Pressure, Second Case

Response without defensive prompt

Bubble-Point Pressure of a Strongly Non-Ideal Binary Liquid

Result

No unique bubble-point pressure can be estimated from the data given. The data determine only the ideal-solution (Raoult's law) reference value, 82 kPa. For a liquid described as strongly non-ideal, that reference value is not an estimate of the bubble-point pressure: the true value can lie well below it or well above it, and the data do not determine which, or by how much.

Symbols and given data
  • x1x_1, the liquid mole fraction of component 1 (dimensionless): x1=0.30x_1 = 0.30
  • x2x_2, the liquid mole fraction of component 2 (dimensionless): x2=1−x1=0.70x_2 = 1 - x_1 = 0.70
  • P1satP_1^{\mathrm{sat}}, the pure-component vapour pressure of component 1 at the stated temperature, in kilopascals (kPa): P1sat=180 kPaP_1^{\mathrm{sat}} = 180\ \mathrm{kPa}
  • P2satP_2^{\mathrm{sat}}, the pure-component vapour pressure of component 2 at the same temperature, in kilopascals (kPa): P2sat=40 kPaP_2^{\mathrm{sat}} = 40\ \mathrm{kPa}
  • PP, the total pressure, in kilopascals (kPa); the bubble-point pressure is the value of PP at which the first vapour bubble forms
  • y1y_1 and y2y_2, the vapour mole fractions of components 1 and 2 (dimensionless), with y1+y2=1y_1 + y_2 = 1
  • γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2, the liquid activity coefficients of components 1 and 2 (dimensionless), defined so that γi=1\gamma_i = 1 for an ideal solution and γi\gamma_i departs from 1 as non-ideality increases
Governing relation

Under the usual low-to-moderate pressure approximation — vapour treated as an ideal gas, pure liquid as the reference state for each component, and pressure (Poynting) correction neglected — equilibrium for each component is given by the modified Raoult's law:

yiP=xi γi Pisaty_i P = x_i \, \gamma_i \, P_i^{\mathrm{sat}}

Summing over the two components and using y1+y2=1y_1 + y_2 = 1 gives the bubble-point pressure:

Pbub=x1 γ1 P1sat+x2 γ2 P2satP_{\mathrm{bub}} = x_1 \, \gamma_1 \, P_1^{\mathrm{sat}} + x_2 \, \gamma_2 \, P_2^{\mathrm{sat}}

Substitution of the given numbers gives:

Pbub=(0.30)(180 kPa) γ1+(0.70)(40 kPa) γ2=54 γ1+28 γ2  kPaP_{\mathrm{bub}} = (0.30)(180\ \mathrm{kPa})\,\gamma_1 + (0.70)(40\ \mathrm{kPa})\,\gamma_2 = 54\,\gamma_1 + 28\,\gamma_2 \ \ \mathrm{kPa}

Evaluation stops at this point. Neither γ1\gamma_1 nor γ2\gamma_2 at x1=0.30x_1 = 0.30 and the stated temperature is supplied, and no model or parameter set from which they could be calculated is supplied.

The ideal-solution reference value

Setting γ1=γ2=1\gamma_1 = \gamma_2 = 1 (Raoult's law, an ideal solution) gives:

Pideal=0.30×180 kPa+0.70×40 kPa=54 kPa+28 kPa=82 kPaP_{\mathrm{ideal}} = 0.30 \times 180\ \mathrm{kPa} + 0.70 \times 40\ \mathrm{kPa} = 54\ \mathrm{kPa} + 28\ \mathrm{kPa} = 82\ \mathrm{kPa}

The corresponding ideal vapour composition, y1=x1P1sat/Pidealy_1 = x_1 P_1^{\mathrm{sat}} / P_{\mathrm{ideal}}, is y1=54/82=0.66y_1 = 54/82 = 0.66.

These two numbers describe the ideal solution only. The problem states that the liquid is strongly non-ideal, which by definition means γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 depart substantially from 1. Reporting 82 kPa as the bubble-point pressure would therefore contradict the stated premise.

Size of the indeterminacy

The unknown coefficients are not a small correction. Two thermodynamically consistent examples, each realisable with a standard two-parameter Margules excess Gibbs energy model at x1=0.30x_1 = 0.30, show the range:

Case γ1\gamma_1 γ2\gamma_2 Pbub=54 γ1+28 γ2P_{\mathrm{bub}} = 54\,\gamma_1 + 28\,\gamma_2
Positive deviation from ideality 3.0 1.5 162+42=204 kPa162 + 42 = 204\ \mathrm{kPa}
Negative deviation from ideality 0.4 0.6 21.6+16.8=38.4 kPa21.6 + 16.8 = 38.4\ \mathrm{kPa}

In the first case the bubble-point pressure exceeds even P1sat=180 kPaP_1^{\mathrm{sat}} = 180\ \mathrm{kPa}, the behaviour associated with a maximum-pressure azeotrope. In the second case it falls below P2sat=40 kPaP_2^{\mathrm{sat}} = 40\ \mathrm{kPa}. Both cases are strongly non-ideal, both satisfy the given data, and they differ by more than a factor of five. No data given select between them, or between them and any intermediate or more extreme case. Activity coefficients are positive quantities with no general upper bound, so the given data place no useful numerical bound on PbubP_{\mathrm{bub}} either.

Data required for a numerical answer

Any one of the following, at the stated temperature and at or near x1=0.30x_1 = 0.30, would close the problem:

  1. Measured values of γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 at that composition, or measured vapour–liquid equilibrium data (composition, pressure) from which they can be obtained.
  2. Fitted parameters for a named activity-coefficient model — for example Margules, van Laar, Wilson, NRTL (non-random two-liquid), or UNIQUAC (universal quasi-chemical) — for this pair of components at that temperature.
  3. A measured bubble-point pressure or a measured azeotropic composition and pressure for the system.

With γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 supplied, the calculation is the single substitution in the governing relation above. At higher pressures, vapour fugacity coefficients and the Poynting correction would also be required; neither is supplied here.

Conclusion
  • Determined by the data: the Raoult's law reference value, Pideal=82 kPaP_{\mathrm{ideal}} = 82\ \mathrm{kPa}, with ideal vapour composition y1=0.66y_1 = 0.66.
  • Not determined by the data: the bubble-point pressure of the stated strongly non-ideal liquid. It equals 54 γ1+28 γ254\,\gamma_1 + 28\,\gamma_2 kPa, and γ1\gamma_1 and γ2\gamma_2 are unknown. A numerical value requires activity-coefficient data or a parameterised activity-coefficient model for the specific pair of components.

  1. Identities of components 1 and 2, and the numerical temperature (so that the stated PisatP_i^{\mathrm{sat}} values can be checked).
  2. A named activity-coefficient model (for example NRTL, Wilson, or UNIQUAC) with its binary interaction parameters, the primary source from which they were taken, the experimental data set they were fitted to, and the temperature and composition range of that fit — with x1=0.30x_1 = 0.30 and the stated temperature inside that range.
  3. A phase-stability check at x1=0.30x_1 = 0.30 confirming a single liquid phase.
  4. A statement of the vapour-phase treatment (ideal gas, or fugacity coefficients from a named equation of state) if pressures or non-ideality make that correction non-negligible.

With items 1–3 supplied, Eq. (1) gives PP directly, and a second independently sourced model should still be run: if the two results differ by more than 10%, the range across models, not a single value, is the result to report.

7. Conclusion

P=54 γ1+28 γ2 kPaP = 54\,\gamma_1 + 28\,\gamma_2\ \mathrm{kPa} at x1=0.30x_1 = 0.30. The ideal-solution value is 82 kPa82\ \mathrm{kPa}. Because no component identities, temperature, activity coefficients, model parameters, parameter source, or data range are given for a liquid stated to be strongly non-ideal, no unique bubble-point pressure exists for this problem as posed. The result is reported as a range and as an under-specification, not as a single value.

A3. Reactive Absorption Capacity — Hydrogen Sulfide Removal

Response without defensive prompt

Amine Solvent Flow for Hydrogen Sulfide Removal

Result

No unique numerical solvent flow can be obtained from the data given. The hydrogen sulfide removal rate and the lean loading fix only one relation between the amine circulation rate and the rich loading. A rich loading, an equilibrium relation together with absorber conditions, or a design loading increase must also be specified.

The governing result, with all symbols defined in Section 1, is

amine molar flow rate = 60 / (rich loading − 0.05) kmol amine/h,

where 60 is in kmol hydrogen sulfide/h, rich loading and 0.05 are in mol hydrogen sulfide/mol amine, and the quotient is therefore in kmol amine/h. The total water-based solution flow requires, in addition, the amine concentration in the solution.

1. Symbols and given data
  • n˙H2S,rem\dot n_{\mathrm{H_2S,rem}} (kilomoles per hour, kmol/h): molar flow rate of hydrogen sulfide (H2S\mathrm{H_2S}) removed in the absorber. Given: n˙H2S,rem=60 kmol/h\dot n_{\mathrm{H_2S,rem}} = 60\ \mathrm{kmol/h}.
  • α\alpha (moles of hydrogen sulfide per mole of amine, mol/mol): loading, moles of H2S\mathrm{H_2S} held by the solvent per mole of amine present.
  • αL\alpha_L (mol/mol): loading of the lean solvent, the solvent leaving the regenerator and entering the absorber. Given: αL=0.05 mol/mol\alpha_L = 0.05\ \mathrm{mol/mol}.
  • αR\alpha_R (mol/mol): loading of the rich solvent, the solvent leaving the absorber. Not given.
  • n˙A\dot n_A (kmol/h): molar flow rate of amine circulated with the solvent. This is the quantity fixed by the loading balance once αR\alpha_R is known.
  • n˙S\dot n_S (kmol/h): molar flow rate of the total aqueous solution (amine plus water).
  • xAx_A (mol/mol): mole fraction of amine in the aqueous solution. Not given.
  • wAw_A (kg/kg): mass fraction of amine in the aqueous solution. Not given.
  • MAM_A (kg/kmol): molar mass of the amine. Not given, because the amine identity is not given.
  • m˙S\dot m_S (kg/h): mass flow rate of the total aqueous solution.
  • ρS\rho_S (kg/m3^3): density of the aqueous solution at the circulation temperature. Not given.
  • V˙S\dot V_S (m3^3/h): volumetric flow rate of the total aqueous solution.
2. Absorber loading balance

A steady-state balance on H2S\mathrm{H_2S} over the absorber, with no H2S\mathrm{H_2S} generated or consumed except by transfer into the solvent (chemical reaction with the amine is represented by the loading α\alpha, in mol/mol), gives

n˙AαR=n˙AαL+n˙H2S,rem.\dot n_A \alpha_R = \dot n_A \alpha_L + \dot n_{\mathrm{H_2S,rem}}.

The left-hand term, n˙AαR\dot n_A \alpha_R (kmol/h), is the H2S\mathrm{H_2S} flow leaving in the rich solvent. The first term on the right, n˙AαL\dot n_A \alpha_L (kmol/h), is the H2S\mathrm{H_2S} flow entering in the lean solvent. The second term on the right, n˙H2S,rem\dot n_{\mathrm{H_2S,rem}} (kmol/h), is the H2S\mathrm{H_2S} transferred from the gas.

Rearrangement gives

n˙A(αR−αL)=n˙H2S,rem,\dot n_A (\alpha_R - \alpha_L) = \dot n_{\mathrm{H_2S,rem}},

n˙A=n˙H2S,remαR−αL=60αR−0.05 kmol amine/h,\dot n_A = \frac{\dot n_{\mathrm{H_2S,rem}}}{\alpha_R - \alpha_L} = \frac{60}{ \alpha_R - 0.05 }\ \mathrm{kmol\ amine/h},

with 6060 in kmol/h and αR\alpha_R and 0.050.05 in mol/mol.

The working capacity of the solvent per pass is the loading increase αR−αL\alpha_R - \alpha_L (mol/mol), not the lean loading αL\alpha_L (mol/mol) alone.

3. Why the lean loading alone is insufficient

Dividing the removal rate by the lean loading alone would give

60/0.05=1200 kmol/h,60 / 0.05 = 1200\ \mathrm{kmol/h},

with 6060 in kmol H2S\mathrm{H_2S}/h and 0.050.05 in mol H2S\mathrm{H_2S}/mol amine. That quotient has no standing as a circulation rate. It would correspond to αR=2αL=0.10 mol/mol\alpha_R = 2\alpha_L = 0.10\ \mathrm{mol/mol}, a special case for which no basis is given, and it ignores the H2S\mathrm{H_2S} already present in the lean solvent entering the absorber.

Two admissible cases show the non-uniqueness:

  • If αR=0.25 mol/mol\alpha_R = 0.25\ \mathrm{mol/mol}, then n˙A=60/(0.25−0.05)=60/0.20=300 kmol amine/h\dot n_A = 60 / (0.25 - 0.05) = 60 / 0.20 = 300\ \mathrm{kmol\ amine/h}.
  • If αR=0.45 mol/mol\alpha_R = 0.45\ \mathrm{mol/mol}, then n˙A=60/(0.45−0.05)=60/0.40=150 kmol amine/h\dot n_A = 60 / (0.45 - 0.05) = 60 / 0.40 = 150\ \mathrm{kmol\ amine/h}.

Both cases satisfy every datum given and remove 60 kmol/h60\ \mathrm{kmol/h} of H2S\mathrm{H_2S}, yet the amine circulation differs by a factor of two. The problem as stated is therefore underdetermined.

4. Parametric answer

Values of n˙A\dot n_A (kmol amine/h) from n˙A=60/(αR−0.05)\dot n_A = 60 / (\alpha_R - 0.05), with 6060 in kmol/h and αR\alpha_R in mol/mol, are:

αR\alpha_R (mol/mol) αR−αL\alpha_R - \alpha_L (mol/mol) n˙A\dot n_A (kmol amine/h)
0.20 0.15 400.0
0.25 0.20 300.0
0.30 0.25 240.0
0.35 0.30 200.0
0.40 0.35 171.4
0.45 0.40 150.0
0.50 0.45 133.3
0.55 0.50 120.0

Any single value from this table is an answer only after the corresponding αR\alpha_R (mol/mol) has been specified, measured, set as a design working capacity, or calculated from an equilibrium (vapour–liquid equilibrium and reaction) model at stated absorber temperature, pressure, and inlet gas H2S\mathrm{H_2S} partial pressure. None of those data is supplied here.

Physical limits that a supplied αR\alpha_R (mol/mol) must respect: αR>αL=0.05 mol/mol\alpha_R > \alpha_L = 0.05\ \mathrm{mol/mol} for net removal, and αR\alpha_R cannot exceed the equilibrium loading at the absorber bottom conditions, nor, for a primary or secondary amine reacting in a 2 amine : 1 H2S\mathrm{H_2S} carbamate-type stoichiometry, a stoichiometric ceiling near 0.5 mol/mol0.5\ \mathrm{mol/mol} unless bicarbonate formation is also counted. A tertiary amine such as methyldiethanolamine has a different (nominally 1 : 1) reaction basis. No ceiling can be selected without the amine identity and the absorber conditions.

5. From amine flow to total solution flow

Even after n˙A\dot n_A (kmol/h) is fixed, the flow of the water-based solution is still not fixed, because the amine concentration is not given.

On a molar basis,

n˙S=n˙A/xA,\dot n_S = \dot n_A / x_A,

with n˙S\dot n_S and n˙A\dot n_A in kmol/h and xAx_A in mol amine/mol solution.

On a mass basis,

m˙S=n˙AMA/wA,\dot m_S = \dot n_A M_A / w_A,

with m˙S\dot m_S in kg/h, n˙A\dot n_A in kmol/h, MAM_A in kg/kmol, and wAw_A in kg amine/kg solution, and

V˙S=m˙S/ρS,\dot V_S = \dot m_S / \rho_S,

with V˙S\dot V_S in m3^3/h, m˙S\dot m_S in kg/h, and ρS\rho_S in kg/m3^3.

Illustration only, not a design answer: if αR=0.45 mol/mol\alpha_R = 0.45\ \mathrm{mol/mol} (so n˙A=150 kmol/h\dot n_A = 150\ \mathrm{kmol/h} from Section 3), if the amine were methyldiethanolamine with MA=119.16 kg/kmolM_A = 119.16\ \mathrm{kg/kmol}, if wA=0.50 kg/kgw_A = 0.50\ \mathrm{kg/kg}, and if ρS=1050 kg/m3\rho_S = 1050\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}, then m˙S=150×119.16/0.50=35 748 kg/h\dot m_S = 150 \times 119.16 / 0.50 = 35\,748\ \mathrm{kg/h} and V˙S=35 748/1050=34.0 m3/h\dot V_S = 35\,748 / 1050 = 34.0\ \mathrm{m^3/h}. Each of those four input values is an added assumption; changing any of them changes the result.

6. Data required for a unique design value
  1. Rich loading αR\alpha_R (mol/mol), or equivalently the design loading increase αR−αL\alpha_R - \alpha_L (mol/mol), or sufficient data to calculate the equilibrium rich loading: amine identity, absorber temperature (K or °C) and pressure (Pa or bar), and inlet gas H2S\mathrm{H_2S} partial pressure (Pa or bar), together with an applicable equilibrium model.
  2. Amine concentration, as xAx_A (mol/mol) or wAw_A (kg/kg), to convert amine flow to total solution flow.
  3. Amine molar mass MAM_A (kg/kmol) and solution density ρS\rho_S (kg/m3^3), if a mass or volumetric solution flow is required.
7. Conclusion

The solvent requirement is n˙A=60/(αR−0.05) kmol amine/h\dot n_A = 60 / (\alpha_R - 0.05)\ \mathrm{kmol\ amine/h}, with 6060 in kmol/h and loadings in mol/mol. With the lean loading αL=0.05 mol/mol\alpha_L = 0.05\ \mathrm{mol/mol} as the only loading datum, no unique amine flow, and hence no unique aqueous solution flow, exists. A representative case at αR=0.45 mol/mol\alpha_R = 0.45\ \mathrm{mol/mol} gives n˙A=150 kmol amine/h\dot n_A = 150\ \mathrm{kmol\ amine/h}; a case at αR=0.25 mol/mol\alpha_R = 0.25\ \mathrm{mol/mol} gives 300 kmol amine/h300\ \mathrm{kmol\ amine/h}; both satisfy the stated data.

Response with defensive prompt

Amine Solvent Flow for Hydrogen Sulfide Removal

Result in brief

No single solvent flow follows from the data given. The data given fix the hydrogen sulfide removal rate and the lean loading only. The rich loading, which sets the circulation, depends on the amine identity, the amine concentration, the absorber temperature, the hydrogen sulfide partial pressure in the feed gas at the absorber bottom, the carbon dioxide content of the feed gas, and the treated-gas specification. None of those conditions is stated in the problem.

Two bounded cases are therefore calculated:

  • Optimistic, corrosion-limited case: 133 kmol of amine per hour, as methyldiethanolamine (MDEA) in a 45 weight percent (wt %) aqueous solution equal to about 35,300 kg of solution per hour.
  • Equilibrium-limited case at low hydrogen sulfide partial pressure: 667 kmol of amine per hour on the same solution basis, equal to about 176,500 kg of solution per hour.

The nominal stoichiometric result, 63 kmol of amine per hour, is calculated in Section 4 only to show why it must not be used.

1. Symbols and given data

Every symbol is defined here, at or before its first use.

  • F(H2S) = molar flow of hydrogen sulfide (H2S) to be removed, in kilomoles per hour (kmol/h). Given: F(H2S) = 60 kmol/h.
  • alpha = loading, in moles of acid gas per mole of amine (mol/mol). Acid gas means H2S plus, where present, carbon dioxide (CO2).
  • alpha_lean = loading of the lean solvent leaving the regenerator and entering the absorber, in mol/mol. Given: alpha_lean = 0.05 mol/mol. Source: the problem statement. This value is taken as stated, for H2S loading. Section 5 notes how it compares with published lean loadings.
  • alpha_rich = loading of the rich solvent leaving the absorber, in mol/mol.
  • alpha_rich,eq = value of alpha_rich in equilibrium with the feed gas at the absorber bottom temperature and feed-gas H2S partial pressure, in mol/mol.
  • Delta_alpha = net pickup per mole of amine circulated, in mol/mol, defined as Delta_alpha = alpha_rich - alpha_lean.
  • n_amine = molar circulation rate of amine itself (not of solution), in kmol of amine per hour (kmol/h).
  • w_amine = mass fraction of amine in the aqueous solution, dimensionless.
  • M_amine = molar mass of the amine, in kilograms per kilomole (kg/kmol).
  • m_solution = mass circulation rate of aqueous solution, in kilograms per hour (kg/h).
  • rho_solution = density of the aqueous solution, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m3).
  • V_solution = volumetric circulation rate of aqueous solution, in cubic metres per hour (m3/h).
  • p(H2S) = partial pressure of H2S in the feed gas, in kilopascals (kPa).
  • T = absorber bottom temperature, in degrees Celsius (deg C).
2. Material balance

The absorber balance on H2S, with no amine loss and no H2S in the treated gas counted in the 60 kmol/h removal figure, is:

n_amine = F(H2S) / Delta_alpha
        = F(H2S) / (alpha_rich - alpha_lean)          (1)

Equation (1) is exact for the stated removal, subject to two conditions:

  1. alpha_rich and alpha_lean are both H2S loadings, or both total acid-gas loadings with F(H2S) replaced by the total acid-gas removal rate. If CO2 is co-absorbed, total acid-gas pickup is larger than 60 kmol/h, the H2S part of Delta_alpha is smaller than the total Delta_alpha, and the circulation required for the H2S duty alone is larger than Equation (1) with H2S loadings gives. A CO2-free basis is assumed in the cases below because no CO2 rate is stated; that assumption is favourable (it gives a lower circulation), not conservative.
  2. alpha_rich cannot exceed alpha_rich,eq at the absorber bottom, and in design it is normally held below equilibrium. Published design guidance places the absorber bottom at no more than about 80 % approach to equilibrium, and amine best-practice guidance at 70 % or less approach at the bottom tray, to retain driving force. An actual rich loading below the equilibrium value raises the circulation above the equilibrium-limited figures in Section 6.

Solution mass and volume follow from n_amine by:

m_solution = n_amine * M_amine / w_amine               (2)
V_solution = m_solution / rho_solution                 (3)
3. Rich and lean loadings: values and sources
3.1 Lean loading
  • alpha_lean = 0.05 mol/mol. Source: given in the problem.
  • Comparison with published ranges, as a check on plausibility only: GPSA Engineering Data Book operating parameters reproduced in Kidnay, Parrish and McCartney, Fundamentals of Natural Gas Processing, give lean residual acid-gas loadings of about 0.12 mol/mol for monoethanolamine (MEA), about 0.08 mol/mol for diethanolamine (DEA), and 0.005 to 0.01 mol/mol for MDEA. A lean loading of 0.05 mol/mol is therefore high for a well-stripped MDEA solvent and low for MEA. It is consistent with, for example, a DEA solvent or a lightly stripped MDEA solvent. Because the amine is not named, the given value is used unchanged in all cases, and the amine-dependence is carried through the rich loading and the solution concentration instead.
3.2 Corrosion limit on the rich loading

Corrosion, not stoichiometry, caps the rich loading in carbon-steel equipment. Published limits, all for total acid-gas loading:

  • Practitioner corrosion limit: most practitioners adopt a rich-amine total acid-gas loading upper limit of 0.40 to 0.50 mol/mol. Source: Jones and Hatcher, "Predicting and Mitigating Corrosion in Amine Units", Laurance Reid Gas Conditioning Conference, 2015. The same source treats 0.40 to 0.45 mol/mol as the recommended range to stay below.
  • API Recommended Practice 581, amine corrosion section: in H2S plus CO2 systems rich loading is often limited to 0.35 to 0.45 mol/mol; in H2S-only systems rich loadings up to 0.70 mol/mol have been satisfactory; lean solution is typically below 0.10 mol/mol. The section also states the common concentrations 20 wt % MEA, 30 wt % DEA, and 40 to 50 wt % MDEA, with corrosion increasing above them.
  • GATE Energy, "H2S Scavenging: Amine Systems": MEA at 15 to 20 wt % and DEA at 25 to 35 wt % are each limited to 0.30 to 0.35 mol/mol in carbon steel; DGA (diglycolamine) is likewise limited to about 0.35 mol/mol; MDEA at 20 to 50 wt % is listed at 0.70 to 0.80 mol/mol, stated to be condition dependent. The MEA limit is corroborated independently for CO2 service: maximum MEA rich loading 0.35 mol/mol without corrosion inhibitors, lean loading at most 0.15 mol/mol, and amine strength at most 20 wt %.
  • GPSA operating table (see Section 3.1): rich loadings of 0.45 to 0.52 mol/mol for MEA, 0.43 to 0.73 mol/mol for DEA, and 0.40 to 0.55 mol/mol for MDEA at 40 to 50 wt %. These tabulated operating values sit at or above the carbon-steel corrosion limits above for MEA, which is why a tabulated operating range must not be read as a corrosion-safe design limit for every metallurgy.

Adopted corrosion limit for the optimistic case: alpha_rich = 0.50 mol/mol, the top of the Jones and Hatcher practitioner range and inside the GPSA MDEA rich range. It is optimistic because it (a) assumes MDEA-type corrosion behaviour rather than MEA/DEA behaviour, (b) assumes no CO2 pickup consuming part of that loading, and (c) takes the top, not the middle, of the range. For an MEA solvent the corresponding corrosion-limited value is alpha_rich = 0.35 mol/mol, calculated separately in Section 5.

3.3 Equilibrium rich loading

alpha_rich,eq is a function of T, p(H2S), amine identity, and w_amine. It rises steeply with p(H2S) and falls with T. Documented points:

  • Aqueous MDEA, T = 40 deg C, p(H2S) = 1 kPa: H2S loading of 0.14 mol/mol in 23.8 wt % MDEA, measured in a screening apparatus and in agreement (4.6 % deviation) with Jou, Mather and Otto, Industrial and Engineering Chemistry Process Design and Development, 1982. Source: Processes 2019, 7, 160, benchmark experiment.
  • Aqueous MDEA, 30 wt %, p(H2S) = 5 kPa: loading of 0.1 to 0.3 mol/mol over T = 100 to 40 deg C, higher at lower T. Sources cited for that range: Li and Shen, Journal of Chemical and Engineering Data, 1993, 38, 105-108, and Huttenhuis et al., Journal of Petroleum Science and Engineering, 2007, 55, 122-134; as worked in the University of Maryland H2S-removal material-balance notes, which apply 0.1 mol/mol at p(H2S) = 5 kPa as the saturation check.
  • General trend, stated in the MDEA solubility literature: at fixed T and w_amine, loading increases with p(H2S); at fixed p(H2S) and T, loading decreases as amine concentration increases.

Adopted equilibrium-limited case: alpha_rich = alpha_rich,eq = 0.14 mol/mol, at the stated conditions T = 40 deg C, p(H2S) = 1 kPa, aqueous MDEA. These conditions are stated here as an illustrative low-pressure case (for example a low-pressure or tail-gas feed), not as conditions given in the problem, because the problem gives no T and no p(H2S). At a high-pressure natural-gas feed, where p(H2S) is tens to hundreds of kPa, alpha_rich,eq is substantially higher and the corrosion limit of Section 3.2, not equilibrium, controls. Which limit controls cannot be decided until T and p(H2S) are supplied.

4. Why the nominal capacity must not be used

The proton-transfer reaction for a tertiary amine is, in words, one amine molecule accepting the proton from one H2S molecule to give a protonated amine cation and a bisulfide anion. The stoichiometric ratio is therefore 1 mol of H2S per mole of amine. Setting alpha_rich = 1.00 mol/mol on that basis gives:

Delta_alpha = 1.00 - 0.05 = 0.95 mol/mol
n_amine     = 60 / 0.95 = 63.2 kmol/h

That result is not a design value, for three stated reasons:

  1. Equilibrium: the equilibrium H2S partial pressure over the solution rises steeply as loading approaches 1 mol/mol (see the Jou et al. data summarised in Section 3.3). Reaching 1.00 mol/mol at the absorber bottom would require a feed p(H2S) far above the low-kPa range of the documented points, at absorber temperature.
  2. Corrosion: 1.00 mol/mol is two to three times the carbon-steel corrosion limits in Section 3.2 (0.35 mol/mol for MEA, 0.40 to 0.50 mol/mol total acid gas as the general practitioner limit).
  3. Approach to equilibrium: a real absorber is designed below, not at, the bottom equilibrium loading (Section 2, condition 2), so even a thermodynamically attainable loading is not fully realised.

The nominal figure understates the optimistic circulation in Section 5 by a factor of about 2.1, and the equilibrium-limited circulation in Section 6 by a factor of about 10.6.

5. Circulation: optimistic (corrosion-limited) case

Basis: alpha_lean = 0.05 mol/mol (given); alpha_rich = 0.50 mol/mol (Section 3.2, corrosion limit, MDEA-type solvent, no CO2 pickup).

Delta_alpha = 0.50 - 0.05 = 0.45 mol/mol
n_amine     = 60 kmol/h / 0.45 mol/mol = 133 kmol/h of amine

Conversion to solution flow, Equations (2) and (3), for MDEA with M_amine = 119.16 kg/kmol (CH3N(CH2CH2OH)2) at w_amine = 0.45 (45 wt %, inside the published 40 to 50 wt % MDEA range):

m_solution = 133.3 * 119.16 / 0.45 = about 35,300 kg/h of solution
V_solution = about 34 m3/h, at rho_solution = about 1,040 kg/m3
             (stated approximation for aqueous MDEA near absorber
             temperature; the mass flow is the primary result)

Sensitivity within the optimistic family:

Case alpha_rich (mol/mol) Delta_alpha (mol/mol) n_amine (kmol/h)
MDEA / mixed acid gas, top of corrosion range 0.50 0.45 133
MDEA, bottom of GPSA rich range 0.40 0.35 171
MEA in carbon steel, corrosion limit 0.35 0.30 200

For the MEA row, with M_amine = 61.08 kg/kmol and w_amine = 0.20 (20 wt %), Equation (2) gives m_solution = 200 * 61.08 / 0.20 = about 61,100 kg/h of solution. The amine identity alone therefore changes the optimistic solution mass flow by a factor of about 1.7, at the same H2S duty.

An H2S-only MDEA case at the API RP 581 upper satisfactory value, alpha_rich = 0.70 mol/mol, would give Delta_alpha = 0.65 mol/mol and n_amine = 92 kmol/h. It is reported here only as a bound: it requires H2S-only service, MDEA, and metallurgy and contaminant control for which 0.70 mol/mol has been satisfactory, and it must not be used for a mixed H2S plus CO2 feed or for MEA/DEA.

6. Circulation: equilibrium-limited case

Basis: alpha_lean = 0.05 mol/mol (given); alpha_rich = alpha_rich,eq = 0.14 mol/mol at T = 40 deg C and p(H2S) = 1 kPa in aqueous MDEA (Section 3.3, Jou et al. data as benchmarked in Processes 2019).

Delta_alpha = 0.14 - 0.05 = 0.09 mol/mol
n_amine     = 60 kmol/h / 0.09 mol/mol = 667 kmol/h of amine

On the same MDEA solution basis as Section 5 (M_amine = 119.16 kg/kmol, w_amine = 0.45):

m_solution = 666.7 * 119.16 / 0.45 = about 176,500 kg/h of solution
V_solution = about 170 m3/h, at rho_solution = about 1,040 kg/m3

This is 5.0 times the optimistic amine circulation. Two further effects raise it, neither included in the figure above:

  • Approach to equilibrium below 100 % at the absorber bottom (Section 2) lowers the realised alpha_rich below 0.14 mol/mol.
  • At p(H2S) = 5 kPa the conservative saturation value applied in the Maryland worked notes is 0.10 mol/mol, which would give Delta_alpha = 0.05 mol/mol and n_amine = 1,200 kmol/h. The range at 5 kPa is 0.1 to 0.3 mol/mol depending on T (Section 3.3), so no single equilibrium circulation can be quoted without T.

Conversely, if the feed is a high-pressure gas with p(H2S) well above 5 kPa, alpha_rich,eq rises above 0.50 mol/mol and the Section 5 corrosion-limited circulation, 133 kmol/h of amine, is the controlling (and larger-duty) bound of the two mechanisms considered here. The controlling case is decided by p(H2S) and T, which are not given.

7. Answer and data required for a single design value
  • Amine circulation, optimistic and corrosion-limited (MDEA-type solvent, alpha_rich = 0.50 mol/mol, alpha_lean = 0.05 mol/mol): n_amine = 133 kmol/h of amine, about 35,300 kg/h of 45 wt % aqueous MDEA solution.
  • Amine circulation, equilibrium-limited at the stated illustrative conditions (40 deg C, p(H2S) = 1 kPa, alpha_rich,eq = 0.14 mol/mol, same lean loading): n_amine = 667 kmol/h of amine, about 176,500 kg/h of the same solution; up to 1,200 kmol/h of amine on the conservative 0.10 mol/mol saturation value at 5 kPa.
  • Corrosion limit applied: total acid-gas rich loading 0.40 to 0.50 mol/mol in carbon steel (0.30 to 0.35 mol/mol for MEA and DEA; up to 0.70 mol/mol reported satisfactory for H2S-only service).
  • Rejected: alpha_rich = 1.00 mol/mol nominal stoichiometric capacity, giving 63 kmol/h of amine (Section 4).

To reduce this to one design circulation, the following must be supplied: amine identity and w_amine; feed-gas total pressure and H2S mole fraction (hence p(H2S)) and CO2 mole fraction and CO2 removal requirement; feed-gas and lean-solvent temperatures at the absorber (hence T); treated-gas H2S specification (which, with alpha_lean, sets the lean-end pinch); and equipment metallurgy (which sets whether the carbon-steel corrosion limits in Section 3.2 apply). A rate-based absorber simulation or vendor equilibrium data for the named solvent at those conditions then fixes alpha_rich,eq, and Equation (1) fixes n_amine.

Sources

A4. Estimated Properties and Compressibility — Second Gas

Response without defensive prompt

Density of an Unnamed Gas at 60 bar and 350 K

Given data and symbols
  • ρ\rho is the mass density of the gas, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m3\mathrm{kg/m^3}); ρ\rho is the quantity to be estimated.
  • PP is the absolute pressure, P=60 bar=6.0×106 PaP = 60\ \mathrm{bar} = 6.0\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{Pa}, where Pa\mathrm{Pa} is the pascal.
  • TT is the absolute temperature, T=350 KT = 350\ \mathrm{K}, where K\mathrm{K} is the kelvin.
  • MM is the molar mass, M=0.044 kg/molM = 0.044\ \mathrm{kg/mol}.
  • RR is the universal gas constant, R=8.314 J/(mol K)R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}.
  • ZZ is the compressibility factor, a dimensionless number defined below; Z=1Z = 1 for an ideal gas.
  • VmV_m is the molar volume, in cubic metres per mole (m3/mol\mathrm{m^3/mol}).

The gas is not named, and no critical properties, no acentric factor, no equation-of-state parameters, and no measured PP–VmV_m–TT data are supplied.

Assumption-free estimate: ideal-gas law

With no information about intermolecular forces, the only density that can be computed from the supplied data alone is the ideal-gas value. The ideal-gas law, in molar form, states that PVm=RTP V_m = R T, and the density follows from ρ=M/Vm\rho = M / V_m. Combining the two relations gives

ρ=PMRT.\rho = \frac{P M}{R T}.

Substitution of the given values gives

ρ=(6.0×106 Pa)(0.044 kg/mol)(8.314 J/(mol K))(350 K)=2.64×1052.910×103 kg/m3≈90.7 kg/m3.\rho = \frac{(6.0\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{Pa})(0.044\ \mathrm{kg/mol})}{(8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\,K)})(350\ \mathrm{K})} = \frac{2.64\times10^{5}}{2.910\times10^{3}}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} \approx 90.7\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}.

The units check: Pa=J/m3\mathrm{Pa} = \mathrm{J/m^3}, so PM/(RT)PM/(RT) has units of (J/m3)(kg/mol)/(J/mol)=kg/m3(\mathrm{J/m^3})(\mathrm{kg/mol}) / (\mathrm{J/mol}) = \mathrm{kg/m^3}, as required.

Result of the ideal-gas estimate: ρ≈91 kg/m3\rho \approx 91\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}.

Why a more accurate real-gas value cannot be obtained from the data given

For a real gas the ideal-gas law is replaced by

PVm=ZRT,soρ=PMZRT=90.7 kg/m3Z.P V_m = Z R T, \qquad \text{so} \qquad \rho = \frac{P M}{Z R T} = \frac{90.7\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}}{Z}.

The compressibility factor ZZ depends on the identity of the gas (through its critical temperature, its critical pressure, and the strength and shape of its intermolecular forces) and on the phase of the material. None of that information is supplied, and MM alone does not supply it: several common gases have a molar mass near 0.044 kg/mol0.044\ \mathrm{kg/mol} but very different critical properties — for example carbon dioxide, nitrous oxide, and propane all have M≈0.044 kg/molM \approx 0.044\ \mathrm{kg/mol}.

At P=60 barP = 60\ \mathrm{bar} the pressure is high enough that ZZ cannot be assumed to be close to 1 without justification, so the correction is not a minor one. Two conditional illustrations, each computed with the Peng–Robinson equation of state using published critical properties for the named gas, show the size and the non-uniqueness of the correction:

  • If the gas were carbon dioxide (critical temperature 304 K304\ \mathrm{K}, critical pressure 73.8 bar73.8\ \mathrm{bar}), the reduced temperature T/TcT/T_c would be 1.151.15 and the reduced pressure P/PcP/P_c would be 0.810.81; the Peng–Robinson equation gives Z≈0.79Z \approx 0.79 and hence ρ≈114 kg/m3\rho \approx 114\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}, about 26%26\% above the ideal-gas value.
  • If the gas were nitrous oxide (critical temperature 310 K310\ \mathrm{K}, critical pressure 72.5 bar72.5\ \mathrm{bar}), the same calculation gives Z≈0.77Z \approx 0.77 and ρ≈118 kg/m3\rho \approx 118\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}.

A third case shows that even the phase is not fixed by the data: propane, with the same nominal MM, has a critical temperature of 370 K370\ \mathrm{K}, above the stated 350 K350\ \mathrm{K}, and a critical pressure of 42.5 bar42.5\ \mathrm{bar}, below the stated 60 bar60\ \mathrm{bar}; at 350 K350\ \mathrm{K} and 60 bar60\ \mathrm{bar} propane is a compressed liquid, not a gas, with a density several times larger than the values above. A single molar mass is therefore compatible with gas densities differing by far more than any rounding in the ideal-gas calculation.

Conclusion
  • The only estimate determined by the stated data is the ideal-gas estimate,

ρ≈91 kg/m3at 60 barand350 K.\rho \approx 91\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} \quad \text{at } 60\ \mathrm{bar and } 350\ \mathrm{K}.

  • This value should be reported as an order-of-magnitude / first estimate, of order 102 kg/m310^{2}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}. A real gas at 60 bar60\ \mathrm{bar} will in general deviate from it — for a carbon-dioxide-like gas, by roughly +25%+25\%, giving ρ≈1.1×102 kg/m3\rho \approx 1.1\times10^{2}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}.
  • A unique, accurate real-gas density cannot be stated until the gas is identified (or, equivalently, its critical properties and acentric factor, an equation of state with its parameters, or measured density / compressibility data at or near 60 bar60\ \mathrm{bar} and 350 K350\ \mathrm{K} are supplied), and until the material is confirmed to be in the gas phase at the stated conditions.

1. Why the identity matters

M=0.044 kg/mol=44 g/molM = 0.044\ \text{kg/mol} = 44\ \text{g/mol} does not identify a substance. At least three common substances match it to the precision given:

  • carbon dioxide, CO2\mathrm{CO_2}, M=0.044010 kg/molM = 0.044010\ \text{kg/mol};
  • nitrous oxide, N2O\mathrm{N_2O}, M=0.044013 kg/molM = 0.044013\ \text{kg/mol};
  • propane, C3H8\mathrm{C_3H_8}, M=0.044096 kg/molM = 0.044096\ \text{kg/mol}.

At low pressure these would have nearly the same density, because the ideal-gas density depends only on MM. At 60 bar60\ \text{bar} the density depends also on how close the state is to condensation, which is set by the critical properties of the specific substance. Those properties cannot be obtained from MM. Any critical temperature or critical pressure inferred from MM alone, or from a group-contribution estimate for an assumed structure, is an estimate for an assumed identity, not a measured property of the unnamed gas. No such estimated critical property is used in the headline range below.

2. Ideal-gas baseline

The universal gas constant is denoted RR, in joules per mole per kelvin (J/(mol K)), with R=8.314 J/(mol K)R = 8.314\ \text{J/(mol K)}. The ideal-gas density is

ρideal=PMRT=(6.0×106)(0.044)(8.314)(350)=90.7 kg/m3.\rho_{\mathrm{ideal}} = \frac{PM}{RT} = \frac{(6.0\times10^{6})(0.044)}{(8.314)(350)} = 90.7\ \text{kg/m}^{3}.

The compressibility factor is denoted ZZ, dimensionless, and is defined by Z=PM/(ρRT)Z = PM/(\rho RT), so that ρ=ρideal/Z\rho = \rho_{\mathrm{ideal}}/Z. An ideal gas has Z=1Z = 1. At 60 bar60\ \text{bar}, attractive intermolecular forces are expected to make Z<1Z < 1 and ρ>ρideal\rho > \rho_{\mathrm{ideal}} for a gas not far above its critical temperature. A value of ZZ is therefore required, and ZZ is substance-specific.

Route 1: Pitzer generalised virial correlation

The Peng–Robinson equation uses a temperature-dependent attraction parameter denoted aa, in pascal square metres per square mole (Pa m6^{6}/mol2^{2}), a co-volume parameter denoted bb, in cubic metres per mole (m3^{3}/mol), a dimensionless temperature function denoted α\alpha (not to be confused with any other quantity), and a dimensionless slope parameter denoted κ\kappa, defined from ω\omega.
