A5. Crystallisation Yield — Second Solute

Response without defensive prompt

Crystal Yield from Cooling a Saturated Solution

Given data and definitions
  • msolventm_{\text{solvent}} (mass of solvent, in grams, g) is the basis mass of solvent, set to msolvent=100 gm_{\text{solvent}} = 100\ \text{g}.
  • S80S_{80} (solubility of the solute at 80 ∘C80\ ^{\circ}\text{C}, in grams of solute per 100 g of solvent, g per 100 g) is S80=45 g per 100 gS_{80} = 45\ \text{g per 100 g}.
  • S25S_{25} (solubility of the solute at 25 ∘C25\ ^{\circ}\text{C}, in grams of solute per 100 g of solvent, g per 100 g) is S25=18 g per 100 gS_{25} = 18\ \text{g per 100 g}.
  • mdissolved,80m_{\text{dissolved,80}} (mass of solute dissolved in the saturated solution at 80 ∘C80\ ^{\circ}\text{C}, in grams, g) is the mass dissolved on the stated basis at 80 ∘C80\ ^{\circ}\text{C}.
  • mdissolved,25m_{\text{dissolved,25}} (mass of solute remaining dissolved in the saturated solution at 25 ∘C25\ ^{\circ}\text{C}, in grams, g) is the mass that can remain dissolved on the stated basis at 25 ∘C25\ ^{\circ}\text{C}.
  • mcrystalm_{\text{crystal}} (mass of solute that crystallises on cooling, the crystal yield, in grams, g) is the mass that leaves solution as solid on cooling from 80 ∘C80\ ^{\circ}\text{C} to 25 ∘C25\ ^{\circ}\text{C}.

The solution is saturated at both temperatures. No solvent is lost on cooling, no solute is lost other than by crystallisation, and the crystals are taken to be pure solute with no solvent of crystallisation or adhering mother liquor. The calculation is therefore a solute mass balance on a fixed solvent basis.

Calculation

On the basis msolvent=100 gm_{\text{solvent}} = 100\ \text{g}:

At 80 ∘C80\ ^{\circ}\text{C}, the saturated solution holds

mdissolved,80=S80=45 gm_{\text{dissolved,80}} = S_{80} = 45\ \text{g}

of solute dissolved.

At 25 ∘C25\ ^{\circ}\text{C}, the saturated solution can hold only

mdissolved,25=S25=18 gm_{\text{dissolved,25}} = S_{25} = 18\ \text{g}

of solute dissolved.

The excess solute must leave solution as crystals. By the solute mass balance,

mcrystal=mdissolved,80−mdissolved,25m_{\text{crystal}} = m_{\text{dissolved,80}} - m_{\text{dissolved,25}}

mcrystal=45 g−18 g=27 gm_{\text{crystal}} = 45\ \text{g} - 18\ \text{g} = 27\ \text{g}

Result

The crystal yield is 27 g of crystals per 100 g of solvent.

As a check, 27 g27\ \text{g} crystallised plus 18 g18\ \text{g} remaining dissolved equals the 45 g45\ \text{g} dissolved initially, so the solute balance closes. The fraction of the initially dissolved solute recovered as crystals is 27/45=0.6027 / 45 = 0.60, i.e. 60%.

Crystal Yield on Cooling a Saturated Solution

Data and assumptions
  • Msolv,0M_{\mathrm{solv},0}: mass of solvent initially present, in grams (g) — Msolv,0=100 gM_{\mathrm{solv},0} = 100\ \mathrm{g}, the basis of the calculation.
  • T1T_1: initial temperature, in degrees Celsius (°C) — T1=80 ∘CT_1 = 80\ \mathrm{^\circ C}.

Source of each solubility: both S80S_{80} and S25S_{25} are taken from the problem statement. No solute is named in the problem statement, so no external solubility table can be identified for the solute, and no external value is substituted for either figure.

Solid form assumed: anhydrous crystals, i.e. f=1f = 1. The problem statement specifies no hydrate, no water of crystallisation, and no solute identity from which a hydrate stoichiometry could be obtained. The calculation therefore assumes that the crystals contain solute only and remove no solvent from the liquid.

Further assumptions, each required for the simple difference below to hold:

  1. The solution is saturated at 80 ∘C80\ \mathrm{^\circ C} and reaches equilibrium saturation at 25 ∘C25\ \mathrm{^\circ C}; no supersaturation persists.
  2. No solvent is lost by evaporation during cooling, and no solvent is incorporated into the crystals (consistent with the anhydrous assumption).
  3. No mother liquor is entrained in the recovered crystals, and no solute is lost by any other route.
  4. The solubility figures are on the stated basis, grams of solute per 100 g of solvent, at both temperatures.
Nominal calculation

Mass of solute dissolved at 80 ∘C80\ \mathrm{^\circ C} on the stated basis:

45 g solute per 100 g solvent45\ \mathrm{g\ solute\ per\ 100\ g\ solvent}

Mass of solute that remains dissolved at 25 ∘C25\ \mathrm{^\circ C}, with the solvent mass unchanged at 100 g under the assumptions above:

18 g solute per 100 g solvent18\ \mathrm{g\ solute\ per\ 100\ g\ solvent}

Because the solvent mass is unchanged, the yield is the difference of the two solubilities:

Y=S80−S25=45−18=27 g per 100 g of initial solventY = S_{80} - S_{25} = 45 - 18 = 27\ \mathrm{g\ per\ 100\ g\ of\ initial\ solvent}

Mass-balance check:

  • Feed solution: 100 g100\ \mathrm{g} solvent + 45 g+\ 45\ \mathrm{g} solute =145 g= 145\ \mathrm{g}.
  • Crystals: 27 g27\ \mathrm{g}.
  • Final mother liquor: 100 g100\ \mathrm{g} solvent + 18 g+\ 18\ \mathrm{g} solute =118 g= 118\ \mathrm{g}.
  • Total out: 27+118=145 g27 + 118 = 145\ \mathrm{g}, equal to the feed mass.

Fraction of the initially dissolved solute recovered as crystals:

27/45=0.6027 / 45 = 0.60

i.e. 60% is crystallised and 40% remains in the mother liquor.

Nominal result: Y=27Y = 27 g of anhydrous crystals per 100 g of initial solvent.

Effect of a hydrate solid form

If the solid were a hydrate, ff would be less than 1, the crystals would remove solvent as water of crystallisation, and the crystal mass would be larger than 27 g per 100 g for the same amount of solute crystallised. A numerical hydrate yield cannot be computed from the data given: it would require the hydrate stoichiometry and the molar masses of the solute and the hydrate, none of which is supplied because no solute is named. The value of 27 g per 100 g is therefore stated strictly as the anhydrous result, not as a hydrate result.

Second-source comparison and uncertainty

No second solubility source can be given: no solute is named, so there is no identified substance whose solubility could be looked up in a second table, and assigning the given figures to a particular solute would be unsupported. The comparison is therefore made over a stated solubility uncertainty instead.

Stated uncertainty adopted for this estimate: each solubility is uncertain by ±5% of its stated value, treated as an illustrative uncertainty for textbook solubility figures quoted to two significant figures. This uncertainty is an assumption of this solution, not a figure from the problem statement.

  • S80=45±2.25S_{80} = 45 \pm 2.25 g per 100 g.
  • S25=18±0.90S_{25} = 18 \pm 0.90 g per 100 g.
  • Nominal difference: Y=45−18=27Y = 45 - 18 = 27 g per 100 g.

Worst-case range (errors in opposite directions):

  • Low: (45−2.25)−(18+0.90)=23.85(45 - 2.25) - (18 + 0.90) = 23.85 g per 100 g.
  • High: (45+2.25)−(18−0.90)=30.15(45 + 2.25) - (18 - 0.90) = 30.15 g per 100 g.

Independent-error (root-sum-square) combination:

  • Combined uncertainty: 2.252+0.902=2.4\sqrt{2.25^{2} + 0.90^{2}} = 2.4 g per 100 g, giving Y=27±2.4Y = 27 \pm 2.4 g per 100 g.

For reference, a smaller assumed uncertainty of ±1 g per 100 g on each solubility would give a worst-case range of 25 to 29 g per 100 g and a root-sum-square result of 27±1.427 \pm 1.4 g per 100 g.

Result
  • Nominal yield (anhydrous crystals, solubilities as given in the problem statement): 27 g per 100 g of initial solvent, corresponding to 60% recovery of the dissolved solute.
  • Over the stated ±5% solubility uncertainty: 27 ± 2.4 g per 100 g (root-sum-square), with a worst-case range of 23.9 to 30.2 g per 100 g.
  • No second-source yield is reported, because the solute is not identified in the problem statement and no external solubility source can therefore be assigned without invention.

B1. Arrhenius Extrapolation — Second Reaction

Response without defensive prompt

Rate Constant at 450 K

Given data
  • k1k_1, the rate constant at the reference temperature, is 0.020 s−10.020\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}.
  • T1T_1, the reference temperature, is 350 K350\ \mathrm{K}.
  • T2T_2, the temperature at which the rate constant is required, is 450 K450\ \mathrm{K}.
  • EaE_a, the activation energy, is 95 kJ mol−1=95,000 J mol−195\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} = 95{,}000\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}.
  • EaE_a was fitted over 340340 to 370 K370\ \mathrm{K}.
Model

The Arrhenius equation is

k=Aexp⁡(−EaRT)k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)

where kk is the rate constant in s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}}, AA is the pre-exponential factor in s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}}, RR is the universal gas constant, 8.314 J mol−1 K−18.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}, and TT is the absolute temperature in K\mathrm{K}.

For the same reaction at two temperatures, AA cancels when the ratio of the two rate constants is taken. With k2k_2 denoting the rate constant at T2T_2:

ln⁡(k2k1)=−EaR(1T2−1T1)\ln\left(\frac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = -\frac{E_a}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right)

This form assumes that AA and EaE_a are constant over the temperature interval between T1T_1 and T2T_2.

Calculation

EaR=95,000 J mol−18.314 J mol−1 K−1=1.143×104 K\frac{E_a}{R} = \frac{95{,}000\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}}{8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}} = 1.143 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{K}

1T2−1T1=1450 K−1350 K=2.222×10−3 K−1−2.857×10−3 K−1=−6.349×10−4 K−1\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1} = \frac{1}{450\ \mathrm{K}} - \frac{1}{350\ \mathrm{K}} = 2.222 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}} - 2.857 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}} = -6.349 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}

ln⁡(k2k1)=−(1.143×104 K)(−6.349×10−4 K−1)=7.25\ln\left(\frac{k_2}{k_1}\right) = -(1.143 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{K})(-6.349 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}) = 7.25

k2k1=exp⁡(7.25)=1.41×103\frac{k_2}{k_1} = \exp(7.25) = 1.41 \times 10^{3}

k2=(0.020 s−1)(1.41×103)=28 s−1k_2 = (0.020\ \mathrm{s^{-1}})(1.41 \times 10^{3}) = 28\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}

Result and scope

The nominal Arrhenius estimate is

k(450 K)≈28 s−1k(450\ \mathrm{K}) \approx 28\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}

This value is an extrapolation, not an interpolation. The fitted range ends at 370 K370\ \mathrm{K}, and 450 K450\ \mathrm{K} is 80 K80\ \mathrm{K} above that limit, a distance larger than the full 30 K30\ \mathrm{K} width of the fitted range. The calculation is valid only if the same reaction mechanism controls over the whole interval and EaE_a and AA remain effectively constant to 450 K450\ \mathrm{K}. A change in mechanism, a temperature-dependent EaE_a, transport limitations, or competing reactions at the higher temperature would change the actual value, and no data are provided to quantify that deviation. The figure of 28 s−128\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} should therefore be reported as a nominal extrapolated estimate requiring experimental confirmation at or near 450 K450\ \mathrm{K} before use for design or safety purposes. The large sensitivity is inherent in the exponential form: for example, an error of only 5 kJ mol−15\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}} in EaE_a changes the extrapolated ratio by a factor of exp⁡[(5,000 J mol−1/8.314 J mol−1 K−1)(6.349×10−4 K−1)]≈1.5\exp\left[(5{,}000\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}} / 8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}})(6.349 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}})\right] \approx 1.5.

k2k1=exp⁡[−EaR(1T2−1T1)]\frac{k_2}{k_1} = \exp\left[ -\frac{E_{\mathrm{a}}}{R} \left( \frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1} \right) \right]

Symbols

Governing relations

For a first-order reaction in an ideal plug-flow reactor at a given instant, with the catalyst activity treated as uniform in the reactor and constant over the residence time of a fluid element, the conversion is

X=1−exp⁡(−kτ a(t))X = 1 - \exp(-k\tau\, a(t))

where exp⁡\exp denotes the exponential function.

Exponential catalyst deactivation is described by

a(t)=exp⁡(−kdt)a(t) = \exp(-k_d t)

kτ a(t)=(1.6)(0.487)=0.779k\tau\, a(t) = (1.6)(0.487) = 0.779

Conversion at that time:

X=1−exp⁡(−0.779)=1−0.459=0.541X = 1 - \exp(-0.779) = 1 - 0.459 = 0.541

For reference, the fresh-catalyst conversion would be X=1−exp⁡(−1.6)=0.798X = 1 - \exp(-1.6) = 0.798.

  • kk is the first-order reaction rate constant for fresh catalyst, in reciprocal time (1/time).
  • τ\tau is the reactor residence time (equivalently, catalyst space time on the basis used to define kk), in time. Only the product kτk\tau is given, so kk and τ\tau are not needed separately.
  • kτ=1.6k\tau = 1.6, dimensionless, for fresh catalyst.
  • aa is the catalyst activity, dimensionless, defined as the reaction rate on the used catalyst divided by the reaction rate on fresh catalyst under the same conditions. Fresh catalyst has a=1a = 1.
  • tt is the time on stream, in days (d). The time of interest is t=240 dt = 240\ \mathrm{d}.
  • kdk_d is the catalyst deactivation constant, in reciprocal days (d−1\mathrm{d^{-1}}). The stated value is kd=0.003 d−1k_d = 0.003\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}.
Deactivation Law and Source

The deactivation law used is first-order decay of activity:

−dadt=kda,a(0)=1-\frac{da}{dt} = k_d a, \qquad a(0) = 1

Integration from a=1a = 1 at t=0t = 0 gives the exponential law stated in the problem:

a(t)=exp⁡(−kdt)a(t) = \exp(-k_d t)

Source: the exponential form is given in the problem statement. It is also the integrated form of the first-order catalyst decay law in the standard treatment of catalyst deactivation by H. Scott Fogler, Elements of Chemical Reaction Engineering, Chapter 10, "Catalysis and Catalytic Reactors," section on catalyst deactivation, where a(t)a(t) is defined as the ratio of the rate on a catalyst used for time tt to the rate on fresh catalyst, and the decay rate is written as a deactivation constant multiplied by a function of activity (p(a)=ap(a) = a for first-order decay). Fogler cites Szepe and Levenspiel, Chemical Engineering Science, 23, 881–894 (1968), for deactivation modelling. No other deactivation mechanism is specified, so no sintering law (second-order in aa in Fogler's treatment), coking law, or concentration-dependent poison term is used.

Plug-Flow Reactor Conversion

For an isothermal, constant-density, first-order reaction in an ideal plug-flow reactor (PFR), with the rate multiplied by the activity aa, integration of the PFR design equation over the residence time gives:

X=1−exp⁡(−kτ a)X = 1 - \exp(-k\tau\, a)

where kτ ak\tau\, a is dimensionless. This expression treats aa as uniform through the bed and constant during the short passage of a fluid element through the reactor, which is appropriate because tt (days) is much longer than τ\tau. The result is therefore the instantaneous conversion at age tt, not a time average over the run.

Check for fresh catalyst (a=1a = 1):

Xfresh=1−exp⁡(−1.6)=1−0.202=0.798X_{\text{fresh}} = 1 - \exp(-1.6) = 1 - 0.202 = 0.798

Fresh conversion is 0.800.80, or about 80%80\%.

Calculation at 240 Days

Activity at t=240 dt = 240\ \mathrm{d} and kd=0.003 d−1k_d = 0.003\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}:

kdt=(0.003 d−1)(240 d)=0.72(dimensionless)k_d t = (0.003\ \mathrm{d^{-1}})(240\ \mathrm{d}) = 0.72 \quad \text{(dimensionless)}

a(240 d)=exp⁡(−0.72)=0.487a(240\ \mathrm{d}) = \exp(-0.72) = 0.487

Effective dimensionless rate group:

kτ a=(1.6)(0.487)=0.779k\tau\, a = (1.6)(0.487) = 0.779

Conversion:

X=1−exp⁡(−0.779)=1−0.459=0.541X = 1 - \exp(-0.779) = 1 - 0.459 = 0.541

Estimated conversion after 240 days on stream: X≈0.54X \approx 0.54, or about 54%54\%, compared with about 80%80\% on fresh catalyst.

Sensitivity to the Deactivation Constant

The same calculation at half and at twice the stated kdk_d, with all other quantities unchanged:

Case kdk_d (d−1\mathrm{d^{-1}}) kdtk_d t at 240 d240\ \mathrm{d}, dimensionless a=exp⁡(−kdt)a = \exp(-k_d t), dimensionless kτak\tau a, dimensionless X=1−exp⁡(−kτa)X = 1 - \exp(-k\tau a), dimensionless
Half kdk_d 0.0015 0.36 0.698 1.116 0.673
Stated kdk_d 0.003 0.72 0.487 0.779 0.541
Twice kdk_d 0.006 1.44 0.237 0.379 0.316

Conversion is 0.670.67 (about 67%67\%) at half the deactivation constant and 0.320.32 (about 32%32\%) at twice the deactivation constant. The response is strongly non-linear: doubling kdk_d more than halves the remaining activity because aa depends exponentially on kdtk_d t, and XX then depends exponentially on aa.

Limits of the Estimate and Earlier End of Run

No feed composition, catalyst identity, poison identity, poison concentration, guard-bed specification, feed specification, product specification, or pressure-drop limit is given. A numerical feed poison limit therefore cannot be stated from the data given; any specific value (for example, a parts-per-million limit for a named poison) would have to come from the feed specification or catalyst supplier limit for the actual system, and stating one here would be unsupported.

Within those limits, the estimate rests on kdk_d remaining constant at 0.003 d−10.003\ \mathrm{d^{-1}} for the full 240 days, on isothermal operation, and on activity remaining uniform and described by the single exponential law. The run could end, or the estimate could cease to apply, before 240 days if any of the following occurred:

  • Feed poison breakthrough or a poison excursion. If a feed poison exceeded the applicable feed or catalyst limit for the actual system, or broke through an upstream guard bed, irreversible poisoning could raise the effective deactivation rate above the stated kdk_d, so deactivation would no longer follow a=exp⁡(−kdt)a = \exp(-k_d t) with the stated constant. A constant low poison level already present from the start could in principle be lumped into the stated kdk_d; a step increase cannot.
  • Conversion or product specification limit. If a minimum required conversion or product specification exists for the actual process, it could be crossed before 240 days, ending the useful run even though the catalyst still has activity a=0.487a = 0.487 at 240 days under the stated law.
  • Fouling or coking pressure-drop limit. Deposit build-up can raise bed pressure drop to the compressor, blower, or mechanical limit and force a shutdown independently of the activity calculation, which contains no pressure-drop term.
  • Temperature excursion and sintering. A hot spot or temperature excursion can sinter the catalyst, a mechanism with a different activity law, and can end the run or invalidate the stated kdk_d.
  • Mechanical or upstream event. Bed damage, support or distributor failure, feed interruption, or an upstream or downstream trip can end a run at any time; none of these is represented in the kinetic model.
Result

At the stated deactivation constant kd=0.003 d−1k_d = 0.003\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}, activity after 240 days is a=0.487a = 0.487 and the instantaneous first-order PFR conversion is X≈0.54X \approx 0.54 (about 54%54\%), down from X≈0.80X \approx 0.80 on fresh catalyst. At half kdk_d, X≈0.67X \approx 0.67; at twice kdk_d, X≈0.32X \approx 0.32. No numerical feed poison limit can be given from the stated data; poison breakthrough above the actual system's feed or catalyst limit, a conversion or product specification limit, a pressure-drop limit, sintering after a temperature excursion, or a mechanical or upstream event could each end the run before 240 days.

B3. Reactor Heat Removal — Second Duty

Response without defensive prompt

Cooling Area for a Reactor Releasing 800 kW

Given data and symbols
  • QQ is the heat removal rate, in watts (W): Q=800 kW=800,000 WQ = 800\ \mathrm{kW} = 800{,}000\ \mathrm{W}.
  • ΔTm\Delta T_{\mathrm{m}} is the mean temperature difference between the reaction mass and the coolant, in kelvin (K): ΔTm=30 K\Delta T_{\mathrm{m}} = 30\ \mathrm{K}.
  • AA is the heat-transfer area, in square metres (m2\mathrm{m^{2}}). AA is to be estimated.
  • UU is the overall heat-transfer coefficient based on area AA, in watts per square metre per kelvin (W m−2 K−1\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}). No value of UU is given in the problem statement.
Governing relation

For steady heat removal through a wall,

Q=UAΔTmQ = U A \Delta T_{\mathrm{m}}

so that

A=QUΔTmA = \frac{Q}{U \Delta T_{\mathrm{m}}}

Data gap

The problem as stated does not determine a unique value of AA, because no value of UU is given and no information is given from which UU can be calculated: no coolant identity or flow rate, no reaction-mass properties, no degree of agitation, no wall material or thickness, and no statement whether cooling is by a jacket, an internal coil, or an external heat exchanger, nor any fouling allowance.

A numerical estimate therefore requires an assumed UU taken from experience with a similar reactor system. The result is an order-of-magnitude design estimate, not a sizing calculation for construction.

Assumed overall heat-transfer coefficient

For an agitated, jacketed or coil-cooled vessel containing a low-viscosity, water-like reaction mass and cooled by water — the usual case implied by a problem of this type — published typical ranges for UU are roughly 300300 to 600 W m−2 K−1600\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}. A representative mid-range value is

U≈400 W m−2 K−1U \approx 400\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}

Higher viscosity, poor agitation, a viscous or fouling reaction mass, or a low coolant flow rate gives a lower UU and therefore a larger required AA. A clean coil or external exchanger with high flow rates on both sides gives a higher UU and a smaller required AA.

Calculation

With Q=800,000 WQ = 800{,}000\ \mathrm{W}, U=400 W m−2 K−1U = 400\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}, and ΔTm=30 K\Delta T_{\mathrm{m}} = 30\ \mathrm{K}:

A=800,000 W(400 W m−2 K−1)(30 K)=800,00012,000 m2≈66.7 m2A = \frac{800{,}000\ \mathrm{W}}{(400\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}})(30\ \mathrm{K})} = \frac{800{,}000}{12{,}000}\ \mathrm{m^{2}} \approx 66.7\ \mathrm{m^{2}}

i.e. about 67 m267\ \mathrm{m^{2}} on the stated assumption for UU.

Sensitivity to the assumed coefficient

The same calculation over the typical range for UU gives:

UU (W m−2 K−1\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}) A=Q/(UΔTm)A = Q/(U\Delta T_{\mathrm{m}}) (m2\mathrm{m^{2}})
200 133
300 88.9
400 66.7
500 53.3
600 44.4
1000 26.7

The value U=200 W m−2 K−1U = 200\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}} in the first row represents a more viscous, poorly agitated or fouled case, and U=1000 W m−2 K−1U = 1000\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}} in the last row represents a favourable external-exchanger case; neither is the base assumption above.

Result

On a representative assumption of U≈400 W m−2 K−1U \approx 400\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}} for an agitated aqueous reactor cooled by water, the required cooling area is approximately 67 m267\ \mathrm{m^{2}}, with a plausible range of about 4545 to 90 m290\ \mathrm{m^{2}} for UU between 600600 and 300 W m−2 K−1300\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-1}}.

A unique, defensible area for detailed design cannot be obtained from QQ and ΔTm\Delta T_{\mathrm{m}} alone. UU must first be established for the actual geometry, agitation, fluid properties, coolant conditions, wall, and fouling allowance. Provision in practice would normally be checked against that established UU and, if the 67 m267\ \mathrm{m^{2}} estimate were carried forward, rounded up with an explicit design margin rather than installed as exactly 67 m267\ \mathrm{m^{2}}.

Response with defensive prompt

Cooling Area for a Reactor Releasing 800 kW

Given quantities and symbols

All symbols are defined here, before first use in any equation.

  • QQ is the rate of heat to be removed, in watts (W). Given: Q=800 kilowatts (kW)=800,000 WQ = 800\ \text{kilowatts (kW)} = 800{,}000\ \text{W}.
  • ΔTm\Delta T_{\mathrm{m}} is the mean temperature difference between the reaction mass and the coolant, in kelvin (K). Given: ΔTm=30 K\Delta T_{\mathrm{m}} = 30\ \text{K}. A temperature difference of 1 K is equal to a temperature difference of 1 degree Celsius, so no conversion is required.
  • UU is the overall heat transfer coefficient, in watts per square metre per kelvin (W m−2^{-2} K−1^{-1}). No value is given in the problem.
  • AA is the heat transfer area, in square metres (m2^{2}), on the same area basis as UU.
Why no single area follows from the given data alone

The steady heat transfer relation is

Q=UAΔTmQ = U A \Delta T_{\mathrm{m}}

so that

A=QUΔTm.A = \frac{Q}{U \Delta T_{\mathrm{m}}}.

QQ and ΔTm\Delta T_{\mathrm{m}} are given, but UU is not. UU depends on the cooling arrangement, the reaction-mass properties (in particular viscosity), the coolant, the vessel or coil material, agitation, and fouling. A single numerical area stated without a stated UU and a stated arrangement is therefore unsupported. The result below is conditional, and is given at both ends of a named published range.

Named published range and configuration used

Arrangement: a well-designed internal (immersed) cooling coil in an agitated reactor vessel, with coolant inside the coil and the reaction mass outside the coil.

Published range: Carpenter, K. J., "Agitated Vessel Heat Transfer", A-to-Z Guide to Thermodynamics, Heat and Mass Transfer, and Fluids Engineering (Thermopedia), DOI 10.1615/AtoZ.a.agitated_vessel_heat_transfer, states, as a general guide: "A typical overall coefficient for a well designed coil would be 400 to 600 W m−2^{-2} K−1^{-1}." The same guide attributes its stirred-batch-reactor coefficient data in part to Fletcher, P. (1987), "Heat Transfer Coefficients for Stirred Batch Reactor Design", The Chemical Engineer.

Configuration to which the area refers: AA is the total external (outside) surface area of the immersed coil tubing that is in contact with the reaction mass. It is not the vessel jacket area, not the vessel cross-sectional area, and not the internal cross-sectional area of the coil tube. UU is taken on that same external coil area basis.

Calculation at both ends of the range

The product in the denominator is evaluated first for each end of the range.

Low end of the range: U=400 W m−2 K−1U = 400\ \text{W m}^{-2}\ \text{K}^{-1}

A=800,000 W(400 W m−2 K−1)(30 K)=800,00012,000 m2=66.7 m2A = \frac{800{,}000\ \text{W}}{(400\ \text{W m}^{-2}\ \text{K}^{-1})(30\ \text{K})} = \frac{800{,}000}{12{,}000}\ \text{m}^{2} = 66.7\ \text{m}^{2}

High end of the range: U=600 W m−2 K−1U = 600\ \text{W m}^{-2}\ \text{K}^{-1}

A=800,000 W(600 W m−2 K−1)(30 K)=800,00018,000 m2=44.4 m2A = \frac{800{,}000\ \text{W}}{(600\ \text{W m}^{-2}\ \text{K}^{-1})(30\ \text{K})} = \frac{800{,}000}{18{,}000}\ \text{m}^{2} = 44.4\ \text{m}^{2}

Unit check: W divided by (W m−2^{-2} K−1^{-1} multiplied by K) gives m2^{2}, as required for an area.

Result

For a well-designed immersed cooling coil in an agitated reactor, on the published range U=400U = 400 to 600 W m−2 K−1600\ \text{W m}^{-2}\ \text{K}^{-1}:

A≈44 to 67 m2 of external immersed-coil surface areaA \approx 44\ \text{to}\ 67\ \text{m}^{2}\ \text{of external immersed-coil surface area}

with 44.4 m244.4\ \text{m}^{2} at U=600 W m−2 K−1U = 600\ \text{W m}^{-2}\ \text{K}^{-1} and 66.7 m266.7\ \text{m}^{2} at U=400 W m−2 K−1U = 400\ \text{W m}^{-2}\ \text{K}^{-1}.

If a single area must be quoted, it must carry its stated coefficient. The conservative single value from this range is:

A=66.7 m2 at the stated U=400 W m−2 K−1A = 66.7\ \text{m}^{2}\ \text{at the stated}\ U = 400\ \text{W m}^{-2}\ \text{K}^{-1}

that is, sizing on the low end of the range gives the largest area and covers the poorer-transfer end of the published range. No fouling allowance, design margin, or excess area has been added; those would increase the installed area beyond the figures above.

Cross-check against a second published table, and sensitivity to arrangement

Towler, G. and Sinnott, R., Chemical Engineering Design, table "Overall Heat Transfer Coefficients for Immersed Coils in Agitated Vessels", gives U=400U = 400 to 700 W m−2 K−1700\ \text{W m}^{-2}\ \text{K}^{-1} for a water or brine coil in aqueous solutions. At U=700 W m−2 K−1U = 700\ \text{W m}^{-2}\ \text{K}^{-1}, A=800,000/(700×30)=38.1 m2A = 800{,}000 / (700 \times 30) = 38.1\ \text{m}^{2}; at U=400 W m−2 K−1U = 400\ \text{W m}^{-2}\ \text{K}^{-1}, A=66.7 m2A = 66.7\ \text{m}^{2}, in agreement with the low end above. This second range is specific to an aqueous reaction mass, which the problem does not state, so it is used here only as a cross-check.

The arrangement matters to the answer. The same Carpenter guide gives single typical cooling values, not ranges, for jacketed vessels: U=350 W m−2 K−1U = 350\ \text{W m}^{-2}\ \text{K}^{-1} for a jacketed carbon or stainless steel vessel, which would give a jacket area of 800,000/(350×30)=76.2 m2800{,}000 / (350 \times 30) = 76.2\ \text{m}^{2}, and U=200 W m−2 K−1U = 200\ \text{W m}^{-2}\ \text{K}^{-1} for a jacketed glass-lined steel vessel, which would give 800,000/(200×30)=133 m2800{,}000 / (200 \times 30) = 133\ \text{m}^{2}. Those are jacket (wetted vessel wall) areas, a different configuration from the coil area reported above, and illustrate why the arrangement and the coefficient must be stated together with any area.

Assumptions
  1. Steady operation, with the full 800 kW removed through the stated cooling surface; heat losses to the surroundings are neglected.
  2. The given 30 K is the applicable mean temperature difference for the whole surface, so no separate log-mean temperature difference calculation is required or possible from the data given.
  3. UU is constant over the area and is based on the external coil area.
  4. No fouling resistance, corrosion allowance, or design margin beyond the published UU range is included.
Sources
  • Carpenter, K. J., "Agitated Vessel Heat Transfer", A-to-Z Guide to Thermodynamics, Heat and Mass Transfer, and Fluids Engineering (Thermopedia), DOI 10.1615/AtoZ.a.agitated_vessel_heat_transfer — coil range 400 to 600 W m−2^{-2} K−1^{-1}; jacketed-vessel cooling values 350 W m−2^{-2} K−1^{-1} (carbon and stainless steel) and 200 W m−2^{-2} K−1^{-1} (glass-lined steel).
  • Towler, G. and Sinnott, R., Chemical Engineering Design (Elsevier), tables of overall heat transfer coefficients for jacketed vessels and for immersed coils in agitated vessels, as reproduced at https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/chemical-engineering/heat-transfer-coefficient — immersed coil, water or brine / aqueous solutions, 400 to 700 W m−2^{-2} K−1^{-1}.
  • Fletcher, P. (1987), "Heat Transfer Coefficients for Stirred Batch Reactor Design", The Chemical Engineer, cited in Carpenter (above).

B4. Mixing Scale-Up — Second Vessel

Response without defensive prompt

Scale-Up of a Stirred Vessel

Result in Brief

No unique large-vessel stirrer speed follows from the data as stated. A scale-up criterion, and the flow regime, must also be specified.

Under the criterion most commonly used for a stirred vessel, namely equal power input per unit volume in turbulent flow, the large-vessel speed is approximately

132 revolutions per minute (rpm).

Speeds under other standard criteria range from 26 rpm to 300 rpm. The derivation and the alternatives are given below.

1. Symbols and Data
  • V1V_1 is the volume of the small vessel, V1=0.05 m3V_1 = 0.05\ \mathrm{m^3}.
  • V2V_2 is the volume of the large vessel, V2=2 m3V_2 = 2\ \mathrm{m^3}.
  • N1N_1 is the stirrer speed in the small vessel, N1=300 rpmN_1 = 300\ \mathrm{rpm}.
  • N2N_2 is the stirrer speed in the large vessel, in rpm, to be found.
  • T1T_1 and T2T_2 are the vessel diameters, in metres (m), of the small and large vessels, respectively.
  • D1D_1 and D2D_2 are the impeller diameters, in m, of the small and large vessels, respectively.
  • SS is the linear scale ratio, dimensionless, defined by S=T2/T1=D2/D1S = T_2/T_1 = D_2/D_1.

Unless a change is stated, the same liquid is used in both vessels and the vessels are geometrically similar.

2. Linear Scale Ratio

Geometric similarity means that every length is multiplied by the same factor SS. A volume is a length cubed, so

V2V1=S3.\frac{V_2}{V_1} = S^3 .

Substitution of V1V_1 and V2V_2 gives

S=(V2V1)1/3=(20.05)1/3=401/3=3.42.S = \left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\frac{2}{0.05}\right)^{1/3} = 40^{1/3} = 3.42 .

Thus every length in the large vessel is 3.42 times the corresponding length in the small vessel. In particular, D2=3.42 D1D_2 = 3.42\,D_1 and T2=3.42 T1T_2 = 3.42\,T_1. Check: 3.423=40.03.42^3 = 40.0, which recovers the volume ratio V2/V1=40V_2/V_1 = 40.

The volume ratio alone fixes SS. It does not fix N2N_2, because N2N_2 depends on which physical quantity is held constant during scale-up.

3. Stirring Relations
  • ρ\rho is the liquid density, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg m−3\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}).
  • μ\mu is the liquid dynamic viscosity, in pascal seconds (Pa s\mathrm{Pa\,s}).
  • P1P_1 and P2P_2 are the stirrer power inputs, in watts (W), in the small and large vessels, respectively.
  • Re\mathrm{Re} is the impeller Reynolds number, dimensionless, defined, with NN in revolutions per second and DD in m, by

Re=ρND2μ,\mathrm{Re} = \frac{\rho N D^2}{\mu},

where NN is a generic stirrer speed and DD is a generic impeller diameter. The factor converting rpm to revolutions per second cancels in every speed ratio used below. - NPN_{\mathrm{P}} is the power number, dimensionless, defined by

NP=PρN3D5,soP=NP ρN3D5,N_{\mathrm{P}} = \frac{P}{\rho N^3 D^5}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad P = N_{\mathrm{P}}\,\rho N^3 D^5,

where PP is a generic stirrer power input, in W. - utipu_{\mathrm{tip}} is the impeller tip speed, in metres per second (m s−1\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}), defined by utip=πDNu_{\mathrm{tip}} = \pi D N, where π\pi is the ratio of a circle circumference to its diameter, dimensionless.

For a baffled vessel in fully turbulent flow, NPN_{\mathrm{P}} is approximately constant for a given geometry, independent of Re\mathrm{Re}. Geometric similarity keeps the geometry, and hence NPN_{\mathrm{P}}, the same in both vessels. With the same liquid, ρ\rho is also the same. Therefore

P∝N3D5.P \propto N^3 D^5 .

Since V∝D3V \propto D^3, where VV is a generic vessel volume, the power input per unit volume, P/VP/V, in W m−3\mathrm{W\,m^{-3}}, obeys

PV∝N3D5D3=N3D2.(1)\frac{P}{V} \propto \frac{N^3 D^5}{D^3} = N^3 D^2 . \tag{1}

Equation (1) is the basis of the standard turbulent scale-up calculation. It is not valid without change in laminar flow; see Section 6.

4. Standard Criterion: Equal Power per Unit Volume

Equal power per unit volume is the usual first criterion when the process result depends on turbulence intensity, gas dispersion, liquid–liquid dispersion, or solids suspension, because P/VP/V is a measure of the mean energy dissipation per unit mass of liquid.

Setting P2/V2=P1/V1P_2/V_2 = P_1/V_1 in equation (1), with the subscripts 1 and 2 denoting the small and large vessels, gives

N23D22=N13D12,N2=N1(D1D2)2/3=N1S−2/3.N_2^3 D_2^2 = N_1^3 D_1^2, \qquad N_2 = N_1 \left(\frac{D_1}{D_2}\right)^{2/3} = N_1 S^{-2/3}.

Substitution of N1=300 rpmN_1 = 300\ \mathrm{rpm} and S=3.42S = 3.42 gives

N2=300×3.42−2/3=132 rpmN_2 = 300 \times 3.42^{-2/3} = 132\ \mathrm{rpm}

to three significant figures.

Check: (132/300)3×3.422=1.00(132/300)^3 \times 3.42^2 = 1.00, so P/VP/V is unchanged, as required. The total power nevertheless rises in proportion to volume: P2/P1=V2/V1=40P_2/P_1 = V_2/V_1 = 40.

Consequences of this choice, relative to the small vessel, are a tip speed utipu_{\mathrm{tip}} increased by a factor S1/3=1.51S^{1/3} = 1.51, and an impeller Reynolds number Re\mathrm{Re} increased by a factor S4/3=5.15S^{4/3} = 5.15. Equal P/VP/V therefore does not preserve maximum shear or flow regime in detail.

5. Other Standard Criteria

Each criterion below holds a different quantity constant, and each gives a different N2N_2. All use S=3.42S = 3.42 and turbulent flow, except where stated.

5.1 Equal impeller tip speed

Equal utipu_{\mathrm{tip}} is used when the maximum shear at the impeller, which scales with utipu_{\mathrm{tip}}, must not increase, for example with shear-sensitive material or a drop size set by maximum shear. From utip=πDNu_{\mathrm{tip}} = \pi D N, constant utipu_{\mathrm{tip}} requires N∝D−1N \propto D^{-1}:

N2=N1S−1=300/3.42=87.7 rpm.N_2 = N_1 S^{-1} = 300/3.42 = 87.7\ \mathrm{rpm}.

The power per unit volume then falls to 1/S=0.2921/S = 0.292 of the small-vessel value, from equation (1).

Equal torque per unit volume gives the same result. Torque is power divided by angular speed, so torque per unit volume scales as N2D2N^2 D^2, and holding torque per unit volume constant also requires N∝D−1N \propto D^{-1}.

5.2 Equal impeller Reynolds number

Equal Re\mathrm{Re} is dynamic similarity for the same liquid. From the definition of Re\mathrm{Re}, constant Re\mathrm{Re} requires N∝D−2N \propto D^{-2}:

N2=N1S−2=300/3.422=25.6 rpm.N_2 = N_1 S^{-2} = 300/3.42^2 = 25.6\ \mathrm{rpm}.

The power per unit volume then falls to 0.007 of the small-vessel value. Equal Re\mathrm{Re} is generally used only in viscous, laminar, or transitional service; in turbulent service it sacrifices nearly all of the power input.

5.3 Equal speed, equal mixing time, and equal turnover time
  • tmt_{\mathrm{m}} is the blend (mixing) time, in seconds (s). In turbulent flow in geometrically similar vessels, the dimensionless product NtmN t_{\mathrm{m}} is approximately constant, so tm∝1/Nt_{\mathrm{m}} \propto 1/N.
  • QQ is the impeller pumping (circulation) rate, in cubic metres per second (m3 s−1\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}). It scales as Q∝ND3Q \propto N D^3, so the turnover time V/QV/Q, in s, also scales as 1/N1/N, because V∝D3V \propto D^3.

Holding tmt_{\mathrm{m}}, or holding V/QV/Q, constant therefore requires

N2=N1=300 rpm.N_2 = N_1 = 300\ \mathrm{rpm}.

The cost is severe: P/VP/V rises by a factor S2=11.7S^2 = 11.7, utipu_{\mathrm{tip}} rises by a factor S=3.42S = 3.42, and total power rises by a factor S5=468S^5 = 468, from P∝N3D5P \propto N^3 D^5 at constant NN.

5.4 Summary table

Ratios in the table are large-vessel value divided by small-vessel value. The P/VP/V ratio is the ratio of power input per unit volume.

Criterion held constant N2N_2 (rpm) Tip-speed ratio Re\mathrm{Re} ratio P/VP/V ratio
Re\mathrm{Re} 25.6 0.292 1.00 0.007
utipu_{\mathrm{tip}} 87.7 1.00 3.42 0.292

No row is preferred in the abstract. The correct row is the one whose held quantity controls the process result: mass transfer and suspension usually point to P/VP/V, shear limits to utipu_{\mathrm{tip}}, blending time to NN, and viscous flow to Re\mathrm{Re}.

6. Effect of Flow Regime

The result N2=132 rpmN_2 = 132\ \mathrm{rpm} assumes fully turbulent flow, with NPN_{\mathrm{P}} constant. In laminar flow, NPN_{\mathrm{P}} is instead approximately inversely proportional to Re\mathrm{Re}, so P∝μN2D3P \propto \mu N^2 D^3 and, since V∝D3V \propto D^3, P/V∝μN2P/V \propto \mu N^2, independent of vessel size. Equal P/VP/V in laminar flow, for the same liquid, then requires N2=N1=300 rpmN_2 = N_1 = 300\ \mathrm{rpm}, not 132 rpm. A calculation for a real vessel therefore requires ρ\rho and μ\mu, and an impeller size, so that Re\mathrm{Re} in each vessel can be checked. None of those quantities is given.

A further practical limit is heat removal. The jacket area, denoted AA, in square metres (m2\mathrm{m^2}), scales as A∝T2A \propto T^2, so the area per unit volume, A/VA/V, falls by a factor S=3.42S = 3.42 on scale-up, whatever N2N_2 is chosen.

7. Conclusion
  • Linear scale ratio: S=401/3=3.42S = 40^{1/3} = 3.42.
  • Conventional answer, equal power per unit volume, turbulent flow, same liquid, geometric similarity: N2≈132 rpmN_2 \approx 132\ \mathrm{rpm}.
  • The problem as stated has no single answer: equal tip speed gives 87.7 rpm, equal Reynolds number gives 25.6 rpm, and equal mixing time gives 300 rpm. A design calculation must name the quantity that controls the process, confirm the flow regime in both vessels, and then check the resulting tip speed, total power, P2=40 P1P_2 = 40\,P_1 under the equal-P/VP/V criterion, and heat-removal area per unit volume.

1. Constant power per volume
Rule

The scale-up rule is P/V=constantP/V = \text{constant} between the two vessels.

For geometrically similar vessels with the same fluid, in the turbulent regime in which the power number is constant, the power input scales as

P∝N3D5P \propto N^3 D^5

where NN is the stirrer speed (in consistent units, so the proportionality is unaffected by using rpm\mathrm{rpm} for both vessels) and DD is the impeller diameter in metres (m\mathrm{m}). Since V∝D3V \propto D^3 under geometric similarity,

PV∝N3D5D3=N3D2\frac{P}{V} \propto \frac{N^3 D^5}{D^3} = N^3 D^2

Setting P/VP/V constant gives N3D2=constantN^3 D^2 = \text{constant}, hence

N∝D−2/3,N2N1=(D2D1)−2/3=λ−2/3N \propto D^{-2/3}, \qquad \frac{N_2}{N_1} = \left(\frac{D_2}{D_1}\right)^{-2/3} = \lambda^{-2/3}

Calculation

N2N1=3.42−2/3=40−2/9=0.441\frac{N_2}{N_1} = 3.42^{-2/3} = 40^{-2/9} = 0.441

N2=300×0.441≈132 rpmN_2 = 300 \times 0.441 \approx 132\ \mathrm{rpm}

Result, constant P/VP/V: N2≈132 rpmN_2 \approx 132\ \mathrm{rpm}.

Process limit protected

Constant P/VP/V holds the mean energy dissipation and the bulk turbulence level per unit volume constant. It therefore protects processes limited by bulk mixing and transport: blending time behaviour, gas–liquid and liquid–liquid mass transfer, heat transfer, solid suspension, and reactions whose rate is limited by mixing. The penalty is that the tip speed rises on scale-up, by a factor λ1/3=1.51\lambda^{1/3} = 1.51 here, so impeller-zone shear is not protected by this rule.

2. Constant tip speed
Rule

The scale-up rule is utip=constantu_{\mathrm{tip}} = \text{constant} between the two vessels, where

utip=πDNu_{\mathrm{tip}} = \pi D N

with π\pi (dimensionless) the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter. The factor π\pi cancels in the ratio, so utip∝NDu_{\mathrm{tip}} \propto ND and constant tip speed gives

N∝D−1,N2N1=(D2D1)−1=λ−1N \propto D^{-1}, \qquad \frac{N_2}{N_1} = \left(\frac{D_2}{D_1}\right)^{-1} = \lambda^{-1}

N2N1=13.42=40−1/3=0.292\frac{N_2}{N_1} = \frac{1}{3.42} = 40^{-1/3} = 0.292

N2=300×0.292≈88 rpmN_2 = 300 \times 0.292 \approx 88\ \mathrm{rpm}

Result, constant tip speed: N2≈88 rpmN_2 \approx 88\ \mathrm{rpm}.

Process limit protected

Constant tip speed holds the maximum impeller speed and, approximately, the maximum shear rate at the impeller tip constant. It therefore protects shear-limited processes: shear-sensitive biological cells, fragile crystals, flocs and droplets, and emulsions in which the maximum droplet size or droplet break-up is set by tip shear, as well as limiting impeller mechanical and erosion severity. The penalty is that P/VP/V falls on scale-up, to a fraction λ−1=0.29\lambda^{-1} = 0.29 of its small-vessel value here, so bulk mixing and mass transfer are not protected by this rule.

Conversion for a First-Order Reaction in a Continuous Reactor

Definitions
  • AA is the reactant.
  • XX is the conversion of AA, dimensionless, defined as the amount of AA consumed divided by the amount of AA fed.
  • CAC_{A} is the molar concentration of AA, in mol m−3\mathrm{mol\,m^{-3}}.
  • CA0C_{A0} is the molar concentration of AA in the feed, in mol m−3\mathrm{mol\,m^{-3}}.
  • kk is the first-order rate constant, in s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}} (reciprocal time in general).
  • τ\tau is the nominal residence time, in s\mathrm{s} (time in general), defined as the reactor volume divided by the volumetric feed rate.
  • DaDa is the Damköhler number for the reaction, dimensionless, defined in the next section.

For constant-density flow, XX is related to the concentrations by

X=1−CACA0,X = 1 - \frac{C_{A}}{C_{A0}},

where CAC_{A} on the right-hand side is the outlet concentration.

The calculation assumes an irreversible, isothermal, first-order reaction, constant density, and steady state. The rate of consumption of AA per unit volume is kCAk C_{A}.

Given quantity

The stated product is

Da=kτ=1.5,Da = k\tau = 1.5,

which is dimensionless, as required: kk has units of reciprocal time and τ\tau has units of time.

Insufficiency of the reactor specification

A numerical value of kτk\tau alone does not give a unique conversion for a continuous reactor. The flow pattern must also be specified. The two standard ideal limits are plug flow and perfect mixing. They give different results at the same kτk\tau, and a real continuous reactor normally lies between them.

Ideal plug-flow reactor

Let tt be the time spent in the reactor by a fluid element, in s\mathrm{s}. Along that element,

dCAdt=−kCA,\frac{dC_{A}}{dt} = -k C_{A},

with CA=CA0C_{A} = C_{A0} at t=0t = 0. Integration to t=τt = \tau gives

CACA0=exp⁡(−kτ)=exp⁡(−Da).\frac{C_{A}}{C_{A0}} = \exp(-k\tau) = \exp(-Da).

Hence

X=1−exp⁡(−Da).X = 1 - \exp(-Da).

For Da=1.5Da = 1.5,

X=1−exp⁡(−1.5)=1−0.2231=0.7769≈0.78.X = 1 - \exp(-1.5) = 1 - 0.2231 = 0.7769 \approx 0.78.

Let VV be the reactor volume, in m3\mathrm{m^{3}}, and let v0v_{0} be the volumetric feed rate, in m3 s−1\mathrm{m^{3}\,s^{-1}}, so that τ=V/v0\tau = V/v_{0}. v0CA0−v0CA−kCAV=0,v_{0} C_{A0} - v_{0} C_{A} - k C_{A} V = 0,

in which the three terms are, in order, feed in, flow out, and consumption by reaction, each in mol s−1\mathrm{mol\,s^{-1}}. Dividing by v0CA0v_{0} C_{A0} and using τ=V/v0\tau = V/v_{0} gives

CACA0=11+kτ=11+Da,\frac{C_{A}}{C_{A0}} = \frac{1}{1 + k\tau} = \frac{1}{1 + Da},

and therefore

X=1−11+Da=Da1+Da.X = 1 - \frac{1}{1 + Da} = \frac{Da}{1 + Da}.

X=1.51+1.5=1.52.5=0.60.X = \frac{1.5}{1 + 1.5} = \frac{1.5}{2.5} = 0.60.

No single conversion follows from kτ=1.5k\tau = 1.5 without a flow model.

  • Plug-flow limit: X≈0.78X \approx 0.78, i.e. about 78%78\% conversion.

Conversion for a First-Order Reaction at a Rate Constant–Residence Time Product of 1.5

Definitions and assumptions
  • AA is the reactant.
  • CAC_A (mol m−3^{-3}) is the concentration of AA at a stated position.
  • CA0C_{A0} (mol m−3^{-3}) is the inlet concentration of AA.
  • CA,outC_{A,\mathrm{out}} (mol m−3^{-3}) is the mixed outlet concentration of AA.
  • XX (dimensionless) is the fractional conversion of AA, defined by X=1−CA,out/CA0X = 1 - C_{A,\mathrm{out}}/C_{A0} for constant-density flow.
  • kk (s−1^{-1}) is the first-order rate constant, for a rate of consumption of AA per unit volume equal to kCAk C_A (mol m−3^{-3} s−1^{-1}).
  • VV (m3^{3}) is the reactor volume.
  • QQ (m3^{3} s−1^{-1}) is the total volumetric flow rate.
  • τ\tau (s) is the nominal residence time, defined by τ=V/Q\tau = V/Q.
  • DaDa (dimensionless) is the first Damköhler number, defined by Da=kτDa = k\tau.

The stated value is

Da=kτ=1.5.Da = k\tau = 1.5.

Assumptions: steady state, isothermal operation, constant density, irreversible first-order reaction, and no side reactions. "Ideal flow" is not one state. The two standard ideal limits are plug flow and perfect mixing, and they give different conversions at the same DaDa. A single number cannot be given until the flow pattern is specified.

1. Ideal flow
1.1 Plug-flow reactor (PFR)

A plug-flow reactor has no axial mixing. A steady-state balance, integrated over τ\tau, gives

CA,outCA0=exp⁡(−kτ)=exp⁡(−Da).\frac{C_{A,\mathrm{out}}}{C_{A0}} = \exp(-k\tau) = \exp(-Da).

Hence

XPFR=1−exp⁡(−1.5)=1−0.2231=0.777.X_{\mathrm{PFR}} = 1 - \exp(-1.5) = 1 - 0.2231 = 0.777.

Conversion, plug flow: X=0.78X = 0.78, i.e. about 78%.

1.2 Continuously stirred tank reactor (CSTR)

A continuously stirred tank reactor has perfect mixing, so the concentration throughout the vessel equals CA,outC_{A,\mathrm{out}}. A steady-state balance gives

CA,outCA0=11+kτ=11+Da.\frac{C_{A,\mathrm{out}}}{C_{A0}} = \frac{1}{1 + k\tau} = \frac{1}{1 + Da}.

Hence

XCSTR=Da1+Da=1.52.5=0.600.X_{\mathrm{CSTR}} = \frac{Da}{1 + Da} = \frac{1.5}{2.5} = 0.600.

Conversion, perfect mixing: X=0.60X = 0.60, i.e. 60%.

The plug-flow result is higher because, in a PFR, fluid retains a high concentration of AA and therefore a high reaction rate over much of its passage. In a CSTR, incoming feed is mixed at once to the low outlet concentration, so the whole volume reacts at the outlet rate. For a first-order reaction, these two values, 0.60 and 0.78, bracket the conversion of most practical single-vessel flow patterns at Da=1.5Da = 1.5, in the absence of bypassing or stagnant regions that exchange only slowly.

2. Bypassing
2.1 Bypass model
  • fbf_b (dimensionless) is the bypass fraction, the fraction of the total flow QQ that passes from inlet to outlet without reacting.
  • QbQ_b (m3^{3} s−1^{-1}) is the bypass flow rate, Qb=fbQQ_b = f_b Q.
  • QaQ_a (m3^{3} s−1^{-1}) is the flow rate through the active (reacting) zone, Qa=(1−fb)QQ_a = (1 - f_b)Q.
  • τa\tau_a (s) is the residence time in the active zone, τa=V/Qa=τ/(1−fb)\tau_a = V/Q_a = \tau/(1 - f_b).
  • DaaDa_a (dimensionless) is the active-zone value, Daa=kτa=Da/(1−fb)Da_a = k\tau_a = Da/(1 - f_b).
  • XaX_a (dimensionless) is the conversion reached by the stream that passes through the active zone.
  • CA,aC_{A,a} (mol m−3^{-3}) is the concentration of AA leaving the active zone, before it is mixed with the bypass stream.

The bypass stream leaves at CA0C_{A0}. Mixing the two outlet streams gives

CA,outCA0=fb+(1−fb) CA,aCA0,\frac{C_{A,\mathrm{out}}}{C_{A0}} = f_b + (1 - f_b)\,\frac{C_{A,a}}{C_{A0}},

so that the overall conversion is

X=(1−fb) Xa.X = (1 - f_b)\,X_a.

The remaining factor 1/(1−fb)1/(1-f_b) in DaaDa_a matters: with VV and total QQ fixed, reducing the flow through the active zone lengthens the time that stream spends in the vessel, which partly offsets the loss to bypassing.

For a plug-flow active zone,

Xa=1−exp⁡(−Daa)=1−exp⁡ ⁣(−Da1−fb).X_a = 1 - \exp(-Da_a) = 1 - \exp\!\left(\frac{-Da}{1 - f_b}\right).

For a perfectly mixed active zone,

Xa=Daa1+Daa=Da/(1−fb)1+Da/(1−fb).X_a = \frac{Da_a}{1 + Da_a} = \frac{Da/(1 - f_b)}{1 + Da/(1 - f_b)}.

In percentage terms:

  • fb=0.05f_b = 0.05: about 75% (plug-flow active zone) or 58% (mixed active zone).
  • fb=0.15f_b = 0.15: about 70% (plug-flow active zone) or 54% (mixed active zone).

2.3 Note on a common simplified convention

A cruder estimate often used for a first pass holds the active-zone residence time at the nominal value τ\tau, rather than at τ/(1−fb)\tau/(1-f_b), and writes X=(1−fb)XidealX = (1 - f_b) X_{\mathrm{ideal}}, with XidealX_{\mathrm{ideal}} taken from Section 1. That convention gives, for a plug-flow active zone, 0.738, 0.660 and 0.544 at fb=0.05f_b = 0.05, 0.15 and 0.30, and, for a mixed active zone, 0.570, 0.510 and 0.420. It is the appropriate form when the bypass flow displaces an equal share of the active volume, rather than merely splitting the flow through a fixed volume. The two sets of numbers differ only through that one modelling choice, which is why the bypass fraction alone, without a statement of what the bypassed fluid displaces, does not fix the conversion exactly. Both sets show the same size and direction of the effect.

3. Evidence that would establish the flow pattern

A measured conversion alone cannot establish the flow pattern. At a single DaDa, a low conversion is equally consistent with a smaller effective kk, a mixed rather than plug-flow pattern, bypassing, or a reduced active volume, and these cannot be separated from one conversion value.

The direct evidence is a residence time distribution (RTD) measurement with an inert tracer, carried out at the operating flow rate and with a fluid of the operating density and viscosity:

  1. Tracer test. Inject a non-reactive, non-adsorbing tracer, either as a short pulse at the inlet or as a step change in inlet tracer concentration, and record the outlet tracer concentration against time. The tracer must not react, adsorb on internals or packing, or change the flow. Recovery of essentially all of the injected tracer is a check on the measurement.
  2. Residence time distribution function. From the pulse response, obtain E(t)E(t) (s−1^{-1}), the residence time distribution function, defined so that E(t) dtE(t)\,\mathrm{d}t (dimensionless) is the fraction of the outlet flow that spent a time between tt (s) and t+dtt + \mathrm{d}t (s) in the vessel. From the step response, obtain F(t)F(t) (dimensionless), the cumulative form, defined as the fraction of the outlet flow that spent a time less than tt in the vessel.
  3. Signatures to read from the measured curves. - Plug flow: a narrow pulse response centred near τ\tau, and a step response that stays near zero until tt is close to τ\tau and then rises sharply. - Perfect mixing: a pulse response that is highest at t=0t = 0 and decays exponentially, and a step response of the form F(t)=1−exp⁡(−t/τ)F(t) = 1 - \exp(-t/\tau). - Bypassing: an immediate response at tt near zero — a sharp early peak in the pulse response, or an immediate jump in the step response — containing a fraction of the tracer close to fbf_b. The height of the initial step in F(t)F(t) is a direct estimate of fbf_b. - Stagnant or dead volume: the mean of E(t)E(t), which is the mean residence time of the flowing fluid, falls below the nominal τ=V/Q\tau = V/Q, and the response shows a long tail from fluid that enters slowly exchanging regions and leaves late. - Degree of mixing: the dimensionless variance of the distribution (the variance of tt divided by the square of the mean of tt) is near 0 for plug flow and near 1 for perfect mixing, with real vessels in between. Fitting a dispersion model or a tanks-in-series model to the curve gives a single index that can be compared between runs.
  4. Confirmatory checks. Repeat the tracer test at several flow rates: bypassing and short-circuiting usually worsen as flow paths and internals dictate, and a pattern that is stable in dimensionless form (plotted against t/τt/\tau) supports a hydrodynamic origin rather than an artefact. Combine the tracer result with conversion measured at several values of τ\tau (several flow rates at fixed kk): a flow model fitted to the tracer curve should predict the whole conversion–τ\tau curve with one value of kk, not merely one point. Dye visualisation, sampling at internal or multiple outlet positions, and temperature or concentration profiling along the vessel give supporting, spatially resolved evidence where access permits.

In practice, an early tracer breakthrough quantifying fbf_b, plus the shape and variance of the rest of the curve distinguishing plug-like from mixed behaviour in the active zone, is the evidence required to select the correct column of the table in Section 2.2.

Answer

At Da=kτ=1.5Da = k\tau = 1.5, the ideal-flow conversion is X=0.78X = 0.78 for plug flow and X=0.60X = 0.60 for perfect mixing. With the fixed-volume bypass model of Section 2, bypass fractions of 0.05, 0.15 and 0.30 reduce the conversion to 0.75, 0.70 and 0.62 respectively for a plug-flow active zone, and to 0.58, 0.54 and 0.48 respectively for a perfectly mixed active zone. An inert-tracer residence time distribution measurement — in particular the size of the response at near-zero time — is the evidence that establishes which case applies and how large the bypass fraction is.

The Fenske equation for the minimum number of theoretical stages at total reflux, for a binary separation with constant α\alpha, is

Nmin⁡=ln⁡Rln⁡α=ln⁡[(xD1−xD)(1−xBxB)]ln⁡αN_{\min} = \frac{\ln R}{\ln \alpha} = \frac{\ln\left[\left(\dfrac{x_D}{1 - x_D}\right)\left(\dfrac{1 - x_B}{x_B}\right)\right]}{\ln \alpha}

The base of the logarithm cancels, so natural logarithms and base-10 logarithms give the same result.

Nmin⁡=ln⁡(24,000)ln⁡(1.22)N_{\min} = \frac{\ln(24{,}000)}{\ln(1.22)}

ln⁡(24,000)=10.0858\ln(24{,}000) = 10.0858

Nmin⁡=10.08580.19885=50.72N_{\min} = \frac{10.0858}{0.19885} = 50.72

Nmin⁡≈50.7N_{\min} \approx 50.7

In practice, a whole number of stages is required, so at least 51 theoretical stages are needed to meet or exceed the specified separation at total reflux. The count Nmin⁡N_{\min} from the Fenske equation is conventionally understood to include the reboiler as one theoretical stage; a total condenser is not counted as a stage.

Response with defensive prompt

Minimum number of theoretical stages — Fenske equation

Given quantities
  • Nmin⁡N_{\min}: minimum number of theoretical stages, dimensionless, attained at total reflux.
  • SS: the product of the distillate and bottoms composition ratios appearing in the Fenske equation, dimensionless. The stated value is S=24,000S = 24{,}000.
  • α\alpha: relative volatility, dimensionless. The stated value is α=1.22\alpha = 1.22.

No component identities, no pressure, no temperature range, and no vapour–liquid equilibrium data are given.

Calculation

For a binary separation, the Fenske equation is

Nmin⁡=ln⁡Sln⁡αN_{\min} = \frac{\ln S}{\ln \alpha}

where ln⁡\ln denotes the natural logarithm. Substitution gives

Nmin⁡=ln⁡(24,000)ln⁡(1.22)=10.0860.1989=50.7N_{\min} = \frac{\ln(24{,}000)}{\ln(1.22)} = \frac{10.086}{0.1989} = 50.7

A fractional stage count is not realisable, so the result is rounded up:

Nmin⁡=51N_{\min} = 51 theoretical stages, including the reboiler, at total reflux.

This is a minimum at total reflux. A column operating at finite reflux requires more stages.

Relative volatility across the composition range

This cannot be reported from the information given.

A single value, α=1.22\alpha = 1.22, is stated. No variation of α\alpha with composition is given, and no data from which such a variation could be calculated are supplied: the two components are not named, and neither the column pressure nor the top and bottom temperatures are stated. Reporting values of α\alpha at the top, at the bottom, or at intermediate compositions would require inventing a component pair and equilibrium data that are not in the problem.

If α\alpha does vary, the standard treatment is to replace the single value in the Fenske equation by a geometric mean, αavg\alpha_{\mathrm{avg}}, defined by

αavg=αtop αbottom\alpha_{\mathrm{avg}} = \sqrt{\alpha_{\mathrm{top}}\,\alpha_{\mathrm{bottom}}}

where αtop\alpha_{\mathrm{top}} is the relative volatility at the top (distillate) conditions, dimensionless, and αbottom\alpha_{\mathrm{bottom}} is the relative volatility at the bottom (bottoms) conditions, dimensionless. Neither αtop\alpha_{\mathrm{top}} nor αbottom\alpha_{\mathrm{bottom}} is known here, so αavg\alpha_{\mathrm{avg}} cannot be evaluated separately from the stated 1.221.22. The calculation above therefore treats 1.221.22 as the effective (mean) relative volatility for the column.

Azeotrope

Whether an azeotrope intervenes cannot be determined from the information given.

An azeotrope is a property of a named component pair at a stated pressure. At an azeotropic composition the relative volatility is 11, and a conventional distillation column cannot cross that composition. Because no components and no pressure are specified, no azeotrope can be confirmed or excluded.

The stated calculation itself rests on an implicit assumption: that an effective α=1.22\alpha = 1.22, greater than 11, applies over the whole composition interval between the bottoms and distillate compositions, with no azeotropic boundary inside that interval. That assumption is part of the problem as posed, not a finding about a real mixture. If a real mixture with an azeotrope between the two product compositions were intended, the specified separation would not be attainable by ordinary distillation at all, regardless of stage count, and the Fenske result would not apply.

Stage count at the lowest and highest plausible relative volatility

No lowest or highest plausible value of α\alpha can be derived from the information given, for the same reason as above: there is no component pair, pressure, or equilibrium data set from which a plausible range could be bounded. Supplying a numerical range, and stage counts at its ends, would be fabrication.

What can be stated exactly is the sensitivity of the result to α\alpha, from Nmin⁡=ln⁡(24,000)/ln⁡αN_{\min} = \ln(24{,}000)/\ln\alpha, rounded up to a whole number of stages:

α\alpha (dimensionless) Nmin⁡N_{\min} (dimensionless) Rounded up
1.15 72.2 73
1.20 55.3 56
1.22 (stated) 50.7 51
1.25 45.2 46
1.30 38.4 39

These entries are a sensitivity illustration, not a plausible range for any particular mixture. They show the practical consequence of the missing data: because α=1.22\alpha = 1.22 is close to 11, the stage count is strongly sensitive to α\alpha, changing by roughly five stages for a change of 0.030.03 in α\alpha near the stated value. A design figure would therefore require measured or correlated equilibrium data for the actual mixture.

Result
  • Minimum theoretical stages at the stated effective relative volatility of 1.221.22: 51 stages, including the reboiler, at total reflux.
  • Relative volatility across the composition range: not determinable — only the single effective value 1.221.22 is given.
  • Azeotrope: not determinable — no components or pressure are specified; the calculation assumes none intervenes between the product compositions.
  • Stage counts at a lowest and highest plausible relative volatility: not determinable — no plausible range can be bounded from the given data; the sensitivity table above quantifies how the count would move if such a range were supplied.

C2. Flooding and Diameter — Second Column

Response without defensive prompt

Packed Column Diameter

Given data

The volumetric gas flow rate, denoted QQ and in cubic metres per second (m3/s\mathrm{m^3/s}), is 1.8 m3/s1.8\ \mathrm{m^3/s}.

The flooding superficial gas velocity, denoted uu and in metres per second (m/s\mathrm{m/s}), is 1.5 m/s1.5\ \mathrm{m/s}. The flooding superficial gas velocity is the maximum usable superficial gas velocity.

Method

The required cross-sectional area of the column, denoted AA and in square metres (m2\mathrm{m^2}), is the volumetric gas flow rate divided by the superficial gas velocity:

A=QuA = \frac{Q}{u}

The column is circular in cross section. The column diameter, denoted DD and in metres (m\mathrm{m}), follows from the area of a circle:

A=πD24A = \frac{\pi D^2}{4}

where π\pi is the mathematical constant pi, approximately 3.14163.1416, and dimensionless.

Rearrangement gives:

D=4AπD = \sqrt{\frac{4A}{\pi}}

Calculation

Substitution of the given data into the area relation gives:

A=1.8 m3/s1.5 m/s=1.2 m2A = \frac{1.8\ \mathrm{m^3/s}}{1.5\ \mathrm{m/s}} = 1.2\ \mathrm{m^2}

Substitution of the area into the diameter relation gives:

D=4×1.2 m2π=1.528 m2=1.236 mD = \sqrt{\frac{4 \times 1.2\ \mathrm{m^2}}{\pi}} = \sqrt{1.528\ \mathrm{m^2}} = 1.236\ \mathrm{m}

Result

The required column diameter is approximately 1.24 m1.24\ \mathrm{m}.

A nominal diameter of 1.24 m1.24\ \mathrm{m} (practically, the next available standard size at or above this value) provides a cross-sectional area of 1.2 m21.2\ \mathrm{m^2} at the stated design condition, so that the superficial gas velocity does not exceed the flooding value of 1.5 m/s1.5\ \mathrm{m/s} at the gas flow rate of 1.8 m3/s1.8\ \mathrm{m^3/s}.

Flooding correlation, scatter, and operating fraction

Correlation. The value uf,nom=1.5 m s−1u_{\mathrm{f,nom}} = 1.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} is of the kind produced by the Sherwood–Leva–Eckert generalised pressure-drop correlation (GPDC) for packed columns — in current form the Strigle version for random packing, and the Kister and Gill GPDC version for structured packing. The correlation plots a capacity parameter, which contains ufu_{\mathrm{f}}, the packing factor, the gas and liquid densities, and the liquid viscosity, against a flow parameter, which contains the liquid-to-gas flow ratio and the density ratio; the flooding curve is the upper boundary of that plot. Its underlying database is predominantly clean test systems, notably air–water and clean hydrocarbon systems. That origin is the reason a system factor is required in Section 4.

Scatter, s=0.20s = 0.20. No single scatter is a property of the correlation alone; it depends on how the correlation is used.

  • With packing-specific flood and pressure-drop data superimposed on the chart (the Kister and Gill interpolation procedure), flood points are reproduced to about ±15%\pm 15\%, most to ±10%\pm 10\%.
  • With a literature packing factor and no packing-specific data — the situation here, since no packing is even named — the fit is materially worse, and reviews of the Sherwood/Eckert family against large flooding databases report average errors of several tens of percent for some packing classes.

The design scatter adopted here is therefore s=0.20s = 0.20, that is, ±20%\pm 20\% in ufu_{\mathrm{f}}. Crediting the tighter ±15%\pm 15\% band would require the packing-specific data that the problem does not supply. The resulting flooding-velocity range is

Values near 0.800.80 are used only for well-characterised, non-foaming systems with a steady gas rate; above the loading region the pressure drop rises steeply and a small surge reaches flooding. uop=f ufu_{\mathrm{op}} = f \, u_{\mathrm{f}}

Response without defensive prompt

Number of Equilibrium Stages for Liquid–Liquid Extraction

Given data

  • ϕ\phi, the fraction of solute remaining in the raffinate, dimensionless: ϕ=0.01\phi = 0.01, i.e. 1 % remaining, 99 % extracted.
  • S/FS/F, the solvent-to-feed ratio, dimensionless, where SS is the solvent flow rate and FF is the feed (raffinate-phase) flow rate, in consistent flow units so that the units cancel: S/F=1.2S/F = 1.2.

Assumptions
  • Countercurrent multistage contact, the standard arrangement for a staged extraction cascade.
  • Equilibrium stages, with the stated constant value of DD on every stage.
  • Essentially immiscible feed and solvent phases, so the raffinate-phase and extract-phase flow rates are approximately constant through the cascade.
  • Dilute solute, so solute transfer does not appreciably change the phase flow rates.
  • Fresh solvent entering the cascade, containing no solute.
Extraction factor

The extraction factor, denoted EE and dimensionless, is the distribution coefficient multiplied by the solvent-to-feed ratio:

E=DSFE = D \frac{S}{F}

E=1.8×1.2=2.16E = 1.8 \times 1.2 = 2.16

An extraction factor greater than 1 means the solute is preferentially carried away in the extract phase, so a finite number of stages can achieve the stated separation.

Kremser equation for countercurrent extraction

For a countercurrent cascade of equilibrium stages with constant EE and solute-free entering solvent, the Kremser equation gives the fraction of solute remaining in the raffinate as

ϕ=E−1E N+1−1,E≠1\phi = \frac{E - 1}{E^{\,N+1} - 1}, \qquad E \ne 1

where ϕ\phi, EE, and NN are as defined above.

Set ϕ=0.01\phi = 0.01 and E=2.16E = 2.16:

0.01=2.16−12.16 N+1−1=1.162.16 N+1−10.01 = \frac{2.16 - 1}{2.16^{\,N+1} - 1} = \frac{1.16}{2.16^{\,N+1} - 1}

2.16 N+1−1=1.160.01=1162.16^{\,N+1} - 1 = \frac{1.16}{0.01} = 116

2.16 N+1=1172.16^{\,N+1} = 117

Take natural logarithms of both sides:

(N+1) ln⁡(2.16)=ln⁡(117)(N+1)\,\ln(2.16) = \ln(117)

N+1=ln⁡(117)ln⁡(2.16)=4.7620.770=6.18N + 1 = \frac{\ln(117)}{\ln(2.16)} = \frac{4.762}{0.770} = 6.18

N=6.18−1=5.18N = 6.18 - 1 = 5.18

The calculated number of theoretical (equilibrium) stages is approximately

N≈5.2N \approx 5.2

A fractional stage cannot be built, so the number is rounded up to the next whole stage.

Number of Equilibrium Stages for Liquid–Liquid Extraction

1. Definitions
  • NN is the number of equilibrium stages, dimensionless. NN must be a whole number in a physical cascade; a non-integer value obtained from the calculation is rounded up to the next whole number.
  • ϕ\phi is the fraction of the feed solute remaining in the raffinate leaving the cascade, dimensionless. The specified target is ϕ=0.01\phi = 0.01.
  • DD is the distribution coefficient, dimensionless, defined as the solute concentration in the extract phase divided by the solute concentration in the raffinate phase at equilibrium. The specified value is D=1.8D = 1.8.
  • SS is the solvent flow rate, in amount per unit time (the unit cancels in the calculation below).
  • FF is the feed flow rate, in the same amount-per-unit-time unit as SS.
  • S/FS/F is the solvent-to-feed ratio, dimensionless. The specified value is S/F=1.2S/F = 1.2.
  • EE is the extraction factor, dimensionless, defined in Section 3.
2. Assumptions

The estimate uses the standard model for a countercurrent multistage extraction cascade:

  1. The solvent entering the cascade is fresh, that is, it contains no solute.
  2. The two liquid phases are immiscible, so the raffinate-phase flow rate and the extract-phase flow rate are constant from stage to stage.
  3. DD is constant, independent of solute concentration, over the concentration range in the cascade.
  4. Every stage is an equilibrium stage.
  5. Flow rates are expressed on a solute-free or otherwise consistent basis, so that EE as defined below is constant.

No data beyond D=1.8D = 1.8, S/F=1.2S/F = 1.2, and ϕ=0.01\phi = 0.01 were supplied with the problem. The consequences of that limit for the distribution-coefficient range, mutual solubility, and solvent loss are stated in Section 6.

3. Extraction Factor

By definition,

E=D SFE = D\,\frac{S}{F}

Substitution of the specified values gives

E=1.8×1.2=2.16E = 1.8 \times 1.2 = 2.16

E>1E > 1 means that the solvent stream has, per pass, more capacity for the solute than the feed stream retains at equilibrium, so a finite cascade can reach ϕ=0.01\phi = 0.01.

4. Stage Calculation

For a countercurrent cascade of equilibrium stages with fresh solvent, constant EE, and E≠1E \neq 1, the Kremser relation for extraction is

ϕ=E−1E N+1−1\phi = \frac{E - 1}{E^{\,N+1} - 1}

Solving for NN:

E N+1=1+E−1ϕE^{\,N+1} = 1 + \frac{E - 1}{\phi}

N=ln⁡ ⁣[1+(E−1)/ϕ]ln⁡E−1N = \frac{\ln\!\left[1 + (E - 1)/\phi\right]}{\ln E} - 1

where ln⁡\ln is the natural logarithm, dimensionless argument in each case.

Substitution of E=2.16E = 2.16 and ϕ=0.01\phi = 0.01:

N=ln⁡ ⁣[1+(2.16−1)/0.01]ln⁡(2.16)−1=ln⁡(117)ln⁡(2.16)−1=6.18−1=5.18N = \frac{\ln\!\left[1 + (2.16 - 1)/0.01\right]}{\ln(2.16)} - 1 = \frac{\ln(117)}{\ln(2.16)} - 1 = 6.18 - 1 = 5.18

The continuous result is N=5.18N = 5.18. A physical cascade requires a whole number of stages, rounded up:

N=6 stagesN = 6\ \text{stages}

Evaluation of ϕ=(E−1)/(E N+1−1)\phi = (E - 1)/(E^{\,N+1} - 1) with E=2.16E = 2.16:

Five stages leave 1.15 % of the solute in the raffinate, which does not meet the 1 % target. Six stages leave 0.531 %, which meets the target. The required number is therefore 6 equilibrium stages under the stated model.

6. Distribution-Coefficient Range, Mutual Solubility, and Solvent Loss
6.1 Stage count at the ends of a distribution-coefficient range

No range for DD was supplied. The problem states a single value, D=1.8D = 1.8. A stage count at the low end and at the high end of a range cannot be calculated without inventing endpoint values, and no endpoint values are reported here.

If endpoint values are supplied, the calculation is direct. Let DlowD_{\mathrm{low}} be the distribution coefficient at the low end of a range, dimensionless, and let DhighD_{\mathrm{high}} be the distribution coefficient at the high end of a range, dimensionless. Let Elow=Dlow(S/F)E_{\mathrm{low}} = D_{\mathrm{low}}(S/F) be the corresponding low-end extraction factor, dimensionless, and let Ehigh=Dhigh(S/F)E_{\mathrm{high}} = D_{\mathrm{high}}(S/F) be the corresponding high-end extraction factor, dimensionless. Then, for the same target ϕ\phi:

Nlow=ln⁡ ⁣[1+(Elow−1)/ϕ]ln⁡Elow−1,Nhigh=ln⁡ ⁣[1+(Ehigh−1)/ϕ]ln⁡Ehigh−1N_{\mathrm{low}} = \frac{\ln\!\left[1 + (E_{\mathrm{low}} - 1)/\phi\right]}{\ln E_{\mathrm{low}}} - 1, \qquad N_{\mathrm{high}} = \frac{\ln\!\left[1 + (E_{\mathrm{high}} - 1)/\phi\right]}{\ln E_{\mathrm{high}}} - 1

with each result rounded up to a whole number of stages. The low end governs the design: a smaller DD gives a smaller EE and requires more stages. The formula requires E>0E > 0; if an endpoint gives E=1E = 1, the limiting form is ϕ=1/(N+1)\phi = 1/(N+1), and if an endpoint gives E<1E < 1, the target ϕ=0.01\phi = 0.01 may be unreachable at any NN, because ϕ\phi then approaches 1−E1 - E as NN increases.

6.2 Mutual solubility

No mutual solubility data were supplied. The problem gives no solubility of the solvent in the raffinate phase, no solubility of the feed carrier in the extract phase, and no phase-composition data of any kind.

The calculation in Sections 3–5 assumes immiscibility, that is, zero mutual solubility, as stated in Assumption 2. That is an assumption of the model, not a measured value, and it must not be reported as the mutual solubility of a real system. If the real phases are partly miscible, the flow rates vary from stage to stage, DD and EE are in general not constant, and the Kremser result is an approximation whose error cannot be assessed from the data supplied.

6.3 Solvent loss

No solvent loss can be quantified from the data supplied, for two independent reasons:

  1. No mutual solubility is given (Section 6.2), so the amount of solvent dissolved in the outgoing raffinate is unknown.

Under the immiscible model assumed above, solvent loss by dissolution in the raffinate is zero by assumption, again not as a measured result.

For reference, if the missing datum were supplied, the loss would be calculated as follows. Let ww be the mass fraction of solvent dissolved in the outgoing raffinate stream, dimensionless, and let RR be the outgoing raffinate flow rate, in mass per unit time. The solvent loss rate, in mass per unit time, is then wRwR. Neither ww nor RR is given in the problem.
