C4. Adsorption Breakthrough — Second Bed

Response without defensive prompt

Breakthrough Time of an Adsorption Bed

Given data
  • MM = mass of adsorbent in the bed, in kilograms (kg): M=5,000 kgM = 5{,}000\ \mathrm{kg}
  • m˙\dot{m} = mass flow rate at which the adsorbate is carried into the bed by the feed stream, in kilograms per hour (kg/h): m˙=6 kg/h\dot{m} = 6\ \mathrm{kg/h}
  • qq = equilibrium capacity of the adsorbent, in kilograms of adsorbate per kilogram of adsorbent (kg/kg): q=0.15 kg/kgq = 0.15\ \mathrm{kg/kg}
Quantity sought
  • tbt_{\mathrm{b}} = breakthrough time, in hours (h): the time at which the adsorbent bed is saturated and the adsorbate begins to appear (break through) at the bed outlet.
Method and assumptions

The estimate is the ideal, stoichiometric breakthrough time. It rests on the following assumptions:

  1. The adsorbent is loaded uniformly to its full equilibrium capacity qq throughout the bed before any adsorbate leaves the bed.
  2. The mass-transfer zone is sharp, so no capacity is left unused at breakthrough. In a real bed the mass-transfer zone has finite length, part of the bed is not fully saturated at breakthrough, and the actual breakthrough time is shorter than the ideal value calculated here.
  3. All adsorbate entering the bed is adsorbed until saturation, so the outlet adsorbate concentration is effectively zero before breakthrough.
  4. The adsorbate feed rate m˙\dot{m} and the equilibrium capacity qq are constant over the run.
  5. No adsorbate is initially present on the adsorbent, and no adsorbate is lost by any route other than adsorption on the bed.

Under these assumptions, breakthrough occurs when the cumulative mass of adsorbate fed to the bed equals the total adsorption capacity of the bed. This is a single overall mass balance; no kinetic, isotherm-shape, or bed-geometry information is required, and none is supplied.

Calculation
Step 1: Total adsorption capacity of the bed

Let WW denote the total mass of adsorbate the bed can hold at equilibrium, in kilograms (kg). WW is the product of the mass of adsorbent and the equilibrium capacity per unit mass of adsorbent:

W=M qW = M \, q

W=(5,000 kg)×(0.15 kg/kg)=750 kgW = (5{,}000\ \mathrm{kg}) \times (0.15\ \mathrm{kg/kg}) = 750\ \mathrm{kg}

The units check: kg×kg/kg=kg\mathrm{kg} \times \mathrm{kg/kg} = \mathrm{kg}, as required for a mass of adsorbate.

Step 2: Time to supply that mass at the feed rate

The time tbt_{\mathrm{b}} required for the feed stream to deliver a mass WW of adsorbate at the constant rate m˙\dot{m} is:

tb=Wm˙=M qm˙t_{\mathrm{b}} = \frac{W}{\dot{m}} = \frac{M \, q}{\dot{m}}

tb=750 kg6 kg/h=125 ht_{\mathrm{b}} = \frac{750\ \mathrm{kg}}{6\ \mathrm{kg/h}} = 125\ \mathrm{h}

The units check: kg÷kg/h=h\mathrm{kg} \div \mathrm{kg/h} = \mathrm{h}, as required for a time.

Equivalently, in days, with a conversion factor of 24 hours per day (h/day):

tb=125 h24 h/day≈5.2 dayst_{\mathrm{b}} = \frac{125\ \mathrm{h}}{24\ \mathrm{h/day}} \approx 5.2\ \mathrm{days}

Result

The ideal breakthrough time is 125 h, approximately 5.2 days.

This value is the stoichiometric (fully utilised bed) estimate. The breakthrough time of a real bed will be shorter, because breakthrough in practice is declared at a small non-zero outlet concentration and because the mass-transfer zone leaves the downstream part of the bed incompletely saturated at that point. A correction for the length of unused bed would require mass-transfer or breakthrough-curve data, which are not supplied in the problem statement.

Response with defensive prompt

Estimate of Breakthrough Time of an Adsorption Bed

Given data and definitions
  • MM is the mass of adsorbent in the bed, in kilograms (kg). M=5,000 kgM = 5{,}000\ \text{kg}.
  • m˙\dot{m} is the mass flow rate of adsorbate in the feed stream, in kilograms per hour (kg/h). m˙=6 kg/h\dot{m} = 6\ \text{kg/h}.
  • qq is the equilibrium capacity of the adsorbent, in kilograms of adsorbate per kilogram of adsorbent (kg/kg). q=0.15 kg/kgq = 0.15\ \text{kg/kg}. Equilibrium capacity is the loading reached when adsorbent is in equilibrium with adsorbate at the feed concentration and operating temperature, after sufficient contact time.
  • tstt_{\mathrm{st}} is the stoichiometric time, in hours (h): the time at which the feed would have supplied exactly the amount of adsorbate required to saturate the whole bed to qq, if capture were complete and the adsorption front were infinitely sharp.
  • qwq_{\mathrm{w}} is the working capacity, in kilograms of adsorbate per kilogram of adsorbent (kg/kg), defined in the section on working capacity below.
  • tbt_{\mathrm{b}} is the breakthrough time, in hours (h): the time at which adsorbate first appears at the bed outlet at the specified breakthrough concentration.

No feed composition beyond the adsorbate rate, no feed adsorbate concentration, no temperature, no isotherm, no isotherm-fit parameters or fit range, no breakthrough concentration, no mass-transfer data, and no regeneration conditions are given in the problem statement.

Ideal calculation

The total amount of adsorbate the bed can hold at equilibrium, denoted MadsM_{\mathrm{ads}} in kilograms (kg), is

Mads=Mq=(5,000 kg)(0.15 kg/kg)=750 kg.M_{\mathrm{ads}} = M q = (5{,}000\ \text{kg})(0.15\ \text{kg/kg}) = 750\ \text{kg}.

At a constant supply rate m˙\dot{m}, the stoichiometric time is

tst=Mqm˙=750 kg6 kg/h=125 h.t_{\mathrm{st}} = \frac{M q}{\dot{m}} = \frac{750\ \text{kg}}{6\ \text{kg/h}} = 125\ \text{h}.

That is, tst=125 ht_{\mathrm{st}} = 125\ \text{h}, approximately 5.25.2 days of continuous operation.

This is the only numerical time determined by the data given.

Interpretation: stoichiometric time and breakthrough time

The value 125 h125\ \text{h} is not, in general, the breakthrough time tbt_{\mathrm{b}}.

  • The calculation assumes complete capture of all adsorbate fed up to saturation, no adsorbate in the outlet before saturation, and a sharp front that uses the whole bed.
  • In a real bed a mass-transfer zone forms. Part of the bed in that zone is only partly loaded when adsorbate first reaches the outlet. Breakthrough therefore occurs before the whole bed reaches qq, so tb<tstt_{\mathrm{b}} < t_{\mathrm{st}} under normal operation.
  • A numerical value for tbt_{\mathrm{b}} would require, at minimum, a breakthrough criterion, mass-transfer or mass-transfer-zone length data (or an equivalent length of unused bed), flow and bed geometry, and the isotherm at the operating conditions. None of these is given.

tst=125 ht_{\mathrm{st}} = 125\ \text{h} is therefore reported as the ideal saturation time and as an upper bound on the useful operating time per cycle, not as a measured or guaranteed breakthrough time.

Equilibrium capacity and working capacity after regeneration

Equilibrium capacity and working capacity are different quantities.

  • Equilibrium capacity, qq: the loading in equilibrium with the feed, as used above. It applies to fresh or fully regenerated adsorbent exposed to the feed long enough to reach equilibrium, and it ignores adsorbate left on the adsorbent from a previous cycle.
  • Working capacity, qwq_{\mathrm{w}}: the amount actually taken up per cycle in cyclic operation. With qresq_{\mathrm{res}} denoting the residual loading remaining on the adsorbent after regeneration, in kilograms of adsorbate per kilogram of adsorbent (kg/kg), and ignoring for this definition the additional loss from the partly used mass-transfer zone,

qw=q−qres.q_{\mathrm{w}} = q - q_{\mathrm{res}}.

Regeneration is normally incomplete: temperature, purge, pressure, or time limits leave a residual heel, so qres>0q_{\mathrm{res}} > 0 and qw<qq_{\mathrm{w}} < q. Bed ageing, fouling, and loss of sites over repeated cycles reduce qwq_{\mathrm{w}} further.

The corresponding ideal operating time based on working capacity, denoted twt_{\mathrm{w}} in hours (h), would be

tw=Mqwm˙=M(q−qres)m˙<125 h.t_{\mathrm{w}} = \frac{M q_{\mathrm{w}}}{\dot{m}} = \frac{M (q - q_{\mathrm{res}})}{\dot{m}} < 125\ \text{h}.

No value of qresq_{\mathrm{res}}, and hence no value of qwq_{\mathrm{w}} or twt_{\mathrm{w}}, is given in the problem statement. A numerical working-capacity time cannot be obtained from q=0.15 kg/kgq = 0.15\ \text{kg/kg} alone, and no such value is invented here.

Isotherm-fit capacity range

No isotherm, isotherm fit, fitted parameters, or range of fitted qq values is supplied in the problem statement. There is therefore no stated lower end or upper end of a capacity range from which two further times could be calculated.

The dependence on qq is linear and is fully stated by

tst=Mm˙ q=833.3 q h,t_{\mathrm{st}} = \frac{M}{\dot{m}}\, q = 833.3\, q\ \text{h},

where qq is in kilograms per kilogram (kg/kg) and the numerical coefficient 833.3833.3 has units of hours divided by (kg/kg), i.e. h/(kg/kg)\text{h}/(\text{kg/kg}).

If a source supplied a fit range from a lower value, denoted qlowq_{\mathrm{low}} in kg/kg, to an upper value, denoted qhighq_{\mathrm{high}} in kg/kg, the two end times would be 833.3 qlow h833.3\, q_{\mathrm{low}}\ \text{h} and 833.3 qhigh h833.3\, q_{\mathrm{high}}\ \text{h}, with the given q=0.15 kg/kgq = 0.15\ \text{kg/kg} giving 125 h125\ \text{h} inside that interval if qlow≤0.15≤qhighq_{\mathrm{low}} \le 0.15 \le q_{\mathrm{high}}. Supplying numerical ends without the range itself would be fabrication.

Competing components

The value q=0.15 kg/kgq = 0.15\ \text{kg/kg} is a single-solute capacity. By construction a single-solute capacity treats only one adsorbate and ignores:

  • competition for adsorption sites by any other adsorbable component present in a real feed;
  • pore blocking, fouling, or reaction caused by other components;
  • displacement of the target adsorbate by a more strongly adsorbed component, which can produce early breakthrough and outlet concentrations above the feed concentration for the displaced component.

No feed composition is given in the problem statement, so no specific competing component in this stream can be named from the data provided. Naming a particular species — for example a particular solvent, water, or a particular gas — as a competitor in this bed would require the stream composition, which is not stated. In any application of this estimate, the full feed composition at operating conditions must be obtained and a multicomponent capacity or a derated working capacity used if other adsorbable components are present.

Result
  • Total equilibrium holding capacity: 750 kg750\ \text{kg} of adsorbate.
  • Stoichiometric (ideal saturation) time: 125 h125\ \text{h}, approximately 5.25.2 days.
  • Actual breakthrough time: less than 125 h125\ \text{h} in a real bed; not numerically determinable from the data given.
  • Working-capacity time after regeneration: less than the equilibrium-capacity time, by an amount set by the residual loading after regeneration; not numerically determinable from the data given.
  • Times at the ends of an isotherm-fit capacity range, and the identity of specific competing components in the feed: not determinable, because no fit range and no feed composition are given.

C5. Membrane Ageing and Fouling — Second Plant

Response without defensive prompt

Membrane Area Sizing

Given data
  • The permeate volumetric flow rate, denoted QpQ_p and expressed in cubic metres per hour (m3^3/h), is Qp=60 m3/hQ_p = 60\ \text{m}^3/\text{h}.
  • The design flux, denoted JJ and expressed in litres per square metre per hour (L/(m2⋅^2\cdoth)), is J=35 L/(m2⋅h)J = 35\ \text{L}/(\text{m}^2\cdot\text{h}).

The flux JJ, in litres per square metre per hour (L/(m2⋅^2\cdoth)), is defined as the permeate volumetric flow rate per unit membrane area.

Required
  • The required membrane area, denoted AA and expressed in square metres (m2^2).
Calculation

By the definition of flux, the permeate volumetric flow rate, denoted QpQ_p and expressed in litres per hour (L/h), the flux JJ, in litres per square metre per hour (L/(m2⋅^2\cdoth)), and the membrane area AA, in square metres (m2^2), are related by:

Qp=JAQ_p = J A

Rearranging for the membrane area AA, in square metres (m2^2):

A=QpJA = \frac{Q_p}{J}

First, convert the permeate volumetric flow rate QpQ_p, in cubic metres per hour (m3^3/h), to litres per hour (L/h). One cubic metre (m3^3) is equal to 1000 litres (L):

Qp=60 m3h×1000 Lm3=60,000 LhQ_p = 60\ \frac{\text{m}^3}{\text{h}} \times 1000\ \frac{\text{L}}{\text{m}^3} = 60{,}000\ \frac{\text{L}}{\text{h}}

Then:

A=60,000 L/h35 L/(m2⋅h)=1714.2857… m2A = \frac{60{,}000\ \text{L}/\text{h}}{35\ \text{L}/(\text{m}^2\cdot\text{h})} = 1714.2857\ldots\ \text{m}^2

The units cancel as litres per hour (L/h) divided by litres per square metre per hour (L/(m2⋅^2\cdoth)), leaving square metres (m2^2), as required.

Result

The required membrane area AA, in square metres (m2^2), is approximately:

A≈1.71×103 m2A \approx 1.71 \times 10^3\ \text{m}^2

That is, approximately 1714 m2^2 of membrane area is required to produce 60 m3^3/h of permeate at a design flux of 35 L/(m2⋅^2\cdoth).

Response with defensive prompt

Membrane Area Sizing

Symbols and given data
  • QpQ_p, permeate volumetric production rate, in cubic metres per hour (m3/h\mathrm{m^3/h}) or litres per hour (L/h\mathrm{L/h}): Qp=60 m3/h=60,000 L/hQ_p = 60\ \mathrm{m^3/h} = 60{,}000\ \mathrm{L/h}.
  • JJ, permeate flux, volumetric permeate flow per unit membrane area per unit time, in litres per square metre per hour (L/(m2⋅h)\mathrm{L/(m^2\cdot h)}, abbreviated LMH): design value J=35 L/(m2⋅h)J = 35\ \mathrm{L/(m^2\cdot h)}.
  • AA, required active membrane area, in square metres (m2\mathrm{m^2}).
  • JwJ_w, clean-water flux, in L/(m2⋅h)\mathrm{L/(m^2\cdot h)}: flux measured with clean (effectively particle-free, low-fouling) water at a stated transmembrane pressure and temperature.
  • JpJ_p, process flux, in L/(m2⋅h)\mathrm{L/(m^2\cdot h)}: flux obtained on the actual feed.
  • JeocJ_{\mathrm{eoc}}, end-of-cycle process flux, in L/(m2⋅h)\mathrm{L/(m^2\cdot h)}: process flux immediately before a cleaning step, after fouling has developed over one operating cycle.
  • ΔPTM\Delta P_{\mathrm{TM}}, transmembrane pressure, in bar: mean feed-side pressure minus permeate pressure.
  • favailf_{\mathrm{avail}}, availability fraction, dimensionless: productive operating time divided by total elapsed time, after deduction of time for backwashing, cleaning, and other planned stops.

No transmembrane pressure, temperature, feed-water quality, recovery, module size, module price, or fouled flux is specified in the problem. Consequences of that absence are stated in Sections 3 to 5; no single fouled area and no single cost figure follows from the given data alone.

1. Nominal area at the design flux

For a pressure-driven separation operated at a stated flux, area and production are related by

A=QpJ.A = \frac{Q_p}{J}.

Substitution gives

A=60,000 L/h35 L/(m2⋅h)=1,714.3 m2≈1,714 m2.A = \frac{60{,}000\ \mathrm{L/h}}{35\ \mathrm{L/(m^2\cdot h)}} = 1{,}714.3\ \mathrm{m^2} \approx 1{,}714\ \mathrm{m^2}.

Result, at the stated design flux and with continuous operation at that flux: A≈1.71×103 m2A \approx 1.71\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{m^2} of active membrane area.

This is an active-area figure. Installed area is larger after rounding up to whole modules and after any allowance for downtime, fouling, and standby capacity (Sections 3 and 4).

2. Clean-water flux and process flux

JwJ_w and JpJ_p are not interchangeable, and an area calculated from JwJ_w does not size a process unit.

  • Clean-water flux JwJ_w: measured on clean water. Resistance is essentially the membrane resistance alone. No cake layer, biofilm, scaling, adsorbed organic matter, concentration polarisation beyond the hydrodynamic boundary layer, or feed osmotic pressure is present. JwJ_w is therefore used for membrane characterisation, integrity and cleaning checks, and comparison of membranes at the same ΔPTM\Delta P_{\mathrm{TM}} and temperature.
  • Process flux JpJ_p: measured on the actual feed at the operating ΔPTM\Delta P_{\mathrm{TM}}, cross-flow or dead-end conditions, temperature, and recovery. Feed viscosity, suspended and dissolved foulants, concentration polarisation, and, for nanofiltration and reverse osmosis, osmotic pressure difference across the membrane all reduce JpJ_p below JwJ_w at the same ΔPTM\Delta P_{\mathrm{TM}}, commonly by a large factor.

Therefore:

  1. If the stated 35 L/(m2⋅h)35\ \mathrm{L/(m^2\cdot h)} is a process design flux — the conventional meaning of a design flux for sizing — the 1,714 m21{,}714\ \mathrm{m^2} in Section 1 is the correct nominal basis.
  2. If 35 L/(m2⋅h)35\ \mathrm{L/(m^2\cdot h)} were instead a clean-water flux, Section 1 would understate the area, by the ratio Jw/JpJ_w/J_p at the operating conditions. That ratio cannot be obtained from the problem statement; it requires pilot or vendor data on the actual feed.
  3. Flux values are comparable only at stated temperature, because flux varies approximately inversely with water viscosity. A flux quoted at one temperature must be viscosity-corrected before use at another temperature.
3. Area at a fouled, end-of-cycle flux

Fouling raises hydraulic resistance during a cycle, so JpJ_p at fixed ΔPTM\Delta P_{\mathrm{TM}} falls, or ΔPTM\Delta P_{\mathrm{TM}} must be raised at fixed JpJ_p to compensate, until a pressure or energy limit is reached. Sizing on an initial, clean process flux therefore delivers 60 m3/h60\ \mathrm{m^3/h} only at the start of a cycle.

The end-of-cycle area for any stated JeocJ_{\mathrm{eoc}} is

Aeoc=QpJeoc,A_{\mathrm{eoc}} = \frac{Q_p}{J_{\mathrm{eoc}}},

where AeocA_{\mathrm{eoc}} is the area required to maintain QpQ_p at the end of the cycle, in m2\mathrm{m^2}.

Because no JeocJ_{\mathrm{eoc}} is given, the defensible output is this relation plus evaluated cases:

JeocJ_{\mathrm{eoc}} (L/(m2⋅h)\mathrm{L/(m^2\cdot h)}) Basis AeocA_{\mathrm{eoc}} (m2\mathrm{m^2})
35.0 No flux decline; design flux maintained to end of cycle 1,714
30.0 Mild decline 2,000
28.0 80% of design flux 2,143

17.5 50% of design flux 3,429

The 70% figure is an assumption stated for illustration, not a value given in the problem or a universal fouling allowance.

The alternative operating strategy must be stated explicitly in a design: (a) install AeocA_{\mathrm{eoc}} and hold production through the cycle; (b) install about 1,714 m21{,}714\ \mathrm{m^2}, accept a falling production rate or a rising ΔPTM\Delta P_{\mathrm{TM}} during the cycle, and restore flux by cleaning more frequently; or (c) install an intermediate area with a stated safety factor. For reference, a 15% margin on the nominal area gives 1.15×1,714=1,971 m21.15 \times 1{,}714 = 1{,}971\ \mathrm{m^2}, which corresponds to holding production down to a flux of 60,000/1,971=30.4 L/(m2⋅h)60{,}000/1{,}971 = 30.4\ \mathrm{L/(m^2\cdot h)}. A percentage margin and an end-of-cycle flux are two statements of the same allowance and must not be applied twice.

The nominal area assumes 60 m3/h60\ \mathrm{m^3/h} is the instantaneous rate while running. If 60 m3/h60\ \mathrm{m^3/h} is instead a required average rate over a day or over a longer period, downtime must be included:

Aavg=QpJ⋅favail,A_{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{Q_p}{J \cdot f_{\mathrm{avail}}},

where AavgA_{\mathrm{avg}} is the area required to meet the average production, in m2\mathrm{m^2}.

Installed area is then rounded up to whole modules. Example only, for a module active area of 40 m240\ \mathrm{m^2} per module: 1,714/40=42.91{,}714/40 = 42.9, so 43 modules, giving 43×40=1,720 m243 \times 40 = 1{,}720\ \mathrm{m^2} installed. Module area, number of trains, and whether one train is held as standby (N+1N+1 redundancy, where NN is the number of duty trains required) are vendor- and duty-specific and are not fixed by the problem. Standby capacity, if required, is additional to every area above.

5. Cleaning, replacement, and cost assumptions

No cost figure is derivable from the problem as stated. Any cost figure quoted for this duty is valid only under cleaning and replacement assumptions of the following kind, which must be stated with the figure. Omitting them makes a cost figure non-comparable and non-auditable.

Cleaning assumptions to state:

  • Cleaning trigger: for example, cleaning-in-place when normalised flux (flux corrected to a reference temperature and ΔPTM\Delta P_{\mathrm{TM}}) has fallen by a stated percentage, commonly of order 10–15%, or when ΔPTM\Delta P_{\mathrm{TM}} has risen by a stated percentage at constant flux.
  • Cleaning frequency and duration that follow from the feed quality and the trigger above, and the downtime charged to favailf_{\mathrm{avail}} in Section 4.
  • Cleaning method and chemicals: backwash and chemically enhanced backwash for routine fouling, and cleaning-in-place with stated chemicals (for example alkali, acid, or oxidant, as compatible with the membrane material) for the periodic clean; chemical consumption, waste disposal, and labour per clean.
  • Flux recovery per clean: cleaning restores only part of the lost flux. A stated assumption is required, for example recovery to 90–95% of the flux after the previous clean, with the unrecovered part treated as irreversible fouling that accumulates over the membrane life. Assuming 100% recovery at every clean overstates life and understates replacement cost.

Replacement assumptions to state:

  • Membrane service life under the stated cleaning regime, for example 5–7 years for many polymeric microfiltration and ultrafiltration installations and of order 3–7 years for reverse osmosis elements, subject to feed quality, cleaning frequency, and oxidant exposure. Life is an assumption to be confirmed for the specific feed and membrane, not a constant.
  • Replacement unit cost: cost per square metre or per module, whether housings, manifolds, and labour are included, and whether replacement is whole-plant at end of life or staggered by train.
  • Annualised replacement charge derived from those two items: replacement cost divided by the assumed life in years, with any discounting method stated.

Cost structure, with all quantities defined before use:

  • CmemC_{\mathrm{mem}}, membrane capital cost, in currency units: Cmem=cA⋅AinstC_{\mathrm{mem}} = c_A \cdot A_{\mathrm{inst}}, where cAc_A is the supplied membrane cost per unit installed area, in currency units per m2\mathrm{m^2}, and AinstA_{\mathrm{inst}} is the installed area after module rounding, in m2\mathrm{m^2}. Total plant capital cost additionally includes housings, pumps, piping, instrumentation, controls, and installation, which are not proportional to area alone and are not estimated here.
  • Crep,yrC_{\mathrm{rep,yr}}, annual replacement allowance, in currency units per year: total membrane replacement cost at the installed area divided by the assumed service life in years.
  • Operating cost per year additionally includes pumping energy, which depends on ΔPTM\Delta P_{\mathrm{TM}} and its rise with fouling, cleaning chemicals and disposal, labour, and downtime losses. None of the inputs for these terms is given.

Accordingly, this solution reports no total cost. A total cost supplied without cAc_A, a service life, a cleaning frequency and recovery, an energy price, and a ΔPTM\Delta P_{\mathrm{TM}} would be a number without a stated basis.

  • That area is valid only if 35 L/(m2⋅h)35\ \mathrm{L/(m^2\cdot h)} is a process flux on the actual feed. An area based on a clean-water flux would be understated and must not be used for sizing.
  • Area to hold the same production at a fouled end-of-cycle flux: Aeoc=60,000/JeocA_{\mathrm{eoc}} = 60{,}000/J_{\mathrm{eoc}}; for example 2,449 m22{,}449\ \mathrm{m^2} at an assumed Jeoc=24.5 L/(m2⋅h)J_{\mathrm{eoc}} = 24.5\ \mathrm{L/(m^2\cdot h)} (70% of the design flux), 2,400 m22{,}400\ \mathrm{m^2} at 25 L/(m2⋅h)25\ \mathrm{L/(m^2\cdot h)}, and 3,000 m23{,}000\ \mathrm{m^2} at 20 L/(m2⋅h)20\ \mathrm{L/(m^2\cdot h)}.

Definition

The overall column efficiency, EoE_{\mathrm{o}} (dimensionless), is defined as the ratio of the number of theoretical stages, NtN_{\mathrm{t}} (dimensionless), to the number of actual trays, NaN_{\mathrm{a}} (dimensionless), that achieve the same separation:

Eo=NtNaE_{\mathrm{o}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{t}}}{N_{\mathrm{a}}}

An efficiency below 1 means an actual tray achieves less separation than an ideal stage, so more actual trays than theoretical stages are required.

Calculation

Rearranging the definition for NaN_{\mathrm{a}} (dimensionless):

Na=NtEoN_{\mathrm{a}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{t}}}{E_{\mathrm{o}}}

Substituting Nt=26N_{\mathrm{t}} = 26 and Eo=0.55E_{\mathrm{o}} = 0.55:

Na=260.55=47.27N_{\mathrm{a}} = \frac{26}{0.55} = 47.27

Result

The calculated value, 47.27 trays, is not a whole number. A column is built with a whole number of trays, and rounding down to 47 trays would provide less than the required separation. The value is therefore rounded up to the next whole tray.

48 actual trays are required.

Conversion of Theoretical Stages to Actual Trays

Definitions
  • NthN_{\mathrm{th}}, the number of theoretical (equilibrium) stages required, is dimensionless. Here Nth=26N_{\mathrm{th}} = 26.
  • NactN_{\mathrm{act}}, the number of actual trays required, is dimensionless (a count).
  • EoE_o, the overall column efficiency, is dimensionless. Here Eo=0.55E_o = 0.55.
Type of efficiency

EoE_o is the overall column efficiency, not a Murphree efficiency.

The overall column efficiency is defined for the whole column as

Eo=NthNactE_o = \frac{N_{\mathrm{th}}}{N_{\mathrm{act}}}

A Murphree efficiency, by contrast, is defined for a single tray from the change in vapour composition across that tray relative to the change that would occur if the vapour leaving the tray were in equilibrium with the liquid leaving the tray. A Murphree efficiency is therefore applied tray by tray in a stage-by-stage calculation; it is not used in the direct whole-column conversion above, and a numerical Murphree value cannot be converted to EoE_o by this formula alone.

Because EoE_o is given, the conversion is direct. No Murphree calculation is required or possible from the data supplied.

Calculation at the stated efficiency

Rearranging the definition of EoE_o, where EoE_o is the overall column efficiency (dimensionless), NthN_{\mathrm{th}} is the number of theoretical stages (dimensionless) and NactN_{\mathrm{act}} is the number of actual trays (dimensionless):

Nact=NthEo=260.55=47.27N_{\mathrm{act}} = \frac{N_{\mathrm{th}}}{E_o} = \frac{26}{0.55} = 47.27

A fractional tray cannot be installed, and rounding down would provide fewer trays than the requirement, so the result is rounded up to the next whole tray:

Nact=48N_{\mathrm{act}} = 48 actual trays

Correlation associated with an overall efficiency of this type

No correlation is needed to obtain the answer, because Eo=0.55E_o = 0.55 is given in the problem. No relative volatility or liquid viscosity is supplied, so EoE_o cannot be calculated from a correlation here.

The standard empirical correlation used to estimate an overall column efficiency when it is not given is the O'Connell correlation (O'Connell, 1946). In the form given by Eduljee (1958), where EoE_o in the equation is expressed in percent, μa\mu_a is the molar average liquid viscosity of the feed at the average column temperature, in millipascal-seconds (mPa·s, numerically equal to centipoise, cP), and αa\alpha_a is the average relative volatility of the light key component relative to the heavy key component, dimensionless:

Eo (%)=51−32.5log⁡10(μaαa)E_o\,(\%) = 51 - 32.5 \log_{10}(\mu_a \alpha_a)

Fitted systems and basis of the O'Connell correlation:

  • Based mainly on data obtained with hydrocarbon systems.
  • The data set also includes some values for chlorinated solvents and water–alcohol mixtures.
  • The underlying data were from commercial columns fitted with bubble-cap trays; predictions for sieve and valve trays are generally taken as slightly conservative.
  • The correlation is reported to give reliable estimates for hydrocarbon systems and only approximate estimates for other systems. It uses only μa\mu_a and αa\alpha_a and takes no account of tray design parameters.

Naming this correlation does not change the calculation above: the value used here remains the given Eo=0.55E_o = 0.55.

For an exchanger rated by an overall coefficient, the rating relation is

1. Given datum and conclusion

The only datum supplied is the liquid-alone frictional pressure gradient, denoted here by (−dp/dz)L(-\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_{L}, where pp is pressure in bar, zz is distance along the pipe in kilometres (km), and the subscript LL denotes liquid flowing alone, at the liquid rate occurring in the two-phase mixture, in the same pipe:

Both standard models below reduce to a multiplier times 0.5 bar/km0.5\ \mathrm{bar/km}, and the multiplier is not determined by the data supplied. It can be close to 1 for a trace of gas and can exceed 100 for a gas-dominated flow. Any single number produced without further data would be an invented gas rate, not an estimate.

The line is horizontal, so the hydrostatic (elevation) contribution is zero. That removes one term only; it does not determine the frictional term, and an acceleration term arising from gas expansion along the line would additionally require inlet and outlet pressures.

2. Separated-flow estimate: Lockhart–Martinelli correlation
2.1 Flow regime assumed

The phases are treated as flowing separately, each occupying part of the pipe cross-section, with a common pressure at the interface and, in general, different phase velocities. The slip ratio SS, defined as S=uG/uLS = u_{G}/u_{L}, where uGu_{G} is the in-situ gas velocity in metres per second (m/s) and uLu_{L} is the in-situ liquid velocity in m/s, is therefore in general greater than 1. The correlation was developed for separated patterns — stratified, slug, and annular flow — in horizontal and near-horizontal pipes. It is not a model of a uniformly dispersed mixture.

2.2 Correlation

Define:

  • CC: empirical Lockhart–Martinelli constant, dimensionless, set by whether each phase alone would be laminar or turbulent: turbulent–turbulent C=20C = 20; laminar liquid–turbulent gas C=12C = 12; turbulent liquid–laminar gas C=10C = 10; laminar–laminar C=5C = 5.

3.1 Flow regime assumed

The two phases are treated as a single uniformly mixed fluid with no slip, S=1S = 1, and with mixture properties averaged between the phases. 3.2 Model

Define:

The frictional gradient is then written as for a single-phase fluid of density ρh\rho_{h} at mass flux GG. Relative to the liquid-alone reference case, with the liquid rate held at the reference rate so that G=GL0/(1−x)G = G_{L0}/(1-x):

These are sensitivity values, not estimates for the unspecified line.

Physically, the large ratios arise because a small gas mass fraction occupies a large volume fraction when ρL/ρG\rho_{L}/\rho_{G} is large, so the mixture velocity, and hence the frictional gradient, rises sharply.

4. Spread between the two models

The two models cannot be differenced numerically here, because each depends on missing quantities, and not even on the same missing quantities: the separated-flow correlation needs (−dp/dz)G(-\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_{G} (and the laminar/turbulent classification of each phase, for CC), whereas the homogeneous model needs xx, ρL/ρG\rho_{L}/\rho_{G}, and a mixture viscosity. The reportable spread is therefore structural, and is as follows.

  1. Both models give (−dp/dz)TP>0.5 bar/km(-\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_{TP} > 0.5\ \mathrm{bar/km} whenever a non-negligible amount of gas is present, because both multipliers exceed 1.
  2. Neither multiplier has a finite upper bound on the data supplied. Values from about 1 bar/km1\ \mathrm{bar/km} to well over 100 bar/km100\ \mathrm{bar/km} are each consistent with the single datum given, under different, equally admissible gas rates and densities.
  3. Where both models can be evaluated for a real case, the homogeneous model normally gives the lower value in stratified and slug flow, because setting S=1S = 1 understates the gas velocity and the interfacial and wall shear; the two models converge for finely dispersed flow, where SS is in fact close to 1. The size of that gap is case-dependent and cannot be stated without the data in §5.

Reporting a single gradient, or a narrow band, would conceal this indeterminacy.

5. Data required for a numerical estimate

Any one of the following sets closes the problem:

  • For Lockhart–Martinelli: (−dp/dz)G(-\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_{G} in bar/km on the same basis as the liquid value, plus the laminar/turbulent state of each phase alone (equivalently, each phase rate with its density and viscosity, and the pipe diameter in metres, m).
  • For the homogeneous model: gas and liquid mass flow rates in kilograms per second (kg/s), ρL\rho_{L} and ρG\rho_{G} in kg/m³, liquid and gas viscosities in pascal-seconds (Pa·s), pipe internal diameter in m, and pipe roughness in m.
  • For either, in practice: operating pressure in bar and temperature in kelvin (K), so that ρG\rho_{G} and gas expansion along the line can be evaluated, and a flow-pattern check (for example a Baker or Taitel–Dukler map), for which surface tension in newtons per metre (N/m) is also needed.
6. Result

(−dp/dz)TP is not determined by the data supplied;(−dp/dz)TP=0.5 ϕL2 bar/km (separated flow),(-\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_{TP}\ \text{is not determined by the data supplied;}\quad (-\mathrm{d}p/\mathrm{d}z)_{TP} = 0.5\,\phi_{L}^{2}\ \mathrm{bar/km}\ \text{(separated flow)},

with ϕL2\phi_{L}^{2} given in §2.2, and the homogeneous counterpart given in §3.2. The firm conclusions available are that the two-phase gradient exceeds the liquid-alone value of 0.5 bar/km0.5\ \mathrm{bar/km}, that it is unbounded above without a gas rate or a gas-alone gradient, and that the separated-flow and homogeneous values coincide only in the dispersed, no-slip limit. Given data

  • PvP_v = vapour pressure of the liquid at the pumping temperature, in kilopascals (kPa): Pv=70 kPaP_v = 70\ \text{kPa}

Definition

The net positive suction head available, NPSHA\text{NPSH}_A, in metres (m), is the absolute inlet head at the pump above the vapour-pressure head, after friction losses in the suction line:

NPSHA=Ps−Pvρg+zs−hf\text{NPSH}_A = \frac{P_s - P_v}{\rho g} + z_s - h_f

where:

  • Ps−Pvρg\frac{P_s - P_v}{\rho g} is the pressure head in excess of the vapour-pressure head, in metres (m),
  • zsz_s is added because the liquid surface is above the pump centreline,
  • hfh_f is subtracted because friction in the suction line reduces the head available at the pump inlet.

All pressures are absolute pressures, so PsP_s and PvP_v are used directly with no addition of atmospheric pressure.

Calculation

Pressure difference:

Ps−Pv=85 kPa−70 kPa=15 kPa=15,000 PaP_s - P_v = 85\ \text{kPa} - 70\ \text{kPa} = 15\ \text{kPa} = 15{,}000\ \text{Pa}

where Pa denotes pascal, 1 Pa=1 kg/(m⋅s2)1\ \text{Pa} = 1\ \text{kg/(m}\cdot\text{s}^2).

Excess pressure head:

Ps−Pvρg=15,000 Pa(680 kg/m3)(9.81 m/s2)=15,0006,670.8 m≈2.25 m\frac{P_s - P_v}{\rho g} = \frac{15{,}000\ \text{Pa}}{(680\ \text{kg/m}^3)(9.81\ \text{m/s}^2)} = \frac{15{,}000}{6{,}670.8}\ \text{m} \approx 2.25\ \text{m}

Net positive suction head available:

NPSHA=2.25 m+1.8 m−2.6 m≈1.45 m\text{NPSH}_A = 2.25\ \text{m} + 1.8\ \text{m} - 2.6\ \text{m} \approx 1.45\ \text{m}

Result

NPSHA≈1.4–1.5 m, nominally 1.45 m\text{NPSH}_A \approx 1.4\text{--}1.5\ \text{m, nominally } 1.45\ \text{m}

The value is positive but small. In practice this available head must exceed the net positive suction head required by the pump, NPSHR\text{NPSH}_R, in metres (m), specified by the pump manufacturer at the operating flow rate, with a suitable margin, to avoid cavitation. NPSHR\text{NPSH}_R was not given, so a cavitation check cannot be completed from the data provided.

  • ww, the specific work input, in kilojoules per kilogram (kJ/kg\text{kJ}/\text{kg}), is to be determined. Specific denotes per unit mass.
Assumptions
  1. The gas is an ideal gas with constant specific heats, so kk and RR are constant over the temperature range.
  2. The compression is reversible and adiabatic. A reversible adiabatic process is isentropic. This assumption is the one that uses kk; no heat-transfer or efficiency data are given for any other model.

Relations

For a reversible adiabatic (isentropic) change of an ideal gas, the temperature and pressure are related by

T2T1=(P2P1)(k−1)/k\frac{T_2}{T_1} = \left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{(k-1)/k}

where every symbol in the relation has been defined above.

For steady-flow adiabatic compression with negligible kinetic and potential energy changes, the specific work input ww in kJ/kg\text{kJ}/\text{kg} equals the increase in specific enthalpy. For an ideal gas with constant specific heats this gives

w=kk−1RT1[(P2P1)(k−1)/k−1]w = \frac{k}{k-1} R T_1 \left[ \left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{(k-1)/k} - 1 \right]

where kk, RR, T1T_1, P1P_1, and P2P_2 have been defined above.

The pressure ratio, dimensionless, is

P2P1=8 bar1 bar=8\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \frac{8\ \text{bar}}{1\ \text{bar}} = 8

The exponent, dimensionless, is

k−1k=1.25−11.25=0.251.25=0.20\frac{k-1}{k} = \frac{1.25 - 1}{1.25} = \frac{0.25}{1.25} = 0.20

The pressure-ratio factor, dimensionless, is

(P2P1)(k−1)/k=80.20=1.516\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{(k-1)/k} = 8^{0.20} = 1.516

The final temperature T2T_2 in K\text{K} is therefore

T2=T1×1.516=300 K×1.516=454.7 KT_2 = T_1 \times 1.516 = 300\ \text{K} \times 1.516 = 454.7\ \text{K}

The prefactor k/(k−1)k/(k-1), dimensionless, is

kk−1=1.250.25=5.00\frac{k}{k-1} = \frac{1.25}{0.25} = 5.00

The product RT1R T_1 in kJ/kg\text{kJ}/\text{kg} is

RT1=0.287 kJ/(kg⋅K)×300 K=86.1 kJ/kgR T_1 = 0.287\ \text{kJ}/(\text{kg}\cdot\text{K}) \times 300\ \text{K} = 86.1\ \text{kJ}/\text{kg}

Substitution into the work relation gives

w=5.00×86.1 kJ/kg×(1.516−1)w = 5.00 \times 86.1\ \text{kJ}/\text{kg} \times (1.516 - 1)

w=430.5 kJ/kg×0.516=222 kJ/kgw = 430.5\ \text{kJ}/\text{kg} \times 0.516 = 222\ \text{kJ}/\text{kg}

A more precise evaluation with 80.20=1.51578^{0.20} = 1.5157 gives w=222.0 kJ/kgw = 222.0\ \text{kJ}/\text{kg}.

Result

The estimated specific work of reversible adiabatic (isentropic) compression is approximately 222 kJ/kg222\ \text{kJ}/\text{kg}, with a discharge temperature of approximately 455 K455\ \text{K}.

This value is per kilogram of gas compressed. The total work for a given mass is the specific work ww in kJ/kg\text{kJ}/\text{kg} multiplied by that mass in kilograms (kg\text{kg}). A real compressor with irreversibilities would require more work for the same pressure ratio.

Governing equation

For laminar flow through the cake and medium in series, the instantaneous filtration rate is given by the Darcy form for filtration:

dVdt=A ΔPμ(Rc+Rm)\frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{A \, \Delta P}{\mu \left( R_{\mathrm{c}} + R_{\mathrm{m}} \right)}

where dV/dtdV/dt is the volumetric filtrate rate, in cubic metres per second (m3/s\mathrm{m^3/s}).

The cake mass deposited after a filtrate volume VV has passed is

mc=c Vm_{\mathrm{c}} = c \, V

The cake resistance is the specific cake resistance multiplied by the cake mass per unit filter area:

Response with defensive prompt

Constant-Pressure Cake Filtration Time — Range Estimate, Not a Tabulated-Value Design

Conclusion

A single design time cannot be obtained from the tabulated specific cake resistance supplied in the problem. That value, inserted in the filtration equation, gives 1.58 h as an arithmetic illustration only. It is refused as a design basis.

The specific cake resistance is not a material constant of the liquid. It is a property of the cake actually formed, and published values span many orders of magnitude. Over the full published range set out below, the cake-resistance term alone gives a filtration time from less than 1 s to about 823 days for the stated volume, pressure difference, area, viscosity and solids loading. Over the narrower, commonly used classification range for industrial cakes the time is still from about 71 s to about 8.2 days.

A bench constant-pressure filtration test on the actual slurry, with the actual filter medium, at the design pressure difference, is required before a design time, a filter area, or a cycle time is stated.

Symbols and given data

Every symbol is defined here, at or before first use.

  • tt: filtration time, in seconds (s), unless stated in minutes (min), hours (h) or days (d).
  • VV: cumulative filtrate volume, in cubic metres (m³). Target V=2 m3V = 2\ \mathrm{m^3}.
  • ΔP\Delta P: constant pressure difference across cake and filter medium, in pascals (Pa). Given $\Delta P = 150\ \mathrm{kPa} = 1.50\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Pa}$.
  • AA: filtration area, in square metres (m²). Given A=3 m2A = 3\ \mathrm{m^2}.
  • μ\mu: filtrate dynamic viscosity, in pascal seconds (Pa·s). Given μ=0.0012 Pa s\mu = 0.0012\ \mathrm{Pa\,s}.
  • cc: dry cake mass deposited per unit volume of filtrate, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³). Given c=40 kg/m3c = 40\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}.
  • α\alpha: average specific cake resistance, in metres per kilogram (m/kg). Tabulated value supplied: α=8×1010 m/kg\alpha = 8\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m/kg}.
  • RmR_{\mathrm{m}}: filter-medium resistance, in reciprocal metres (m⁻¹). No value is supplied.
  • dV/dt\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}t: instantaneous filtrate volumetric flow rate, in cubic metres per second (m³/s).
  • ss: cake compressibility exponent, dimensionless, in α=α0(ΔP)s\alpha = \alpha_{0}(\Delta P)^{s}, where α0\alpha_{0} is a fitted constant whose units depend on ss. s=0s = 0 for an incompressible cake; ss approaches 1 for a highly compressible cake.
  • AbA_{\mathrm{b}}: bench-test filtration area, in square metres (m²).
  • mpm_{\mathrm{p}}: slope of a plot of t/Vt/V against VV, in seconds per metre to the sixth power (s/m⁶).

The dry cake mass deposited at the target volume is $cV = 40 \times 2 = 80\ \mathrm{kg},i.e., i.e.cV/A = 26.7\ \mathrm{kg/m^2}$ of dry cake per unit filter area. A bench test that stops at a much smaller cake loading does not reproduce the design cake.

Governing equation

For laminar flow through cake and medium in series, the general filtration equation is

1AdVdt=ΔPμ(αcV/A+Rm).\frac{1}{A}\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\Delta P}{\mu\left(\alpha c V/A + R_{\mathrm{m}}\right)} .

At constant ΔP\Delta P, with α\alpha, cc and RmR_{\mathrm{m}} treated as constant during a run, integration from V=0V = 0 at t=0t = 0 gives the integrated constant-pressure (Ruth) equation

t=μαc2A2ΔP V2+μRmAΔP V.t = \frac{\mu\alpha c}{2A^{2}\Delta P}\,V^{2} + \frac{\mu R_{\mathrm{m}}}{A\Delta P}\,V .

The first term is the cake-resistance term. The second term is the filter-medium term. Because no RmR_{\mathrm{m}} is supplied, every time calculated below is the cake-resistance term only, and is therefore a lower bound on the total time. In rearranged linear form,

tV=μαc2A2ΔP V+μRmAΔP,\frac{t}{V} = \frac{\mu\alpha c}{2A^{2}\Delta P}\,V + \frac{\mu R_{\mathrm{m}}}{A\Delta P},

so a plot of t/Vt/V against VV is a straight line whose slope mp=μαc/(2A2ΔP)m_{\mathrm{p}} = \mu\alpha c/(2A^{2}\Delta P) carries α\alpha and whose intercept carries RmR_{\mathrm{m}}. This linear form is the basis of the bench test specified below.

Arithmetic with the tabulated value

Inserting the given values in the cake-resistance term:

t=(0.0012)(8×1010)(40)2(3)2(1.50×105) (2)2=1.536×10102.70×106=5.69×103 s.t = \frac{(0.0012)(8\times10^{10})(40)} {2(3)^{2}(1.50\times10^{5})}\,(2)^{2} = \frac{1.536\times10^{10}}{2.70\times10^{6}} = 5.69\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{s}.

That is t=94.8 min=1.58 ht = 94.8\ \mathrm{min} = 1.58\ \mathrm{h}, cake term only, at exactly α=8×1010 m/kg\alpha = 8\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m/kg}.

Collecting the given constants, the cake term for any α\alpha is

t  [s]=7.11×10−8  α  [m/kg],t\;[\mathrm{s}] = 7.11\times10^{-8}\;\alpha\;[\mathrm{m/kg}],

so tt is directly proportional to α\alpha. Every factor of 10 of error or of real variation in α\alpha is a factor of 10 in tt. No other given quantity has this uncertainty: μ\mu, cc, AA, VV and ΔP\Delta P are measured or set quantities with percent-level uncertainty, whereas α\alpha is uncertain by orders of magnitude.

Why a tabulated specific cake resistance is not a design basis
  1. α\alpha depends on the solids, not only on the liquid: particle size distribution (approximately as the inverse square of the surface-mean particle size in the Carman–Kozeny picture), particle shape, fines content, cake porosity, and whether the solids are crystalline, fibrous, flocculent, gelatinous or biological.
  2. α\alpha depends on slurry state: solids concentration, pH, ionic strength, flocculant or filter-aid dose and conditioning history, ageing, and break-up of flocs or crystals by pumping and agitation.
  3. α\alpha depends on operating conditions. Most real cakes are compressible: α\alpha increases with ΔP\Delta P, described by α=α0(ΔP)s\alpha = \alpha_{0}(\Delta P)^{s} with ss commonly from about 0.1–0.3 for crystalline inorganic solids to about 0.4–0.9 for biological sludges and metal hydroxides. A value tabulated at an unspecified pressure difference is therefore not transferable to 150 kPa150\ \mathrm{kPa}, even for nominally the same solid.
  4. α\alpha depends on the medium through blinding, particle penetration into the cloth, and pre-coat practice, which also set RmR_{\mathrm{m}}.

Consequently a handbook or problem-statement value of α\alpha establishes only the order of magnitude that one unspecified cake once showed. Using it to commit a cycle time, an area or a production rate is not supported.

Full published range and the corresponding time

Published values do not form a narrow band. The sub-ranges reported in standard compilations and handbooks include:

  • Coarse, rigid, crystalline cakes: about 10710^{7} to 109 m/kg10^{9}\ \mathrm{m/kg}.
  • The Leu ease-of-separation classification, reproduced in the Coulson and Richardson tradition: about 109 m/kg10^{9}\ \mathrm{m/kg} very easy, 1010 m/kg10^{10}\ \mathrm{m/kg} easy, 1011 m/kg10^{11}\ \mathrm{m/kg} moderate, 1012 m/kg10^{12}\ \mathrm{m/kg} difficult, 1013 m/kg10^{13}\ \mathrm{m/kg} very difficult.
  • General textbook and reference compilations for industrial cakes: commonly quoted spans of 10910^{9} to 1012 m/kg10^{12}\ \mathrm{m/kg} and of 101010^{10} to 1013 m/kg10^{13}\ \mathrm{m/kg}.
  • Sludges: about 101110^{11} to 1012 m/kg10^{12}\ \mathrm{m/kg} for well conditioned sludges, and about 101310^{13} to 1015 m/kg10^{15}\ \mathrm{m/kg} for raw, unconditioned sludges; mixed urban wastewater sludge is reported at about 101410^{14} to 1015 m/kg10^{15}\ \mathrm{m/kg} before conditioning.

The union of these published values is therefore approximately

107 m/kg  ≲  α  ≲  1015 m/kg,10^{7}\ \mathrm{m/kg} \;\lesssim\; \alpha \;\lesssim\; 10^{15}\ \mathrm{m/kg},

eight orders of magnitude. The tabulated 8×1010 m/kg8\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m/kg} lies inside the union, between the "easy" and "moderate" classes. Nothing in the problem statement — no solid identity, particle size, shape, porosity, conditioning or compressibility — places the actual cake at that point, or in any one decade, of the range.

101310^{13} 7.11×1057.11\times10^{5} 8.23 d
101410^{14} 7.11×1067.11\times10^{6} 82.3 d
101510^{15} 7.11×1077.11\times10^{7} 823 d (about 2.3 years)

The supplied value gives 5.69×1035.69\times10^{3} s (1.58 h), between the 101010^{10} and 101110^{11} rows, as expected.

Reading of the table:

  • Full published range: about 0.7 s to about 823 days, cake term only.
  • Industrial-cake classification range, 10910^{9} to 1013 m/kg10^{13}\ \mathrm{m/kg}: about 71 s to about 8.2 days, cake term only.
  • The filter-medium term, $\mu R_{\mathrm{m}}V/(A\Delta P) = 5.33\times10^{-9} R_{\mathrm{m}}$ seconds with RmR_{\mathrm{m}} in m⁻¹, adds to every entry. For published medium resistances of order 10910^{9} to 1011 m−110^{11}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}} this is about 5 s to 533 s: negligible beside the high-α\alpha entries, but larger than the cake term itself at the low-α\alpha end. The low-end times are therefore lower bounds, not predictions.
  • The upper entries are not practical operating times. They state that, if the actual cake is a difficult or raw-sludge-like cake, the specified area and pressure difference cannot deliver 2 m32\ \mathrm{m^3} on any usable cycle, and the design — area, pressure, conditioning, filter aid, or separation method — must change. A range that ends in an infeasible design is the correct output at this stage; a single mid-range time would conceal the infeasibility.
Bench test required to narrow the range

The required test is a constant-pressure bench filtration test on the actual slurry — a pressure leaf test or a pressure filtration cell ("bomb" filter) — carried out as follows. A vacuum Büchner funnel test is not a substitute at the design condition, because vacuum cannot reach ΔP=150 kPa\Delta P = 150\ \mathrm{kPa} and a compressible cake has a different α\alpha at a different ΔP\Delta P.

  1. Representative sample. Use fresh, actual process slurry at plant solids concentration, particle size distribution, pH, temperature and conditioning or flocculant dose, prepared and handled as in the plant (no extra milling, settling, dilution or ageing). Keep the sample homogeneous during the test without breaking flocs.
  2. Actual medium. Fit the plant filter medium (same cloth, grade and pre-coat, if any) in a cell of known bench area AbA_{\mathrm{b}}.
  3. Design pressure. Run at constant ΔP=150 kPa\Delta P = 150\ \mathrm{kPa}, with filtrate viscosity μ\mu measured at the test temperature. Also run at bracketing pressure differences, for example about 75 kPa and about 300 kPa, to obtain ss from the slope of a plot of log⁡α\log\alpha against log⁡ΔP\log\Delta P and to confirm the value at 150 kPa by interpolation, not extrapolation.
  4. Data. Record cumulative filtrate volume VV against time tt at many points, and continue the run to at least the design cake loading cV/A=26.7 kg/m2cV/A = 26.7\ \mathrm{kg/m^2} of dry cake per unit area, or to the maximum cake thickness proposed for the plant, whichever governs. Weigh the dried cake to measure cc directly as dry cake mass divided by total filtrate volume, rather than assuming the nominal feed concentration.
  5. Reduction. Plot t/Vt/V against VV. From the straight-line region, take the slope mpm_{\mathrm{p}} and the intercept. Then α=2Ab2ΔP mp/(μc)\alpha = 2A_{\mathrm{b}}^{2}\Delta P\,m_{\mathrm{p}}/(\mu c) and Rm=(intercept) AbΔP/μR_{\mathrm{m}} = (\text{intercept})\,A_{\mathrm{b}}\Delta P/\mu. Report curvature or a poor straight-line fit if it occurs: curvature indicates compressibility during the run, medium blinding, settling in the cell, or cake cracking, and invalidates a single constant-α\alpha reduction until the cause is resolved.
  6. Replication. Run at least duplicate tests at 150 kPa and report α\alpha and RmR_{\mathrm{m}} with their replicate spread. Insert the measured α\alpha at 150 kPa, and the measured RmR_{\mathrm{m}}, into the full integrated equation — both terms — to obtain the design time, and state the spread in tt that follows from the replicate spread in α\alpha.

Only after that test is a single time, with an uncertainty interval, a legitimate design figure. Until then the defensible estimate is the range above: nominally 1.58 h at the tabulated resistance, but about 71 s to 8.2 days over the industrial-cake classification range, and about 0.7 s to 823 days over the full published range of specific cake resistance, in every case for the cake-resistance term alone.

E1. Relief Sizing — Second Valve

Response without defensive prompt

Relief Orifice Sizing

Given data and definitions

The required relieving rate, denoted WW, in kilograms per second (kg/s), is:

W=5 kg/sW = 5\ \text{kg/s}

The orifice mass flux under the vapour-only assumption, denoted GG, in kilograms per square metre per second (kg/(m2⋅^{2}\cdots)), is:

G=900 kg/(m2⋅s)G = 900\ \text{kg/(m}^{2}\cdot\text{s)}

The required effective orifice area, denoted ArequiredA_{\text{required}}, in square metres (m2^{2}), is to be determined.

The equivalent circular orifice diameter corresponding to ArequiredA_{\text{required}}, denoted drequiredd_{\text{required}}, in metres (m), is to be determined.

No inlet pressure, temperature, molar mass, compressibility, heat-capacity ratio, back pressure, or discharge coefficient is given, and none is needed: GG is supplied directly, so the choked-flow mass-flux calculation that would otherwise be required to obtain GG is not part of this sizing.

Governing relation

By definition, the mass flux GG is the relieving rate WW divided by the effective orifice area ArequiredA_{\text{required}}:

G=W/ArequiredG = W / A_{\text{required}}

Rearrangement gives:

Arequired=W/GA_{\text{required}} = W / G

Required area

Substitution of W=5 kg/sW = 5\ \text{kg/s} and G=900 kg/(m2⋅s)G = 900\ \text{kg/(m}^{2}\cdot\text{s)} gives:

Arequired=5/900 m2=0.00556 m2A_{\text{required}} = 5 / 900\ \text{m}^{2} = 0.00556\ \text{m}^{2}

Unit conversions of ArequiredA_{\text{required}}:

  • Arequired=0.00556 m2=55.6 cm2A_{\text{required}} = 0.00556\ \text{m}^{2} = 55.6\ \text{cm}^{2}
  • Arequired=5,556 mm2A_{\text{required}} = 5{,}556\ \text{mm}^{2}

Dimensional check: (kg/s)/(kg/(m2⋅s))=m2(\text{kg/s}) / (\text{kg/(m}^{2}\cdot\text{s)}) = \text{m}^{2}, as required for an area.

Equivalent diameter

For a circular orifice, the area ArequiredA_{\text{required}} and the diameter drequiredd_{\text{required}} are related by:

Arequired=πdrequired2/4A_{\text{required}} = \pi d_{\text{required}}^{2} / 4

where π\pi is the dimensionless constant pi, approximately 3.14163.1416.

Rearrangement and substitution give:

drequired=4Arequired/π=4×0.00556/π m=0.0841 md_{\text{required}} = \sqrt{4 A_{\text{required}} / \pi} = \sqrt{4 \times 0.00556 / \pi}\ \text{m} = 0.0841\ \text{m}

That is:

drequired=84.1 mm=3.31 ind_{\text{required}} = 84.1\ \text{mm} = 3.31\ \text{in}

AQ=7,129 mm2=0.007129 m2A_{\text{Q}} = 7{,}129\ \text{mm}^{2} = 0.007129\ \text{m}^{2}
