Response with defensive prompt

Relief Orifice Sizing

1. Given data and scope limit

The relieving rate is denoted by WW, in kilograms per second (kg/s). The orifice mass flux is denoted by GG, in kilograms per square metre per second (kg/(m²·s)). The required effective discharge area is denoted by AA, in square metres (m²).

Given values:

  • W=5 kg/sW = 5\ \text{kg/s}
  • G=900 kg/(m2⋅s)G = 900\ \text{kg/(m}^2\text{·s)}, stated on a vapour-only basis

No other design data are supplied: no protected equipment, no maximum allowable working pressure (MAWP, in kilopascals gauge or pounds per square inch gauge), no set pressure, no relieving pressure or temperature, no fluid identity or composition, no liquid inventory or liquid level, no inlet or outlet piping data, and no per-scenario relieving rates. The calculation in Section 6 is therefore the area that corresponds to the two given numbers. It is not, on the supplied data, a completed relief-device design.

2. Code editions used
  • American Petroleum Institute (API) Standard 520, Part I, Sizing, Selection, and Installation of Pressure-relieving Devices — Part I: Sizing and Selection, Tenth Edition, October 2020, including Errata 1 (2023): sizing method.
  • API Standard 521, Pressure-relieving and Depressuring Systems, Seventh Edition, June 2020, including Errata 1 (November 2022): identification of overpressure causes and determination of individual relieving rates.
  • API Standard 526, Flanged Steel Pressure-relief Valves, Eighth Edition, August 2023: standard orifice letter designations and effective areas, used in Section 7 only.

No project-specified edition was supplied, so the current editions above are reported as the basis used. A project that contractually adopts an earlier edition must be re-stated on that edition; the arithmetic in Section 6 does not depend on the edition.

3. Relief scenarios

The governing scenario is defined in Section 4. Before any governing scenario can be selected, every credible cause of overpressure for the protected system must be listed and a relieving rate obtained for each. The standard checklist of causes, following API Standard 521, is:

  1. Closed or blocked outlets on vessels (vapour outlet blocked, liquid outlet blocked, or both).
  2. Cooling-water failure to a condenser.
  3. Top-tower reflux failure.
  4. Sidestream reflux failure.
  5. Lean-oil failure to an absorber.
  6. Accumulation of non-condensables.
  7. Entrance of highly volatile material into a system.
  8. Overfilling of a storage or surge vessel.
  9. Failure of automatic control, including a control valve failing open, a control valve failing closed, and gas blow-by from a high-pressure source into lower-pressure equipment through a failed or open valve.
  10. Abnormal heat input or abnormal vapour input.
  11. Split heat-exchanger tube (tube rupture), relieving the low-pressure side.
  12. Internal explosion.
  13. Chemical reaction, including runaway reaction.
  14. Hydraulic expansion (thermal expansion of liquid blocked in between closed valves or in a liquid-full item).
  15. Exterior fire.
  16. Power failure (electric, steam, or other), and the related utility failures that follow from it, such as loss of cooling, loss of instrument air, and loss of reflux.

Check-valve failure with reverse flow, inadvertent opening of a valve connecting a high-pressure source, and loss of a utility not listed separately are treated under items 1, 9, and 16; they are not additional physical mechanisms.

Status of each item on the supplied data: not evaluable, and not excludable. No equipment list, piping and instrumentation arrangement, inventory, operating pressure and temperature, or control configuration is given, so no item can be marked credible or non-credible, and no relieving rate can be computed for any item. Any document that marked one of these items as the governing case, or deleted the others, on the present data would be stating a result that the data do not contain.

4. Governing scenario

The governing scenario is the credible scenario that requires the largest effective discharge area, AA, in m². It is not necessarily the scenario with the largest WW, in kg/s, because GG, in kg/(m²·s), depends on the relieving pressure, relieving temperature, fluid properties, and phase in that scenario; a smaller WW at a smaller GG can require the larger AA.

On the supplied data, no governing scenario can be identified. Only one value of WW is supplied, with no statement of which scenario it comes from and no competing values to compare it with.

The calculation in Section 6 therefore proceeds on the following conditional basis only: if the supplied W=5 kg/sW = 5\ \text{kg/s} is the already-determined governing relieving rate, obtained elsewhere from the scenario analysis of Section 3, then the area in Section 6 is the required area for that governing case. If the supplied WW is instead the rate for one non-governing scenario, the area in Section 6 is the area for that scenario alone and the device would be undersized for the true governing case.

5. Phase of the relieving stream: vapour, liquid, or two-phase

Classification on the supplied data: vapour, by stated assumption only — not by demonstration.

Reason: the problem states a vapour-only assumption and supplies a single GG, in kg/(m²·s), on that basis. With WW and a vapour GG as the only inputs, the arithmetic of Section 6 is a vapour calculation. Nothing further can be claimed, for the following reasons.

  • Whether a relief stream is single-phase vapour, single-phase liquid, or two-phase depends on the state at the device inlet at relieving conditions: whether the inlet draws from a vapour space or from below a liquid level, whether a saturated liquid flashes on the pressure drop through the device, and whether liquid is entrained or carried over by level swell. None of the quantities needed for that determination — composition, saturation condition, liquid level relative to the inlet, vessel geometry, or a flashing calculation — is supplied.
  • Several scenarios in Section 3 are characteristically not vapour-only: hydraulic expansion (item 14) relieves liquid; overfilling (item 8) and a blocked liquid outlet (item 1) can relieve liquid; external fire (item 15) on a liquid-containing vessel, tube rupture (item 11), and runaway reaction (item 13) can relieve a two-phase mixture.
  • A vapour-only result is valid only where the inlet is in the vapour space, the liquid level at relieving conditions remains below the inlet with adequate disengagement, and the fluid does not flash or entrain liquid through the device. None of those conditions is established here.

Consequence: if the actual governing stream is liquid or two-phase, the area in Section 6 does not apply. Two-phase sizing requires a two-phase method under API Standard 520, Part I (for example a homogeneous-equilibrium or omega-method calculation, with the fluid properties at relieving conditions), and generally gives a different — for flashing mixtures, a larger — required area than a vapour-only calculation at the same WW. The vapour-only assumption must be proved for the governing scenario, with the level and flashing evidence recorded, before the area below is used for selection.

6. Required area calculation

By definition of mass flux, the mass flow through an area is the mass flux multiplied by that area:

W=G⋅AW = G \cdot A

where WW is the relieving rate in kg/s, GG is the orifice mass flux in kg/(m²·s), and AA is the required effective discharge area in m². Solving for AA:

A=WG=5 kg/s900 kg/(m2⋅s)=5.56×10−3 m2A = \frac{W}{G} = \frac{5\ \text{kg/s}}{900\ \text{kg/(m}^2\text{·s)}} = 5.56 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2

Unit conversions of the same area:

  • A=5,556 mm2A = 5{,}556\ \text{mm}^2 (square millimetres)
  • A=55.6 cm2A = 55.6\ \text{cm}^2 (square centimetres)
  • A=8.61 in2A = 8.61\ \text{in}^2 (square inches)

Check: G⋅A=900×5.56×10−3=5.00 kg/sG \cdot A = 900 \times 5.56 \times 10^{-3} = 5.00\ \text{kg/s}, which reproduces the given WW.

The equivalent circular diameter, denoted by dd, in metres (m), defined by A=πd2/4A = \pi d^{2} / 4, where π\pi is the mathematical constant (dimensionless), is:

d=4Aπ=4×5.56×10−3π=0.0841 m=84.1 mmd = \sqrt{\frac{4A}{\pi}} = \sqrt{\frac{4 \times 5.56 \times 10^{-3}}{\pi}} = 0.0841\ \text{m} = 84.1\ \text{mm}

Basis of the flux value: GG is taken here as the applicable effective mass flux at the relieving conditions for the device, that is, the flux actually achieved through the effective area. No discharge coefficient, back-pressure correction factor, rupture-disc combination factor, or viscosity correction factor is supplied, and none has been applied in addition to GG. Applying such a factor on top of an already-effective GG would double-count it; conversely, if the given GG were an ideal (theoretical) flux, those factors would still have to be applied and AA would increase. Which of these the given GG represents must be confirmed in the source calculation.

7. Standard orifice selection

The selected standard effective area is denoted by AselA_{\text{sel}}, in square inches (in²) or square centimetres (cm²). The selected standard orifice must have AselA_{\text{sel}} equal to or greater than the required AA of 8.61 in28.61\ \text{in}^2 (55.6 cm255.6\ \text{cm}^2).

Under API Standard 526, Eighth Edition:

  • Orifice letter P: Asel=6.38 in2A_{\text{sel}} = 6.38\ \text{in}^2 (41.2 cm241.2\ \text{cm}^2) — smaller than required; not acceptable.
  • Orifice letter Q: Asel=11.05 in2A_{\text{sel}} = 11.05\ \text{in}^2 (71.3 cm271.3\ \text{cm}^2) — the smallest single standard orifice that meets the requirement.

A single-valve selection on the conditional basis of Sections 4–6 is therefore a Q orifice, with an area 28.3%28.3\% above the required area, computed as (11.05/8.61−1)×100%(11.05 / 8.61 - 1) \times 100\%.

Note on notation: the mass flux GG used in this calculation is not the API Standard 526 orifice letter G. Orifice letter G has an effective area of 0.503 in20.503\ \text{in}^2 (3.24 cm23.24\ \text{cm}^2), which is far below the required area and must not be selected on the basis of the shared letter.

Selection cautions: a Q orifice is a large single device. Whether one Q device or multiple smaller devices in parallel are used, and whether the resulting oversizing causes unstable operation (chatter) at the rates of the non-governing scenarios, cannot be assessed without the per-scenario rates, set pressure, and back pressure. Those checks are part of final selection under API Standard 520, Part I, and API Standard 520, Part II (installation, including inlet pressure loss and built-up back pressure).

8. Result and data required to complete the design

Result, on the conditional vapour-only basis stated above:

  • Required effective discharge area: A=5.56×10−3 m2=55.6 cm2=8.61 in2A = 5.56 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2 = 55.6\ \text{cm}^2 = 8.61\ \text{in}^2
  • Smallest single standard orifice meeting that area: API Standard 526 letter Q (11.05 in211.05\ \text{in}^2, 71.3 cm271.3\ \text{cm}^2)
  • Phase basis: vapour only, by assumption given in the problem, not demonstrated
  • Governing scenario: not identifiable from the supplied data; W=5 kg/sW = 5\ \text{kg/s} is treated, conditionally, as the governing rate

Data required before this sizing can be issued as a design: protected equipment and its MAWP; set pressure and allowable overpressure for each case (operating cases and the fire case have different allowable overpressures); relieving pressure and temperature for each scenario; fluid composition and properties at relieving conditions, including molecular weight, ratio of specific heats (dimensionless), and compressibility factor (dimensionless) for vapour and density for liquid; liquid inventory, normal and maximum liquid level, and inlet location for the phase determination in Section 5; a relieving rate for every credible scenario in Section 3; superimposed and built-up back pressure; and the discharge-coefficient and correction-factor basis of the given GG.

E2. Thermal Runaway Time — Second Reaction

Response without defensive prompt

Time to Maximum Rate Under Adiabatic Conditions

Given data
  • T0T_{0}, the initial temperature, in kelvin (K\mathrm{K}): T0=420 KT_{0} = 420\ \mathrm{K}
  • cpc_{p}, the specific heat of the reaction mass, in kilojoules per kilogram per kelvin (kJ/(kg⋅K)\mathrm{kJ/(kg \cdot K)}): cp=2.2 kJ/(kg⋅K)=2200 J/(kg⋅K)c_{p} = 2.2\ \mathrm{kJ/(kg \cdot K)} = 2200\ \mathrm{J/(kg \cdot K)}, where J\mathrm{J} denotes joule
  • q0q_{0}, the heat release rate at T0T_{0}, in watts per kilogram (W/kg\mathrm{W/kg}): q0=6 W/kg=6 J/(s⋅kg)q_{0} = 6\ \mathrm{W/kg} = 6\ \mathrm{J/(s \cdot kg)}, where s\mathrm{s} denotes second
  • EaE_{a}, the activation energy, in kilojoules per mole (kJ/mol\mathrm{kJ/mol}): Ea=110 kJ/mol=110 000 J/molE_{a} = 110\ \mathrm{kJ/mol} = 110\,000\ \mathrm{J/mol}
  • RR, the universal gas constant, in joules per mole per kelvin (J/(mol⋅K)\mathrm{J/(mol \cdot K)}): R=8.314 J/(mol⋅K)R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol \cdot K)}

The quantity to be estimated is TMRad\mathrm{TMR_{ad}}, the time to maximum rate under adiabatic conditions, in seconds (s\mathrm{s}).

Model

Let TT, the temperature of the reaction mass, in kelvin (K\mathrm{K}), and tt, the time, in seconds (s\mathrm{s}), be the variables.

Under adiabatic conditions there is no heat loss to the surroundings, so the heat released by the reaction raises the temperature of the reaction mass. The energy balance per unit mass is

cpdTdt=q(T)c_{p} \frac{dT}{dt} = q(T)

where q(T)q(T), the heat release rate at temperature TT, in watts per kilogram (W/kg\mathrm{W/kg}), is the temperature-dependent value corresponding to q0q_{0} at T0T_{0}, and dT/dtdT/dt, the self-heating rate, is in kelvin per second (K/s\mathrm{K/s}).

The temperature dependence of q(T)q(T) is taken as Arrhenius in form:

q(T)=q0exp⁡[−EaR(1T−1T0)]q(T) = q_{0} \exp\left[-\frac{E_{a}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T} - \frac{1}{T_{0}}\right)\right]

where exp⁡\exp, the exponential function, is dimensionless, as is its argument.

For TT close to T0T_{0},

1T0−1T≈T−T0T02\frac{1}{T_{0}} - \frac{1}{T} \approx \frac{T - T_{0}}{T_{0}^{2}}

so that

q(T)≈q0exp⁡[EaRT02 (T−T0)]q(T) \approx q_{0} \exp\left[\frac{E_{a}}{R T_{0}^{2}}\,(T - T_{0})\right]

This approximation neglects reactant consumption; the reaction is treated as zero-order in concentration, with the rate governed by temperature alone. The energy balance becomes

dTdt=q0cpexp⁡[EaRT02 (T−T0)]\frac{dT}{dt} = \frac{q_{0}}{c_{p}} \exp\left[\frac{E_{a}}{R T_{0}^{2}}\,(T - T_{0})\right]

Initial self-heating rate

At T=T0T = T_{0} the exponential factor is 11, so the initial self-heating rate, denoted (dT/dt)0(dT/dt)_{0} and expressed in kelvin per second (K/s\mathrm{K/s}), is

(dTdt)0=q0cp=6 J/(s⋅kg)2200 J/(kg⋅K)=2.73×10−3 K/s=0.164 K/min\left(\frac{dT}{dt}\right)_{0} = \frac{q_{0}}{c_{p}} = \frac{6\ \mathrm{J/(s \cdot kg)}}{2200\ \mathrm{J/(kg \cdot K)}} = 2.73 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K/s} = 0.164\ \mathrm{K/min}

where min\mathrm{min}, minute, is used in the final value.

Integration to the time to maximum rate

Let θ\theta, the temperature rise above T0T_{0}, in kelvin (K\mathrm{K}), be defined by θ=T−T0\theta = T - T_{0}. Let kk, the coefficient of θ\theta in the exponent, in reciprocal kelvin (K−1\mathrm{K^{-1}}), be defined by

k=EaRT02=110 000 J/mol(8.314 J/(mol⋅K))(420 K)2=0.0750 K−1k = \frac{E_{a}}{R T_{0}^{2}} = \frac{110\,000\ \mathrm{J/mol}}{(8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol \cdot K)})(420\ \mathrm{K})^{2}} = 0.0750\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}

Separating variables in the energy balance and integrating θ\theta from 00 to infinity (in this model the rate increases without bound as TT rises, and the integral converges) gives

TMRad=cpq0∫0∞exp⁡(−kθ) dθ=cpq0⋅1k=cpRT02q0Ea\mathrm{TMR_{ad}} = \frac{c_{p}}{q_{0}} \int_{0}^{\infty} \exp(-k\theta)\, d\theta = \frac{c_{p}}{q_{0}} \cdot \frac{1}{k} = \frac{c_{p} R T_{0}^{2}}{q_{0} E_{a}}

Substitution gives

TMRad=(2200 J/(kg⋅K))(8.314 J/(mol⋅K))(420 K)2(6 J/(s⋅kg))(110 000 J/mol)=4.89×103 s\mathrm{TMR_{ad}} = \frac{(2200\ \mathrm{J/(kg \cdot K)})(8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol \cdot K)})(420\ \mathrm{K})^{2}}{(6\ \mathrm{J/(s \cdot kg)})(110\,000\ \mathrm{J/mol})} = 4.89 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{s}

Unit check: the joules (J\mathrm{J}), kilograms (kg\mathrm{kg}), and moles (mol\mathrm{mol}) cancel, and (K)2(\mathrm{K})^{2} in the numerator cancels one kelvin (K\mathrm{K}) from cpc_{p} and one kelvin (K\mathrm{K}) from RR, leaving seconds (s\mathrm{s}), as required for a time.

Converting,

TMRad≈4 889 s≈81 min≈1.36 h\mathrm{TMR_{ad}} \approx 4\,889\ \mathrm{s} \approx 81\ \mathrm{min} \approx 1.36\ \mathrm{h}

where h\mathrm{h}, hour, is used in the final value.

Result

TMRad≈1.4 h (about 80 min) from 420 K\mathrm{TMR_{ad}} \approx 1.4\ \mathrm{h}\ \text{(about 80 min) from } 420\ \mathrm{K}

Scope of the estimate
  • The conditions are adiabatic: no heat loss, no cooling, and uniform temperature in the reaction mass.
  • Reactant consumption is neglected. Consumption reduces the rate at a given temperature, so the value above is a conservative (short) estimate of the time available before the rate reaches its maximum.
  • The result is an estimate from the Arrhenius approximation near T0T_{0}, not an exact integration with full kinetics. It is suitable for screening and for emergency-response time assessment, not as a substitute for calorimetric TMRad\mathrm{TMR_{ad}} measurement or a full kinetic simulation.
Response with defensive prompt

Time to Maximum Rate under Adiabatic Conditions at 420 K

Result

The estimated time to maximum rate under adiabatic conditions, denoted TMRad and expressed in hours (h), is approximately 1.36 h (81.5 min, or 4.89 × 10³ s) at an initial temperature of 420 K.

This is the standard zeroth-order estimate. It assumes a thermal inertia (phi) factor, denoted φ and dimensionless, of φ = 1. Reactant consumption is neglected, so the estimate is on the conservative (short) side.

Symbols and given data

Each symbol is defined at its first use here:

  • TMRad: time to maximum rate under adiabatic conditions, in seconds (s), minutes (min), or hours (h).
  • T₀: initial temperature, in kelvin (K); T₀ = 420 K.
  • T: temperature during the self-heating, in kelvin (K).
  • t: time, in seconds (s).
  • cp: specific heat capacity of the reaction mass, in joules per kilogram per kelvin (J/(kg·K)).
  • q₀: specific heat release rate at T₀, in watts per kilogram (W/kg), where 1 W = 1 J/s.
  • Ea: activation energy, in joules per mole (J/mol).
  • R: universal gas constant, R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).
  • (dT/dt)₀: initial self-heating rate at T₀, in kelvin per second (K/s), where dT/dt is the rate of change of temperature with time.
  • φ: thermal inertia (phi) factor, dimensionless; φ is the ratio of the total heat capacity of the reaction mass plus its container to the heat capacity of the reaction mass alone. φ = 1 means that no heat is taken up by a container.
Quantity Stated value Converted value Calorimetric basis
cp 2.2 kJ/(kg·K) 2 200 J/(kg·K) Per kilogram of reaction mass. The problem does not name the instrument or method (for example, differential scanning calorimetry, adiabatic calorimetry, or reaction calorimetry), so no instrument is attributed to this value.
q₀ at 420 K 6 W/kg 6 J/(s·kg) Per kilogram of reaction mass, at 420 K. The problem does not name the instrument or method that produced this rate, so no instrument is attributed to this value.
Ea 110 kJ/mol 110 000 J/mol Per mole, as an Arrhenius activation energy. The problem does not name the calorimetric data set or fitting method from which Ea was obtained, so no instrument or method is attributed to this value.
T₀ 420 K 420 K Stated initial (starting) temperature for the adiabatic estimate; not itself a calorimetric measurement.

The calculation requires only that cp and q₀ share the same basis, per kilogram of reaction mass, which the stated units show. It does not require, and the problem does not supply, the identity of a specific calorimeter.

Data-range check

The problem states single values, not ranges, for both q₀ and Ea: q₀ = 6 W/kg only, and Ea = 110 kJ/mol only. No second end value for either quantity is given. Distinct times for two different ends therefore cannot be computed from the stated data without inventing end values, and none are invented here.

The formal end-of-range evaluation is consequently the same at both ends:

Range end q₀ (W/kg) Ea (kJ/mol) TMRad (s) TMRad (min) TMRad (h)
Lower stated end 6 110 4.89 × 10³ 81.5 1.36
Upper stated end 6 110 4.89 × 10³ 81.5 1.36

For later use if genuine range limits are supplied, TMRad at fixed T₀ and cp varies in inverse proportion to the product q₀ × Ea. The shortest time in a genuine range would use the largest q₀ and the largest Ea, and the longest time would use the smallest q₀ and the smallest Ea.

Thermal inertia assumed

φ = 1 is assumed. This is the definition of the adiabatic case requested: all heat released heats the reaction mass alone, with no heat loss to the surroundings and no heat taken up by a test bomb, vessel wall, or other container.

Equivalently, cp and q₀ are treated as already on a φ = 1, reaction-mass basis. The problem gives no φ value greater than 1 and no container mass or container heat capacity, so no φ correction can be, or is, applied. If the quoted q₀ were an uncorrected rate measured in a container with φ > 1, a correction would be required before use and the numerical result above would not apply unchanged.

Method

Under adiabatic conditions with φ = 1, the heat released raises the temperature of the reaction mass, so the initial self-heating rate is

(dT/dt)₀ = q₀ / cp.

Substitution gives

(dT/dt)₀ = 6 J/(s·kg) / 2 200 J/(kg·K) = 2.73 × 10⁻³ K/s = 0.164 K/min = 9.82 K/h.

For a zeroth-order Arrhenius reaction, in which the fall in reactant concentration during the induction period is neglected, expansion of the Arrhenius temperature dependence about T₀ gives the standard Townsend–Tou / Frank-Kamenetskii estimate

TMRad = cp × R × T₀² / (q₀ × Ea).

This is the expression used for the headline result. It is an approximation: cp, Ea, and the reaction order treatment are held constant over the induction period.

Calculation

T₀² = (420 K)² = 176 400 K².

Numerator, cp × R × T₀²:

2 200 J/(kg·K) × 8.314 J/(mol·K) × 176 400 K² = 3.226 × 10⁹ J²/(kg·mol) (units combine as shown below).

Denominator, q₀ × Ea:

6 J/(s·kg) × 110 000 J/mol = 6.60 × 10⁵ J²/(s·kg·mol).

Therefore

TMRad = 3.226 × 10⁹ / 6.60 × 10⁵ s = 4 889 s = 81.5 min = 1.36 h.

The unit check is: [J/(kg·K)] × [J/(mol·K)] × [K²] divided by ([J/(s·kg)] × [J/mol]) leaves seconds (s), as required for a time.

Rounded to the precision justified by the input data (two to three significant figures), TMRad ≈ 1.4 h at 420 K, for φ = 1.

Consistency check and scope

Numerical integration of the full Arrhenius temperature dependence, retaining the same zeroth-order treatment, the same constant cp, and no reactant consumption, gives 5.23 × 10³ s (87.2 min, 1.45 h). The standard closed-form estimate above, 4.89 × 10³ s, is about 7 % shorter, which is the expected direction for that approximation and is conservative for a screening estimate.

The result applies only under the stated conditions:

  1. Adiabatic operation: no heat loss and no cooling.
  2. φ = 1, as stated above.
  3. Constant cp and constant Ea over the temperature rise.
  4. Zeroth-order treatment with reactant consumption neglected; a real reaction that consumes reactant reaches its maximum rate later, so the estimate is conservative in that respect.
  5. The starting point is exactly 420 K with a heat release rate of 6 W/kg at that temperature. At a higher starting temperature the time would be substantially shorter; at a lower starting temperature it would be substantially longer.

E3. Gas Dispersion — Second Release

Response without defensive prompt

Ground-Level Centreline Concentration at 400 m Downwind

Given data and symbols

The following symbols are defined before use, with SI units in parentheses:

  • QQ = continuous mass release rate (kilograms per second, kg/s) = 0.8 kg/s0.8\ \mathrm{kg/s}
  • uu = mean wind speed (metres per second, m/s) = 4 m/s4\ \mathrm{m/s}
  • xx = downwind distance from the source (metres, m) = 400 m400\ \mathrm{m}
  • yy = crosswind distance from the plume centreline (m); on the centreline, y=0 my = 0\ \mathrm{m}
  • zz = height above ground (m); at ground level, z=0 mz = 0\ \mathrm{m}
  • HH = effective release height above ground (m)
  • σy\sigma_y = standard deviation of the concentration distribution in the crosswind direction (m), at distance xx
  • σz\sigma_z = standard deviation of the concentration distribution in the vertical direction (m), at distance xx
  • C(x,y,z)C(x,y,z) = mean gas concentration (kilograms per cubic metre, kg/m3^3) at position (x,y,z)(x, y, z), where (x,y,z)(x, y, z) is the position coordinate set in m

Stability class: Pasquill class D (neutral), which applies to overcast conditions by day or by night. Class D therefore fixes σy\sigma_y and σz\sigma_z.

Assumptions
  1. Steady, continuous release at constant QQ and constant uu, with a steady wind direction.
  2. Gaussian plume model with total reflection at the ground (no deposition, no chemical reaction, no washout).
  3. Flat, open-country terrain, for which the Briggs dispersion formulae below are intended.
  4. No release height is stated in the problem. The calculation is therefore made for a ground-level release, H=0 mH = 0\ \mathrm{m}. This is the highest ground-level result for a given QQ: an elevated release would reduce the ground-level concentration by the factor stated in the note at the end.
Model

For a continuous point source with ground reflection, the Gaussian plume equation is:

C(x,y,z)=Q2πuσyσzexp⁡(−y22σy2)[exp⁡(−(z−H)22σz2)+exp⁡(−(z+H)22σz2)]C(x,y,z) = \frac{Q}{2\pi u \sigma_y \sigma_z} \exp\left(-\frac{y^2}{2\sigma_y^2}\right) \left[ \exp\left(-\frac{(z-H)^2}{2\sigma_z^2}\right) + \exp\left(-\frac{(z+H)^2}{2\sigma_z^2}\right) \right]

where π\pi is the mathematical constant pi (dimensionless) and exp⁡\exp denotes the exponential function.

On the centreline at ground level, y=0 my = 0\ \mathrm{m} and z=0 mz = 0\ \mathrm{m}. The crosswind exponential is then 1, and the two vertical exponentials are equal, so the equation reduces to:

C(x,0,0)=Qπuσyσzexp⁡(−H22σz2)C(x,0,0) = \frac{Q}{\pi u \sigma_y \sigma_z} \exp\left(-\frac{H^2}{2\sigma_z^2}\right)

With H=0 mH = 0\ \mathrm{m} the remaining exponential is also 1, giving:

C(x,0,0)=QπuσyσzC(x,0,0) = \frac{Q}{\pi u \sigma_y \sigma_z}

Dispersion coefficients for class D at 400 m

The Briggs formulae for open country, class D, with xx in m, are:

σy=0.08 x1+0.0001 x\sigma_y = \frac{0.08\,x}{\sqrt{1 + 0.0001\,x}}

σz=0.06 x1+0.0015 x\sigma_z = \frac{0.06\,x}{\sqrt{1 + 0.0015\,x}}

where the numerical coefficients 0.08, 0.06, 0.0001 and 0.0015 are empirical constants of the class D formulae (the constants multiplying xx inside the square roots carry implied units of inverse metres, m−1^{-1}, so that each product with xx is dimensionless).

At x=400 mx = 400\ \mathrm{m}:

σy=0.08×4001+0.0001×400=321.04=321.020=31.4 m\sigma_y = \frac{0.08 \times 400}{\sqrt{1 + 0.0001 \times 400}} = \frac{32}{\sqrt{1.04}} = \frac{32}{1.020} = 31.4\ \mathrm{m}

σz=0.06×4001+0.0015×400=241.60=241.265=19.0 m\sigma_z = \frac{0.06 \times 400}{\sqrt{1 + 0.0015 \times 400}} = \frac{24}{\sqrt{1.60}} = \frac{24}{1.265} = 19.0\ \mathrm{m}

These values agree with a direct reading of the Pasquill–Gifford curves for class D at 400 m, which gives σy\sigma_y of about 30–35 m and σz\sigma_z of about 15–20 m.

Calculation

C(400,0,0)=0.8π×4×31.4×19.0 kg/m3C(400,0,0) = \frac{0.8}{\pi \times 4 \times 31.4 \times 19.0}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}

The denominator is:

π×4×31.4×19.0=7.50×103 m3/s\pi \times 4 \times 31.4 \times 19.0 = 7.50 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{m^3/s}

Hence:

C(400,0,0)=0.87.50×103=1.07×10−4 kg/m3C(400,0,0) = \frac{0.8}{7.50 \times 10^{3}} = 1.07 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}

Unit check: QQ in kg/s divided by (uu in m/s multiplied by σy\sigma_y in m and σz\sigma_z in m) gives kg/s divided by m3^3/s, which is kg/m3^3, as required for a concentration.

In more convenient units:

C(400,0,0)=1.07×10−4 kg/m3=0.107 g/m3=107 mg/m3C(400,0,0) = 1.07 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} = 0.107\ \mathrm{g/m^3} = 107\ \mathrm{mg/m^3}

where g/m3^3 is grams per cubic metre and mg/m3^3 is milligrams per cubic metre.

Result

The estimated ground-level centreline concentration 400 m downwind is approximately 1.1×10−4 kg/m31.1 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}, i.e. about 110 mg/m3110\ \mathrm{mg/m^3}.

Given the scatter in graphical readings of σy\sigma_y and σz\sigma_z, a defensible reported range is about 9090–130 mg/m3130\ \mathrm{mg/m^3}; the central estimate is 107 mg/m3107\ \mathrm{mg/m^3}.

Scope and limits
  • The result is a time-averaged (typically about 10-minute average) plume concentration under steady class D conditions; short-term peak concentrations at a fixed point are higher because of plume meander and concentration fluctuations.
  • If the release is in fact elevated, with H>0 mH > 0\ \mathrm{m}, the ground-level centreline value is the value above multiplied by exp⁡(−H2/(2σz2))\exp\left(-H^2 / (2\sigma_z^2)\right), with σz=19.0 m\sigma_z = 19.0\ \mathrm{m} at this distance. For example, that factor is 0.61 for H=19.0 mH = 19.0\ \mathrm{m} and 0.14 for H=38 mH = 38\ \mathrm{m}.
  • No conversion to parts per million by volume is given, because the identity, molar mass and temperature of the gas are not stated.

Ground-Level Plume Concentration at 400 m

Notation and Given Data
  • CC is the gas concentration, in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m3\mathrm{kg/m^3}), with values also reported in milligrams per cubic metre (mg/m3\mathrm{mg/m^3}).
  • QQ is the continuous release rate (source strength), in kilograms per second (kg/s\mathrm{kg/s}); Q=0.8 kg/sQ = 0.8\ \mathrm{kg/s}.
  • uu is the mean wind speed, in metres per second (m/s\mathrm{m/s}), taken as constant with height and time; u=4 m/su = 4\ \mathrm{m/s}.
  • xx is the downwind distance from the source, in metres (m\mathrm{m}); x=400 mx = 400\ \mathrm{m}.
  • yy is the crosswind distance from the plume centreline, in metres (m\mathrm{m}); on the centreline y=0 my = 0\ \mathrm{m}.
  • zz is the height above ground, in metres (m\mathrm{m}); at ground level z=0 mz = 0\ \mathrm{m}.
  • HH is the effective release height, in metres (m\mathrm{m}). No release height is stated in the problem, so the release is taken to be at ground level, H=0 mH = 0\ \mathrm{m}. The effect of a non-zero value of HH is given in the section on scope.
  • σy\sigma_y is the lateral (crosswind) dispersion coefficient, in metres (m\mathrm{m}): the standard deviation of the concentration distribution in the yy direction defined above.
  • σz\sigma_z is the vertical dispersion coefficient, in metres (m\mathrm{m}): the standard deviation of the concentration distribution in the zz direction defined above.
  • π\pi is the mathematical constant pi, dimensionless, π=3.14159…\pi = 3.14159\ldots
  • exp⁡(w)\exp(w) is the exponential function of the dimensionless quantity ww, where ww is any quantity appearing as its argument in an equation below.

The letters A, B, C, D, E and F are labels for the Pasquill atmospheric stability classes: A is extremely unstable, B is moderately unstable, C is slightly unstable, D is neutral, E is slightly stable, and F is moderately stable.

Result

For stability class D, the ground-level centreline concentration at x=400 mx = 400\ \mathrm{m} is

C≈1.1×10−4 kg/m3≈107 mg/m3.C \approx 1.1 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} \approx 107\ \mathrm{mg/m^3}.

The value is a time-averaged concentration with an averaging time of about 10 minutes (see the section on averaging time). Section 5 gives the corresponding values for all six stability classes A to F. Two significant figures are appropriate: direct reading of the Pasquill–Gifford curves instead of the analytical fits used here shifts the class D value by tens of percent, and Gaussian plume estimates of this type are normally regarded as accurate to within about a factor of two.

1. Stability Class

In the Pasquill classification scheme, the neutral category D is used, regardless of wind speed, for overcast (heavily clouded) conditions during the day or the night. The stated weather — overcast, day or night — therefore gives class D directly. No insolation or night-time cloud-cover entry in the classification table needs to be resolved further.

2. Model

The model is the steady-state Gaussian plume model for a continuous point source of a passive (neutrally buoyant) gas, with total reflection at the ground and no loss by deposition, reaction or washout. The general form is

C(x,y,z)=Q2πu σyσzexp⁡ ⁣(−y22σy2)[exp⁡ ⁣(−(z−H)22σz2)+exp⁡ ⁣(−(z+H)22σz2)],C(x, y, z) = \frac{Q}{2\pi u\, \sigma_y \sigma_z} \exp\!\left(-\frac{y^2}{2\sigma_y^2}\right) \left[ \exp\!\left(-\frac{(z-H)^2}{2\sigma_z^2}\right) + \exp\!\left(-\frac{(z+H)^2}{2\sigma_z^2}\right) \right],

where every symbol in the equation is defined in the notation section above. The second term inside the square brackets is the ground-reflection (image source) term.

Setting y=0 my = 0\ \mathrm{m} and z=0 mz = 0\ \mathrm{m} gives the ground-level centreline form:

C(x,0,0)=Qπu σyσzexp⁡ ⁣(−H22σz2).C(x, 0, 0) = \frac{Q}{\pi u\, \sigma_y \sigma_z} \exp\!\left(-\frac{H^2}{2\sigma_z^2}\right).

With H=0 mH = 0\ \mathrm{m} the exponential factor is exp⁡(0)=1\exp(0) = 1, so the working equation is

C=Qπu σyσz.C = \frac{Q}{\pi u\, \sigma_y \sigma_z}.

Dimensional check: (kg/s)/[(m/s)(m)(m)]=kg/m3(\mathrm{kg/s}) / [(\mathrm{m/s})(\mathrm{m})(\mathrm{m})] = \mathrm{kg/m^3}, as required for CC.

3. Dispersion Coefficients: Source and Values for Class D

Model name: Gaussian plume model. Source of the dispersion coefficients: the analytical formulas of Briggs (1973), which are fits to the Pasquill–Gifford dispersion curves of Pasquill (1961) as presented by Gifford. The open-country (rural, flat terrain) set of the Briggs formulas is used, since the Pasquill–Gifford curves were obtained over open terrain and no urban setting is stated. In the formulas below, xx is in metres (m\mathrm{m}) and the resulting values of σy\sigma_y and σz\sigma_z are in metres (m\mathrm{m}); the formulas are stated for xx between 100 m100\ \mathrm{m} and 10 000 m10\,000\ \mathrm{m}, so x=400 mx = 400\ \mathrm{m} is inside the stated range.

For class D the Briggs open-country formulas are

σy=0.08 x (1+0.0001 x)−1/2,σz=0.06 x (1+0.0015 x)−1/2,\sigma_y = 0.08\, x\, (1 + 0.0001\, x)^{-1/2}, \qquad \sigma_z = 0.06\, x\, (1 + 0.0015\, x)^{-1/2},

where the numerical coefficients in the σy\sigma_y equation and the σz\sigma_z equation are those tabulated by Briggs for class D. At x=400 mx = 400\ \mathrm{m}:

σy=0.08×400×(1+0.0001×400)−1/2=32(1.04)1/2=31.4 m,\sigma_y = 0.08 \times 400 \times (1 + 0.0001 \times 400)^{-1/2} = \frac{32}{(1.04)^{1/2}} = 31.4\ \mathrm{m},

σz=0.06×400×(1+0.0015×400)−1/2=24(1.60)1/2=19.0 m.\sigma_z = 0.06 \times 400 \times (1 + 0.0015 \times 400)^{-1/2} = \frac{24}{(1.60)^{1/2}} = 19.0\ \mathrm{m}.

C=1.07×10−4 kg/m3=107 mg/m3.C = 1.07 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} = 107\ \mathrm{mg/m^3}.

The unit conversion used is 1 kg/m3=106 mg/m31\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} = 10^{6}\ \mathrm{mg/m^3}.

For a ground-level release the pattern in the table is monotonic: from class A to class F the atmosphere becomes more stable, σy\sigma_y and σz\sigma_z decrease, the plume spreads less, and the ground-level centreline value of CC rises — by a factor of about 77 between class A and class F at this distance. This ordering is specific to a ground-level release; for an elevated release a more stable class can give a lower ground-level value at a fixed distance because the plume has spread less towards the ground.

6. Averaging Time

The result is a mean concentration, not an instantaneous value. The Pasquill–Gifford curves, and hence the Briggs fits to them, carry the sampling (averaging) time of the field data behind the curves, conventionally quoted as about 10 minutes; values in the range 3 to 15 minutes are quoted in the literature for the same curves. The concentration calculated here is therefore stated as an approximately 10-minute average. Instantaneous concentrations at a fixed point fluctuate about this mean as the plume meanders, and can exceed it by roughly a factor of two; a mean over a longer period, such as one hour, would in general be lower at a fixed point because the plume spends part of the period directed elsewhere. The plume travel time to the receptor, x/u=400/4=100 sx/u = 400/4 = 100\ \mathrm{s}, where the division is the value of xx in metres (m\mathrm{m}) divided by the value of uu in metres per second (m/s\mathrm{m/s}) to give a time in seconds (s\mathrm{s}), is a separate quantity and is not the averaging time.

7. Assumptions and Scope
  1. Ground-level release: H=0 mH = 0\ \mathrm{m}, because no release height is stated. If the effective release height were not zero, every value in the table of section 5 would be multiplied by exp⁡(−H2/2σz2)\exp(-H^2 / 2\sigma_z^2), with HH and σz\sigma_z in metres (m\mathrm{m}), using the value of σz\sigma_z for the class concerned. For class D at 400 m400\ \mathrm{m}, where σz=19.0 m\sigma_z = 19.0\ \mathrm{m}, even a modest elevated release reduces the ground-level value substantially, so the result is conditional on this assumption.
  2. Steady, continuous release at constant QQ; constant wind speed uu and constant wind direction over the averaging period.
  3. Passive gas: neutral buoyancy, no dense-gas slumping, no chemical reaction, no dry or wet deposition, and no radioactive or other decay during transport.
  4. Flat, open-country terrain with no buildings or other obstacles, matching the open-country Briggs coefficient set. An urban coefficient set gives larger values of σy\sigma_y and σz\sigma_z and therefore lower concentrations, so the terrain setting must match the site before the numbers are applied to a specific location.
  5. Total reflection at the ground and no capping inversion or mixing-layer lid taken into account; at x=400 mx = 400\ \mathrm{m} with the values of σz\sigma_z tabulated above, a lid well above the plume does not affect the result.
  6. The receptor is exactly on the centreline at ground level. Off-centreline values are lower by the factor exp⁡(−y2/2σy2)\exp(-y^2 / 2\sigma_y^2), with yy and σy\sigma_y in metres (m\mathrm{m}).

F1. Control-Loop Tuning — Second Loop

Response without defensive prompt

PI Controller Tuning for a First-Order-Plus-Dead-Time Process

1. Given data and process model

The process gain is Kp=1.8K_{\mathrm{p}} = 1.8 (dimensionless), the process time constant is τ=45 s\tau = 45\ \mathrm{s}, and the dead time is θ=12 s\theta = 12\ \mathrm{s}, where KpK_{\mathrm{p}}, τ\tau, and θ\theta are the three parameters of the process model defined below.

The Laplace variable is ss, with unit s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}}. The process transfer function, Gp(s)G_{\mathrm{p}}(s) (dimensionless), for a first-order-plus-dead-time (FOPDT) process is

Gp(s)=Kp e−θsτs+1=1.8 e−12s45s+1G_{\mathrm{p}}(s) = \frac{K_{\mathrm{p}}\, e^{-\theta s}}{\tau s + 1} = \frac{1.8\, e^{-12 s}}{45 s + 1}

where e−θse^{-\theta s} is the dead-time term, which produces no change in the output for 12 s12\ \mathrm{s} after a change in the input, and 1/(τs+1)1/(\tau s + 1) is the first-order lag, which produces a response that reaches 63.2%63.2\% of its final value one time constant (45 s45\ \mathrm{s}) after the dead time has elapsed.

The ratio of dead time to time constant is

θτ=12 s45 s=0.27\frac{\theta}{\tau} = \frac{12\ \mathrm{s}}{45\ \mathrm{s}} = 0.27

A value of θ/τ\theta/\tau (dimensionless) below about 0.10.1 denotes a lag-dominant process and a value above about 11 denotes a dead-time-dominant process. The value 0.270.27 lies between these limits, so the process is moderately difficult to control: the dead time is large enough to limit the attainable closed-loop speed, but it does not dominate the response. No derivative action is specified in the problem, and none is required at this ratio; a proportional-integral (PI) controller is sufficient.

2. Controller form

The controller gain is KcK_{\mathrm{c}} (dimensionless, because KpK_{\mathrm{p}} is dimensionless and the controller input and output are taken in consistent scaled units), and the integral time (also called the reset time) is τI\tau_{\mathrm{I}}, in seconds (s\mathrm{s}). The PI controller transfer function, Gc(s)G_{\mathrm{c}}(s) (dimensionless), in the standard (non-interacting, ideal) form is

Gc(s)=Kc(1+1τIs)G_{\mathrm{c}}(s) = K_{\mathrm{c}} \left( 1 + \frac{1}{\tau_{\mathrm{I}} s} \right)

where the first term in parentheses, 11, is the proportional action and the second term, 1/(τIs)1/(\tau_{\mathrm{I}} s), is the integral action. The integral action removes steady-state offset after a set-point change or a sustained load disturbance. A smaller τI\tau_{\mathrm{I}} corresponds to stronger integral action.

The sign convention is that the control error, ee (in the units of the controlled variable), is the set point minus the measured value of the controlled variable. With Kp>0K_{\mathrm{p}} > 0, a positive KcK_{\mathrm{c}} under this convention is reverse-acting: an increase in the measured value above the set point decreases the controller output.

3. Recommended tuning: SIMC (Skogestad internal model control) rule

The tuning method used for the recommendation is the SIMC rule (Skogestad internal model control), a direct-synthesis/internal-model-control rule with one adjustable parameter. That parameter is the desired closed-loop time constant, λ\lambda, in seconds (s\mathrm{s}). The value λ=θ=12 s\lambda = \theta = 12\ \mathrm{s} is the standard SIMC choice for a balance of speed of response and robustness; a smaller λ\lambda gives a faster but less robust loop, and a larger λ\lambda gives a slower but more robust loop.

For a PI controller applied to a FOPDT process, the SIMC settings are

Kc=1Kp⋅τλ+θ,τI=min⁡ ⁣(τ,  4(λ+θ))K_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{1}{K_{\mathrm{p}}} \cdot \frac{\tau}{\lambda + \theta}, \qquad \tau_{\mathrm{I}} = \min\!\left( \tau,\; 4(\lambda + \theta) \right)

where min⁡(a,b)\min(a, b) denotes the smaller of the two quantities aa and bb, in seconds (s\mathrm{s}).

Substitution of Kp=1.8K_{\mathrm{p}} = 1.8, τ=45 s\tau = 45\ \mathrm{s}, θ=12 s\theta = 12\ \mathrm{s}, and λ=12 s\lambda = 12\ \mathrm{s} gives

Kc=11.8⋅45 s12 s+12 s=0.5556×1.875=1.04K_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{1}{1.8} \cdot \frac{45\ \mathrm{s}}{12\ \mathrm{s} + 12\ \mathrm{s}} = 0.5556 \times 1.875 = 1.04

τI=min⁡ ⁣(45 s,  4×24 s)=min⁡(45 s,  96 s)=45 s\tau_{\mathrm{I}} = \min\!\left( 45\ \mathrm{s},\; 4 \times 24\ \mathrm{s} \right) = \min(45\ \mathrm{s},\; 96\ \mathrm{s}) = 45\ \mathrm{s}

The corresponding reset rate, 1/τI1/\tau_{\mathrm{I}} (unit: s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}}), is 1/(45 s)=0.022 s−11/(45\ \mathrm{s}) = 0.022\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}, equivalent to 1.331.33 repeats per minute.

The tuned controller is therefore

Gc(s)=1.04(1+145s)G_{\mathrm{c}}(s) = 1.04 \left( 1 + \frac{1}{45 s} \right)

with ss in s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}} and the integral time 4545 in the denominator in seconds (s\mathrm{s}).

4. Robustness of the recommended tuning

The gain crossover frequency is ωgc\omega_{\mathrm{gc}}, in radians per second (rad s−1\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}), defined as the frequency at which the magnitude of the open-loop transfer function equals 11. The phase margin is ϕm\phi_{\mathrm{m}}, in degrees (∘^{\circ}), defined as 180∘180^{\circ} plus the open-loop phase at ωgc\omega_{\mathrm{gc}}. The gain margin is GmG_{\mathrm{m}} (dimensionless), defined as the reciprocal of the open-loop magnitude at the frequency at which the open-loop phase equals −180∘-180^{\circ}.

Numerical evaluation of the open loop formed by Gc(s)G_{\mathrm{c}}(s) from Section 3 in series with Gp(s)G_{\mathrm{p}}(s) from Section 1 gives

  • ωgc=0.042 rad s−1\omega_{\mathrm{gc}} = 0.042\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}},
  • ϕm=61∘\phi_{\mathrm{m}} = 61^{\circ},
  • Gm=3.1G_{\mathrm{m}} = 3.1, equivalent to 9.9 dB9.9\ \mathrm{dB}, where dB\mathrm{dB} denotes decibels, 20log⁡10Gm20 \log_{10} G_{\mathrm{m}}.

A phase margin in the range 45∘45^{\circ} to 60∘60^{\circ} and a gain margin above about 22 are commonly taken as indicating a robust loop. The values above meet the gain-margin condition and lie at the upper end of the phase-margin range, so the recommended tuning is expected to remain stable under moderate errors in KpK_{\mathrm{p}}, τ\tau, and θ\theta, with a set-point response that is close to first order with time constant λ=12 s\lambda = 12\ \mathrm{s} after the dead time: the output begins to move after 12 s12\ \mathrm{s} and approaches the new set point over roughly the following 3λ3\lambda to 4λ4\lambda, that is, 36 s36\ \mathrm{s} to 48 s48\ \mathrm{s}. Overshoot for a set-point step is expected to be small. Integral action gives zero steady-state offset for a step set-point change and for a step load disturbance, subject to the controller output not saturating.

A more conservative variant, obtained from the same formulas with λ=24 s\lambda = 24\ \mathrm{s}, is Kc=(1/1.8)×45 s/(24 s+12 s)=0.69K_{\mathrm{c}} = (1/1.8) \times 45\ \mathrm{s} / (24\ \mathrm{s} + 12\ \mathrm{s}) = 0.69 and τI=min⁡(45 s, 4×36 s)=45 s\tau_{\mathrm{I}} = \min(45\ \mathrm{s},\, 4 \times 36\ \mathrm{s}) = 45\ \mathrm{s}. This variant is appropriate if the model parameters are uncertain or the manipulated variable must move less.

5. Comparison with classical reaction-curve and ultimate-gain rules

The table below places the recommendation beside three classical PI tunings computed from the same KpK_{\mathrm{p}}, τ\tau, and θ\theta. All controller gains KcK_{\mathrm{c}} in the table are dimensionless and all integral times τI\tau_{\mathrm{I}} are in seconds (s\mathrm{s}).

Method KcK_{\mathrm{c}} τI\tau_{\mathrm{I}} (s\mathrm{s})
SIMC, λ=θ\lambda = \theta (recommended) 1.04 45
Ziegler–Nichols reaction curve 1.88 40
Cohen–Coon 1.92 26
Tyreus–Luyben (ultimate-gain based) 1.14 96

The Ziegler–Nichols reaction-curve PI settings are Kc=(0.9/Kp)(τ/θ)=0.9×3.75/1.8=1.88K_{\mathrm{c}} = (0.9/K_{\mathrm{p}})(\tau/\theta) = 0.9 \times 3.75 / 1.8 = 1.88 and τI=θ/0.3=12 s/0.3=40 s\tau_{\mathrm{I}} = \theta/0.3 = 12\ \mathrm{s}/0.3 = 40\ \mathrm{s}. These settings target a quarter-amplitude-decay response and give an oscillatory response with a phase margin of about 36∘36^{\circ} for this process.

The Cohen–Coon PI settings are Kc=(1/Kp)(τ/θ)(0.9+θ/(12τ))=1.92K_{\mathrm{c}} = (1/K_{\mathrm{p}})(\tau/\theta)\left(0.9 + \theta/(12\tau)\right) = 1.92 and τI=θ(30+3θ/τ)/(9+20θ/τ)=26 s\tau_{\mathrm{I}} = \theta \left(30 + 3\theta/\tau\right)/\left(9 + 20\theta/\tau\right) = 26\ \mathrm{s}. These settings are more aggressive still, principally through the shorter integral time.

For the ultimate-gain entries, the ultimate frequency is ωu\omega_{\mathrm{u}}, in radians per second (rad s−1\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}), defined by the phase condition θωu+arctan⁡(τωu)=π\theta \omega_{\mathrm{u}} + \arctan(\tau \omega_{\mathrm{u}}) = \pi, where π\pi is in radians. Solution gives ωu=0.144 rad s−1\omega_{\mathrm{u}} = 0.144\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}. The ultimate period is Pu=2π/ωu=43.7 sP_{\mathrm{u}} = 2\pi/\omega_{\mathrm{u}} = 43.7\ \mathrm{s}, where PuP_{\mathrm{u}} is in seconds (s\mathrm{s}). The ultimate gain is Ku=1+(τωu)2/Kp=3.63K_{\mathrm{u}} = \sqrt{1 + (\tau \omega_{\mathrm{u}})^{2}}/K_{\mathrm{p}} = 3.63 (dimensionless), where KuK_{\mathrm{u}} is the proportional-only controller gain at which the loop is on the boundary of stability. The Tyreus–Luyben PI settings, Kc=Ku/3.2=1.14K_{\mathrm{c}} = K_{\mathrm{u}}/3.2 = 1.14 and τI=2.2Pu=96 s\tau_{\mathrm{I}} = 2.2 P_{\mathrm{u}} = 96\ \mathrm{s}, are conservative and are intended mainly for lag-dominant processes; the long integral time gives slow removal of offset here. The Ziegler–Nichols ultimate-gain PI settings, Kc=0.45Ku=1.64K_{\mathrm{c}} = 0.45 K_{\mathrm{u}} = 1.64 and τI=Pu/1.2=36 s\tau_{\mathrm{I}} = P_{\mathrm{u}}/1.2 = 36\ \mathrm{s}, lie between the reaction-curve settings and the recommendation in aggressiveness.

The classical reaction-curve rules give controller gains roughly 1.81.8 times the recommended value. For a process with θ/τ=0.27\theta/\tau = 0.27, those gains produce noticeable overshoot and oscillation and reduced robustness to model error. The SIMC settings are therefore retained as the recommendation.

6. Implementation notes
  1. Anti-windup protection is required: when the controller output reaches a limit, integration must stop or be back-calculated, otherwise the accumulated integral term produces a large overshoot on recovery.
  2. In a digital implementation, the sampling period, Δt\Delta t, in seconds (s\mathrm{s}), should be no larger than about θ/10=1.2 s\theta/10 = 1.2\ \mathrm{s}, so that the dead time is resolved and the discretisation does not add appreciable phase lag.
  3. A set-point step applied directly through both proportional and integral action produces a proportional kick in the controller output of magnitude KcK_{\mathrm{c}} times the step size. Set-point weighting on the proportional term, or a set-point ramp, removes the kick where the manipulated variable must not move abruptly.
  4. If the actual process gain differs from 1.81.8 by a factor ff (dimensionless), the loop gain changes by the same factor, because the loop gain is proportional to the product KcKpK_{\mathrm{c}} K_{\mathrm{p}}. The gain margin of 3.13.1 in Section 4 states the factor by which that product can increase before the boundary of stability is reached, within the accuracy of the FOPDT model.
  5. The tuning is a starting point for commissioning. It should be checked on the plant with a small set-point step, and λ\lambda increased (equivalently, KcK_{\mathrm{c}} decreased at unchanged τI=45 s\tau_{\mathrm{I}} = 45\ \mathrm{s}) if the response oscillates or the manipulated variable moves excessively.
7. Result

Recommended PI settings for Kp=1.8K_{\mathrm{p}} = 1.8, τ=45 s\tau = 45\ \mathrm{s}, and θ=12 s\theta = 12\ \mathrm{s}:

  • Controller gain: Kc=1.04K_{\mathrm{c}} = 1.04 (dimensionless), reverse-acting under the error convention of Section 2.
  • Integral time: τI=45 s\tau_{\mathrm{I}} = 45\ \mathrm{s} (reset rate 0.022 s−10.022\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}).
  • Controller: Gc(s)=1.04(1+1/(45s))G_{\mathrm{c}}(s) = 1.04 \left( 1 + 1/(45 s) \right).
  • Expected margins: phase margin 61∘61^{\circ}, gain margin 3.13.1.

  • TiT_{i} (s) is the integral (reset) time of the proportional-integral controller.

The process model is the first-order-plus-dead-time (FOPDT) model

P(s)=Kp e−θsτs+1P(s) = \frac{K_{p}\,e^{-\theta s}}{\tau s + 1}

with the given values Kp=1.8K_{p} = 1.8, τ=45 s\tau = 45\ \mathrm{s}, and θ=12 s\theta = 12\ \mathrm{s}. The dead-time ratio, defined as θ/τ\theta/\tau, is 12/45=0.26712/45 = 0.267 (dimensionless).

The controller is taken in the standard (ideal, non-interacting) proportional-integral form

C(s)=Kc(1+1Tis).C(s) = K_{c}\left(1 + \frac{1}{T_{i}s}\right).

Primary tuning: Skogestad Internal Model Control (SIMC) rule

Tuning rule named: the Skogestad Internal Model Control (SIMC) rule.

Model the rule was derived for: an FOPDT model, i.e. exactly the model form above. The SIMC rule is the Skogestad simplification of internal model control (IMC) tuning applied to an FOPDT process.

The rule introduces one design parameter, τc\tau_{c} (s), the desired closed-loop time constant. The standard robust SIMC choice is τc=θ\tau_{c} = \theta, giving τc=12 s\tau_{c} = 12\ \mathrm{s}. The SIMC proportional-integral settings for an FOPDT process are

Kc=1Kp ττc+θ,Ti=min⁡ ⁣(τ,  4(τc+θ)).K_{c} = \frac{1}{K_{p}}\,\frac{\tau}{\tau_{c} + \theta}, \qquad T_{i} = \min\!\left(\tau,\; 4(\tau_{c} + \theta)\right).

Substitution gives

Kc=11.8×4512+12=0.5556×1.875=1.04K_{c} = \frac{1}{1.8}\times\frac{45}{12 + 12} = 0.5556 \times 1.875 = 1.04

and

Ti=min⁡(45,  4×24)=min⁡(45,  96)=45 s.T_{i} = \min(45,\; 4 \times 24) = \min(45,\; 96) = 45\ \mathrm{s}.

Recommended settings: Kc=1.04K_{c} = 1.04 and Ti=45 sT_{i} = 45\ \mathrm{s}. In parallel form, the integral gain, defined as Ki=Kc/TiK_{i} = K_{c}/T_{i} with KiK_{i} in s−1\mathrm{s^{-1}}, is Ki=1.04/45=0.023 s−1K_{i} = 1.04/45 = 0.023\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}.

Gain under a second named rule: Ziegler–Nichols

Second tuning rule named: the Ziegler–Nichols process-reaction-curve (open-loop) rule, which is also fitted to an FOPDT model (the tangent-at-inflection representation of the step response). For proportional-integral control that rule gives

Kc=0.9 τKpθ,Ti=θ0.3.K_{c} = 0.9\,\frac{\tau}{K_{p}\theta}, \qquad T_{i} = \frac{\theta}{0.3}.

Substitution gives

Kc=0.9×451.8×12=0.9×2.083=1.88,K_{c} = 0.9 \times \frac{45}{1.8 \times 12} = 0.9 \times 2.083 = 1.88,

Ti=120.3=40 s.T_{i} = \frac{12}{0.3} = 40\ \mathrm{s}.

The controller gain under the second (Ziegler–Nichols) rule is therefore Kc=1.88K_{c} = 1.88, with Ti=40 sT_{i} = 40\ \mathrm{s}. This gain is about 1.8 times the SIMC gain (1.88/1.04=1.801.88/1.04 = 1.80), which is consistent with the known character of the two rules: the Ziegler–Nichols settings target fast, quarter-amplitude-decay response and are considerably more aggressive and less robust than the SIMC settings.

Dead-time uncertainty

No dead-time uncertainty is specified in the problem statement. The problem gives a single nominal dead time, θ=12 s\theta = 12\ \mathrm{s}, with no tolerance, no range, and no required robustness specification. A required dead-time uncertainty that the tuning "must tolerate" therefore cannot be stated as a given datum; any specific required value (for example ±3 s\pm 3\ \mathrm{s} or ±25%\pm 25\%) would be invented, not derived from the information supplied.

What can be stated, because it is computed from the given model and the recommended tuning, is the dead-time tolerance the SIMC loop actually achieves:

  • With KcKp=1.04×1.8=1.875K_{c}K_{p} = 1.04 \times 1.8 = 1.875 (dimensionless) and Ti=τ=45 sT_{i} = \tau = 45\ \mathrm{s}, the controller zero cancels the process pole, so the open-loop transfer function reduces to a gain, an integrator, and the dead time.
  • The gain crossover frequency, ωc\omega_{c} (rad s−1\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}), defined as the frequency at which the open-loop magnitude equals 1, is ωc=1.875/45=0.0417 rad s−1\omega_{c} = 1.875/45 = 0.0417\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}.
  • The phase margin, defined as 180∘180^{\circ} plus the open-loop phase at ωc\omega_{c}, is 180∘−90∘−ωcθ×(180∘/π)=90∘−28.6∘=61.3∘180^{\circ} - 90^{\circ} - \omega_{c}\theta \times (180^{\circ}/\pi) = 90^{\circ} - 28.6^{\circ} = 61.3^{\circ}.
  • The delay margin, defined as the phase margin in radians divided by ωc\omega_{c}, is 1.071/0.0417=25.7 s1.071 / 0.0417 = 25.7\ \mathrm{s}. The gain margin, defined as the reciprocal of the open-loop magnitude at the frequency where the phase is −180∘-180^{\circ}, is 3.143.14 (dimensionless, about 9.9 dB9.9\ \mathrm{dB}).

So the recommended SIMC tuning tolerates, in the nominal linear model, up to about 26 s26\ \mathrm{s} of additional dead time beyond the nominal 12 s12\ \mathrm{s} before the stability boundary is reached. This 26 s26\ \mathrm{s} is a computed achieved margin, not a specified requirement. It also assumes KpK_{p} and τ\tau are exact and that dead time is the only model error, so it must not be read as an allowable operating uncertainty; a practical dead-time error would consume only part of this margin, alongside errors in KpK_{p} and τ\tau.

F2. Data Reconciliation — Second Plant

Response without defensive prompt

Data Reconciliation — Reconciled Product Flow

Symbols and data

All flows are in the same (unspecified) flow units.

  • FmF_m — measured feed flow, Fm=210F_m = 210
  • PmP_m — measured product flow, Pm=132P_m = 132
  • RmR_m — measured residue flow, Rm=74R_m = 74
  • F^\hat{F} — reconciled (adjusted) feed flow, to be found
  • P^\hat{P} — reconciled (adjusted) product flow, to be found
  • R^\hat{R} — reconciled (adjusted) residue flow, to be found
  • σF\sigma_F — standard uncertainty of the feed meter, in flow units
  • σP\sigma_P — standard uncertainty of the product meter, in flow units
  • σR\sigma_R — standard uncertainty of the residue meter, in flow units
  • σF2\sigma_F^2, σP2\sigma_P^2, σR2\sigma_R^2 — the corresponding variances, in (flow units)2^2

Standard uncertainties, converted from a percentage of each reading:

  • σF=0.015×210=3.15\sigma_F = 0.015 \times 210 = 3.15, so σF2=9.9225\sigma_F^2 = 9.9225
  • σP=0.020×132=2.64\sigma_P = 0.020 \times 132 = 2.64, so σP2=6.9696\sigma_P^2 = 6.9696
  • σR=0.020×74=1.48\sigma_R = 0.020 \times 74 = 1.48, so σR2=2.1904\sigma_R^2 = 2.1904
Balance discrepancy

The material balance that the reconciled flows must satisfy exactly is

F^=P^+R^.\hat{F} = \hat{P} + \hat{R}.

The measured flows do not satisfy the balance:

Pm+Rm=132+74=206≠210=Fm,P_m + R_m = 132 + 74 = 206 \ne 210 = F_m,

so the imbalance, defined as Fm−Pm−RmF_m - P_m - R_m, is

Fm−Pm−Rm=210−132−74=4.F_m - P_m - R_m = 210 - 132 - 74 = 4.

A total correction of 4 flow units must be distributed among the three meters. It is not distributed equally: in weighted least-squares reconciliation a meter is adjusted more when its measurement is less certain, i.e. in proportion to its variance.

Reconciliation principle

The reconciled flows minimise the weighted sum of squared adjustments,

(F^−Fm)2σF2+(P^−Pm)2σP2+(R^−Rm)2σR2,\frac{(\hat{F} - F_m)^2}{\sigma_F^2} + \frac{(\hat{P} - P_m)^2}{\sigma_P^2} + \frac{(\hat{R} - R_m)^2}{\sigma_R^2},

subject to the exact balance F^−P^−R^=0\hat{F} - \hat{P} - \hat{R} = 0.

Solving this constrained minimisation (for example by a Lagrange multiplier for the balance constraint) gives each adjustment proportional to that meter's variance, with a common factor set by the imbalance divided by the sum of the variances. The sum of the variances is

σF2+σP2+σR2=9.9225+6.9696+2.1904=19.0825.\sigma_F^2 + \sigma_P^2 + \sigma_R^2 = 9.9225 + 6.9696 + 2.1904 = 19.0825.

The common factor is

419.0825=0.2096.\frac{4}{19.0825} = 0.2096.

Hence:

  • Feed adjustment: −σF2×0.2096=−9.9225×0.2096=−2.08-\sigma_F^2 \times 0.2096 = -9.9225 \times 0.2096 = -2.08
  • Product adjustment: +σP2×0.2096=+6.9696×0.2096=+1.46+\sigma_P^2 \times 0.2096 = +6.9696 \times 0.2096 = +1.46
  • Residue adjustment: +σR2×0.2096=+2.1904×0.2096=+0.46+\sigma_R^2 \times 0.2096 = +2.1904 \times 0.2096 = +0.46

The signs follow from the imbalance: the feed reading is reduced and the product and residue readings are increased, so that the three meet at a common balanced value. Note that the smallest, most precise meter in absolute terms (the residue meter, σR=1.48\sigma_R = 1.48) receives the smallest adjustment, and the feed meter (σF=3.15\sigma_F = 3.15) receives the largest.

Reconciled flows
  • F^=210−2.08=207.92\hat{F} = 210 - 2.08 = 207.92
  • P^=132+1.46=133.46\hat{P} = 132 + 1.46 = 133.46
  • R^=74+0.46=74.46\hat{R} = 74 + 0.46 = 74.46

Check of the balance:

P^+R^=133.46+74.46=207.92=F^,\hat{P} + \hat{R} = 133.46 + 74.46 = 207.92 = \hat{F},

which satisfies the balance exactly (to rounding).

Answer

The reconciled product flow is approximately 133.5 flow units (133.46 before rounding), increased from the measured 132 because the combined product-plus-residue reading fell 4 units short of the feed reading, and the product meter carries the larger share of that correction on account of its larger variance.

  • RR (unit): residue flow.
  • FmF_{\mathrm{m}} (unit), PmP_{\mathrm{m}} (unit), RmR_{\mathrm{m}} (unit): measured (raw) values of FF, PP, RR.

  • u(Fm)u(F_{\mathrm{m}}) (unit), u(Pm)u(P_{\mathrm{m}}) (unit), u(Rm)u(R_{\mathrm{m}}) (unit): standard uncertainties (1 standard deviation) of the measured values FmF_{\mathrm{m}}, PmP_{\mathrm{m}}, RmR_{\mathrm{m}}.
  • vFv_F (unit²), vPv_P (unit²), vRv_R (unit²): variances of FmF_{\mathrm{m}}, PmP_{\mathrm{m}}, RmR_{\mathrm{m}}, equal to u(Fm)2u(F_{\mathrm{m}})^2, u(Pm)2u(P_{\mathrm{m}})^2, u(Rm)2u(R_{\mathrm{m}})^2 respectively.

  • pp (dimensionless): two-sided probability value for the test in Section 3.

The steady-state material balance to be satisfied exactly by the reconciled values is

F^−P^−R^=0.(0)\hat{F} - \hat{P} - \hat{R} = 0. \tag{0}

The three meter errors are taken as independent, as no correlation is stated.

2. Raw imbalance and its uncertainty

The raw imbalance dd (unit) is

d=Fm−Pm−Rm.(1)d = F_{\mathrm{m}} - P_{\mathrm{m}} - R_{\mathrm{m}}. \tag{1}

Numerically,

d=210−132−74=210−206=+4 unit.(2)d = 210 - 132 - 74 = 210 - 206 = +4\ \text{unit}. \tag{2}

3. Test of whether the imbalance is only random error

The standardised imbalance zz (dimensionless) is

z=du(d)=44.368=0.92.(4)z = \frac{d}{u(d)} = \frac{4}{4.368} = 0.92. \tag{4}

Equivalently, z2=0.84z^2 = 0.84, a chi-square statistic with 1 degree of freedom (one balance constraint).

  • ∣z∣=0.92<1.96|z| = 0.92 < 1.96, the 95 % (two-sided) normal limit.
  • The two-sided probability value is p≈0.36p \approx 0.36, well above 0.05.

Result of the test: the null hypothesis that all three meters are free of gross (systematic) error is not rejected at the 95 % level. An imbalance of 4 unit, or larger, would arise from the stated random uncertainties alone with probability about 36 %. The imbalance is therefore consistent with random error only; there is no statistical evidence, from these three readings alone, of a faulty (grossly biased) meter. Reconciliation by weighted least squares (Section 4) is the appropriate treatment. Section 5 is a sensitivity calculation, not a conclusion that any meter is in fact faulty.

4. Reconciliation by weighted least squares

The reconciled values F^\hat{F}, P^\hat{P}, R^\hat{R} (unit) are the values that minimise the sum of the squared adjustments, each adjustment divided by the variance of its meter,

(F^−Fm)2vF+(P^−Pm)2vP+(R^−Rm)2vR,\frac{(\hat{F}-F_{\mathrm{m}})^2}{v_F} + \frac{(\hat{P}-P_{\mathrm{m}})^2}{v_P} + \frac{(\hat{R}-R_{\mathrm{m}})^2}{v_R},

subject to Eq. (0). A meter with a larger variance receives a larger adjustment. Solving this constrained problem (for example by a Lagrange multiplier) gives each adjustment proportional to the variance of that meter, with a common factor d/(vF+vP+vR)d/(v_F+v_P+v_R), and a sign such that the imbalance is removed:

F^=Fm−vF dvF+vP+vR,P^=Pm+vP dvF+vP+vR,R^=Rm+vR dvF+vP+vR.(5)\hat{F} = F_{\mathrm{m}} - v_F\,\frac{d}{v_F+v_P+v_R}, \qquad \hat{P} = P_{\mathrm{m}} + v_P\,\frac{d}{v_F+v_P+v_R}, \qquad \hat{R} = R_{\mathrm{m}} + v_R\,\frac{d}{v_F+v_P+v_R}. \tag{5}

The common factor is

dvF+vP+vR=419.0825=0.2096 unit−1.\frac{d}{v_F+v_P+v_R} = \frac{4}{19.0825} = 0.2096\ \text{unit}^{-1}.
