F3. Corrosion and Remaining Life — Second Vessel

Response without defensive prompt

Remaining Life of a Vessel — Estimate

Given data
  • Measured wall thickness, denoted tmeasuredt_{\mathrm{measured}} (millimetres, mm): tmeasured=15 mmt_{\mathrm{measured}} = 15\ \mathrm{mm}
  • Minimum required thickness, denoted tminimumt_{\mathrm{minimum}} (millimetres, mm): tminimum=9 mmt_{\mathrm{minimum}} = 9\ \mathrm{mm}
  • General corrosion rate, denoted rr (millimetres per year, mm/year): r=0.22 mm/yearr = 0.22\ \mathrm{mm/year}
Available metal loss

Available metal loss, denoted aa (millimetres, mm), is the measured thickness minus the minimum required thickness:

a=tmeasured−tminimuma = t_{\mathrm{measured}} - t_{\mathrm{minimum}}

a=15 mm−9 mm=6 mma = 15\ \mathrm{mm} - 9\ \mathrm{mm} = 6\ \mathrm{mm}

The value of a=6 mma = 6\ \mathrm{mm} agrees with the value stated in the problem.

Remaining life

Remaining life, denoted LL (years, year), is the available metal loss divided by the general corrosion rate, under the assumptions stated below:

L=arL = \frac{a}{r}

L=6 mm0.22 mm/year=27.2727… yearL = \frac{6\ \mathrm{mm}}{0.22\ \mathrm{mm/year}} = 27.2727\ldots\ \mathrm{year}

L≈27 yearL \approx 27\ \mathrm{year}

That is, approximately 27.3 years if three significant figures are retained, matching the two significant figures in r=0.22 mm/yearr = 0.22\ \mathrm{mm/year} to approximately 27 years.

Assumptions
  1. Corrosion is uniform (general) over the vessel wall, so a single general corrosion rate rr describes the metal loss.
  2. The corrosion rate rr remains constant at 0.22 mm/year0.22\ \mathrm{mm/year} over the remaining life.
  3. The minimum required thickness tminimum=9 mmt_{\mathrm{minimum}} = 9\ \mathrm{mm} remains unchanged (no change in design pressure, temperature, material allowable stress, or applicable code requirement).
  4. No additional allowance is deducted for localized corrosion, pitting, erosion, cracking, or future inspection uncertainty beyond the stated values.

Under these assumptions, the vessel reaches its minimum required thickness after approximately 27 years of further metal loss at the stated rate.

Answer

The estimated remaining life is approximately 27 years.

Response with defensive prompt

Remaining Life of a Vessel — Uniform-Corrosion Estimate

1. Calculation

Symbols, defined before first use:

  • tmt_{\mathrm{m}} (millimetres, mm) is the measured wall thickness.
  • tmint_{\mathrm{min}} (mm) is the minimum required wall thickness, i.e. the thickness needed for the design pressure, design temperature, loads, material allowable stress and weld joint efficiency, with no allowance left for further metal loss.
  • Δt\Delta t (mm) is the available metal loss, Δt=tm−tmin\Delta t = t_{\mathrm{m}} - t_{\mathrm{min}}.
  • rr (millimetres per year, mm/year) is the general, i.e. uniform, corrosion rate.
  • RLRL (years) is the remaining life under uniform corrosion at a constant rate rr.

Given data:

  • tm=15 mmt_{\mathrm{m}} = 15\ \mathrm{mm}
  • tmin=9 mmt_{\mathrm{min}} = 9\ \mathrm{mm}
  • r=0.22 mm/yearr = 0.22\ \mathrm{mm/year}

Available metal loss:

Δt=tm−tmin=15 mm−9 mm=6 mm\Delta t = t_{\mathrm{m}} - t_{\mathrm{min}} = 15\ \mathrm{mm} - 9\ \mathrm{mm} = 6\ \mathrm{mm}

Remaining life, assuming linear uniform loss at the stated constant rate:

RL=Δtr=6 mm0.22 mm/year=27.3 yearsRL = \frac{\Delta t}{r} = \frac{6\ \mathrm{mm}}{0.22\ \mathrm{mm/year}} = 27.3\ \mathrm{years}

Nominal result: approximately 27 years.

This result is valid only if all of the following hold:

  1. tm=15t_{\mathrm{m}} = 15 mm is the minimum measured thickness at the governing location, not an average thickness and not a nominal or original thickness.
  2. tmin=9t_{\mathrm{min}} = 9 mm is correct for the current design and operating conditions.
  3. Metal loss is uniform, proceeds at the constant rate r=0.22r = 0.22 mm/year, and will continue at that rate, with no change in fluid, temperature, pressure, flow, chemistry or operating practice.
  4. No localised attack, cracking, or other time-dependent damage is active at a rate faster than rr.

If any condition does not hold, 27.3 years is not a safe remaining life. In particular, condition 4 is not established by the data given.

2. Rate range — no range was given

No rate range was given in the problem. Only one value of the general corrosion rate was given, r=0.22r = 0.22 mm/year. Distinct remaining lives at the two ends of a rate range therefore cannot be calculated from the given data, and no low and high rates are invented here.

For any rate interval that is later established from inspection data, with rlowr_{\mathrm{low}} (mm/year) defined as the lowest credible rate and rhighr_{\mathrm{high}} (mm/year) defined as the highest credible rate, the two end values are obtained from the same relation, and the higher rate gives the shorter life:

  • Longest life, at rlowr_{\mathrm{low}}: RLmax=Δt/rlow=6/rlowRL_{\mathrm{max}} = \Delta t / r_{\mathrm{low}} = 6 / r_{\mathrm{low}} years
  • Shortest life, at rhighr_{\mathrm{high}}: RLmin=Δt/rhigh=6/rhighRL_{\mathrm{min}} = \Delta t / r_{\mathrm{high}} = 6 / r_{\mathrm{high}} years

Illustrative sensitivity only — the following rates are not data for this vessel, and the corresponding lives are not predictions for this vessel. The table states only how strongly the result depends on the rate actually established:

Rate rr (mm/year) RL=6/rRL = 6 / r (years)
0.11 (one-half of the given rate) 54.5
0.22 (given rate) 27.3
0.44 (twice the given rate) 13.6
1.00 (illustrative fast localised rate) 6.0

A factor of two error in the rate produces a factor of two error in the remaining life. Establishing the rate, and whether localised attack is present, is therefore the controlling task, not refinement of the arithmetic.

3. Damage mechanisms

The given rate rr describes general (uniform) corrosion only: metal loss spread broadly over a surface, for which an average thickness trend and the calculation in Section 1 are meaningful. Other mechanisms that can govern a pressure vessel, depending on material, fluid, temperature and environment — none of which were given — include:

3.1 Localised attack
  • Pitting corrosion: deep, narrow pits. The deepest pit, not the average wall loss, governs perforation. Pit penetration rates commonly exceed the general rate by a large factor, so a vessel can leak while the average thickness still appears to give a long life.
  • Crevice corrosion: accelerated attack in shielded gaps, under gaskets, lap joints, deposits and supports, where the local chemistry differs from the bulk fluid.
  • Under-deposit corrosion: attack beneath scale, sludge, corrosion product or other deposits, often combined with pitting.
  • Galvanic corrosion: accelerated loss of the less noble metal at a dissimilar-metal contact, localised near the junction.
  • Erosion-corrosion and flow-accelerated corrosion: removal of metal or of a protective film by flowing fluid, localised at inlets, bends, restrictions, impingement zones and areas of turbulence or phase change.
  • Microbiologically influenced corrosion (MIC): pitting and under-deposit attack associated with bacterial activity, commonly in stagnant or low-flow water-containing zones.
  • Corrosion under insulation (CUI): external corrosion, often highly localised and hidden, under wet or damaged insulation and cladding, especially at supports, nozzles and insulation breaches.
  • Selective leaching: removal of one element from an alloy, e.g. dezincification of brass or graphitic corrosion of cast iron, leaving a weakened porous structure with little visible thickness change.
3.2 Other mechanisms not described by a uniform rate
  • Stress corrosion cracking (SCC): cracking under tensile stress in a specific environment, e.g. chloride SCC of austenitic stainless steel, caustic cracking and amine cracking of carbon steel. Cracking can cause failure with negligible general thinning, and a thickness-based remaining life does not apply.
  • Hydrogen damage: hydrogen-induced cracking (HIC), stress-oriented HIC, blistering, and high-temperature hydrogen attack, depending on service.
  • Environmental and high-temperature mechanisms: carbon dioxide (sweet) corrosion, hydrogen sulfide (sour) corrosion, sulfidation, oxidation, carburisation and naphthenic acid corrosion, each strongly dependent on fluid composition and temperature.
  • Fatigue, creep and brittle fracture: not corrosion, but relevant to vessel life at cyclic or high-temperature service and not captured by a corrosion-rate calculation.

Which of these mechanisms, if any, are active in this vessel cannot be determined from a thickness, a required thickness and one general rate. Naming a mechanism as active for this item, or ruling one out, requires the item-specific data in Section 4.

4. Item-specific inspection data required to narrow the range

To replace the single assumed rate with a defensible rate range, and to test for localised attack, the following data for this specific vessel are required:

4.1 Identity, design and material
  • Vessel identifier, construction code and year, design pressure and temperature, maximum allowable working pressure (MAWP), and the calculation from which tmin=9t_{\mathrm{min}} = 9 mm was obtained, including material allowable stress and weld joint efficiency.
  • Material specification and grade for shell, heads, nozzles and welds; original nominal thickness and original corrosion allowance.
  • Confirmation that current operating pressure and temperature remain within the basis used for tmint_{\mathrm{min}}.
4.2 Service and operating history
  • Fluid or fluids handled, phase, and composition, including water content, pH (a measure of acidity, defined as the negative base-10 logarithm of hydrogen-ion activity), chloride content, carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulfide partial pressures, oxygen ingress, solids and contaminants.
  • Operating temperature, pressure, flow velocity and flow regime, in particular at inlets, bends and liquid-level and vapour–liquid interface zones.
  • Changes of service, feed, chemistry or operating conditions, excursions, shutdown and stagnant periods, and any leaks, repairs, replacements or previous failures on this vessel or on similar vessels in the same service.
4.3 Thickness and localised-attack data
  • Previous inspection reports for this vessel, with dates, so that short-term and long-term corrosion rates can be calculated separately from thickness readings taken at the same locations over time; the governing rate is normally the larger of the two.
  • Current thickness readings at defined condition monitoring locations (CMLs), i.e. marked inspection points revisited at each inspection, reported as the minimum reading at each location, with the instrument, calibration, surface preparation and measurement uncertainty stated.
  • Thickness grids or scans over areas of suspected thinning, sufficient to establish the extent as well as the depth of thinning, for assessment of a local thin area where needed.
  • Direct evidence on localised attack: maximum pit depth and pit density from pit-depth measurement, surface replication, laser or profilometry scanning, or internal visual inspection; depth and extent of attack under deposits, at crevices, at the liquid level, and under insulation at selected insulation-removal locations.
  • Internal and external visual inspection findings, coating and insulation condition, and deposit, scale and corrosion-product samples with analysis, including microbiological testing where MIC is a candidate mechanism.
4.4 Cracking and monitoring data
  • Non-destructive examination (NDE) for cracking where SCC or hydrogen damage is a candidate, e.g. wet fluorescent magnetic particle testing, liquid penetrant testing, phased-array ultrasonic testing or time-of-flight diffraction, with the locations and coverage stated.
  • Corrosion monitoring data for this service: corrosion coupon mass-loss results, electrical resistance or linear polarisation probe trends, process chemistry trends, and iron or other metal counts in the fluid, each with dates that can be aligned with thickness trends.
  • Planned future operation: any intended change in fluid, temperature, pressure or throughput that would change the future rate relative to the historical rate.

With at least two reliable thickness data sets at the same CMLs, a measured maximum pit depth, and the service data above, a low and a high credible rate can be stated from evidence, the two end lives can then be calculated by the relations in Section 2, and the governing mechanism — uniform loss or localised attack — can be identified.

5. Conclusion
  • Available metal loss: Δt=6\Delta t = 6 mm.
  • Remaining life at the single given general corrosion rate r=0.22r = 0.22 mm/year: RL=27.3RL = 27.3 years, approximately 27 years.
  • Remaining life at both ends of a rate range: not calculable from the data given, because no rate range was given. The end values follow from RL=6/rRL = 6 / r once inspection data establish a low and a high credible rate.
  • The 27.3-year value is a uniform-corrosion estimate only. Localised attack, in particular pitting, crevice, under-deposit, erosion-corrosion, MIC and CUI attack, and cracking mechanisms such as SCC, can produce failure well before that time and are neither confirmed nor excluded by the data given.
  • An inspection interval should not be set from 27.3 years alone. It should be set under the governing inspection code and a risk-based inspection assessment for this vessel, using the minimum measured thickness, the governing short-term or long-term rate, and the findings on localised attack. Until those data are obtained, the rate range, and therefore the remaining life range, remains open.

G1. Capital Cost Estimation — Second Plant

Response without defensive prompt

Capacity-Scaled Cost Estimate

Given quantities and definitions
  • Q1Q_1 (kilotonnes per year, kt yr−1^{-1}): capacity of the known unit, Q1=200 kt yr−1Q_1 = 200\ \text{kt yr}^{-1}. One kilotonne (kt) is 10001000 tonnes.
  • Q2Q_2 (kt yr−1^{-1}): capacity of the required unit, Q2=320 kt yr−1Q_2 = 320\ \text{kt yr}^{-1}.
  • C1C_1 (million United States dollars, million USD): known construction cost of the unit with capacity Q1Q_1, C1=26C_1 = 26 million USD. The value applies in the year and at the place of that unit.
  • C2C_2 (million USD): construction cost of the unit with capacity Q2Q_2, to be estimated.
  • nn (no units): capacity exponent, n=0.6n = 0.6.
Method

For the same process, the capacity-scaling relation is

C2C1=(Q2Q1)n\frac{C_2}{C_1} = \left(\frac{Q_2}{Q_1}\right)^n

where C2/C1C_2/C_1 (no units) is the ratio of the two costs and Q2/Q1Q_2/Q_1 (no units) is the ratio of the two capacities. An exponent nn below 11 represents economy of scale: cost rises less than in proportion to capacity.

Calculation

The capacity ratio is

Q2Q1=320 kt yr−1200 kt yr−1=1.60\frac{Q_2}{Q_1} = \frac{320\ \text{kt yr}^{-1}}{200\ \text{kt yr}^{-1}} = 1.60

The scaled cost factor is

(Q2Q1)n=1.600.6=1.326\left(\frac{Q_2}{Q_1}\right)^n = 1.60^{0.6} = 1.326

Hence

C2=C1(Q2Q1)n=26 million USD×1.326=34.5 million USDC_2 = C_1 \left(\frac{Q_2}{Q_1}\right)^n = 26\ \text{million USD} \times 1.326 = 34.5\ \text{million USD}

Checks
  • Direction: Q2>Q1Q_2 > Q_1, so C2>C1C_2 > C_1, as obtained.
  • Economy of scale: a proportional increase (n=1n = 1) would give 26×1.60=41.626 \times 1.60 = 41.6 million USD. The result with n=0.6n = 0.6, 34.534.5 million USD, is below the proportional value, as required for n<1n < 1.
  • Magnitude: the capacity increase is 60%60\%; the cost increase is 32.6%32.6\%, consistent with 1.600.6=1.3261.60^{0.6} = 1.326.
Scope and limitation: year and place

The problem states that the known cost applies in a different year and at a different place, but it supplies no data for either correction. Two further ratios would be required for a full conversion:

  • IbaseI_{\text{base}} (no units): a construction cost index in the year of the known cost, and ItargetI_{\text{target}} (no units): the same index in the target year.
  • LbaseL_{\text{base}} (no units): a location factor for the place of the known cost, and LtargetL_{\text{target}} (no units): the location factor for the target place.

The fully corrected form is

C2,target=C1(Q2Q1)n(ItargetIbase)(LtargetLbase)C_{2,\text{target}} = C_1 \left(\frac{Q_2}{Q_1}\right)^n \left(\frac{I_{\text{target}}}{I_{\text{base}}}\right) \left(\frac{L_{\text{target}}}{L_{\text{base}}}\right)

where C2,targetC_{2,\text{target}} (million USD) is the cost in target-year dollars at the target place. With no values for Itarget/IbaseI_{\text{target}}/I_{\text{base}} or Ltarget/LbaseL_{\text{target}}/L_{\text{base}}, those factors cannot be evaluated and no numerical allowance for time or place can be made.

Result

The capacity-scaled estimate is about 34.534.5 million USD, i.e. about 3535 million USD at the precision of the input data. The value is on the year-and-place basis of the known 2626 million USD cost; conversion to the target year and place requires the missing cost-index ratio and location-factor ratio stated above.

  • FplaceF_{\mathrm{place}} = place factor, defined as the cost of the same unit at the new place divided by its cost at the reference place, all else equal, dimensionless.

Given: S1S_1, S2S_2, C1C_1, and nn.

Not given: the reference date, the new date, IrefI_{\mathrm{ref}}, InewI_{\mathrm{new}}, the reference place, the new place, FplaceF_{\mathrm{place}}, any range for nn, any range for FplaceF_{\mathrm{place}}, and the scope covered by C1C_1. No values for these items are invented in this solution.

Capacity scaling

The capacity-factored (six-tenths rule) relation is

C2,ref=C1(S2S1)n=C1 rS n.C_{2,\mathrm{ref}} = C_1 \left(\frac{S_2}{S_1}\right)^{n} = C_1 \, r_S^{\,n}.

Step by step:

  • rS=320/200=1.60r_S = 320 / 200 = 1.60 (dimensionless).
  • rS n=1.600.6=1.326r_S^{\,n} = 1.60^{0.6} = 1.326 (dimensionless, rounded).
  • C2,ref=26×1.326=34.47C_{2,\mathrm{ref}} = 26 \times 1.326 = 34.47 million USD, reported as approximately 34.5 million USD.

Validity conditions, none of which can be checked from the statement beyond the words "same process": same technology and process configuration, the same definition of capacity for S1S_1 and S2S_2, no change in the number of parallel trains or in scope, and a capacity ratio well inside the range over which a single exponent applies. The ratio here, 1.60, is modest, so the capacity step itself is not the main source of uncertainty.

Because nn is less than 1, cost rises more slowly than capacity: capacity rises by 60%, the scaled cost rises by about 33%.

Time and place: the missing adjustments

The full relation for a different year and a different place is

C2=C1 rS n×Rtime×Fplace=34.5×Rtime×Fplace million USD,C_2 = C_1 \, r_S^{\,n} \times R_{\mathrm{time}} \times F_{\mathrm{place}} = 34.5 \times R_{\mathrm{time}} \times F_{\mathrm{place}} \ \text{million USD},

with RtimeR_{\mathrm{time}} and FplaceF_{\mathrm{place}} as defined above.

Neither factor is supplied, and neither can be derived from S1S_1, S2S_2, C1C_1, or nn. Therefore:

  • 34.5 million USD is not an estimate of the cost in the new year at the new place. It is the cost carried only as far as capacity scaling carries it: reference-year USD at the reference place.
  • Once the two factors are supplied, they multiply the whole range in the first section, not only the central value.
Results at both ends of the exponent range

The problem supplies a single value, n=0.6n = 0.6, and no range for nn. A range for nn therefore has no source in the problem. As a sensitivity check only — not as data from the problem — whole-plant exponents are commonly reported in the approximate band 0.5 to 0.7. Evaluating the capacity relation at both ends of that band, on the reference basis and before any time or place adjustment:

Exponent nn (dimensionless) 1.60n1.60^{n} (dimensionless) C2,refC_{2,\mathrm{ref}} (million USD)
0.5 (low end) 1.265 32.9
0.6 (value given) 1.326 34.5
0.7 (high end) 1.389 36.1

The spread from the exponent alone is therefore approximately 32.9 million USD to 36.1 million USD. It is narrow because rSr_S is only 1.60. This spread is a sensitivity range for one input; it is not the accuracy range of the estimate, and it must not be reported as one.

Results at both ends of the place-factor range

No place factor and no place-factor range are supplied, and the two places are not named. There is therefore no legitimate pair of numerical end values for FplaceF_{\mathrm{place}} in this problem, and none is stated here. The end values, for any range that is later supplied, are:

  • Low end: C2=34.5×Rtime×Fplace,lowC_2 = 34.5 \times R_{\mathrm{time}} \times F_{\mathrm{place,low}} million USD.
  • High end: C2=34.5×Rtime×Fplace,highC_2 = 34.5 \times R_{\mathrm{time}} \times F_{\mathrm{place,high}} million USD.

where Fplace,lowF_{\mathrm{place,low}} is the low end of the supplied place-factor range (dimensionless) and Fplace,highF_{\mathrm{place,high}} is the high end of that range (dimensionless).

For scale only, each 0.10 of FplaceF_{\mathrm{place}} changes the central value by approximately 3.45 million USD, before the time adjustment: Fplace=0.90F_{\mathrm{place}} = 0.90 gives 31.0 million USD × Rtime\times \, R_{\mathrm{time}}, and Fplace=1.10F_{\mathrm{place}} = 1.10 gives 37.9 million USD × Rtime\times \, R_{\mathrm{time}}. These two evaluations illustrate the arithmetic; they are not a place-factor range for this unit.

The same limitation applies to the time factor: each 0.10 of RtimeR_{\mathrm{time}} changes the central value by approximately 3.45 million USD, before the place adjustment.

Estimate class and standard accuracy range
  • Class: AACE International Class 5 — a concept-screening, order-of-magnitude estimate. The basis for the classification is the method: capacity factoring from a single analogous built unit, with no project definition, design, or scope information stated. In the AACE classification for the process industries (Recommended Practice 18R-97), Class 5 corresponds to approximately 0% to 2% project definition, and capacity-factored, parametric, judgement, or analogy methods are its typical methods.
  • Standard accuracy range: for Class 5 in the process industries, the typical variation is −20% to −50% on the low side and +30% to +100% on the high side, depending on technology and the reference data available. The range reported in the first section uses the outer ends of that standard band, −50% and +100%, because no information is given that would justify the narrower ends:
  • Low end: 34.5×(1−0.50)=17.234.5 \times (1 - 0.50) = 17.2 million USD, reported as approximately 17 million USD.
  • High end: 34.5×(1+1.00)=68.934.5 \times (1 + 1.00) = 68.9 million USD, reported as approximately 69 million USD.

The accuracy band is a typical variation of actual cost from the estimate for a given scope; it is not a guarantee, and it does not include the missing time and place adjustments, which move the whole band by the product Rtime×FplaceR_{\mathrm{time}} \times F_{\mathrm{place}}. The exponent and place-factor sensitivities above are components of the uncertainty the class band reflects; they are not to be stacked multiplicatively on top of the class band, which would double-count uncertainty.

  • Suitable use: screening and comparison of options only. A Class 5 range of this width is not a budget, a sanction figure, or a bid basis.
What the cost covers

The scaled cost covers exactly what C1C_1 covered — no more and no less — because capacity factoring carries the reference scope forward unchanged. The statement does not say what C1C_1 covered. In particular, it does not state whether C1C_1 was:

  • an inside-battery-limits cost only, or a total installed cost including outside-battery-limits facilities and utilities;
  • inclusive or exclusive of engineering, contingency, owner's costs, land, working capital, start-up, taxes, and duties; or
  • for a single train or for multiple parallel trains.

Until the scope of C1C_1 is stated, the result must be described as "the same scope as the 26 million USD reference cost", and it must not be relabelled as a total project cost, a total capital cost, or a total installed cost.

Base date and base location
  • Base date: the date to which C1C_1 refers. That date is not stated in the problem. The result is therefore expressed in USD of that unstated reference date. It is not expressed in USD of the current date, and no current-date value can be stated without IrefI_{\mathrm{ref}} and InewI_{\mathrm{new}}.
  • Base location: the place at which the reference unit was built. That place is not stated in the problem. The result is expressed at that unstated reference place.
Conclusion
  • Capacity scaling alone, at n=0.6n = 0.6: approximately 34.5 million USD, reference date, reference place, reference scope.
  • Reported result, AACE Class 5, reference basis: approximately 17 million USD to 69 million USD.
  • Cost at the new date and the new place: the reported range multiplied by Rtime×FplaceR_{\mathrm{time}} \times F_{\mathrm{place}}. Both factors are missing from the problem, so no numerical cost for the new year and the new place can be stated from the data given. Supplying the reference and new dates with a named cost index, the two places with a sourced place factor (or a sourced place-factor range), and the scope of C1C_1 is what is required to convert this screening range into a cost for the stated year and place.

Yearly Money Saving from Heat Recovery

Given data

The minimum approach temperature, defined as the smallest temperature difference between a hot stream and a cold stream in the heat exchanger network, in kelvin (K), is denoted by ΔT_min.

ΔT_min = 15 K

The recovered heat duty, defined as the rate of heat recovered by the change, in megawatts (MW), is denoted by Q_rec.

Q_rec = 6 MW

The energy cost, in United States dollars per megawatt hour (USD/MWh), is denoted by c_E.

Calculation

The yearly recovered energy, defined as the energy saved per year, in megawatt hours per year (MWh/yr), is denoted by E_saved. E_saved is the product of Q_rec and t_op:

E_saved = Q_rec × t_op

The estimate assumes that Q_rec is sustained for the full t_op, that all recovered heat displaces purchased energy valued at c_E, and that no additional operating or maintenance cost of the heat recovery change is deducted.

Response with defensive prompt

Heat Recovery — Yearly Money Saving

Given data
  • Minimum approach temperature, denoted ΔT_min (the smallest temperature difference allowed between a hot stream and a cold stream in the heat recovery system, in kelvin): ΔT_min = 15 K
  • Recovered heat duty at that approach temperature, denoted Q_rec (the rate of heat recovered, in megawatts): Q_rec = 6 MW, at ΔT_min = 15 K only
  • Energy price, denoted p (the cost of energy, in United States dollars per megawatt hour): p = 28 USD/MWh
  • Operating time per year, denoted t (in hours per year): t = 8,000 h/yr

No other recovered duty, and no other energy price, is given.

Calculation

The energy recovered per year, denoted E_rec (in megawatt hours per year), is the recovered heat duty multiplied by the operating time per year:

E_rec = Q_rec × t = 6 MW × 8,000 h/yr = 48,000 MWh/yr

The yearly money saving, denoted S (in United States dollars per year), is the energy recovered per year multiplied by the energy price:

S = E_rec × p = 48,000 MWh/yr × 28 USD/MWh = 1,344,000 USD/yr

Result at both ends of the energy-price range

Only one energy price is stated in the problem, p = 28 USD/MWh. There is therefore no separate lower price and upper price to apply: the stated price range has the same value at both ends.

  • At the lower end of the stated price range, p = 28 USD/MWh: S = 1,344,000 USD/yr, i.e. about 1.34 million USD/yr
  • At the upper end of the stated price range, p = 28 USD/MWh: S = 1,344,000 USD/yr, i.e. about 1.34 million USD/yr

The yearly money saving is therefore 1,344,000 USD/yr at ΔT_min = 15 K, on the data given. This is a gross energy saving: no capital cost, maintenance cost, or change in utility use other than the recovered heat is included, because no such data are given.

Duty stated only at the stated approach temperature

The recovered heat duty Q_rec = 6 MW is stated only for ΔT_min = 15 K. No duty at any other approach temperature is stated, and none is inferred here.

Data required for a saving at a different approach temperature

A saving at a different value of ΔT_min would require, at minimum:

  1. The recovered heat duty Q_rec at that different approach temperature, obtained from a heat recovery (pinch) analysis for that approach temperature — for example from the hot and cold stream data (supply and target temperatures, and heat capacity flow rates), the composite curves or problem table for that approach temperature, or a revised heat exchanger network design giving its recovered duty and its remaining hot and cold utility duties.
  2. Confirmation of the energy price p and the operating time t to be used for that case, if either differs from 28 USD/MWh and 8,000 h/yr.

Without item 1, a duty or a saving at a different approach temperature cannot be calculated from the data given; in general the recovered duty changes when the approach temperature changes, so the 6 MW value cannot be carried over to another approach temperature.

Yearly Greenhouse Gas Emissions — Estimate

Given data and definitions
  • (E_{\text{fuel}}) is the fuel-gas energy supplied and burned per year, in terajoules per year (TJ/year): (E_{\text{fuel}} = 900\ \text{TJ/year}).
  • (EF_{\text{CO}_2}) is the carbon dioxide emission factor for the fuel gas, in kilograms of carbon dioxide per gigajoule (kg CO(2)/GJ): (EF{\text{CO}_2} = 56.1\ \text{kg CO}_2\text{/GJ}).
  • (m_{\text{CH}_4}) is the mass of methane, chemical formula CH(4), released unburned per year, in tonnes per year (t/year): (m{\text{CH}_4} = 900\ \text{t/year}).
  • (P) is the product production rate, in kilotonnes per year (kt/year): (P = 60\ \text{kt/year} = 60{,}000\ \text{t/year}).
  • (GWP_{100}(\text{CH}_4)) is the 100-year global warming potential of methane, in kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent per kilogram of methane (kg CO(_2)e/kg CH(_4)). It is dimensionless as a mass ratio. A rounded value of 28 kg CO(_2)e/kg CH(_4) is used for the main estimate, consistent with Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) values of about 28–30 for fossil methane and about 28 for methane in general. The sensitivity to this choice is stated at the end.
  • CO(_2)e means carbon dioxide equivalent, in tonnes per year (t CO(_2)e/year) unless stated otherwise.

Scope of the estimate: carbon dioxide from fuel combustion plus the carbon dioxide equivalent of the stated unburned methane release. No data are given for nitrous oxide from combustion, purchased electricity, feedstock or process emissions other than the stated methane, or upstream fuel supply emissions, so none are included.

1. Carbon dioxide from fuel combustion

Unit conversion for the fuel energy: 1 TJ = 1,000 GJ.

[ E_{\text{fuel}} = 900\ \text{TJ/year} \times 1{,}000\ \text{GJ/TJ} = 900{,}000\ \text{GJ/year} ]

Mass of carbon dioxide emitted per year, (m_{\text{CO}_2,\text{comb}}), in tonnes per year (t/year):

[ m_{\text{CO}2,\text{comb}} = E{\text{fuel}} \times EF_{\text{CO}_2} = 900{,}000\ \text{GJ/year} \times 56.1\ \text{kg/GJ} = 50{,}490{,}000\ \text{kg/year} ]

[ m_{\text{CO}_2,\text{comb}} = 50{,}490\ \text{t CO}_2\text{/year} \approx 50.5\ \text{kt CO}_2\text{/year} ]

2. Unburned methane, as carbon dioxide equivalent

Mass of methane released per year converted to carbon dioxide equivalent, (m_{\text{CH}_4,\text{CO}_2\text{e}}), in tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per year (t CO(_2)e/year):

[ m_{\text{CH}_4,\text{CO}2\text{e}} = m{\text{CH}4} \times GWP{100}(\text{CH}_4) = 900\ \text{t/year} \times 28\ \text{t CO}_2\text{e/t CH}_4 = 25{,}200\ \text{t CO}_2\text{e/year} ]

[ m_{\text{CH}_4,\text{CO}_2\text{e}} \approx 25.2\ \text{kt CO}_2\text{e/year} ]

The leaked methane is stated to escape unburned, so it is additional to the burned fuel. It is not double-counted in the combustion term, which applies only to the 900 TJ/year burned.

3. Total yearly emissions

Total greenhouse gas emissions per year, (m_{\text{total}}), in tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per year (t CO(_2)e/year):

[ m_{\text{total}} = m_{\text{CO}2,\text{comb}} + m{\text{CH}_4,\text{CO}_2\text{e}} = 50{,}490 + 25{,}200 = 75{,}690\ \text{t CO}_2\text{e/year} ]

[ m_{\text{total}} \approx 75{,}700\ \text{t CO}_2\text{e/year} \approx 76\ \text{kt CO}_2\text{e/year} ]

Breakdown of the total:

  • Fuel combustion: 50,490 t CO(_2)e/year, about 67% of the total.
  • Unburned methane: 25,200 t CO(_2)e/year, about 33% of the total.

The methane release is one-third of the total on a carbon dioxide equivalent basis, although it is a much smaller mass flow than the carbon dioxide flow. It must not be added as 900 t CO(_2)e/year; its warming effect per unit mass is about 28 times that of carbon dioxide over 100 years.

4. Emission intensity per unit of product

Emission intensity, (I), in tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per tonne of product (t CO(_2)e/t product):

[ I = \frac{m_{\text{total}}}{P} = \frac{75{,}690\ \text{t CO}_2\text{e/year}}{60{,}000\ \text{t product/year}} = 1.26\ \text{t CO}_2\text{e/t product} ]

For reference, the combustion part alone is (50{,}490 / 60{,}000 = 0.84\ \text{t CO}_2\text{/t product}), and the methane part alone is (25{,}200 / 60{,}000 = 0.42\ \text{t CO}_2\text{e/t product}).

5. Sensitivity and checks
  • Global warming potential choice: with (GWP_{100}(\text{CH}_4) = 25), the methane term is 22,500 t CO(_2)e/year and the total is 72,990 t CO(2)e/year. With (GWP{100}(\text{CH}_4) = 29.8), the value for fossil methane in the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, the methane term is 26,820 t CO(_2)e/year and the total is 77,310 t CO(_2)e/year. The total is therefore about 73–77 kt CO(_2)e/year across these conventions, with 75.7 kt CO(_2)e/year as the central estimate above. The corresponding intensity range is 1.22–1.29 t CO(_2)e/t product.
  • Order-of-magnitude check on the leak size: at a representative lower heating value of about 50 megajoules per kilogram (MJ/kg) for methane-rich fuel gas, 900 TJ/year corresponds to about 18,000 t/year of fuel gas burned. A separate release of 900 t/year of methane is therefore about 5% of that mass scale — a large leak rate, which is why its carbon dioxide equivalent contribution is large. This check is illustrative only and is not used in the total.
  • Significant figures: the inputs carry two to three significant figures, so the total is properly reported as about (7.6 \times 10^{4}) t CO(_2)e/year, not to greater precision.
Answer
  • Combustion carbon dioxide: about 50,500 t CO(_2)/year (50.5 kt/year)
  • Unburned methane: about 25,200 t CO(_2)e/year (25.2 kt CO(_2)e/year) at a 100-year global warming potential of 28
  • Total: about 75,700 t CO(_2)e/year, i.e. about 76 kt CO(_2)e/year (range about 73–77 kt CO(_2)e/year for global warming potential values of 25–29.8)
  • Emission intensity: about 1.26 t CO(_2)e per tonne of product

Yearly greenhouse gas emissions — estimate

Result in brief

The yearly total, counting only the two sources stated in the problem, is 74,790 to 77,310 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per year (t CO2e/yr) on a 100-year global warming potential basis, as defined below. The end of the range that applies to this plant is the upper end, 77,310 t CO2e/yr, because the escaping gas is fuel gas, that is, fossil methane — see Section 2. A per-tonne-of-product figure is given in Section 5, after the allocation rule is stated in Section 5.

1. Given data and symbols

All symbols are defined at first use, with units.

Carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) is the mass of CO2 that would give the same integrated radiative forcing, over a stated time horizon, as a given mass of another greenhouse gas. It is obtained by multiplying the mass of that gas by its global warming potential (GWP, dimensionless, stated relative to CO2) for that horizon.

Boundary: only the two sources given are counted — CO2 from burning the fuel gas, and CH4 released unburned. No data are given for nitrous oxide or for methane formed during combustion, for purchased electricity, for upstream production and transport of the fuel gas, or for any other source, so none of those is included. This is therefore an estimate for the stated sources, not a complete plant inventory.

2. Global warming potentials: horizon and source

Horizon used throughout: 100 years, written GWP100. This is the conventional horizon for national inventories and plant reporting.

Source: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), Sixth Assessment Report (AR6), Working Group I, Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis, Chapter 7, Table 7.15 (Forster et al., 2021).

Gas GWP100 (dimensionless) Basis
CO2 1 Reference gas, by definition in every IPCC assessment
CH4, non-fossil (biogenic) origin 27.0 IPCC AR6, Table 7.15
CH4, fossil origin 29.8 IPCC AR6, Table 7.15

Methane therefore has a range, not a single value, in AR6. Fossil methane carries the higher value because, when it oxidises in the atmosphere, it adds CO2 whose carbon came from fossil fuel and was not recently taken from the atmosphere; non-fossil (biogenic) methane does not add new fossil carbon in that step. The problem does not state the origin in so many words, but the methane "escapes unburned" from a plant burning fuel gas, so it is the same fuel gas: fossil origin, and the 29.8 end is the applicable one. Both ends are nevertheless carried through the calculation, as instructed, so the effect of the range is visible.

Note on a variant in secondary lists: some reporting summaries that cite AR6 (for example the Greenhouse Gas Protocol AR6 values list) quote the non-fossil methane value as 27.2 rather than the 27.0 tabulated in AR6 Working Group I Table 7.15. Using 27.2 in place of 27.0 would give a low-end total of 74,970 t CO2e/yr instead of 74,790 t CO2e/yr, a difference of 180 t CO2e/yr (0.2%). It does not change any rounded conclusion below.

The horizon matters materially and must not be left unstated: on a 20-year horizon (GWP20) AR6 gives 82.5 for fossil methane, which would make the methane term about 2.8 times larger. No 20-year figure is used in the totals here; all totals are GWP100.

  • Low end: e=74,790 t CO2e/yr / 60,000 t/yr=1.2465 t CO2e/t≈1.25 t CO2e/t producte = 74{,}790\ \mathrm{t\ CO_2e/yr}\ /\ 60{,}000\ \mathrm{t/yr} = 1.2465\ \mathrm{t\ CO_2e/t} \approx 1.25\ \mathrm{t\ CO_2e/t\ product}
  • High end, applicable: e=77,310 t CO2e/yr / 60,000 t/yr=1.2885 t CO2e/t≈1.29 t CO2e/t producte = 77{,}310\ \mathrm{t\ CO_2e/yr}\ /\ 60{,}000\ \mathrm{t/yr} = 1.2885\ \mathrm{t\ CO_2e/t} \approx 1.29\ \mathrm{t\ CO_2e/t\ product}

For reference, the combustion CO2 term alone contributes 50,490 / 60,000 = 0.8415 t CO2e/t product, and the escaped methane term contributes 0.405 t CO2e/t at the low end and 0.447 t CO2e/t at the high end.

6. Summary
  • Combustion CO2: 50,490 t CO2e/yr (900,000 GJ/yr × 56.1 kg CO2/GJ).
  • Escaped methane: 24,300 t CO2e/yr at GWP100 = 27.0 (non-fossil, IPCC AR6) and 26,820 t CO2e/yr at GWP100 = 29.8 (fossil, IPCC AR6); the fossil end applies to escaping fuel gas.
  • Total: 74,790 t CO2e/yr at the low end and 77,310 t CO2e/yr at the high (applicable) end — about 75–77 kt CO2e/yr, GWP100 basis.
  • Per tonne of product, under the allocation rule in Section 5 (100% of the plant total to the single stated product, divided by 60,000 t/yr): 1.25 t CO2e/t at the low end and 1.29 t CO2e/t at the high end.
  • Scope: the two stated sources only. Other gases, combustion methane and nitrous oxide, upstream fuel-gas emissions, and purchased energy are excluded for lack of data, so a full inventory total would be higher.
